exp.0:3:
This verse continues the list of Jesus' ancestors: Aram was the father of Aminadab, Aminadab the father of Naasson, and Naasson the father of Salmon. The phrase "was the father of" is how the list reads at each step. These are names from the tribe of Judah, and they may sound unfamiliar, but they were real people within the history of Israel.

Matthew, who writes this Gospel, begins by presenting Jesus as the promised Messiah, a descendant of Abraham and of David. This genealogy shows that God kept his promises step by step. The names in this verse connect Judah to Salmon, who later appears alongside Rahab. Some scholars think the list summarizes and selects generations, and does not necessarily name every one.

For today: God works through ordinary people, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your daily faithfulness, though it may seem small, can be part of what God does in your family and in the generations to come.
exp.0:7:
This verse continues the list of Jesus' ancestors. Here appear Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram and Uzziah, kings of Judah. Uzziah is also known as Azariah.

Matthew, the author of the gospel according to tradition, writes for Jewish readers. He wants to show that Jesus is the promised Messiah, a descendant of David. The list is abbreviated: between Joram and Uzziah it leaves out some kings whom other books of the Old Testament mention. In Hebrew usage, "father of" could also mean ancestor.

God keeps his promises across many generations, even through imperfect people. Your faithfulness today, though it may seem small, can be part of what God is doing for the future of your family.
exp.0:17:
This verse tells how the life of Jesus on earth began. Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, that is, formally engaged, and at that time this bond was a very serious one. The phrase "before they came together" means before they lived together as husband and wife. At that time it was found that she had conceived by the work of the Holy Spirit, not by a man.

Matthew, the author, has just presented the genealogy of Jesus, which links him to Abraham and David. Now he explains something special: Jesus did not come in an ordinary way. The verses that follow show Joseph's reaction, as he wanted to act with kindness, and the clarification given by the angel.

For today: God can work in ways we do not understand and did not expect. When our life becomes complicated by something unexpected, we can trust that He still keeps His promises and can guide us step by step.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that Joseph, Mary's husband, was a righteous man. Because he did not want to expose her to public shame, he decided to leave her quietly. The phrase "Her husband" is used because they were betrothed, a formal commitment almost as binding as marriage, though they did not yet live together.

Matthew tells here the story of Jesus' birth. Joseph learns that Mary is pregnant and does not understand what has happened. His righteousness leads him to respect the law, but also to treat Mary with kindness. Some understand that he did not want to expose her to a severe punishment. The text says nothing more about his feelings. Soon after, an angel explains everything to him.

For today: when someone fails you or when you do not understand a situation, seek to act with justice and mercy, without humiliating anyone. And wait for God's guidance before you decide.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that King Herod was troubled, that is, he was disturbed and alarmed, when he heard the news from the magi. And he was not the only one: all of Jerusalem was troubled along with him.

The narrator, Matthew, tells us that some magi from the east arrived asking about the newborn King of the Jews. Herod governed under Roman authority and feared losing his power. The Bible does not explain in detail why the city was troubled. It is often thought that the people knew Herod's violent character and feared what he might do, but that is an interpretation.

For today: the arrival of Jesus can make uncomfortable those who cling to their own control. We can ask ourselves whether we receive Christ with joy and openness, or whether we prefer to defend our own place. Handing over control to him frees us from fear.
exp.1:4:
The chief priests and scribes answer Herod's question: the Christ would be born in Bethlehem of Judea. They say that a prophet announced this, that is, that it was already written in the Scriptures. The word "Bethlehem" is the older spelling of the town's name.

Herod was troubled by the news from the wise men about the birth of a king. So he gathered the religious leaders, experts in the Scriptures, to learn where the Christ would be born. They cite the prophecy of Micah (with a phrase that also recalls 2 Samuel 5:2). It is striking that they knew the answer, but the text does not say that they went to look for the child.

We can know the Bible well and still not respond to it. Let us not stop at knowing facts, but let the Word lead us to seek Jesus and to worship him.
exp.1:7:
Herod sends the wise men to Bethlehem. He asks them to search carefully for the child and, when they find him, to bring him word. He says he also wants to go and worship him.

King Herod ruled with a great fear of losing his power. He had just learned from the chief priests and scribes that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem. His request sounds devout, but the account shows later that his intentions were evil: he wanted to destroy the child (Matthew 2:16). The wise men, by contrast, truly sought to worship him.

For today: not everything that sounds religious comes from a sincere heart. Let us ask God to examine our motives, so that our faith is true worship and not just pretty words. And let us be wise to tell the difference between words and deeds.
exp.1:8:
What it says: The wise men heard King Herod and set out toward Bethlehem. The star they had seen in the east, that is, in their homeland to the east, guided them again. It went before them until it came to a stop right over the place where the child Jesus was.

Context: The narrator is Matthew. Herod had asked the wise men to tell him when they found the child, saying that he wanted to worship him. But the account shows that his intentions were not good. The wise men, on the other hand, were sincerely seeking Jesus. It is not known with certainty what the star was exactly; there are several explanations, and the text only says that God guided them.

For today: God knows how to guide those who seek him sincerely, even in the midst of people with evil intentions. Keep seeking Jesus with humility, and trust that God will show you the way step by step.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that when the wise men from the east saw the star again, they felt an enormous joy. Their rejoicing means they were filled with happiness, and the words that describe it in the verse emphasize that their joy was intense. The phrase "when they saw the star" simply means that they saw the star.

Matthew narrates here what happened after Herod sent them to Bethlehem. They had traveled from far away looking for the king of the Jews, and they had lost sight of the star. Seeing it again going ahead of them, they understood that God was guiding them. What exactly that star was like, we do not know; it has been explained in various ways.

For today: when we seek God with sincerity, he knows how to give us signs of his guidance at just the right moment. Trust that he does not leave you alone on the road, and let that assurance fill you with joy, even if the journey has been long or uncertain.
exp.1:14:
Joseph, Mary, and Jesus stayed in Egypt until King Herod died.

The one speaking here is Matthew, the author of the Gospel. Herod wanted to kill the child, and for that reason an angel warned Joseph to flee. Matthew quotes Hosea 11:1, which originally spoke of Israel coming out of Egypt in the Exodus. Matthew sees in Jesus the one who lives again the story of Israel. Scholars explain this connection in different ways.

For today: God watches over his plans even in times of danger and uncertainty. When your path changes in an unexpected way, trust that God can guide you step by step, as he guided Joseph, and obey him with faith.
exp.1:20:
This verse tells us that Joseph obeyed right away. He got up, took the young child Jesus and his mother Mary, and went with them into the land of Israel.

Mateo is the one who narrates. Earlier, an angel had told Joseph in a dream that he could now return from Egypt, because those who had sought to kill the child had died. Herod had tried to destroy Jesus, and that is why the family fled. Here we see that God watched over his Son and guided Joseph step by step.

For today: when we know what God asks of us, it is wise to obey without delay. Joseph did not have the whole picture, but he trusted and acted. We can ask God for direction in our decisions, and take the next step we already know, trusting that He continues to care for his own.
exp.1:21:
This verse tells that Joseph, returning from Egypt with Mary and Jesus, heard that Archelaus was ruling in Judea after his father, Herod. He was afraid to go there. Then God guided him in a dream, and he went to the region of Galilee.

The one speaking is the evangelist Matthew, narrating what happened. Herod had died, but his son ruled part of the territory. Ancient history remembers him as a harsh ruler, though here Matthew mentions only Joseph's fear. God cares for the child Jesus and leads him to Nazareth, in Galilee.

For today: Joseph's fear was not a lack of faith, but prudence. When we do not know which path to take, we can ask God for direction, stay attentive to his guidance, and take sensible steps, trusting that he cares for his own.
exp.2:0:
In those days John the Baptist appeared and began to preach in the wilderness of Judea. "Came" means that he presented himself publicly, and "preaching" means that he proclaimed a message out loud. The wilderness of Judea is a dry, sparsely populated region near the Jordan River and the Dead Sea.

Here the writer of the gospel, Matthew, presents John as the messenger who prepares the way for Jesus. The verses that follow explain his message: repent, because the kingdom of heaven is near. Matthew connects it with Isaiah's prophecy about a voice crying out in the wilderness. "In those days" is a general expression; the text does not specify an exact date.

For today: before seeking God in great things, it is good to pause and listen with humility. Ask yourself which areas of your life need a sincere change, and give God that space today.
exp.2:3:
This verse describes how John the Baptist dressed and what he ate. He wore clothing made of camel's hair, with a leather belt around his waist. He ate locusts, which were edible insects, and wild honey, that is, honey from bees in the fields.

Matthew is the one who tells us this. His description recalls the prophet Elijah, who also dressed simply (2 Kings 1:8), though not all scholars see it as a direct reference. John lived in the desert, called people to repentance, and prepared the way of the Lord. His austere life gave strength to his message.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our lives are consistent with what we say we believe. John did not seek comfort or fame; he wanted people to look to God. Let us ask God to help us live with simplicity and sincerity, so that our actions support our words.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that no one should be complacent, thinking, "I am right with God because I am a descendant of Abraham." John the Baptist warns them that this does not save them. "Raise up children" means to bring forth or raise up children. God has the power to bring children to Abraham even from stones, that is, it does not depend on family inheritance.

John the Baptist speaks to many Pharisees and Sadducees who came to be baptized. He notices that some were seeking to escape judgment without a real change. So he asks them for fruit worthy of repentance: a transformed life. He says the ax is already ready and that someone more powerful is coming, Jesus.

For today: do not rest on your church, your family, or your religious history. Ask yourself honestly whether your life shows repentance, humility, and obedience to God today.
exp.2:9:
God's judgment is already very close. The axe is the tool in view, and it is already set against the root of the trees, ready to strike. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. It is a strong picture meant to warn that there is no time to waste.

The one speaking is John the Baptist, in the wilderness, addressing people who were coming to be baptized, including Pharisees and Sadducees. Many of them trusted that they were descendants of Abraham, as if that alone secured God's favor. John tells them that what matters is genuine repentance, something that shows in the way they live. He also announces the coming of someone more powerful: Jesus.

For today: it is not enough to say that we believe, or to belong to a church or a believing family. Ask God to show you an attitude or habit you need to change, and take one concrete step toward it today.
exp.2:11:
He says that Christ holds a winnowing fork in his hand, a tool like a shovel or a pitchfork used to toss freshly threshed grain into the air. The wind carries off the chaff, the light outer husk, and the heavy wheat falls to the ground. The threshing floor is the place where the grain is threshed. The granary is the storehouse. Christ will gather the wheat into his barn and burn the chaff with a fire that will never go out.

John the Baptist is speaking to the crowds who were coming to the Jordan, and also to Pharisees and Sadducees. He warns them that their repentance must produce good fruit, because the coming Messiah will separate the true from the false. Christians often understand this fire as the final judgment, though some interpret it in other ways.

Today, examine your life honestly. It is not enough to appear to be a believer; ask God to produce real fruit in you, such as humility, righteousness, and mercy.
exp.2:12:
This verse tells that Jesus left the region of Galilee, in the north, and walked to the Jordan River, where John was. His purpose was clear: he wanted to be baptized by him.

The one telling the story is Matthew. John had been announcing that someone more powerful would come, and suddenly that same Jesus presents himself before him. What is surprising is that Jesus, who had no sin, places himself in line alongside those who were repenting. Later he will say that this was fitting in order to fulfill all righteousness, that is, to do what God wanted. Scholars explain the exact meaning of that phrase in various ways.

Today we can learn from the humility of Jesus. He took a step of simple obedience and identified himself with us. If God asks something of you, do not wait to understand everything: obey with humility.
exp.2:14:
Jesus asks John to let him be baptized. Then John agrees and baptizes him.

Jesus speaks in response to John the Baptist, who felt unworthy to baptize someone greater than himself. John's baptism called people to repentance, and Jesus had no sin. For this reason, scholars explain this act in several ways: as obedience to the Father, as identification with his people, or as the public beginning of his mission. Right afterward, the Father affirms him from heaven.

For today: obeying God, even when we do not understand everything, is an act of humility. Jesus shows us that simple obedience pleases the Father.
exp.2:15:
This verse tells how Jesus, as soon as he was baptized, came up out of the water. At that moment the heavens were opened to him, meaning the sky opened up. He saw the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and resting on him.

Matthew tells us what happened at the Jordan River. John the Baptist did not want to baptize Jesus, but Jesus told him that this was fitting, to do what God required. Right after that, the Father speaks from heaven. In this way, Matthew shows the Son, the Spirit, and the Father together.

For today: Jesus began his mission by obeying God with humility. We can do the same, trusting that the Father is pleased with a heart willing to obey, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.2:16:
Matthew 3:17 says that when Jesus came up out of the water, a voice came from heaven. That voice declared that Jesus is his beloved Son. The phrase "in whom I am well pleased" points to the Father's deep approval and joy in his Son.

The one speaking is God the Father. Jesús had just been baptized by John, and the Spirit was descending on him like a dove. Many Christians see here the Father, the Son, and the Spirit all acting at once. This happens before Jesus begins his public ministry, and the voice confirms who he is and affirms him before everyone.

For today: the Father expressed his love and his delight in Jesus before he performed any miracles or taught anyone. A person who trusts in Christ can rest in the fact that God's love does not depend on their achievements. You can begin your day by remembering that God loves you, and then serve from that security, not to earn his approval.
exp.3:1:
It says that Jesus went forty days and forty nights without eating, and that afterward He was hungry. The idea of fasting here means that He did not eat, as a deliberate decision to seek God. The text shows that Jesus was truly human: He had a body with real needs.

Matthew tells us that the Spirit led Jesus into the desert before He began His public ministry. There the devil tempted Him just when He was at His weakest and most hungry. For many readers, the forty days recall the forty years of Israel in the desert, although the text does not say this directly. Jesus answers with Scripture, not with His power.

For today: when you are tired, in need, or weak, do not be surprised when temptations come. Jesus understands that weakness. Learn from Him to answer with the Word of God, keeping it in your heart for those difficult moments.
exp.3:2:
The tempter, that is the devil, came to Jesus and challenged him: "If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread."

Jesús had just been led by the Spirit into the desert, and after forty days of fasting he was hungry. The devil speaks here and takes advantage of that real need. Some understand that he was questioning Jesus' identity; others, that he was inviting him to use his power on his own account, without depending on the Father. Jesus answers with the Scriptures, trusting in God.

For today: temptation often comes in moments of tiredness or need, offering a quick way out that lies outside God's will. We can respond as Jesus did, keeping the Word in our hearts and trusting that God cares for us.
exp.3:3:
Jesus answers the tempter with Scripture. He says that a human being does not live on bread alone, meaning on what the body eats and needs. A person also lives by every word that comes out of the mouth of God.

Jesus speaks this after fasting forty days in the desert. He was hungry, and the devil proposed that he use his power to turn stones into bread. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3, where Moses reminded Israel that God sustained them in the desert. Jesus chooses to trust his Father and not to act on his own.

Today, real needs, such as work, food, or health, are not wrong. But they should not rule our decisions. Before acting under pressure from urgency, we can read the Bible and pray, trusting that God also cares for us.
exp.3:5:
Satan says to Jesus, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here." To persuade him, he quotes Scripture (Psalm 91:11-12): God will command his angels to watch over him, and they will bear him up in their hands so that he will not even strike his foot against a stone. The high edges of the temple, and the word for striking or falling, are the parts of the verse he is pointing to here.

Here the devil speaks, during Jesus' temptation in the desert. He had already tried to make Jesus doubt God through the bread; now he uses the Scriptures, but he bends them to his purpose. He wants Jesus to test God with a spectacular sign, instead of trusting Him. Jesus will answer with another text: one must not put God to the test.

For today: it is not enough to quote a verse; we must understand it in full and in the light of everything God teaches. Trusting God does not mean demanding proof or taking senseless risks, but obeying Him with humility.
exp.3:11:
This verse tells us that Jesus heard that John the Baptist had been thrown into prison, and then he withdrew to the region of Galilee.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just overcome temptation in the wilderness. Now his public ministry begins. Matthew does not explain in detail why Jesus went to Galilee. Some think he went to avoid danger; others think it was the time to begin his work. The text that follows connects this with the prophecy of Isaiah.

For today: When things become difficult, such as the arrest of someone who served God, we do not have to stop. Jesus moved forward with confidence in God's plan. Let us ask him for wisdom to take the next faithful step.
exp.3:16:
It says that, from that time, Jesus began to proclaim a public message: "Repent," that is, turn around and change the way you think, because the kingdom of heaven is at hand, meaning it is very near. Preach means to announce openly.

He speaks as he begins his ministry in Galilee. Matthew has just quoted Isaiah: the people who lived in darkness saw a great light. Jesus is that light, and his call to repentance prepares hearts. Soon he calls his first disciples, fishermen, to follow him.

For today: repenting is not only feeling guilt, but turning back to God. Today you can think of one area of your life where you need to change direction, tell God about it honestly, and take one concrete step, such as asking forgiveness or giving up a bad habit.
exp.3:17:
This verse tells that Jesus was walking along the shore of the Sea of Galilee, which is a large lake. There he saw two brothers, Simon, also called Peter, and Andrew. They were casting the net into the water, because they were fishermen.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just begun his preaching, announcing that the kingdom of heaven was near. Now he starts calling his first disciples. Matthew presents this as a fulfillment of the light that came to a people sitting in darkness. Jesus finds them at work, not in the temple.

For today: Jesus draws near to people in their everyday life, in their work and in ordinary things. We can be attentive to his calling us there, and answer him with willingness.
exp.3:18:
Jesus invites Simon Peter and Andrew to follow him. The phrase "follow me" in the verse is simply a request to come after him, that is, to follow him. He promises that he will make them fishers of men, meaning that he will use them to lead other people toward God, just as they once caught fish with their nets.

Jesus had just begun his ministry in Galilee, calling people to repent because the kingdom of heaven was near. He speaks with two brothers who worked as fishermen. He calls them in the middle of their daily work, and the text says they followed him at once, leaving their nets.

For today: Jesus calls us to follow him, and he also gives us a purpose. We can ask him to use what we already are and what we already do to serve others and share his hope with love and simplicity.
exp.3:20:
This verse tells that Jesus, going a little further on, saw two other brothers: James (Santiago) and John, sons of Zebedee. They were in the boat with their father, getting their nets in order. "Mending" means they were repairing them, sewing up the tears. Then Jesus called them. The word "saw" is written here as it is in the verse you have read.

It is part of Matthew's account of the beginning of Jesus' ministry in Galilee. Shortly before, Jesus had called Peter and Andrew, who were also fishermen. Here the narrator is Matthew, and he shows that Jesus invites ordinary people, in the middle of their daily work, to follow him. The verses that follow say that they answered at once.

Jesus often calls us in the midst of everyday life, not only in special moments. Today you can be attentive to his voice while you work or care for your family, and answer him with willingness, even when you cannot see the whole road ahead.
exp.3:21:
This verse tells how James and John, who were in the boat with their father Zebedee, immediately left everything and followed Jesus. The words "immediately" and "the boat" in the verse above are not quoted here; the verse simply points out that they answered without delay and set out with him as his disciples.

It is an account from the Gospel of Matthew. Jesus was walking along the Sea of Galilee and had already called Simon and Andrew. Then he called these two other brothers, who were mending their nets. Matthew shows that Jesus calls ordinary people in the middle of their work, and that they responded promptly. The text does not explain what they thought or how their father reacted, so it is better not to assume more.

For today: when you sense that God invites you to obey him, do not put it off. Ask him for the courage to take a concrete step today, even if it means letting go of something comfortable or familiar.
exp.3:24:
This verse says that great crowds were following Jesus. They came from Galilee, from the Decapolis (a region of ten cities east of the Jordan), from Jerusalem, from Judea, and from beyond the Jordan, that is, from the eastern side of the river.

Here the narrator, Matthew, speaks. He summarizes what happened after Jesus traveled through Galilee teaching and healing. His fame spread, and people from very different places, both Jews and probably non-Jews, began to follow him. This verse sets the scene for the Sermon on the Mount, which comes right after.

For today: following Jesus is not just admiring his miracles or his fame. Those crowds sought him out out of need. We can come to Him just as we are, with our burdens, and ask him to teach and guide us as well, not only to help us.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that Jesus began to speak and to teach. It means nothing strange: only that he began to speak with purpose and care.

Here Matthew speaks, telling how Jesus saw the crowds, went up the mountain, and sat down. His disciples came near to him. Sitting was the normal posture of a Jewish teacher when teaching. What follows is the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount, addressed first to the disciples, though the crowds were also close by. Some think he taught everyone; the text leaves both possibilities open.

For today: before speaking, Jesus sat down and waited for people to come near. We can imitate him by keeping a moment of calm to listen to his Word, without rushing, with a heart ready to learn.
exp.4:3:
Jesus says that those who mourn are happy, or blessed, because they will receive comfort, that is, consolation. The word translated "blessed" means blessed, favored by God. Mourning can refer to grief over a loss, to sorrow over one's own sin, or to sorrow over the evil in the world. Scholars understand it in several ways, and perhaps it includes all of them.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, with the crowd nearby, at the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount. He has just said that the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit, those who recognize their need for God. Here he continues along that line: God does not abandon those who suffer, and he promises comfort. The text does not say exactly when it will come, and it may include comfort both now and in the future.

Today, you do not have to hide your sadness or pretend to be strong. Bring it to God honestly, and gently accompany others who mourn, without rushing them.
exp.4:5:
They are happy and blessed, Jesus says, who want righteousness as strongly as a person longs to eat when hungry or drink when thirsty. "Blessed" means happy or favored. "Filled" means completely satisfied, full. "Righteousness" can be understood as living uprightly before God, and also as a longing for what is right to be done in the world.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples, with others listening nearby. The Beatitudes describe what the citizens of God's kingdom are like. Here Jesus says that the desire for righteousness will not go unanswered: God promises to satisfy it. Some understand that this fullness begins now, and others that it will be completed when God restores all things.

For today: ask yourself what you long for most. Spend a few minutes praying and reading the Bible, asking God to teach you to live with honesty and to treat others well.
exp.4:7:
Jesus says that those whose heart is pure are happy, because they will see God. "Blessed" means happy, favored. In the Bible, the heart is the center of a person: their thoughts, desires, and intentions. "Pure" points to a sincere life, without duplicity. "Will see God" is a promise of closeness with Him; some understand it as something present, and others as something that will be fully fulfilled in the future.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Earlier he spoke of those who seek righteousness and of the merciful. Here he shows that God cares about what is inward, not only about outward religious appearances.

For today: ask God to examine your motives. Before you serve, pray, or help, ask yourself why you are doing it, and honestly confess whatever you find. He cleanses and renews.
exp.4:15:
Jesus says that the light of his followers should shine in the sight of everyone. Then he explains the purpose: the good works others see should lead them to give glory, that is, to honor and praise, God, their Father in heaven. The good works are acts of kindness and love that people can see. The final purpose is not that people admire us, but that they glorify God, our heavenly Father.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Just before this, he called them the light of the world and used the picture of a lamp that is not hidden under a bushel (a measure or vessel for grain). Later he clarifies that he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, so good works are rooted in what God has always asked.

Today, look for one concrete act of service or kindness this week, such as helping a neighbor or patiently dealing with someone difficult. Do it simply, without seeking applause, and let God receive the glory.
exp.4:16:
Jesus says that he did not come to "abolish" the law or the prophets, which are the Scriptures of the Old Testament. He came "to fulfil" them, that is, to bring them to their full meaning and true purpose. The word "fulfil" can be understood as obeying, making what was announced come true, and completing its purpose.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, addressing his disciples and the crowd. He has just told them that they are the light of the world and that their good works should bring glory to the Father. Now he makes clear that his teaching does not contradict God, but follows and completes what God had already said. Then he speaks of the importance of obeying and teaching his commandments.

For today: Read the whole Bible as one message that points to Christ, and ask him to teach you to obey with love, not only with rules.
exp.4:18:
Jesus says that whoever breaks even one of the least of the commandments, and teaches others to do the same, will be called "least" in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever keeps them and teaches them will be called "great" in the kingdom of heaven. To break a commandment is to violate it. The phrase "will be called" speaks of how a person will be regarded in the kingdom.

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just said that he did not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them. With this he corrects anyone who might think he was loosening the call to obedience. He then says that true righteousness must exceed that of the Pharisees, that is, it must come from the heart and not only from outward appearance.

For today: do not despise the small matters of obeying God. Be careful also about what you teach by your example, because your life speaks. Obey sincerely, trusting in the grace of Christ.
exp.4:19:
Jesus says that the righteousness of his followers must be greater than that of the scribes (the teachers of the law) and the Pharisees, a group held in high regard for their care in keeping religious rules. If it is not, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. "Righteousness" here means living uprightly before God.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just said that he did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it. The verses that follow show what this greater righteousness looks like: it is not enough to avoid murder; one must also guard against anger and contempt in the heart. Interpreters debate the details, but the emphasis falls on what is inward.

Today, do not be satisfied with keeping only the outward rules. Ask God to transform your heart: your attitudes, your words, and how you treat others, especially at home.
exp.4:23:
Jesus says that if you are about to offer your gift at the altar and you remember that a brother has something against you, you must leave your gift there. First go and seek to be reconciled with that person, and then come back and offer your gift. "Gift" means an offering or present; "brother" here means your neighbor, especially a fellow believer.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just taught that anger and insults harm the heart, not only murder. For him, sincere worship cannot be separated from how we treat others. The sayings that follow about the adversary and the judge reinforce the urgency of settling matters quickly.

For today: if you know you have wronged someone, do not let it pass. Before you pray, sing, or serve in the church, look for a humble way to ask forgiveness or clear things up, without waiting for the other person to take the first step.
exp.4:24:
Jesus says that if someone has a dispute with you, you should make peace with that person quickly, while you are still together on the way.

The verse of his words is simple: if you do not do this, the accuser may bring you before the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer who carried out the sentence, until you end up in prison.

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He is explaining that the righteousness God wants goes beyond not murdering: it touches anger and broken relationships. That is why he continues the theme of the previous verse, where reconciliation is more urgent than the offering at the altar.

For today: if there is an unresolved conflict with someone, do not let it cool or grow. Take one concrete step today, such as a phone call, an apology, or a sincere conversation, and seek peace while there is still time.
exp.4:31:
Jesus says that if a man sends away his wife without there having been sexual unfaithfulness or immorality, he exposes her to committing adultery, and that whoever marries her also commits adultery. To put away a wife means to send her away and divorce her. To commit adultery means to fall into adultery.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, correcting common interpretations of the law of Moses. Some used a written certificate of divorce as an excuse to send a woman away easily. In that society, a woman who was sent away was left very unprotected. Jesus defends the value of marriage and the most vulnerable person. Christians understand the scope of the exception and the difficult cases in different ways.

For today: take care of your marriage and your promises, and never treat another person as disposable. If there is pain or divorce in your story, turn to God and to a community that will walk with you in grace and truth.
exp.4:35:
Jesus says that we should not swear by our own head either. The reason is simple: we cannot even make one hair white or black. It also notes that a certain small word in the original wording means something like "or" in older usage. The idea is that we do not have full control even over our own bodies, so we cannot guarantee anything with that kind of oath.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He corrects the habit of using oaths to give more weight to words, sometimes mentioning sacred things without keeping what was promised. He teaches that everything belongs to God, not to us. Some think he forbids every kind of oath; others think he condemns the careless and deceptive use of them.

For today: be a person of your word. Before promising something, think humbly about whether you will be able to keep it, and speak simply and truthfully, without needing embellishments to be believed.
exp.4:45:
Jesus says that loving only those who love us is nothing out of the ordinary. The word "reward" here refers to the payment or fruit that God gives. The tax collectors were agents who collected taxes for the Roman empire, and many Jews despised them. Even they loved those who were kind to them.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just asked them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. He wants his followers to reflect the character of the Father, who gives sun and rain to both good and evil people. The love of the kingdom goes beyond what is common.

Today, think of someone who rubs you the wrong way or has hurt you. This week, pray for that person and do one concrete act of kindness, even if they never thank you. Ask God to give you his love so you can do it.
exp.4:46:
Jesus asks: if you greet only your own brothers and sisters, meaning your close circle, what makes you different? Greeting someone warmly means you show them affection through a kind word or embrace. Even they treated their own people well.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just taught them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. His point is that God's children should reflect their Father, who gives sun and rain to everyone without distinction. He then calls them to a life that is complete and mature in love.

For today: this week, do one concrete act of kindness toward someone outside your circle, such as a distant neighbor, a difficult coworker, or someone you disagree with. Greet, help, or pray for that person.
exp.5:2:
When we help those in need, the text says we should do it so discreetly that not even our left hand finds out what our right hand is giving. It is an exaggerated way of speaking to say: do not announce it or boast about it.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and the crowd. He has just criticized hypocrites, who gave so that they would be admired. He wants to correct the motives of the heart: what matters is pleasing God, not impressing people.

For today: when you help someone, do it without publicizing it or expecting applause. You can give help quietly, without posting about it online or telling your friends, trusting that God sees what you do.
exp.5:15:
Jesus says that when someone fasts, they should not put on a gloomy, neglected face like the hypocrites. Old words: the phrase about looking gloomy and severe refers to a face that looks serious and somber; to "disfigure their faces" means to change or spoil their appearance; and "reward" is what they receive. They make themselves look worn out so that people will notice they are fasting, and Jesus states that this human admiration is all they will get.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Earlier he taught about giving to the needy and praying without seeking applause. Here he applies the same principle to fasting, a common Jewish religious practice. His point is the heart: not acting to impress others, but acting for God.

For today: when you pray, give, serve, or fast, ask yourself who you are doing it for. Try to keep some of your life with God private, between Him and you, without seeking the admiration of others.
exp.5:16:
Jesus says that when someone fasts, they should anoint their head and wash their face. "Anoint" means putting oil or perfume on the hair, something common in that time for looking presentable. "Face" is the visage. In other words, one should look normal and well cared for, not sad or neglected.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Earlier he corrected the hypocrites, who put on a suffering look so that people would admire them. He wants fasting to be something between the person and God, not a spectacle. The Father sees in secret and rewards.

If you pray, fast, or serve, do it with sincerity and without seeking applause. You do not need to announce it or show weariness. Present yourself simply and offer that moment to God alone, trusting that He sees your heart.
exp.5:18:
Jesus says that we should not pile up riches while thinking they will be safe here on earth. The insect that destroys fine clothing and the rust that spoils metals both show how goods are damaged. Thieves who dig through mud walls to get inside to steal show how goods are lost. Everything we store up here gets used up, damaged, or lost.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just taught about giving, praying, and fasting without seeking the applause of people, but rather the gaze of the Father. Now he moves from the same theme to money: there too it matters whom we want to please and what we trust in.

For today: review how you use your time and your money. Without neglecting your responsibilities, set aside something to help others, support your church, or do good in secret. In this way your heart learns to trust God and not your possessions.
exp.5:19:
Jesus says that we should store up treasures in heaven and not on earth. Some of the words in this verse are older ones: rust is the corrosion that eats away at metal, and a moth is the insect that destroys clothing. Breaking through a wall to get in and steal is what the verse describes as thieves who break through and steal. In heaven, nothing of that kind can harm or take away what we keep there.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. He had been teaching them to give, pray, and fast without seeking applause, but rather the gaze of the Father. Now he turns to the subject of money and possessions. The verses that follow explain that the heart follows what we value most.

Today we can ask ourselves: where am I investing my time and my money? One practical way is to set something aside to help someone in need or to support the work of the church, trusting that God values what we do out of love.
exp.5:20:
Jesus says that the heart follows the treasure. A "treasure" is whatever we value most and take the most care of. In other words, what we consider most valuable is what governs our affections, thoughts, and decisions.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Before this, he warns that earthly treasures are damaged or lost: by moths, by rust, and by thieves. Afterward, he speaks about the eye as a lamp, to show that what we look at and desire affects our whole life.

For today: review how you spend your time, your money, and your thoughts. This shows where your heart is. Today, decide to give something to God or to someone in need, and ask him to put his Kingdom first in your life.
exp.5:24:
Jesus tells us not to live filled with anxiety about what we will eat, drink, or wear. The word "worry" means to be troubled and anxious. Then he asks a question: isn't life worth more than food, and the body worth more than clothing? If God gave us what is greatest, our life and our body, we can trust that he will also take care of what we need.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Just before this, he said that no one can serve God and money, that is, riches. That is why he begins with "Therefore": worry about money and possessions competes with trust in God. Then he invites them to look at the birds.

For today: when worry about providing for yourself overtakes you, pray and hand that burden over to God. Do what is yours to do with responsibility, but do not let fear rule your heart.
exp.5:25:
Jesus invites us to look at the birds of the air. They do not sow, nor reap, nor gather food into barns (the barns of that time were storehouses for grain). Even so, God, our heavenly Father, feeds them. Then Jesus asks: are you not worth much more than they?

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, to his disciples and to the crowd listening to him. He has just said that no one can serve God and riches. For this reason he asks them not to live anxious about food or clothing, because life is worth more than that.

Today we can do what Jesus says: stop to observe creation and remember that God cares for us. This does not take away our work or our responsibility, but it helps us hand over our worries to God in prayer.
exp.5:26:
This verse asks a question: which of you, by worrying a great deal, can make yourself one cubit taller? A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly half a meter. Some translators think it could also refer to adding a little time to one's life; the Greek word allows both ideas.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just told them to look at the birds, and soon he will speak about the lilies. He wants to show them that the Father takes care of them, so they should not live controlled by anxiety.

For today: when worry steals your peace, ask yourself whether worrying changes anything. What you can do is do your part, hand the burden over to God in prayer, and trust in his care.
exp.5:27:
Jesus asks why we worry, that is, why we are anxious and troubled, about clothing. He invites us to consider the lilies of the field: they grow without working or spinning, meaning they do not make their own cloth.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, addressing his disciples and the crowd. He has just spoken about the birds and how the Father cares for them. His purpose is to teach trust in God and not to live controlled by anxiety about material things. Some think that "lilies" refers to wildflowers in general, not to one exact species.

For today: when worry about money or possessions takes away your peace, stop for a moment, look at something God has made, such as a plant or a bird, and pray, handing that need over to God. Keep doing your part responsibly, but without anxiety.
exp.5:31:
Jesus says that the Gentiles, that is, those who did not know the God of Israel, strive after food, drink, and clothing. But his disciples have a heavenly Father who already knows that they need all these things. The phrase "need" in the verse above matches the verse's point that this is the sense of the word.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just spoken about the birds and the lilies, and now he corrects anxiety about material things. He reminds them that they are not like those who live without knowing God as Father.

For today: when worry about money, work, or family takes away your peace, bring it to God in prayer with the confidence of a child. Then do with diligence what is yours to do today, without carrying the burden of tomorrow.
exp.6:0:
Jesus says that we should not judge others, so that we will not be judged.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples and the crowd how to live in the kingdom of God. Afterward he explains that the measure we use with others will be used with us, and he gives the example of the speck and the plank: we notice the small fault of another person and do not see our own, which is much larger. Some understand that the one who will judge us is God; others understand that people will judge us too.

For today: before criticizing someone, examine your own heart, pray for that person, and treat them with the same mercy you want to receive.
exp.6:5:
He says we should not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw our pearls before pigs. If we do, they will trample them underfoot (the word for trample means to tread down) and turn on us to tear us apart (the word for tear apart means to rip to pieces). Dogs and pigs were despised animals, and here they stand for people who scornfully reject what is precious from God.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount. Just before, he asked us not to judge with hypocrisy, but to first remove the plank from our own eye. Here he adds that discernment is also necessary. Interpreters explain this in different ways, but nearly all agree that Jesus asks for wisdom when sharing what is sacred. He then encourages us to ask God, who gives generously.

For today: share your faith with humility and love, but with wisdom. If someone mocks and rejects again and again, do not argue or insist. Pray for that person and wait for a better opportunity.
exp.6:7:
Jesus explains why it is worth asking, seeking, and knocking: everyone who does so receives an answer. Whoever asks receives; whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks on the door, it is opened. The word "everyone" in the verse means that no one is left out. The verbs are in the present tense and suggest a constant attitude: keep on asking, keep on seeking.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Just before this, he spoke about not judging and about guarding what is holy. Here he encourages trust in God as Father. What follows makes it clear: a good father would not give a stone to his child, and much less would God.

For today: bring your needs to God with confidence and without giving up, as a child speaks with his father. Ask also for wisdom and seek his will, knowing that he responds with goodness, though not always in the way we expect.
exp.6:12:
Jesus invites us to enter through the narrow gate. He says there are two roads: one wide and easy, which ends in ruin (complete loss and destruction), and another narrow, which leads to life. Many go by the wide one.

Jesus speaks at the end of the Sermon on the Mount, addressing his disciples and the crowd. He has just taught about trusting the Father, asking him, and treating others the way we would want to be treated. Now he calls them to decide: it is not enough to listen, one must choose to follow him. Then he warns about false prophets.

For today: do not follow something only because most people do it. Before deciding, ask yourself: "Does this agree with the teachings of Jesus?" Even when it is costly, trust that his way leads to life.
exp.6:13:
Jesus says that the gate that leads to life is narrow and the way is difficult, and that few find it. "Find" is the meaning of the word in question; it is a contrast with the broad and easy road, where many people enter and which ends in destruction.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, near the end of his teaching. He has just spoken about treating others as we want to be treated, and right after this he warns about false prophets. With this image he invites his hearers to decide seriously whether they will follow him, without letting themselves be carried along by the crowd. Scholars debate how literal the idea of "few" is, but the call to choose carefully is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I follow Jesus out of conviction, or only out of habit and comfort? Today, choose one simple decision where obeying him will cost you something, and do it with trust in his guidance.
exp.6:15:
Jesus says that people are recognized by what they produce, that is, by their conduct and their results. He asks whether anyone gathers grapes from thorn bushes or figs from thistles. The "thistles" here are prickly plants, like the cardos. The obvious answer is no, because each plant produces its own kind of fruit.

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just warned that the road to life is narrow and that there are false prophets, who look like sheep but are wolves inside. He gives them a practical way to discern: it is not enough to look at words or appearance; one must observe the whole life and its effects over time.

For today: before following a leader or a teaching, watch patiently for the character it produces: humility, truth, love, self-control. And examine your own fruit honestly as well.
exp.6:17:
It says that a tree's nature shows in what it produces. A healthy tree gives good fruit, and a tree that is spoiled gives bad fruit. It is a comparison: the tree is the person, and the fruit is their words, attitudes and actions.

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount. Just before, he warned about false prophets, who look like sheep but inside are wolves. Here he gives a way to recognize them: not by their appearance or their speeches, but by the fruit they leave in life. He then adds that the tree without good fruit is cut down.

For today: before I follow a leader or judge my own life, I look at the long-term fruit: love, truth, humility, patience. And I ask God to heal my heart, because what I give comes from there.
exp.6:26:
It says a strong storm came upon the house of the foolish man: the rain fell, the rivers rose, and the winds blew.

Jesus speaks at the end of the Sermon on the Mount. With this image he closes his teaching and warns that it is not enough to hear his words; they must be put into practice. The crowd was amazed, because Jesus taught with authority, not like the scribes.

For today: do not be content with hearing the Bible or with agreeing with it. Choose one of Jesus' teachings, for example forgiving, being honest, or trusting God, and obey it this week. When the storms come, that simple obedience will be your firmness.
exp.6:28:
This verse says that the crowd was amazed because Jesus taught with real authority, and not the way the scribes did. The scribes were the teachers of Jewish law. Jesus was teaching the crowds, so he was instructing them directly.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking as he finishes the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7). The scribes usually supported their teaching by quoting other respected teachers. Jesus, by contrast, spoke directly, saying things like "You have heard that it was said... but I say to you." This surprised the people, because it showed that his word carried weight in itself.

For today: it is not enough to admire the words of Jesus, as the people of that time did. He had just spoken about building on the rock, that is, about obeying. Today you can choose one of his teachings and put it into practice this week.
exp.7:3:
Jesus tells the man healed of leprosy not to tell anyone, but to go and show himself to the priest and bring the offering that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.

Jesus speaks right after touching and cleansing the leper. The law of Moses (Leviticus 14) required that the priest confirm a leper's healing. That is why Jesus respects this order. It is not known for certain why he asked for silence; it has been understood as a wish to avoid crowds who sought only miracles, or misunderstandings about who he was.

For today: God works with power, but also with order and humility. When he helps you, do not use it to draw attention to yourself. Thank him with simple obedience, and let your changed life be the testimony.
exp.7:5:
It says that a centurion, an officer of the Roman army, came to Jesus in Capernaum and told him about his problem. Here the word for the servant is rendered as a servant or a young attendant. This man was lying in bed, unable to move, and he was suffering greatly, grievously tormented. It notes that the centurion does not directly ask for anything; he simply lays out the need.

The one speaking is the centurion, a foreigner who was not part of the people of Israel. He comes right after Jesus healed a leper. Although his position gave him authority, he approaches Jesus with humility and pleads for someone who, in that time, had little social worth. Jesus replies at once that he will go and heal him.

For today: we can bring the needs of others to Jesus with simplicity and compassion. No elaborate words are required; it is enough to tell him honestly what is happening to someone we love, trusting that he cares.
exp.7:7:
Here a Roman officer responds to Jesus with humility. He says he is not worthy for Jesus to come into his house, and he asks only that Jesus speak a word so that his servant will be healed. The "roof" in the verse is the house itself, the place under his roof. The servant is a young man who serves him.

The speaker is a centurion, an officer over about one hundred soldiers, probably not a Jew. His servant was paralyzed and suffering greatly. Jesus had already said he would go and heal him, but the centurion trusts that Jesus' authority is enough, even from a distance. Jesus marvels at his faith.

For today: we can approach God with humility and trust his word, even when we do not yet see the result. Prayer is not earning his help, but believing that he is good and has the power to act.
exp.7:14:
He says Jesus touched the hand of Peter's mother-in-law, and the fever left her immediately. She got up from her bed and began to serve them.

Mateo recounts this event right after Jesus healed the servant of the centurion. Jesus arrives at Peter's house, sees the sick woman, and acts without anyone asking him to, according to this account. Later, when evening came, he healed many more. Matthew sees in this the fulfillment of Isaiah 53:4, where it speaks of the one who bore our sicknesses. Interpreters explain in different ways how that prophecy applies, but all of them see in it the care of Jesus.

Jesus pays attention to people's needs, even in the home and in everyday life. When he restores us, our natural response can be to serve with gratitude. Today we can bring him our burdens and use what we have received to help others.
exp.7:15:
When evening came, the people brought to Jesus many who were tormented by demons. He drove out the spirits with only a word and healed all who were sick. Those described as tormented are people afflicted by evil spirits. The phrase about it being late indicates that the day was ending.

Matthew tells this as a narrator. Jesus had just healed Peter's mother-in-law in Capernaum. It was late, and it is likely that the people waited until the Sabbath had ended before carrying the sick to him, though the text does not say so. Matthew then explains that this fulfills what Isaiah had announced: Jesus takes our infirmities and diseases. Interpreters debate the exact scope of that phrase.

For today: if you are weary or the night of your life seems long, you can come to Jesus with your burdens and those of others. He turns no one away. Bring to him, in prayer and with confidence, those you love.
exp.7:16:
Matthew says that Jesus' healings fulfilled what Isaiah had foretold: that the Servant of the Lord would take our infirmities and bear our sicknesses. Infirmities are the pains and ailments of the body.

Here the speaker is Matthew, the author of the Gospel, not Jesus. He has just recounted how Jesus healed Peter's mother-in-law and, in the evening, many who were sick and possessed by demons. He cites Isaiah 53:4 to show that Jesus is the promised Servant. How this connects to the cross is a matter of debate among Christians: some see here a promise of physical healing, while others see mainly a compassionate care that points to the complete work of Christ.

For today: when you are sick, weary, or burdened, bring it to Jesus with confidence. He sympathizes with your suffering and does not regard you from a distance. Pray for healing, but also rest in the knowledge that He cares for you.
exp.7:20:
Here a disciple asks Jesus for permission to go first and bury his father, and then follow him. The request is for leave to go first and then follow him.

After a scribe offered to follow Jesus and He spoke to him about the cost of following, another disciple sets a condition. We do not know whether his father had already died or whether he wanted to wait until he died; interpreters understand this in different ways. Jesus replies that following him comes first, using a strong expression to show the urgency of the call.

For today: Jesus deserves first place, even above good and legitimate things. Ask yourself what you usually put before obeying him, and give it to him with confidence, knowing that he cares for what you leave behind.
exp.7:29:
This verse tells us that, at some distance from Jesus and the two men, there was a large herd of pigs feeding on the grass. The word "herd" in this verse refers to a group of animals kept together, and "feeding" means they were grazing or eating.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Jesus has just arrived in the region of the Gergesenes, where two men tormented by demons come out to meet him. The demons recognize Jesus as the Son of God and fear his judgment. This herd appears right away as the place they ask to go. The detail shows that Jesus has authority over the demons, and that they can act only if he allows it.

For today: When you feel that something dominates you or frightens you, remember that Jesus has authority over every evil. Come to him with confidence.
exp.8:0:
This verse tells how Jesus got into a boat, crossed the lake, and came to his own town. Quoted wording and old spellings from the source are not repeated here. The town of Jesus is usually understood to be Capernaum, which served as a home base during his ministry in Galilee.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just returned from the region of the Gadarenes, where he had healed people who were possessed by demons, and the people there had asked him to leave. Matthew shows Jesus going back to a familiar place, and soon a paralyzed man is brought to him. This verse serves as a bridge to that scene.

For today: Jesus does not stay stuck in the rejection he faced. He keeps moving forward and serves those who need him. When something goes wrong for you or a door closes, do not dwell on it. Keep doing good wherever God has placed you.
exp.8:1:
Some people brought to Jesus a man who was paralyzed, lying on a bed. Jesus saw their faith and said to the sick man: "Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you."

Jesus had just returned by boat to his city, which was probably Capernaum, though the text does not say so in those words. The narrator is Matthew. Jesus speaks tenderly and first attends to the man's deepest need: forgiveness. This provokes the reaction of the scribes, who accuse him in their minds of blasphemy.

Today we can learn to bring others before Jesus in prayer, with simple faith. He sees our heart, speaks to us with kindness, and cares about our deepest need, not only the visible problem.
exp.8:10:
The Pharisees see that Jesus is sitting down to eat with tax collectors and sinners. So instead of speaking to Him directly, they ask His disciples why their Master does this. Tax collectors were disliked for working for Rome and, very often, for collecting more than they should. Sinners were people who lived outside the law.

The Pharisees were a religious group who took great care to keep themselves pure. Sharing a meal meant acceptance and closeness, so for them this was a scandal. Jesus had just called Matthew, a tax collector, and Matthew welcomed Him into his house along with his friends. Jesus then answers that He came as a physician for the sick.

We might ask ourselves whether it is hard for us to draw near to people we consider far from God. Jesus shows us another way: to approach them with mercy, to share life with them, and to offer hope, without failing to call them to repentance.
exp.8:11:
Jesus answers a criticism with a simple comparison: those who are well do not seek the doctor, but those who are sick. The word "hearing" means that Jesus heard the complaint. "Doctor" refers to the one who heals. With this, Jesus presents himself as someone who heals, and he calls those who recognize their need "the sick."

The Pharisees, who were very strict about the law, were scandalized that Jesus ate with tax collectors (collectors of taxes, looked down on by many) and with sinners. Jesus answers them. Some understand that he speaks with a touch of irony, since the Pharisees also needed healing, though they did not acknowledge it. Then Jesus quotes Hosea: he desires mercy, not only rituals.

For today: do not distance yourself from God because you feel unworthy. Come near with sincerity, and treat with compassion those who struggle, without looking down on them.
exp.8:13:
The disciples of John the Baptist come to Jesus with a sincere question. They notice that they and the Pharisees fast often, but Jesus' disciples do not.

This happens right after Jesus has eaten with sinners and tax collectors. John's disciples, who lived a life of repentance and simplicity, wonder why Jesus' followers do not practice the same fasting. Jesus answers with the picture of a wedding: people do not mourn while the bridegroom is present.

For today: before judging the practices of other believers, ask yourself what is in the heart. Fasting and other spiritual disciplines are valuable when they draw us closer to God, and Jesus teaches us that there are times to celebrate his presence and times to seek him with humility.
exp.8:14:
Jesus answers with a simple question: can the guests at a wedding mourn while the bridegroom is still with them? It is impossible, because a wedding is a time of celebration. Then he says that a time will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, carried far from them, and then they will fast. The word "taken" here refers to sorrow and fasting.

The disciples of John the Baptist asked him why they and the Pharisees fasted, but his disciples did not. Jesus presents himself as the bridegroom. His presence is a reason for joy. Many understand that he is announcing his death, although the text says it in few words.

For today: do not live your faith only as a list of duties. Enjoy the closeness of Christ with gratitude, and when you fast or pray with sorrow, do it with a heart that longs for God, not out of mere custom.
exp.8:15:
Nobody puts a patch of new cloth, one that has not yet been washed or shrunk, onto an old garment. The verse describes new, unwashed fabric that is strong and has never been used. When it shrinks, it pulls on the old cloth and leaves the tear bigger than before.

Jesus is speaking with the disciples of John the Baptist, who ask him why his disciples do not fast. He answers that while the bridegroom is present, it is a time for celebration, and he uses examples from everyday life. Many understand that what Jesus brings is not a simple repair of the old way of practicing faith, although some interpret it in other ways.

For today: do not use Jesus as a patch on your life as it has always been. Let him transform your habits, priorities, and motives, rather than settling for touch-ups that do not change the heart.
exp.8:16:
Jesus says that no one puts new wine into old wineskins. The wineskins mentioned here are bags made from animal skin for storing wine. An old wineskin is stiff and can no longer stretch. New wine keeps fermenting and builds up pressure, so the old skin bursts and everything is lost. That is why new wine is put into new skins, which are flexible, and so both are preserved.

Jesus is responding to a question about why his disciples did not fast, as other religious groups did. He explains that with him is the joy of a wedding, and that what he brings is something new. The two examples, the patch and the wine, show that his work does not fit into old, rigid molds. Some see here an invitation to give up only rigidity, while others see that Jesus is introducing something truly different.

Today, ask God for a heart willing to learn. Do not cling to customs just because they have always been done that way. Examine whether they help you follow Christ.
exp.8:17:
While Jesus was still speaking these things to them, a certain ruler came in and knelt before him. He said that his daughter had just died. But he asked Jesus to come and place his hand on her, convinced that she would live. Here the phrase can be understood as him falling down before Jesus with great reverence.

Jesus had been answering a question about fasting and used the images of patches and new wineskins. The man speaks with grief, but with faith. Matthew does not give his name; Mark and Luke identify him as Jairus, the leader of the synagogue. Jesus follows him at once, and along the way the healing of the sick woman takes place.

When a situation strikes us that seems lost, we can come to Jesus with humility and with confidence. He is not troubled by our desperation; he invites us to bring to him whatever hurts most.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that Jesus got up and went with the man who had asked him for help. His disciples went with him too. The phrase about following him means that Jesus went behind that man, or along with him, toward his house.

Here the narrator is Matthew. A ruler, that is, a leader or person in authority, came up to Jesus while he was teaching. That man bowed before him with respect and begged him on behalf of his daughter, who had died. Jesus stopped teaching and responded at once to her need.

For today: Jesus does not stay in theory, but moves toward the one who is suffering. We can imitate him. When someone asks us for help or needs company, let us set aside what we are doing, if possible, and go to their side. Sometimes the best gesture is simply to be present.
exp.8:22:
This verse tells us that Jesus came to the house of the ruler, an important man who had asked him for help for his daughter. When he went in, he saw the musicians who played the flutes and a large crowd making a commotion, that is, noise and uproar. It was the scene of a funeral.

The narrator is Matthew. Jesus had been interrupted on the way by the woman who touched his clothing and was healed. Now he continues toward the house where the girl had just died. In that time, musicians and mourning women were hired for funerals. That is why the atmosphere was full of noise and sorrow.

When everything seems finished and the noise of hopelessness covers everything, Jesus is still hope. We can bring to him with confidence our situations that seem lost.
exp.8:33:
This verse shows the reaction of the Pharisees to the miracle. They say that Jesus casts out demons through the prince of the devils, that is, through the chief of the evil spirits. The word "But" means the people marveled, but they rejected him.

The Pharisees were a religious group who were highly respected among the Jews. They had just seen a mute man speak, and the people said that nothing like this had ever been seen in Israel. They could not deny the fact, so they explained it in the worst way possible. Later, in Matthew 12, they make this accusation again and Jesus answers them.

For today: sometimes a closed heart sees a good work and still criticizes it. Let us ask God for humility to recognize his work, to rejoice when someone is helped, and not to let pride or envy blind us.
exp.8:36:
Here Jesus compares people to a field of wheat ready for harvest. The crop that is mature and can already be gathered is the harvest, and the workers who gather it are the labourers. He says there are many people who need help and hope, but few who devote themselves to serving them.

The one speaking is Jesus, and he says it to his disciples. He had just travelled through towns and villages teaching, proclaiming the kingdom and healing. Seeing the crowd, he felt compassion, because they were lost, like sheep without a shepherd. From that compassion this teaching arises, and right away he invites them to pray for more labourers.

For today: look around you with the compassionate eyes of Jesus. Pray for those who serve others in God's name, and ask him how you can help, with a visit, a kind word or a concrete gesture.
exp.8:37:
Jesus asks his disciples to pray to the Lord of the harvest, that is, to God, the owner of the harvest. The harvest is the field of grain ready to be gathered, and here it stands for the people who need to hear God's message. The laborers are those who work in that harvest. He asks that God send out workers.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after going through the cities and villages. Seeing the people weary and scattered, like sheep that have no shepherd, he felt compassion. His first response is prayer: the need is great and the workers are few.

Today, when faced with the needs of those around us, we can begin by praying sincerely. Let us ask God to raise up workers and to make us available to serve, helping, listening, or sharing his love with someone close to us.
exp.9:0:
It says that Jesus called together his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, that is, evil spirits, so that they could cast them out. He also empowered them to heal every sickness and every ailment. "Authority" means power to act or command; the old spellings in the source are not carried over here.

The one acting here is Jesus, and the narrator is Matthew. Before this, Jesus had gone through the towns teaching and healing, and he had felt compassion for the crowds (Matthew 9:35-38). Now he makes his disciples partners in that same work. Then the text names the twelve apostles, the ones sent out.

For today: Jesus does not call anyone to serve with their own strength alone. If God gives you a task of caring for or helping others, ask him for strength and wisdom, and take the first step trusting that he is with you.
exp.9:1:
This verse begins the list of the twelve apostles. It first names Simon, whom Jesus called Peter, and his brother Andrew. Then it names James (that is, Santiago), the son of Zebedee, and his brother John.

Here the narrator is Matthew, who was also one of the twelve. Jesus had just called his disciples and given them authority to heal and to cast out evil spirits. Now Matthew gives their names, to show that Jesus chose specific people, with their own histories and families, to be sent out to serve. Two pairs of brothers lead the list.

Today we can remember that God calls ordinary people, with names and faces, to serve him. You do not have to be perfect. Ask yourself: who can I help or encourage this week, perhaps together with a family member or friend?
exp.9:4:
Jesus sends out his twelve disciples with a clear instruction: do not go along the roads of the Gentiles (those who were not Jews), and do not enter any city of the Samaritans.

Jesus speaks right after choosing the twelve. He sends them first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, that is, to the Jewish people. Many understand this as an initial stage of the mission, since later Jesus sends them to all nations (Matthew 28:19). Some also explain that God chose to begin with Israel because of his promises to that people.

For today: when God gives you a task, carry it out in obedience, in the place and at the time he indicates, without becoming discouraged because others called later will come after you. Start with the people closest to you, with love and simplicity.
exp.9:9:
Jesus tells his disciples not to take a scrip (a travel bag for carrying food or belongings), nor two coats, nor extra shoes, nor a staff (a walking stick). The reason: the workman is worthy of being supported with what he needs to live.

Jesus is speaking to the twelve apostles when he sends them out for the first time to preach in the cities of Israel. He asks them to travel light and to trust in God, who would care for them through the hospitality of the people. Some scholars note that other gospels mention the staff and the sandals differently; it is usually understood that Jesus emphasizes urgency and dependence on God, rather than a fixed rule.

For today: serve others generously and without turning your service into a business, and support with gratitude those who devote their time to serving God and the community.
exp.9:22:
Jesus tells his disciples that if they are persecuted in one town, they should not stay there but go on to another. He assures them that they will not finish going through all the towns of Israel before "the Son of man" comes.

Jesus is sending the twelve out to preach in the towns of Israel and warns them of rejection and persecution. The phrase about the coming of the Son of man is understood in several ways: his coming in judgment on Jerusalem, his resurrection and the advance of the kingdom, or his final return. Interpreters do not agree, and we can acknowledge that with humility.

For today: obeying God does not mean seeking suffering without need. If a situation becomes dangerous or closed, being wise and changing course can also be faith, trusting that God is still at work.
exp.9:23:
Jesus says that a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. In today's words: whoever follows Jesus should not expect better treatment than He received. The "servant" is the one who serves another, and the "master" is the one he serves.

Jesus speaks to the twelve apostles as He sends them out to proclaim the kingdom. He has just warned them that they will be rejected and persecuted. With this saying He prepares their hearts: if they called Him Beelzebul, an insulting name for the prince of demons, they will also insult His followers. But He asks them not to be afraid.

For today: if someone rejects you or mocks you for following Christ, do not be discouraged or surprised. Remember that you are on the same road as your Teacher, and ask Him for courage to respond with gentleness and firmness.
exp.9:27:
Jesus says not to fear those who can take away the life of the body, because they cannot touch the soul. Instead, we should have a reverent awe of God, who has power over the whole person.

The old form of a word is not explained here, and the word for "hell" is not discussed, since the verse above does not use it. Some believe that "destroy" means total ruin, others that it means eternal punishment; Christians have understood this in different ways.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples, just before sending them out to preach. He warns them that they will be rejected and even persecuted. For this reason he encourages them to speak with courage. And right away he reminds them that the Father cares even for the sparrows and has counted every hair on their heads.

When fear of criticism or rejection silences you, remember that God cares for you. Ask him for courage to be faithful to him, even when it costs you, and trust in his care.
exp.9:28:
Jesus asks whether two sparrows are not sold for a farthing, a coin of very little value. Yet he says that not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. Some understand this to mean without your Father knowing it; others, without his will. Both emphasize his care.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom, warning them that they will face rejection and persecution. He tells them not to fear those who can only harm the body. Through this simple example he shows them that God cares even for the smallest things, and that they are worth far more.

For today: when you feel afraid or think you are insignificant, remember that God sees you and knows you. Bring your worry to him in prayer and keep doing what is right with confidence.
exp.9:30:
