Jesus says not to be afraid, because each of us is worth more than many sparrows. The sparrows are small, inexpensive birds. If God takes care even of these birds, how much more does he care for his children.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples when he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom. He warns them that there will be rejection and persecution. For this reason he encourages them: the Father knows everything that happens to them, down to the smallest details, such as the number of their hairs. Afterward he asks them to confess him with courage.

For today: when fear holds you back from living or from speaking about your faith, remember that God knows you and values you. His care does not promise that there will be no difficulties, but it does mean you do not face them alone. Give him that worry today in prayer.
exp.9:38:
He who holds tightly to his own life, trying to secure it and living only for himself, will end up losing it. But whoever gives up his life for the sake of Jesus will find it. The verb "find" here means to come upon or obtain, while the verb "lose" means to let go or give up.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom. He warns them that following him may bring rejection, even from within their own family. Earlier he had asked them to love him more than anyone else and to take up their cross. This saying explains why it is worth it: what is given to Christ is not truly lost.

For today: think of an area where you cling to control, such as your time, your plans, or your comfort. Bring it to Jesus in prayer today and ask him how to serve him in it, trusting that he gives true life.
exp.9:39:
Jesus says that receiving his disciples is the same as receiving him, and receiving him is receiving God the Father, who sent him. "Receive" means welcoming them, giving them a good reception, and accepting their message.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles as he sends them out to preach in the towns of Israel. He has just warned them that following him is costly, even to the point of carrying the cross. Here he comforts them: some will reject them, but those who welcome them will be welcoming God himself. The verses that follow speak of reward for whoever helps them.

For today: when someone shares the Word of God with sincerity, or needs help because they serve the Lord, receive them with respect and generosity. A simple gesture, such as offering food, prayer, or lodging, is seen by God as done to him.
exp.9:40:
It says that whoever welcomes a prophet because he is a prophet will receive the same kind of reward the prophet receives. The same holds for whoever welcomes a righteous person because he is righteous.

Jesus is speaking to his twelve disciples when he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom. He warns them of rejection and sacrifice, but he also assures them that whoever receives them receives him, and through him, the Father. The verses that follow extend the promise even to someone who gives just a cup of cold water. Some think that "prophet" and "righteous" refer to different kinds of believers; others think they refer to the very disciples who are being sent.

Today we can support those who serve God: a pastor, a missionary, or a faithful brother or sister. Inviting them to a meal, praying for them, or helping them in their needs is a service that God sees and rewards.
exp.9:41:
It says that if anyone gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water, only because they are a disciple of Jesus, God will notice it and reward them.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles as he sends them out to preach. He warns them that they will be rejected, but also that there will be those who receive them. Closing this discourse, Jesus teaches that welcoming his messengers is welcoming him and the Father. For this reason, even the smallest gesture has value.

For today: do not underestimate small acts of kindness. A cup of water, a meal, a word of encouragement, or a favor to a believer who serves God, done sincerely, is seen by the Lord. Look today for someone you can help.
exp.10:2:
John the Baptist sends two of his disciples with a question: "Are you the one who was to come, or should we look for another?" "The one who was to come" refers to the promised Messiah.

John is in prison and hears about the works of Jesus. The disciples speak on John's behalf. We do not know for certain why he asks: some think he had doubts, others that he wanted to encourage his disciples to believe. Jesus answers by pointing to his works, which fulfill what the prophets announced, as in Isaiah.

Even faithful people can have questions when they suffer or when things do not turn out as they hoped. You can bring your doubts to Jesus honestly. He is not angered by questions; he answers by making himself known to those who seek him.
exp.10:7:
Jesus asks the crowd what they expected to find when they went out into the wilderness to see John. Was it a man dressed in fine, soft clothing? He answers his own question: those who dress in luxury live in the houses of kings, not in the wilderness.

John the Baptist's disciples, who were in prison, had just asked Jesus whether He was the one who was to come. When they left, Jesus defended John before the crowd. John was not weak like a reed, nor one who loved comforts. He was firm, simple, and faithful to his mission as a prophet.

For today: let us not look for messengers who flatter us or give us comfort. Let us value those who speak the truth with firmness and humility, even when their lives are simple.
exp.10:12:
Jesus says that all the earlier Scripture, that is, the prophets and the law of Moses, announced what God would do, and that this announcement reached as far as John the Baptist. "Prophesied" means that they spoke on God's behalf about what was to come.

Jesus is speaking to the crowds, after John, who was in prison, sent messengers to ask whether He was the Messiah. Jesus praises John and explains his place: he is the last great messenger of the period of promise, and with Jesus comes the fulfillment. The verses that follow connect him with Elijah, according to the promise in Malachi.

For today: read the whole Bible looking toward Christ. When you read the Old Testament, ask yourself: how does this show me Jesus? In this way you will better understand God's promises and trust Him more.
exp.10:15:
Jesus asks what he can compare the people of his time to. He answers with an everyday image: children sitting in the marketplace, the town square, calling out to their playmates.

Jesus is speaking to the crowds, right after speaking about John the Baptist. Both John and Jesus had been rejected, although they came in very different ways. Jesus uses this children's game to show that many people were looking for excuses not to respond to God. What follows in the text explains the comparison.

For today: let us examine whether we sometimes set conditions for God, expecting him to speak in our own way. Let us ask him for a humble heart, willing to listen and obey, even when his message comes in unexpected or uncomfortable ways.
exp.10:16:
The children playing in the marketplace complain to their companions: "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang songs of mourning, and you did not weep." To pipe is to play a wind instrument, and to lament is to sing sorrowful songs for someone who has died.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and compares this generation to those children. John the Baptist lived with self-denial, and Jesus came sharing meals with everyone. They rejected both. According to the context, the people were making excuses so that they would not respond to God, no matter how the message reached them.

For today: examine whether you are looking for excuses not to listen. God can speak to us in different ways, and sometimes we reject him because his message does not come in the form we prefer. Ask him for a humble heart, ready to respond.
exp.10:18:
Jesus says that he came eating and drinking like any other person, and people accused him of being a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors (despised tax collectors) and of sinners. At the end he says that wisdom is justified, that is, shown to be true, by her children, meaning by her results and fruits.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd, right after praising John the Baptist. He compares that generation to capricious children who will not play at being happy or at being sad. John lived in strict self-denial and they called him demon-possessed; Jesus lived sociably and they called him a libertine. Nothing seemed right to them, because they did not want to believe.

For today: let us not look for excuses to reject the truth. Rather, let us look humbly at the fruits of Jesus' life and of those who follow him, and not let ourselves be carried away by criticism or by what people think.
exp.10:24:
Jesus prays and praises the Father, whom he calls Lord of heaven and earth. He thanks him because these things were hidden from the wise and understanding, yet were revealed to little children. Hidden means concealed, and revealed means made known.

Jesus speaks just after rebuking cities such as Capernaum, which saw his miracles and did not repent. The wise were people proud of their knowledge, and the children are those who receive with humility and simplicity. Jesus does not despise learning; he points out that pride closes the heart. The following verse says that this pleased the Father.

For today: draw near to God and to his Word with humility, ready to learn and not to presume. Before reading the Bible, ask God to open your eyes and teach you, even if you already think you know the passage.
exp.10:26:
Jesus says that the Father has placed all things in his hands. No one truly knows the Son except the Father, and no one truly knows the Father except the Son. But the Son can make the Father known to whomever he chooses. The word "know" here speaks of a deep, personal knowing, not just having information. To "reveal" is to make known something that was hidden.

Jesus speaks in prayer, praising the Father because these truths were not opened to those who consider themselves wise, but to the humble. Right after this, he invites the weary and burdened to come to him. In this way, knowing God is not an intellectual achievement, but a gift that comes through Jesus.

For today: you do not need to understand everything to know God. Come to Jesus with humility, ask him to show you the Father, and rest in his invitation.
exp.10:27:
Jesus invites everyone who is weary and burdened by the weight of life to come to Him. He promises that He will give them rest.

Jesus speaks just after saying that only He truly knows the Father and reveals Him to whomever He chooses. Many understand the burdens to include the weight of the religious rules of His time, though it can also cover any weariness of the soul. Then Jesus invites them to learn from Him, for He is gentle and humble.

Today, instead of carrying only your worries, bring them to Jesus in sincere prayer. Tell Him what weighs on you, and stay for a moment in silence, trusting that He sustains you and teaches you to walk with more peace.
exp.10:29:
Jesus says that his yoke is "easy" and his burden is "light." A yoke was a wooden piece that joined two animals so they could pull a load together. Here "easy" means kind, well fitted, and not painful. "Light" means that it does not weigh too much.

Jesus speaks to people who are tired and weighed down. Shortly before, he invited them to come to him and learn from him, for he is gentle and humble. In his time, "yoke" was also used to speak of a teacher's teaching. Some think Jesus is contrasting his teaching with heavy religious burdens; the text does not spell this out here, but it fits the tone of the invitation.

For today: when you feel worn out by demands, guilt, or fear, go to Jesus in prayer and ask him what he really asks of you. Learn from his kind way of dealing with people, and do not carry alone what he has not given you to carry.
exp.11:8:
Here the verse says that Jesus left the place where he had been speaking with the Pharisees about the Sabbath, and went into their synagogue. The verse's notes on the wording of the verse are not needed for the English reader, so they are omitted here. The synagogue was the place where the Jews gathered to read Scripture and to pray.

Here the narrator is Matthew. He has just recounted the dispute about the disciples who picked heads of grain on the Sabbath. Jesus reminded them that God prefers mercy to ritual. Now he enters the synagogue, and there he will meet a man in need. The phrase "their synagogue" may suggest some distance from those who were questioning him, although scholars explain it in various ways.

For today: faith is not measured only by keeping religious customs, but by how much it moves us to help those who suffer. Today you can ask yourself to whom you might show mercy, even if that disrupts your routine.
exp.11:9:
This verse tells that in the synagogue there was a man with a withered hand, that is, paralyzed or shriveled. Some people asked Jesus whether it was allowed to heal on the Sabbath. The text makes clear that they were asking so that they might accuse him: they were not seeking the truth, but a reason to blame him.

Matthew tells this right after Jesus said that he is Lord of the Sabbath. The people who ask are, according to the context, people who were watching Jesus closely, and the text gives no further details about them. Jesus answers with the example of a sheep that falls into a pit: if someone helps an animal on the Sabbath, how much more should a person be helped. In this way he teaches that the Sabbath is a day for doing good.

For today: before we use rules or customs to judge someone, let us ask ourselves whether we are helping the person who is suffering. Doing good, with humility and compassion, reflects the heart of God.
exp.11:10:
Jesus asks his listeners: if any of you has a sheep and it falls into a pit on the sabbath day, will you not take hold of it and lift it out? A pit is a deep hole in the ground, the sabbath is the day of rest, and to take hold of something means to grab it in order to help.

Jesus speaks in a synagogue, in front of a man with a withered hand. Some people, looking for a reason to accuse him, ask whether it is lawful to heal on the sabbath. He answers with an everyday example that they themselves would accept. If helping an animal was reasonable, helping a person was even more so. Then he heals the man.

For today: let us not allow rules or religious customs to make us indifferent to the pain of others. Doing good, such as visiting a sick person or helping someone in trouble, pleases God on any day.
exp.11:17:
This verse presents a special servant of God. God himself chose him, loves him, and takes great delight in him. He promises to put his Spirit upon him, and that he will bring justice to the Gentiles, that is, to the peoples who were not Jews. The verse calls him "beloved," which means very dear, and it says that God's soul is well pleased with him, meaning that God rejoices deeply in him.

Matthew quotes here from Isaiah 42:1-4. In the passage, God is the one speaking about his servant. Jesus had just healed many people and asked them not to make him known. Matthew sees in that humble and quiet attitude the fulfillment of this prophecy.

For today: God does not measure greatness as the world does, with noise and fame. We can serve with humility and tenderness, trusting that God sees and takes pleasure in what is done simply and with love.
exp.11:21:
It says that people brought to Jesus a man who had a demon and was also unable to see or speak. Jesús healed him, and the man was set free and began to speak and see.

Here the narrator, Matthew, speaks. Shortly before, he quotes the prophet Isaiah, who described a servant of God who was gentle with the weak, like a bruised reed that is not broken. This healing shows that same compassion. Afterward, the crowd is amazed and asks whether Jesus might be the Son of David, that is, the promised Messiah. The Pharisees, however, reject the sign and say that his power comes from Beelzebub.

Today we can come to Jesus with our burdens and with the burdens of others, trusting in his tenderness. We should also ask him for an open heart, so that we recognize his work and do not harden ourselves against it.
exp.11:23:
The Pharisees heard that the crowd was asking whether Jesus was the Son of David, that is, the promised Messiah. Then they said that Jesus cast out demons only by the power of Beelzebub, the ruler of the devils.

Jesus had just healed a man who was possessed, blind, and mute. The crowd was amazed, but the Pharisees, who were already opposed to Jesus, could not deny the miracle and attributed it to the enemy. Beelzebub was a name used for the chief of the demons, and its exact origin is debated. Jesus answered with simple logic: a kingdom divided cannot stand.

For today: when God does something good, let us guard our hearts so that we do not deny it out of pride or prejudice. Let us ask for humility to recognize his hand, even when it does not fit what we expected.
exp.11:24:
Jesus knew what the Pharisees were thinking in their hearts, and he answered them with a simple truth: a kingdom that fights against itself is laid waste, that is, ruined and destroyed. The same is true of a city or a household divided against itself: it will not be able to stand.

Jesus had just healed a man who was possessed by a demon. The crowd was wondering whether he might be the Son of David, the Messiah. The Pharisees, in order to discredit him, said that he drove out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons. Jesus shows them that their accusation makes no sense: Satan would not tear himself apart.

For today: divisions weaken homes, churches, and friendships. Before we feed a quarrel, we can ask ourselves what unity and humility would do in that situation, and seek peace with those around us.
exp.11:28:
Jesus says that no one can enter the house of a strong man and carry off his belongings (his goods or possessions) unless he first ties up or restrains the strong man. Only after he has subdued him can he plunder the house.

Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees, who accused him of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of the demons. He answers that his authority comes from the Spirit of God. Many understand that the strong man is Satan and that Jesus, by freeing the oppressed, shows that he has already defeated him and that the kingdom of God is present.

For today: if Christ has authority over all evil, we can come to him with confidence when we feel bound by fear, addiction, or guilt. He can set us free. Let us ask him to deliver us and walk with him each day.
exp.11:29:
Jesus says there is no middle ground when it comes to Him: whoever is not on his side is against him. And whoever does not gather with him scatters. The image is that of a shepherd who gathers the flock or a reaper who brings in the harvest; the one who does not help gather ends up scattering.

Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees, who were accusing him of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul. He shows them that his work comes from the Spirit of God and that the kingdom is already present. There can be no neutrality before that truth: either the work of God is recognized, or it is rejected.

For today: let us not live a lukewarm or indifferent faith. Let us ask ourselves honestly whether, through our words and actions, we are helping to gather others to Christ, with love and humility, or whether, without realizing it, we are pushing them away.
exp.11:30:
Jesus says that God can forgive every kind of sin and every offensive word spoken against him. But there is one exception: blasphemy against the Spirit. Blaspheming means speaking with contempt or insult against God.

Jesus speaks here after healing a man who was possessed by a demon. The Pharisees said he was doing it by the power of Satan. Jesus answers that he defeats the strong one, Satan, by the power of God. Attributing the clear work of the Spirit to evil is what he warns against. Some believe it is a persistent and deliberate rejection of God; others see it as a sin of that particular historical moment. The question is debated.

If you are worried that you have committed this sin, that very concern usually shows a heart that is sensitive to God. Come to him with humility, and do not harden your heart against his work.
exp.11:31:
It says that speaking a word against the Son of Man, that is, against Jesus, can be forgiven. But speaking against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age (the present era) nor in the age to come (the era that is coming).

Jesus is speaking to some Pharisees who had just seen him heal a man possessed by a demon. They were saying that he did it by the power of Satan. Jesus warns them that calling the clear work of the Spirit evil is a very serious thing. Interpreters explain this in several ways, but almost all of them see it as a hard and persistent rejection of God's work.

For today: if you are worried that you have committed this sin, notice that your concern already shows a heart that is sensitive to God. Rather, take care with what comes out of your mouth, and draw near to God with humility.
exp.11:38:
Jesus answers the scribes and Pharisees who ask for a sign. He tells them that an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but that no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonas.

Jesus speaks to religious leaders who had already seen his miracles, yet still attributed them to another power and did not believe. They were not asking for a sign out of faith but to test him. Jesus then explains that the sign of Jonas points to his death and resurrection, and he recalls that Nineveh did repent at the preaching of Jonas.

For today: let us not make our faith depend on God giving us special proofs. We already have what He has shown us in Christ. Let us ask for a humble heart that listens and responds with repentance and trust.
exp.11:39:
Jesus compares his own future with what happened to Jonah. Just as Jonah was inside a great fish for three days and three nights, the Son of man, a title Jesus uses for himself, would be in the heart of the earth, a way of speaking about the tomb. Many understand the phrase "three days and three nights" as a common way of counting time, not necessarily exactly seventy-two hours.

Jesus is speaking. Some scribes and Pharisees were asking him for a miraculous sign to prove his authority, even though they had already seen many miracles. He answers that the only sign they will get is the sign of Jonah: his death and resurrection.

For today: God has given us enough reasons to trust Jesus. Instead of demanding proof every time we doubt, we can look at his resurrection and respond with repentance and sincere faith.
exp.11:40:
Jesus says that the people of Nineveh, a pagan city, will stand up on the day of judgment alongside the people of his time and will condemn them. The reason is that the Ninevites repented when Jonah preached to them. And here is someone greater than Jonah.

Jesus speaks to some scribes and Pharisees who were asking him for a miraculous sign, even though they had already seen many of his works. He calls them an evil generation because they did not believe. He compares their hardness with the response of Nineveh, which listened to a prophet without receiving any special sign. Jesus presents himself as greater than Jonah.

For today: do not harden your heart. If God speaks to you through his Word, respond with humility and change what you need to change, without waiting for extraordinary proofs.
exp.11:41:
Jesus says that the queen of the South, that is, the queen of the south, will rise up at the day of judgment together with the people of his time and will condemn them. She traveled from very distant lands, "the ends of the earth", to hear the wisdom of Solomon. And Jesus declares that now there is someone greater than Solomon present there. "Hear" here means to listen with attention.

Jesus speaks to some scribes and Pharisees who were asking him for a miraculous sign, even though they had already seen many miracles. He compares their unbelief with the attitude of the Ninevites and of this queen, who responded to less evidence. Many believe the queen is the queen of Sheba, although the text does not give her name.

If a queen made such a long journey to seek wisdom, we should not neglect the word of Jesus, which we have so close at hand. We can set apart a time each day to listen to him with humility.
exp.11:43:
Here Jesus tells of the unclean spirit which, after leaving a person, decides to return to his house, as if it still belonged to him. Upon arriving, he finds the house empty, swept clean, and put in order. It is tidy on the outside, but there is no one living in it.

Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees and the crowds, after they had asked him for a sign and had attributed his miracles to the power of the devil. Through this scene he describes this evil generation: a surface cleansing, without a change of heart or a surrender to him. Some scholars see it as a warning to Israel; others also read it as a principle for the individual.

For today: it is not enough to leave bad habits behind or to tidy up one's life on the outside. The heart must be filled with Christ, his Word, prayer, and fellowship with other believers.
exp.11:45:
This verse tells us that Jesus was still speaking to the crowd when his mother and his brothers arrived. They stayed outside because they wanted to speak with him.

The account follows Jesus' harsh words against a generation that rejected him. Matthew is the one who tells the story. Jesus' "brothers" are mentioned several times in the gospels; some Christians understand them as children of Mary, others as close relatives. The Bible does not explain their reasons for seeking him here. The scene sets up the teaching that comes next about Jesus' true family.

For today: even the most cherished relationships must come after listening to God. Ask yourself whether you are attentive to his voice, and willing to follow him, even when other things draw your attention.
exp.11:46:
Someone in the crowd tells Jesus that his mother and his brothers are outside and want to speak with him. "Brothers" here refers to Jesus' close relatives. Some believe they were children of Mary and Joseph; others, that they were cousins or children of Joseph from an earlier marriage. The Bible does not make this clear in this passage.

The one speaking is a man from the crowd. Jesus was teaching and had just given a warning about this evil generation. His family arrives, perhaps out of concern for him, and wants to talk with him. Jesus uses the moment to teach that those who do the will of the Father form his true spiritual family.

Loving one's family is good, but God invites us into a larger family: that of those who obey him. This week, look for a concrete way to serve or encourage a brother or sister in your church.
exp.11:48:
He stretches out his hand toward his disciples and says, "Look, here are my mother and my brothers." Earlier, someone had told him that his mother and his brothers were waiting outside. With this gesture, Jesus answers that question by pointing to those who were following him.

Jesus is teaching the crowd, and his relatives arrive wanting to speak with him. He does not look down on his family; the Gospels do not describe it that way. Rather, he teaches that true closeness to him does not depend only on blood. He explains this in the next verse: whoever does the will of the heavenly Father is part of his family.

Today, this passage invites us to see other believers as true family. We can reach out to someone in the church who is alone, offer friendship, pray with that person, and help with whatever they need.
exp.12:1:
Many people gathered around Jesus. So he got into a boat and sat down, while the whole crowd stood on the shore. The word "gathered" in the verse above matches the idea of coming close, and the boat here is a fishing boat, and the shore is the edge of the lake.

It is the same day on which Jesus left a house and sat down by the Sea of Galilee. Matthew reports what Jesus did, not a speech of his. The boat served so that everyone could see him and hear him well. Right away he spoke to them in parables, beginning with the one about the sower.

For today: Jesus made himself accessible, and the people came eager to listen. We can set aside a specific time to draw near to him through his Word, with attention and without rushing, ready to truly listen.
exp.12:3:
Here Jesus tells of a sower scattering seed, and that some of it fell by the way side, that is, on the edge of the path, where the ground was hard and trampled. "Seed" here is the word for seed. Since it could not get into the soil, the birds came and ate it.

Jesus is sitting in a boat by the lake, and a great crowd listens to him from the shore. He teaches them in parables, simple stories with a deeper message. Later in this same chapter, He himself explains that this seed stands for the word of the kingdom, and that the path speaks of a heart that does not understand it, and the evil one snatches it away.

For today: when you hear the Word of God, do not let it pass you by. Stop, think about it, and ask God for a soft and attentive heart.
exp.12:10:
Jesus answers the disciples' question. He tells them that it has been given to them by God, that is, they have been granted the privilege of knowing the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, the truths of God that had previously been hidden. But to others, it has not been given.

Jesus is teaching the crowds in parables, and the disciples come to ask him why he does it this way. His answer shows that not everyone receives the truth in the same way. Christians have understood this in different ways: some emphasize God's action in revealing, while others also emphasize the hardness of heart of those who do not want to hear.

For today: approach the Bible with humility and ask God to open your understanding. Understanding his Word is a gift received with a willing heart.
exp.12:12:
Jesus explains why he teaches in parables. He says that many people look and listen, but they do not grasp what truly matters. They see the miracles and hear his words, but they do not understand their meaning. Divine truths that are known only when God reveals them are the things the verse calls secrets of the kingdom.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, who had asked him why he used parables. There were many people around, and many of them had hard hearts. The parables revealed the truth to those who sought it sincerely, and to others they showed their stubbornness. Scholars debate how much of this was judgment and how much was an invitation to seek more; the text shows both sides.

Today we can approach the Bible with humility and a hunger to learn. Before reading, ask God to open your eyes and your heart. Then ask what it teaches you and what you should obey.
exp.12:13:
Jesus says that what the prophet Isaiah foretold is fulfilled in the people of his time. They hear with their ears, but do not understand; they look with their eyes, but do not truly perceive the real meaning of what they see. Seeing, in this case, means truly seeing, really grasping what is in front of them.

Jesus speaks to the crowds and explains why he teaches in parables. He quotes Isaiah 6:9-10, where the people had hardened their hearts. Many heard Jesus, but did not want to change. The parables revealed the truth to those who had open hearts, and hid it from those who had already decided not to believe. Interpreters explain in various ways how the people's hardness and God's action are related.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Bible; it must be received with humility. Before reading it, ask God for a willing heart, and then obey one concrete thing you have understood.
exp.12:14:
Jesus says that the heart of this people has grown hard, like something fattened and unfeeling. They hear with difficulty, and they have shut their eyes. The purpose is that they should not see, nor hear, nor understand with their heart, nor turn back to be healed.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd and to his disciples, explaining why he teaches in parables. He quotes Isaiah 6, where the people were already resisting God. Many listened without wanting to change. Scholars explain in different ways whether God hardens or only confirms a hardness that already existed, but the text shows that the hardness was real and willful.

Today, ask God for a soft heart before you read his Word. Do not be satisfied with just hearing it: ask yourself what change he is asking of you, and obey it with humility.
exp.12:17:
Jesus invites his disciples to listen closely to the verse of the parable of the sower. The verse below is what the verse is introducing, so the reader can see how the teaching is being framed.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the parable to the crowds. They had asked him why he taught in parables. He has just told them that they are blessed because they see and hear what many prophets and righteous people longed to know. Now he gives them the verse of what happens when the word of the kingdom is sown in different hearts.

Today we can ask ourselves how we are listening to the Word of God. Truly hearing means paying attention, thinking, and obeying. Before reading the Bible, we can pray, asking for an attentive and willing heart.
exp.12:18:
Jesus says that when someone hears the message of God's kingdom and does not understand it, the wicked one comes and snatches away what had been sown in their heart. That person is like the seed that falls beside the path, on hard ground where it cannot get in.

Jesus is explaining the parable of the sower to his disciples. Shortly before, he told them they were blessed to see and hear what many prophets and righteous people longed for. He teaches them that merely hearing is not enough; the way the word is received matters greatly.

Today we can listen to the Bible with attention, pray asking for understanding, and ask about what we do not grasp. A soft and willing heart helps the word take root and not be lost.
exp.12:21:
Jesus explains that the seed sown among thorns represents the one who hears the word of God, but who lets the care of this world (the worries of present life) and the deceitfulness of riches (the false idea that money gives security and happiness) choke it. In this way the word is left without fruit, that is, unfruitful.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, in private, after telling the parable of the sower to the crowd. He makes clear to them why the same seed produces different results: it depends on the heart that receives it. Earlier he spoke of the stony ground; later he will speak of the good soil.

Today we can ask ourselves what thorns grow in our lives: debts, hurry, ambition, or anxiety. A practical help is to set aside a moment each day to read the Bible without distractions and to remove, little by little, whatever steals our time and our peace.
exp.12:23:
Jesus tells another story to teach what the kingdom of heaven is like. He says it is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. "Sowed" means he scattered seed on the ground to plant it, and "parable" is a simple comparison taken from everyday life.

Jesus is speaking to the crowds beside the Sea of Galilee. Shortly before, he explained the parable of the sower, where the seed falls on different kinds of ground. Now he changes the focus: he no longer looks at the ground, but at what happens in the field when someone plants something good. The verses that follow show that an enemy will appear.

For today: God plants good things in your life and in your community. Do not be discouraged if you also see bad things nearby. Keep trusting in Him, take care of the good He has planted, and remember that He knows how and when to act.
exp.12:29:
Jesus says that the wheat and the tares must grow together until the harvest. When that time comes, the owner will tell the reapers to gather the tares first, bind them in bundles and burn them, and to store the wheat in his barn, which is a granary or storehouse.

Jesus is telling the parable of the wheat and the tares to the crowds. An enemy sowed bad seed in the field, and the servants wanted to pull it up right away. The owner stops them so the wheat is not harmed. Later Jesus explains that the harvest represents the end of the age (Matthew 13:39).

Today it reminds us that it is not our place to judge who belongs to God and who does not. We can live patiently among people who are different from us, trusting that God will do justice in his own time.
exp.12:30:
Jesus tells another parable, that is, a simple story meant to teach a truth. He says that the kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man takes and sows in his field.

Jesus is speaking to the crowds, after telling the parable of the wheat and the weeds. There he explained that God lets everything grow until the final time. Now he uses a very small seed to show how the kingdom of God begins: without much noise, but with a sure growth, as the following verse says.

For today: do not despise small beginnings. A prayer, an act of kindness, or a word of faith planted today can grow more than you imagine, even if you cannot see it yet.
exp.12:32:
Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to yeast, which is a small amount of fermented dough. A woman takes it and mixes it into three measures of flour, which is a large quantity, enough to feed many people. Over time, the whole batch of dough rises and swells.

Jesus speaks to the crowds, right after the parable of the mustard seed. Both show a small beginning that grows into something large. Some see here a quiet growth from within; others point out that yeast sometimes symbolizes something negative in the Bible, so the exact meaning is debated. What is clear is the contrast between the small and the great.

God often works quietly and patiently. Do not be discouraged if your faith, your prayer, or your good example seem small; trust that God can make them grow over time.
exp.12:36:
Jesus answers his disciples and explains that the one who sows the good seed is "the Son of man." That expression was a title Jesus used for himself. The word "seed" in the verse above is the same as the word "seed" in the sentence about sowing, so Jesus is saying that he is the one who sows what is good in the world.

The disciples had asked him to explain the parable of the tares, a bad weed that grows among the wheat. Jesus had spoken to the crowds in parables, and now, back at home, he makes the meaning clear to his followers. Here the verse begins, and the first detail is that the sower is himself.

For today: if Jesus is the one who sows what is good, we do not have to carry the whole weight of producing fruit on our own. We can ask him to let his word grow in us, and share it with others trusting that he makes it sprout.
exp.12:37:
Jesus explains that the field where the seed is sown is the whole world. The good seed represents the children of the kingdom, that is, those who belong to God and follow him. The tares, a weed that looks like wheat, represent the children of the wicked one, those who belong to the evil one.

Jesus speaks privately with his disciples, at home, after telling the parable to the crowd. They did not understand it and asked him to explain it. He makes it clear that people who are very different live side by side in this world, and that the final judgment is not ours to make.

For today: do not be discouraged because believers and unbelievers live together. Live as good seed, with love and truth, and leave the judgment of each person to God.
exp.12:38:
Jesus explains three parts of his parable here. The enemy who sowed the weeds is the devil. The harvest, or reaping, is the end of the world, that is, the close of this age. And the reapers, those who gather the harvest, are the angels.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in private, after telling the parable of the wheat and the weeds to the crowd. They had not understood it, so they asked him for an explanation. He shows them that the children of the kingdom and the children of the evil one live side by side in the world, and that the final separation is not made by people but by God through his angels.

For today: we do not need to judge or pull anyone out from among us. We can live with patience, guarding our own hearts, and trust that God will do justice in his time.
exp.12:40:
Jesus says that the Son of Man, that is, he himself, will send his angels at the end of the age. They will gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, meaning whatever causes others to stumble into sin, and also those who practice iniquity.

Jesus is explaining to his disciples the parable of the wheat and the tares. The wheat represents the children of the kingdom, and the tares represent the children of the wicked one. Now he looks ahead to the end: God himself will carry out the separation, not us. Until then, both grow together.

For today: it is not your place to judge or to pull anyone out of the kingdom. With patience, live in what is good, ask God to examine your own heart, and trust that he will do justice in his time.
exp.12:43:
The kingdom of heaven, he says, is like a treasure hidden in a field. A man finds it and hides it again. Full of joy, he sells everything he has and buys that field so that he can keep the treasure.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, at home, after telling several parables to the crowd. With this image he teaches that the kingdom of God has enormous value. Some scholars think the treasure speaks of Christ and his kingdom, and that the man represents the one who discovers it. Others see the man as Jesus himself. Both readings are debated.

For today: ask yourself what place God holds in your priorities. Following Jesus is not a sad burden but a discovery that brings joy. Today, let that joy lead you to let go of something that gets in the way of following him more closely.
exp.12:44:
Jesus says that the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant, a man who goes about seeking fine pearls. A merchant is someone who buys and sells goods. This man is not wandering by chance: he searches eagerly for things of great value.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in a series of parables about the kingdom. Just before, he told the parable of the treasure hidden in a field, where a man sells everything out of joy. This parable adds another view: the kingdom has enormous worth. Some find it without looking for it, and others seek it with determination. Interpreters explain in various ways who the merchant is, but the central message is the supreme value of the kingdom.

Today we can ask ourselves: what do I desire most eagerly? Let us ask God for a heart that values his kingdom above everything else.
exp.12:46:
Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to a fishing net that is cast into the sea and gathers fish of every kind.

Jesus is speaking in parables to his disciples, after the parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl. This parable closes the series. The verses that follow explain that, at the end, the angels will separate the wicked from the righteous. Jesus wants to show that the kingdom invites everyone, but there will be a judgment at the end.

For today: the gospel is announced to all, and in the church there may be people who are very different from one another. Instead of hurrying to judge others, we can examine our own hearts and live with sincerity, trusting that God will make the separation in his time.
exp.12:50:
Jesus asks his disciples whether they have understood everything he has just taught in the parables.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, apart from the crowds. He has just told them parables about the kingdom of heaven: the seed, the weeds, the treasure, the pearl, and the net. He even explained the final judgment to them. That is why he asks whether they truly grasped the message. Scholars debate how deep their understanding really was, since other passages show that they still had a great deal to learn.

Understanding the Word is not only hearing it, but receiving it and living it. You can honestly ask yourself: what have I understood of what God has shown me, and how am I going to put it into practice this week?
exp.12:53:
This verse tells that Jesus returned to Nazareth, the town where he grew up, and taught in the synagogue, the place where the Jews gathered. The people were astonished, that is, greatly amazed, and asked where this man got such wisdom and such mighty works, meaning these miracles.

The narrator is Matthew, and then the people of his hometown speak. Jesus had just told parables. His neighbors had known him since childhood, and so it was hard for them to accept that someone so familiar had such authority. Their amazement, as becomes clear afterward, ended in stumbling and lack of faith.

For today: do not confine God to what you already know. Sometimes He works through ordinary people or situations. Ask Him for a humble and open heart, so that you can recognize His voice even when it comes in a simple or unexpected way.
exp.13:2:
This verse explains why John the Baptist was in prison. Herod Antipas, the ruler of the region, had arrested him, tied him up, and put him in jail. The reason was Herodias, who had been the wife of his brother Philip and was now living with Herod.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Herod becomes frightened when he hears about Jesus and thinks John has risen from the dead. Matthew looks back to the past to explain that fear: John had spoken the truth about that marriage, and this led him to prison. Herod's conscience was not at peace.

For today: speaking the truth in love can cost a great deal, but it is still the right thing to do. Let us ask God for courage and humility to speak honestly, without seeking to please everyone, and also for ears willing to hear correction.
exp.13:5:
Matthew tells us that while Herod was celebrating his birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced before all the guests, and Herod was very pleased with her.

Here Matthew speaks as the narrator. He explains how John the Baptist ended up dead. John had told Herod that it was not right for him to live with Herodias, his brother's wife. Herod wanted to kill him, but he feared the people. This feast sets the stage for a hasty promise that will change everything.

For today: a decision made in a moment of pleasure, pride or pressure can cause enormous harm. Before promising something, it is wise to stop, think, and ask God for wisdom to do what is right, even when others are watching us.
exp.13:6:
This verse says that Herod made a solemn promise to Herodias's daughter. He swore to her, that is, he called God as witness, that he would give her anything she asked for. The words "asked" and "promised" are clear; "with an oath" means that it was a very serious promise.

Matthew tells this to explain how John the Baptist died. Herod Antipas had him imprisoned because John had told him it was not right for him to live with Herodias, the wife of his brother. Herod was carried away by the moment, during his birthday feast, and spoke without thinking. His promise, made lightly, ended up being used by Herodias to get what she wanted.

For today: let us think carefully before promising something, especially in moments of emotion or pressure. And if we have already made a bad promise, it is better to admit the mistake than to hurt others out of pride or fear of looking foolish.
exp.13:9:
He sent word and had John beheaded in the prison. This verse says Herod sent an executioner to the prison and ordered that John the Baptist's head be cut off.

Mateo tells this as a memory. Herod Antipas had heard about Jesus and thought he was John risen from the dead. John was in prison because he had rebuked Herod for his marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife. During a feast, Herodias's daughter pleased the king, and at her mother's urging she asked for John's head. Herod gave in because of his oath and because he did not want to look bad in front of his guests.

For today: let us not allow pride or fear of what others think to lead us into doing wrong. And if telling the truth costs us, let us remember that God sees and values faithfulness.
exp.13:10:
This verse tells how Herod's order ended. John the Baptist's head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, the daughter of Herodias, and she carried it to her mother.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Herod had made a vow in front of his guests, and the girl, urged on by her mother, asked for John's head. John had rebuked Herod for his marriage to Herodias. Matthew shows how pride, resentment, and fear of looking foolish can lead to a terrible injustice.

For today: let us think before we promise something, and not let the pressure of others silence our conscience. And when following the truth costs us dearly, let us remember that God sees and cares for his own, just as Jesus saw the pain of this moment.
exp.13:12:
When Jesus heard about it, the verse says, he left by boat for a quiet place where no people lived. But the crowds found out and followed him on foot from their towns.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just received the news that John the Baptist had been executed by Herod. Many readers understand that Jesus was looking for a time alone to be with God and carry his grief, although the text does not say this in so many words.

For today: when you suffer a loss, it is good to step away for a while to pray and rest. And if God interrupts you to serve others, ask him to give you compassion, as Jesus had.
exp.13:13:
He says that Jesus went out of the boat and found a large crowd waiting for him. When he saw them, he felt compassion, that is, a deep sorrow for the people and a desire to help them. For this reason he healed the sick who were among them. Some older words: the word "saw" is "saw", "crowd" means a large group of people, and "sick" are those who were unwell.

Here the narrator, Matthew, speaks. Jesus had just learned that John the Baptist had been killed, and he withdrew to a lonely place, probably to be alone. But the people followed him on foot. Instead of being annoyed at losing his rest, Jesus attended to them. This prepares the account that follows, when he feeds the crowd.

For today: when someone interrupts us in a moment of tiredness or sadness, we can ask God for a compassionate heart like Jesus'. Sometimes helping others, with a visit, a phone call, or a little time spent paying attention, is a way of following him.
exp.13:14:
The disciples come to Jesus as evening falls and tell him that the place is deserted and that it is already late. They ask him to send the crowd away so that they can go to the villages and buy food for themselves.

The disciples speak. A large crowd had followed Jesus on foot, and he had healed the sick with compassion. The disciples see a practical problem: there is no food or shops nearby. Their suggestion seems sensible, but Jesus will answer differently. Through this, he shows them that he wanted to act through them.

When you see a need that seems greater than your resources, do not dismiss it right away. Bring it to Jesus and ask him what he wants you to do with the little you have. He can use your simple help.
exp.13:20:
This verse says that in that meal about five thousand men ate, not counting the women and children. That means the total crowd was probably much larger. The phrase "about five thousand" indicates an approximate figure.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Jesus has just received the people who followed him to a remote place, and his disciples told him they did not have enough food. Matthew emphasizes the size of the crowd to highlight that Jesus fed everyone with very little: five loaves and two fish. After this, Jesus sends the people away and goes up to pray alone.

For today: whatever little you have, if you give it to God, it can reach more people than you imagine. Offer your time, your gifts, or your resources with confidence.
exp.13:35:
This verse tells that the sick people of Gennesaret asked Jesus for something very simple: to touch only the edge of his cloak. The cloak was the outer garment he wore, and the edge was the hem, where there were often fringes or tassels. Everyone who touched it was made whole. The word "begged" means they asked with persistence and humility.

The one who tells the story is Matthew. Jesus and his disciples had just crossed the lake and arrived at Gennesaret, a region by the Sea of Galilee. The men of the place recognized him, alerted everyone in the area, and brought their sick. We do not know for certain why they asked only to touch his cloak, but it shows their faith and their desire not to trouble him.

For today: come to Jesus with confidence, even when your faith feels small. You do not need perfect words; it is enough to come to Him with humility and bring to Him the needs of others too, as those neighbors did.
exp.14:0:
This verse tells us that some scribes and Pharisees came from Jerusalem to where Jesus was. The scribes were experts in the Law of Moses who taught it, and the Pharisees were a religious group that was very careful about the rules.

The context is that Jesus was already well known for his teaching and his miracles. These leaders came from the most important religious city, probably to examine him or to correct him. Right away they question him about the tradition of the elders, rules handed down from generation to generation that were not commandments written by God. Jesus will answer them firmly.

For today: let us consider whether we give more importance to our religious customs than to obeying God with a sincere heart. Traditions can help, but they must never take the place of the Word of God.
exp.14:4:
Jesus says that the Pharisees and the teachers of the law were teaching something contrary to God's law. If someone told his father or mother, "What you might have gained from me is already a gift dedicated to God," that person was free from helping them.

Jesus answers scribes and Pharisees who came from Jerusalem and criticized him because his disciples did not follow the traditions of the elders. He shows them that their tradition set aside the command to honor one's parents, which included material support. Scholars explain in several ways how exactly that practice worked, but Jesus' accusation is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use religious excuses, such as service, work, or customs, to avoid caring for our family. Honoring God includes lovingly helping those who raised us.
exp.14:11:
Then his disciples came and told him that the Pharisees were upset and felt offended by what he had just said. The disciples are the ones speaking. Jesus had taught the crowd that what defiles a person is not the food that goes into the mouth, but what comes out of the heart. This clashed with the Pharisees' traditions about washing hands and food. The disciples seem worried about how these religious leaders would react.

Today, telling the truth with love can make some people uncomfortable, even very religious people. We should not seek to offend anyone, but neither should we stay silent about what God teaches only because we fear the reaction. Let us ask God for wisdom and humility to speak clearly and to listen with a heart ready to change.
exp.14:16:
Jesus asks whether they still do not understand something simple: food enters through the mouth, passes into the stomach, and then leaves the body.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, and Peter asked him to explain the earlier parable. The Pharisees were criticizing the disciples for eating without washing their hands according to tradition. Jesus teaches that what makes us unclean before God is not the food, but what is in the heart, from which come evil words and actions.

For today: instead of worrying only about appearances or religious customs, let us ask God to cleanse our hearts. Before we speak or act, we can ask ourselves: what is really inside me?
exp.14:18:
Jesus says that from inside a person, from the heart, come harmful things: evil thoughts, murders, adultery, sexual relations outside of marriage, thefts, lies told against others (false witness), and words that insult God (blasphemies). In the Bible, the heart speaks of the center of a person: their thoughts, desires, and decisions.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd. The Pharisees and scribes had criticized him because his disciples ate without washing their hands according to tradition. Jesus teaches that what makes a person unclean before God is not the food, but what comes out from within.

Today, instead of caring only about appearances, we can ask God to heal our heart. When you notice anger, envy, or lying, do not hide them: confess them and ask for help to change from the inside.
exp.14:19:
Jesus ends his teaching by saying that what truly makes us unclean is the evil that comes out of the heart: harmful thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, lies, and offenses against God. By contrast, eating without performing the ceremonial handwashing does not make us unclean before God. "Defile" here means making someone impure or unworthy before God.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples and with some Pharisees and scribes, who criticized him because his followers did not keep the tradition of washing their hands before eating. That custom came from the elders, not from a command of the law of Moses. Jesus shows them that what matters is the heart, not only the outward things.

We can be more concerned about the condition of our heart than about outward religious appearance. Today you can ask God to cleanse you within and to help you take care of your thoughts and words.
exp.14:20:
This verse says that Jesus left the place where he was and went toward the region of Tyre and Sidon, two ancient cities by the Mediterranean Sea.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Jesus had just argued with the Pharisees about what truly defiles a person: it is not unwashed hands, but what comes out of the heart. Afterward he withdraws from that conflict and enters an area with a mostly non-Jewish population. Some believe he went there to rest; the text does not explain this. There he will meet the Canaanite woman.

For today: God can lead you to unexpected places to meet people who are seeking him. Stay alert and willing to listen, and do not let prejudice close your heart.
exp.14:30:
This verse tells how the crowd was amazed at what they saw happening: the mute were speaking, those with a limb injured or unable to be used, such as a hand, were made whole, the lame walked, and the blind could see. As a result, everyone praised the God of Israel.

Here it is not Jesus who speaks, but the narrator, Matthew, who describes the reaction of the crowd. Jesus was beside the Sea of Galilee, on a mountain, and the people brought their sick and laid them at his feet. He healed them. Then his compassion is seen, for soon he is concerned because the people have nothing to eat.

When we see God's goodness at work, we can respond with wonder and gratitude. Today we can pause to give glory to him for what he does in our lives and in the lives of others, and also bring our sick and our burdens to him with confidence.
exp.14:31:
Jesus gathers his disciples and tells them he feels compassion for the crowd. They have been with him for three days and now have no food left. He does not want to send them away without eating, because they might grow weak and collapse from exhaustion on the road.

He speaks right after healing many lame, blind, mute, and sick people, and the crowd praised the God of Israel. Now Jesus notices a simpler need: hunger. The disciples answer with doubt, since they are in a deserted place. Some see here a scene similar to the first feeding of the bread, although this is a different occasion.

Jesus cares about our daily needs, not only our spiritual ones. We can bring him with confidence whatever worries us, and also open our eyes to help someone beside us who is hungry or tired.
exp.14:32:
The disciples ask Jesus where they could get so much bread, in an empty place, to feed such a great crowd. To feed a crowd until they are satisfied and full is what the verse means by having enough bread, and the crowd here is simply the large group of people.

Jesus had just healed many sick people, and the crowd had been with him for three days. He felt compassion and did not want to send them away hungry. The disciples answer by thinking only about what they lacked. It is striking that they had already seen Jesus heal many people; some think that this is why their question shows little faith, although the text does not say so directly.

When God asks us to help someone, it is easy to look only at what we do not have. We can instead place in his hands the little that we do have, like the seven loaves, and trust that he knows what to do with it.
exp.14:33:
Jesus asks his disciples how many loaves they have. They answer seven, and a few little fish. The word "have" here is simply the ordinary word for possessing something. It is a simple question, but Jesus asks it so that they can see clearly how little there is.

It is Jesus who speaks, and he feels compassion for a crowd that has been with him for three days in a remote place with no food. The disciples had just said there was no way to feed so many people. Jesus does not ignore the problem; he starts with what they do have, even though it seems very little. Then he gives thanks and distributes the food.

For today: when a need seems too great, do not just stand there looking at what is missing. Place in Jesus' hands the little you have, with gratitude, and trust that he can use it.
exp.14:35:
This verse tells how Jesus took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks to God, broke them, and handed them to his disciples. The disciples, in turn, distributed them to the crowd.

Jesus is with a large crowd that had been with him for three days, listening and seeking healing. He feels compassion because they have nothing to eat, and he does not want to send them away hungry. The disciples had very little, but Jesus uses what they have. It is a similar but distinct account to that of the five thousand.

For today: whatever little you have, whether time, talent, or money, offer it to God with gratitude. He can use it to bless others, and you have a part in the chain that distributes it.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that the Pharisees and the Sadducees came to Jesus to test him, that is, to put him to the test with bad intentions. They asked him for a sign from heaven, meaning a spectacular miracle that would come directly from God and prove that he was the Messiah.

The Pharisees and the Sadducees were religious groups that almost always disagreed with each other, but here they join together against Jesus. They had already seen his miracles, so they were not seeking to understand, but to trap him. In the verses that follow, Jesus answers that they know how to read the weather, but they do not recognize what God is doing in their time.

For today: we can ask God with a sincere heart, not to test him. If he has already shown us his work and his Word, the question is whether we are willing to believe and obey.
exp.15:3:
Jesus says that the people of that time, who were unfaithful to God, ask for a miraculous sign in order to believe. But they will not receive any, except the sign of the prophet Jonas. "Adulterous" means unfaithful to God, like someone who breaks a covenant of love. Then Jesus left them and went away.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees and Sadducees, who wanted to test him by asking for a sign from heaven. He had already performed many miracles, so they had no lack of evidence, but rather a heart unwilling to believe. In Matthew 12:40 Jesus connects the sign of Jonas with his death and resurrection. Here he does not explain it, but many understand it that way.

For today: instead of demanding extra proof from God, look at what he has already shown you, above all in Jesus, and respond with faith and obedience.
exp.15:4:
They say the disciples crossed to the other side of the Sea of Galilee and realized they had not brought any bread. It is a simple detail: a forgetting.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Jesus had just left the Pharisees and Sadducees, who were asking him for a sign from heaven. This forgotten bread sets the scene for what follows: Jesus warns them about the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the disciples think he is talking about food. Their minds seem fixed on the material, while Jesus was speaking of a teaching that spreads like yeast through dough.

For today: sometimes we worry so much about what we lack that we do not listen to what God wants to teach us. Before you become anxious, pause and ask him: "Lord, what are you trying to tell me in this?"
exp.15:5:
Jesus warns his disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Leaven is what makes bread dough rise; here it is a picture of something small that spreads and changes everything.

Jesus speaks right after these groups asked him for a sign from heaven. The disciples, worried that they have no bread, misunderstand his words. Later the text makes clear that he was referring to their teaching (v. 12): their unbelief and their hypocritical religiosity.

Today we can ask ourselves what ideas or attitudes are creeping little by little into our hearts, such as religious pride or doubt. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and ask God for a humble and trusting heart.
exp.15:9:
Jesus reminds them of another miracle: when he fed four thousand people with seven loaves. He asks them how many baskets they gathered up afterward. The baskets of that miracle were large baskets, the kind that could hold a great deal, and the leftovers filled many of them. The disciples saw this with their own eyes.

Jesus speaks with his disciples in the boat. They are worried because they forgot to bring bread. He warns them about the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and they think he is talking about food. Jesus reminds them that they have already seen how God provides, and so they should not worry about bread. His warning was about false teachings.

For today: when you worry about what you lack, remember how God has cared for you before. And stay alert, because Jesus wants you to guard your heart against ideas that spread like yeast and draw you away from the truth.
exp.15:11:
This verse says that the disciples finally understood what Jesus meant. He was not speaking about bread that is baked, but about the teaching of the Pharisees and the Sadducees. Yeast is what makes dough rise, and here it serves as an image of something small that spreads and changes everything.

Jesus had warned them about yeast, but the disciples thought he was rebuking them for not bringing bread. Then he reminded them how he had multiplied the loaves for thousands of people. With this, he showed them that lack of bread was not the problem. His real warning was against teachings that pull people away from God.

Today we can examine what we hear and believe by comparing it with the Bible. A wrong idea may seem small, but little by little it can bend our faith and the way we live.
exp.15:14:
Jesus asks his disciples a direct question. He wants to know what they themselves think of him, not just what the crowds think. It is a personal question, one that calls for an answer of your own.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples near Caesarea Philippi. Earlier he had asked them what people were saying, and they mentioned John the Baptist, Elijah, and Jeremiah. These were respectful opinions, but they fell short. Now Jesus moves from what others say to what each one believes. Peter answers that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Today this question still stands. It is not enough to repeat what others think or what we learned as children. Take a moment to answer Jesus honestly: who is he to you?
exp.15:18:
Jesus tells Peter that he will give him "the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Binding and loosing were words used for forbidding and permitting, or for declaring something required or free.

Jesus speaks right after Peter confessed that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus responds by giving him a special responsibility. Christians understand this in different ways: some see a particular authority given to Peter, others see it as authority for the whole church that proclaims the gospel. Shortly afterward, Jesus announces his death and resurrection.

For today: each believer can open doors for others by humbly sharing the message of Jesus, never forgetting that the authority comes from him.
exp.15:20:
Jesus begins to explain plainly to his disciples what is going to happen to him. He must go to Jerusalem, suffer greatly at the hands of the elders (the leaders of the people), the chief priests (the principal priests) and the scribes (the teachers of the Law). He will be killed, and on the third day he will rise again. The phrase "he must" means it was necessary, part of God's plan.

Shortly before, Peter had recognized that Jesus is the Christ. Now Jesus, who is the one speaking, reveals what kind of Messiah he will be: one who suffers before being glorified. That is why Peter reacts with objection, since he was expecting something else.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we want a Jesus on our own terms or as he really is. Trusting God sometimes includes accepting that his path goes through sacrifice and self-giving, and that there is hope there too.
exp.15:25:
Jesus asks two questions. The first: what good is it for a person to gain the whole world if they lose their soul? The word "gain" here means to win or obtain. The second: what could someone give in exchange for their soul? The implied answer is that nothing is worth as much. Here "soul" can also be understood as the life or the whole person.

Jesus speaks to his disciples shortly after announcing his death. He teaches them that following him means denying themselves and taking up the cross. Whoever clings to their own life loses it, but whoever gives it up for Christ finds it. This saying explains why that cost is worth paying.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are chasing most strongly: money, success, or approval. These things are not bad in themselves, but they must not take the place of God. Today, put Christ first in one concrete decision.
exp.16:2:
This verse says that, while Jesus was transfigured, Moses and Elijah suddenly appeared and were talking with him.

The account is told by Matthew. Jesus had taken Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and there he showed himself in glory. Moses stands for the Law and Elijah for the prophets, so their presence shows that Jesus is the center of everything God had said before. Matthew does not explain what they were talking about; Luke says they spoke of his departure to Jerusalem. Afterward, the voice from heaven says that Jesus must be listened to.

For today: when you read the Bible, read it looking at Jesus. Before you look only for rules or examples, ask what it teaches you about him, and then pay attention to him.
exp.16:7:
It says that when the disciples lifted up their eyes, they no longer saw Moses or Elijah, nor the cloud, nor the bright glory. They saw only Jesus.

This happens after the transfiguration. Peter, James, and John, on the mountain with Jesus, saw his glory and heard the voice of the Father telling them to listen to his Son. Frightened, they fell to the ground. Jesus touched them and encouraged them to rise without fear. The account does not explain this in words, but many understand that the final focus on Jesus shows that he is the one who should hold the center.

For today: in moments of excitement, fear, or confusion, turn your eyes back to Jesus. Read the Gospels and ask him to be your center, above experiences or ideas.
exp.16:11:
Jesus says that Elijah has already come, but the people did not recognize him. Instead, they did to him whatever they wished. And he announces that the Son of Man will suffer in a similar way at their hands.

Jesus speaks with Peter, James, and John after coming down from the mountain of the transfiguration. They ask him why the scribes taught that Elijah must come first, based on Malachi 4:5. Jesus answers that this Elijah has already come, and the text makes clear that he was referring to John the Baptist, who was rejected and killed. Jesus links the fate of John with his own.

For today: God sometimes acts in ways we do not expect. Let us ask for humility to recognize his work, even when it comes in a simple form or in a different way than we had imagined.
exp.16:12:
This verse says that the disciples understood that Jesus, when speaking of Elijah, was referring to John the Baptist. "Understood" here means that they finally grasped the meaning of his words.

The disciples had just seen Jesus transfigured alongside Moses and Elijah, and they asked him why the teachers of the law said that Elijah had to come first. Jesus explained that Elijah had already come, but they did not recognize him and treated him badly. He was referring to John, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). Jesus added that he too would suffer in the same way.

For today: God sometimes works in ways we do not expect. Let us ask him for attentive eyes and a humble heart to recognize what he does, rather than rejecting it because it does not fit our ideas.
exp.16:20:
Jesus says that "this kind," meaning this class of evil spirit, does not go out except by prayer and fasting. The word "kind" means type or class. Important note: many ancient manuscripts do not include this verse, and several modern translations omit it or place it in a footnote. Even so, a very similar phrase appears in Mark 9:29.

Jesus has just healed a boy whom the disciples could not free. They ask him privately why they failed. Jesus answers that it was because of their little faith, and he teaches that faith, though small, has great power. He then adds this teaching about prayer and fasting.

For today: do not depend on your own strength in difficult problems. Seek God steadily in prayer, and if you can, join it with fasting, to strengthen your trust in him.
exp.16:22:
Jesus announces that they will kill him, but that on the third day he will be raised. "They will kill him" means that they will murder him, and "he will be raised" means that he will come back to life. The disciples were exceedingly sorry, because they heard the part about the death, and it grieved them deeply.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples while they are in Galilee. Shortly before, he healed a boy whom they had not been able to heal. Now he prepares them for what is coming: he will be delivered into the hands of men. The text does not say that they understood the part about the resurrection; their sorrow shows that the news of the death struck them harder. Afterward they arrive at Capernaum, and the temple tax is mentioned.

Jesus does not hide hard things, and he teaches us to look beyond pain. When we go through a loss or a trial, we can bring our sadness to God honestly and remember that suffering does not have the last word. The hope of the risen Christ sustains us.
exp.16:25:
Peter answers that kings collect tax from strangers, that is, from those who are not of the family. Jesus concludes: then the children are free, that is, exempt from paying.

The collectors of the temple tax, which was two drachmas, asked whether Jesus paid it. Peter said yes, and Jesus spoke with him in private. With this comparison he shows that he, as the Son of God, was not obligated to pay for the house of his Father. Even so, in the following verse he decides to pay so as not to cause offense. Some scholars see here a reference to his divine identity; the text does not explain this further.

For today: sometimes we have a right to something and yet can give it up out of love, so as not to be a stumbling block to others. Ask yourself whether there is a situation where giving up your right would help more than insisting on it.
exp.16:26:
Jesus tells Peter to go to the lake, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When he opens its mouth, he will find a coin, a stater, enough to pay the tax for the two of them. The word "offend" in this verse means to cause someone to stumble or to give offense. "Sea" here is the Sea of Galilee.

The collectors of the temple tax had asked whether Jesus paid it. Jesus explains that, as the Son, he was not obligated, since the children of a king do not pay tribute. Even so, he decides to pay it so as not to cause a stumbling block. The miracle shows his authority and his care for Peter.

For today: sometimes we can give way in things that are not essential, even when we have the right to insist, so as not to place obstacles in the path of others. And we can trust that God provides what is needed when we obey.
exp.17:0:
The disciples came to Jesus and asked him a question: who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? The word "greatest" here means the one who is the most important or who holds the highest rank.

The ones speaking are the disciples, and Jesus answers them right away. Matthew does not fully explain why they ask, but it seems they were concerned about position or the importance of each one. Jesus calls a child, places him in the middle of them, and teaches them that they must become humble and trusting, like a child, in order to enter the kingdom.

Today, this scene invites us to examine the heart. It is easy to want recognition, even in church or at work. We can ask God for humility and seek to serve others without comparing ourselves.
exp.17:3:
This verse says that the greatest person in the kingdom of heaven is the one who humbles himself like a child. To humble oneself means to make oneself small, to set aside pride and not seek to be above others. Jesus is not speaking of being naive, but of having a simple attitude, without pretensions of importance.

Jesus speaks with his disciples, who had asked him who was the greatest in the kingdom of heaven (v. 1). They were thinking about ranks and honors. Then Jesus placed a child in the middle of them and turned the question around: greatness is measured by humility, not by power. He then warns that the little ones must be cared for and welcomed.

For today: this week, look for an opportunity to serve someone without anyone noticing or thanking you for it. Ask God for a simple heart, one that does not need applause in order to feel valued.
exp.17:8:
It says that if your eye makes you stumble or leads you into sin, you should pluck it out and throw it away. It is better to enter life with one eye than to be thrown into the fire of hell with both. A cause of stumbling means something that makes you sin. The fire of hell is Gehenna, a picture of the final judgment.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, right after warning against causing little ones to stumble. He uses deliberately exaggerated language, as was common in Jewish teaching, to show that nothing is worth more than life with God. Almost everyone understands that he is not asking for self-mutilation, but for taking seriously the step of cutting off whatever leads us into sin.
