For today: identify one concrete thing that makes you fall, such as certain content online, a friendship, or a habit, and make a firm decision to stay away from it this week. Ask God for the strength to do it.
exp.17:10:
Jesus says that the Son of Man, that is, he himself, came to save what was lost. By "lost" he means people who have turned away from God and cannot come back on their own. His mission is to rescue them.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, who had just asked who was the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. He answers them with care toward the little ones, the humble and the simple. This verse gives the reason: Jesus came for those who go astray, and so no one should look down on them. It should be added that some early manuscripts do not include this verse, although the idea appears in Luke 19:10.

Today we can look with patience on someone who has drifted away from faith or from the church. If Jesus went out to seek them, we too can draw near with kindness, without judging.
exp.17:13:
This verse says that God, our Father who is in heaven, does not want even one of these little ones to perish. "Perish" means to go astray and end up destroyed. The "little ones" refers to the simple and humble disciples, and also to children.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after they asked him who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. He sets a child in the midst of them and warns them not to despise the weak. Then he tells the parable of the lost sheep to show how much each person is worth to God. After that he teaches how to seek a brother who has sinned.

For today: if someone has turned away from the faith or from the church, do not judge them or ignore them. Pray for that person and seek them out with care, because God cares about them.
exp.17:15:
If your brother does not listen to you when you speak with him privately, then go back and take one or two others with you. This way, the matter can be settled by the testimony of two or three witnesses, so that the truth is confirmed and not left to one person's word alone.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples about how to deal with sin within the community. Earlier in this chapter he showed that God does not want even one of the little ones to be lost. So this step is meant to win back your brother, not to shame him. It also recalls the principle from the law of Moses about witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

For today: if someone has wronged you and will not listen to you, do not spread it among everyone. Seek out one or two mature people who love the truth and peace, so they can go with you in humility. Let their goal be to restore the relationship and to care for your brother.
exp.17:16:
Matthew 18:17 says that if a brother who sinned against you does not listen to the witnesses, the matter is taken to the church, that is, the community of believers. If he also refuses to listen to the church, he should be regarded as a gentile and a tax collector. A gentile is someone from outside God's people, and a tax collector was a person looked down on at that time.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and teaches them how to care for relationships within their community. The verse comes from the parable of the lost sheep, so the purpose is to win back the brother, not to punish him. Some understand the phrase to mark a formal separation; others remember that Jesus also sought out tax collectors and gentiles with love.

For today: if someone offends you, speak with them first in private, with humility and a desire for reconciliation. Avoid gossip, and seek help only when it is necessary.
exp.17:23:
He says the king began to settle accounts with his servants, and one man was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. A talent was a unit of weight for precious metals, and ten thousand talents was an enormous sum, almost impossible for an ordinary person to repay.

Jesus tells this parable in answer to Peter, who asked how many times he should forgive his brother. Jesus told him seventy times seven, meaning forgive without keeping count. With this story, Jesus wants to show that God forgives us an immense debt.

For today: before we hold on to an offense someone committed against us, let us remember how much we have received from the grace of God. That helps us forgive with a more humble and generous heart.
exp.17:24:
He says that the servant had no way to pay his enormous debt. So the king commanded that he be sold, along with his wife, his children, and everything he owned, to recover at least part of what was owed.

Jesus tells this parable after Peter asked him how many times he should forgive his brother. The debt of ten thousand talents was an impossible amount to repay, and it shows how great is what God forgives us. The sale of the family reflects the debt laws of that time. The parable does not say that God approves of that practice; it only describes how serious the debt was.

For today: remember how much you have received from God's mercy. That will help you forgive others with humility, even when it costs you.
exp.17:28:
Here the fellow servant, who owed a small sum, falls to his knees before the servant who had just been forgiven. He asks for time, pleading "Have patience with me," and promises to pay everything. A fellow servant is someone who serves alongside you under the same master, and falling down at someone's feet was a sign of humility and urgent pleading.

Jesus tells this parable in answer to Peter, who asked how many times he should forgive his brother. The plea of this man sounds almost exactly like the one the forgiven servant made earlier to his lord, but he does not remember it. A hundred denarii was a real debt, though very small compared with the one that was cancelled.

For today: when someone asks you for forgiveness or patience, remember how much you have received from God. That memory helps you respond with mercy rather than harshness.
exp.17:29:
This verse says that the forgiven servant refused his fellow servant's plea. He did not want to give him time. Instead, he went and had him thrown into prison until he paid what he owed.

Jesus tells this parable in response to Peter, who asked how many times he should forgive a brother. The king in the story had already forgiven this servant an enormous debt. That is why his harshness toward a small debt is so shocking. Jesus wants to show how contradictory it is to receive mercy and not give it.

For today: before holding on to resentment, remember how much you have been forgiven by God. Ask him to soften your heart, and look for a concrete way today to show patience or forgiveness to someone who owes you something, whether money, an apology, or an offense.
exp.17:30:
This verse tells that the other servants saw how the forgiven servant had treated his fellow servant without mercy. They were very sad, and they went to the king to tell him everything. The fellow servants are the ones who worked alongside him, and the king is the lord of the story.

Jesus tells this parable when Peter asks him how many times he must forgive. A king forgave a servant an enormous debt, but that servant would not forgive a small debt. Jesus teaches that whoever has received God's mercy must extend it to others. As for whether the servants did right in reporting it, the text only shows their grief at the injustice.

Today we can remember how much God has forgiven us before refusing forgiveness to someone else. If something hurts us or seems unfair, the best thing is to bring it to God in prayer and ask him for a compassionate heart.
exp.18:9:
The disciples react with surprise to what Jesus has just said about divorce. They think that if marriage is so serious and cannot easily be undone, then it is better not to marry.

Jesus had been answering some Pharisees who wanted to test him about divorce. He led them back to God's original plan: that a man and a woman become one flesh. The disciples, hearing this, feel that the demand is very high. Jesus does not correct them harshly, but explains that not everyone understands this, and speaks of the call to remain single for the sake of the kingdom.

For today: before you marry, or if you are already married, take the commitment seriously. Ask God for the grace to be faithful and to love with constancy.
exp.18:11:
Jesus mentions three kinds of eunuchs, that is, men who have no married life or children: those who were born that way, those whom others made that way, and those who live in voluntary singleness for the kingdom of heaven's sake. He says that whoever is able to receive this should receive it.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after teaching that marriage is a serious and lasting union. They react by saying that then it is better not to marry. He answers that not everyone can receive this teaching, but only those to whom God grants it. Many understand that singleness for the kingdom is a special calling, not a general obligation.

For today: value your situation, whether married or single, as a place where God can use you. No one is less because of their marital status. Ask God how to serve him with what you have.
exp.18:12:
Here, some parents or people close to them bring children to Jesus so that he will put his hands on them and pray for them. It was a common gesture of blessing. The disciples "rebuked" them, that is, scolded them or told them off, probably so as not to bother the Master.

Matthew tells this right after Jesus' teachings about marriage and about those who give up marriage for the kingdom. The one speaking here is the narrator, Matthew. The disciples act according to what they thought was right, but Jesus will correct them immediately. Children at that time had little social importance, and that may explain the disciples' reaction, although the text does not say so exactly.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, without meaning to, we put up barriers that keep others from coming to Jesus, especially children. We can make room for them with patience, prayer, and affection.
exp.18:18:
Jesus continues listing the commandments to the young man who asked him how to enter life. Now he mentions two more: honor your father and your mother, which means respecting them and caring for them, and love your neighbor as yourself. "Neighbor" is the person we have close to us.

Jesus speaks with a rich young man who asks what good he must do to have eternal life. Jesus lists commandments that deal with how we treat others. Then the young man says he has kept them, and Jesus takes him deeper: he shows him that his heart was attached to his riches. Some scholars see here an invitation to examine the heart, not only conduct.

Today we can ask ourselves: how do I treat my parents and those near me? Choose one concrete action this week, such as calling your parents or helping a neighbor, and do it with sincere love, not only out of duty.
exp.18:19:
Here a young man tells Jesus that he has kept all those commandments since his youth. "Young man" is the word used for a young person, and the question that follows, "what do I still lack?", shows that he feels something is still missing.

The speaker is the rich young man, who had asked how to attain eternal life. Jesus cited commandments that concern how we treat our neighbor. Then Jesus asks him to sell what he has, help the poor, and follow him. The young man went away sad, because he had many possessions. In this way we see where his heart was attached.

Today we can honestly ask ourselves: is there something I find hard to let go of in order to follow Jesus? Keeping rules is not enough; God seeks a heart willing to trust in him and to love truly.
exp.18:29:
Matthew 19:30 says that many who now seem to be first, important, or admired will end up last, and that others who seem to be last, humble, or ignored will end up first.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after Peter asked what they would receive for having left everything. Jesus promises a reward to those who give something up for him, but he adds this warning: the reward does not depend on position or human merit. This saying is linked to the parable of the workers in the vineyard, which follows in chapter 20, where God acts with generosity and justice in his own way.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or think yourself superior because of your service or your background. Serve God with humility and gratitude, trusting that he values the heart and rewards with kindness.
exp.19:0:
Jesus says that the kingdom of heaven is like a man who owns a house. Very early in the morning he went out to hire workers to labor in his vineyard. To hire here means to engage workers and agree on their pay. The householder is the head of a household, the owner of the property.

Jesus speaks, and he does so through a parable. It comes after the rich young man went away sad, and after Peter asked what those who have left everything to follow him would receive. With this story, Jesus teaches how God acts with generosity. Many interpreters see here a lesson about grace, although the details are explained in several ways.

Today we can remember that serving God is not a competition. Instead of comparing ourselves with others or claiming merits, we can work with gratitude, trusting that God is good and just.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that the owner of the vineyard came to an agreement with the first workers to pay them a denarius for the day's work, and then sent them into his vineyard. "Agreed" means they reached an understanding. A denarius was a Roman coin, and it is generally understood to have been the normal pay for a day's work.

Jesus tells this parable to explain what the kingdom of heaven is like. It comes right after Peter's question about what those who had left everything to follow Jesus would receive (Matthew 19:27). Here the owner acts with order and fairness: there is a clear arrangement and a known wage. Interpreters explain the different groups of workers in various ways, but all agree that the parable highlights the generosity of God.

For today: serve God with gratitude and not with a spirit of bargaining. He is just and keeps what He promises, so we can trust Him without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.19:2:
He says that the owner of the vineyard went back to the marketplace around nine in the morning, which was the third hour of the Jewish day. There he found other men who were standing idle, that is, without work and without anyone having hired them. The marketplace was the public place where day laborers waited for someone to call them.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples, after speaking with the rich young man and after saying that the first will be last and the last will be first. The owner represents God, who goes out again and again to invite more people into his kingdom. Many understand that the vineyard speaks of serving God.

Today we can remember that God keeps calling, regardless of each person's age or past. If you feel you have wasted time, respond today to his invitation and serve him with gratitude.
exp.19:4:
He says the owner of the vineyard went out again to the square, around noon (the sixth hour) and around three in the afternoon (the ninth hour), and hired workers again in the same way.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. An owner hires workers at different times of the day, and at the end he pays everyone the same. Jesus tells it after speaking with Peter about the disciples' reward, and he teaches that God gives generously and not according to our calculations. Some scholars see it as a lesson about grace; others also highlight humility before God.

God keeps calling and offering people a place in his work, no matter when they arrive. Today, rejoice when God blesses others and do not compare yourself to them.
exp.19:6:
The workers hired at the last hour explain that they were standing idle because no one had hired them. The owner answers them: "Go you also into the vineyard, and you will receive whatever is right." He does not promise an exact amount, but trusts in their fairness.

Jesus tells this parable of a vineyard owner who hires workers at different hours. He speaks of the kingdom of heaven. The eleventh hour is almost at the end of the working day, around five in the afternoon. Interpreters understand it as a teaching about the generous grace of God, who invites everyone and gives more than is expected.

For today: it is never too late to respond to God's call. If you feel you have come late or that you have little to offer, go anyway and trust that he is good and just.
exp.19:7:
In the evening, the owner of the vineyard told his manager to call the workers and pay them their wages. He would pay them beginning with those who came last and ending with those who came first.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. It comes right after he said that many who are first will be last, and the last will be first. The owner represents God, and the way he pays shows that his generosity does not follow our accounting. Some scholars see here a teaching about grace; others also highlight the surprise of those who worked the longest.

Today, this invites us to rejoice when God is generous to others, without comparing ourselves or feeling envy. We can serve him with gratitude, remembering that everything we receive comes from his goodness.
exp.19:8:
This verse says that the workers who started at almost the end of the day, around the eleventh hour (about five in the afternoon), were the first to be paid. Each one received a denarius, which was the normal wage for a full day's work.

Jesus is telling a parable about the kingdom of heaven. The owner of the vineyard represents God. Jesus tells it after speaking with his disciples about rewards, and it shows that God gives with a goodness that goes beyond what we calculate.

For today: instead of comparing your service with that of others or feeling envy, be thankful that God's grace is generous. Rejoice when God blesses someone else, remembering that you too live from his goodness and not from your merits.
exp.19:17:
Jesus says they are on their way to Jerusalem, and that there the Son of man will be handed over to the chief priests and to the teachers of the law. They will condemn him to death.

Jesus speaks privately to his twelve disciples while they travel toward Jerusalem. This is the third time he tells them about his death. He does so to prepare them, because they were still thinking about greatness and about a kingdom that would come right away. Just after this, the mother of James and John asks him for places of honor, which shows that they had not understood well.

Jesus was not caught off guard by suffering; he accepted it with purpose. Today, when we go through trials, we can trust that God works even in difficult moments, and learn to follow Christ with humility, not only looking for comfort or recognition.
exp.19:18:
Jesus says that he will be handed over to the Gentiles, that is, to the non-Jews, meaning the Romans. They will mock him, flog him, and crucify him. "Mock" means to make fun of someone with contempt. But on the third day he will rise again.

Jesus speaks privately with his twelve disciples as they travel on the road to Jerusalem. This is the third time in this gospel that he announces his death. He speaks to them plainly so that they will understand what is coming. Yet right after this, the mother of James and John asks him for places of honor, which shows that they still did not grasp the road of suffering he was going to walk.

For today: Jesus chose the cross out of love, without hiding its cost. If we want to follow him, let us ask him for a humble heart that seeks to serve rather than to be recognized, trusting that God has the last word.
exp.19:22:
Jesus tells James and John that they will indeed drink from his cup, meaning they will share his suffering, and that they will be baptized with his same baptism, meaning they will be plunged into pain and trial. But the places at his right and left hand are not his to hand out; they belong to those for whom the Father has already prepared them.

Jesus speaks this on the way to Jerusalem, where he will suffer and die. The mother of the brothers asked him for the places of honor in his kingdom. They answered that they were able, without yet understanding the cost. Afterward, the other ten disciples became angry, and Jesus taught that leadership in his kingdom means serving.

For today: before wanting recognition or an important place, ask yourself whether you are willing to serve and to remain faithful even when it costs you. Leave the rewards in God's hands and devote yourself to following Jesus with humility.
exp.19:29:
This verse says that two blind men were sitting by the roadside. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they began to cry out. They called him "Lord" and "Son of David," and they asked him to have mercy on them, which means compassion and help they did not deserve.

Matthew tells this as Jesus was leaving Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, followed by a crowd. Just before this, Jesus had said that he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. "Son of David" was a title for the promised Messiah, so these men were recognizing him as the King sent by God, even though they could not see him.

For today: when you feel you cannot manage alone, do not wait until you have the perfect words. Cry out to Jesus with sincerity and trust, even if others do not understand. He listens to those in need.
exp.19:32:
The two blind men answer Jesus's question with a clear and direct request. They say "Lord," acknowledging his authority, and ask that their eyes be opened, that is, that they may see. They do not ask for money or anything else, but for what they truly need.

The two blind men were sitting along the road when Jesus passed by, on his way to Jerusalem. The crowd told them to be quiet, but they cried out all the more loudly. Jesus stopped, called them, and asked what they wanted. Their answer shows simple faith and hope that Jesus could heal them.

For today: Jesus invites us to tell him honestly what we need, without pretense or shame. Speak with him about your real need, even when others tell you it is not worth the trouble, and trust in his compassion.
exp.19:33:
This verse tells how Jesus felt compassion for two blind men and touched their eyes. At once they could see, and instead of going off on their own way, they began to follow him. The word "compassion" here means a deep kind of pity that moves a person to act.

The one telling the story is Matthew. The two blind men were sitting by the road and had shouted for help, even though the crowd tried to quiet them. Jesus stopped, called them over, and asked what they wanted. They answered plainly: they wanted their eyes to be opened. This happens while Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem.

Jesus stops at our needs and listens to us with compassion. We can speak to him honestly, as they did, telling him what we truly need. And when we receive his help, a natural response is to follow him with thankfulness, walking with him each day.
exp.20:4:
This verse says that the people of Jerusalem, called "daughter of Zion," should know that their King is coming to them. He does not come with weapons or pride, but meek, that is, humble and without violence. He rides on a female donkey and on a colt, the young of a beast of burden.

Matthew explains why Jesus asked for the animals. He quotes the prophet Zechariah (9:9), with some words from Isaiah 62:11 at the beginning. Jesus enters Jerusalem a few days before his death, and Matthew wants to show that Jesus is the promised King. Some think he sat on the colt, and others that the cloaks covered both animals; the text does not fully clarify this.

Jesus shows that his greatness is lived out with humility. Today we can follow him by treating others with gentleness, without imposing ourselves or seeking applause, and trusting that his way is the right one.
exp.20:6:
What it says: The disciples brought Jesus a female donkey and her young, a little donkey. They put their cloaks, that is, their capes or outer garments, on the animals, and Jesus sat on top. The verse says "on them," and it can be understood in several ways as to whether Jesus rode one or both; many believe it refers to the cloaks.

Context: Matthew, the narrator, tells of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. The disciples obeyed his command. Matthew explains that this fulfills the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9, where the King comes gentle. Jesus presents himself as King, but not with a warhorse, rather with humility.

For today: Jesus shows that true greatness is lived with gentleness and service. Today we can ask ourselves where we seek to assert ourselves, and ask God to teach us to obey and serve with humility, as the disciples did and as Jesus himself did.
exp.20:9:
This verse says that when Jesus entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and filled with commotion. The people asked, "Who is this?" The word for "stirred" here means there was great movement, unrest, and excitement. "Jerusalem" is the same city name you see in the verse.

The one speaking here is the writer, Matthew, and then the people of the city. Jesus was riding on an animal, and the crowd was welcoming him as the son of David, a title pointing to the promised king. The people of Jerusalem did not know him well, which is why they ask. The crowd's answer is that Jesus is the prophet from Nazareth. That is true, but it does not say everything Matthew wants to show about him.

Today there are also many opinions about Jesus. Let us ask this question honestly: who is he to me? Let us not settle for what others say; let us read the Gospels and come to know him personally.
exp.20:11:
Jesus came to the temple in Jerusalem and drove out all who were selling and buying there. He overturned the tables of the money changers, that is, those who exchanged money, and also the seats of those who sold doves. The doves were the offerings of the poor.

Jesus had just entered Jerusalem, and the city was in a great stir, asking who he was. Here he acts with authority in the house of God. Shortly afterward he explains his action by quoting the Scriptures: the temple was meant to be a house of prayer, but they had turned it into a place of unfair business. Interpreters explain in various ways what troubled him most: the abuse, the trade itself, or the hindrance to worship.

Today we can ask what things have taken the place of prayer and sincerity before God. Ask him to cleanse your heart of everything that gets in the way of your closeness to him.
exp.20:18:
Jesus is on his way to the city and he is hungry. He sees a fig tree beside the road, goes up to it, and finds no fruit, only leaves. Then he tells it that it will never bear fruit again, and the tree dries up at once.

Jesus speaks to his disciples during the last days before the cross, in Jerusalem. A fig tree with leaves gave the impression that it had fruit, but it was empty. Many believe it is a sign about religious appearance without fruit, though others stress the lesson about faith. Jesus himself goes on to speak about faith and prayer.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith has only leaves or also the fruit of love, honesty, and obedience. Let us ask God that our lives reflect what we say we believe, and let us trust him with a sincere faith.
exp.20:22:
Jesus arrives at the temple, and while he is teaching, the chief priests and the elders of the people approach him. They ask him by what authority he does these things and who gave him that authority. The chief priests were the leading priests, and the elders were respected leaders of the community.

A day earlier, Jesus had entered Jerusalem with a large crowd and had driven the merchants out of the temple. Now the religious leaders, who felt they were the rightful owners of that place, challenge him. They were probably trying to trap him or discredit him. Jesus answers with a question about John the Baptist, and in doing so he reveals what was really in their hearts.

For today: We can ask ourselves whether we seek the truth sincerely or only defend our own position. God asks us for a humble heart, willing to recognize his voice even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.20:26:
They answered Jesus, saying they did not know, when he asked them about the baptism of John. Then Jesus said that he would not tell them by what authority he did these things.

Jesus was in the temple, and the religious leaders asked him who had given him authority. He answered them with a question about John the Baptist. They calculated what would be best for them to say, not what was true. They feared looking bad before Jesus or the people, so they said they did not know. Their answer showed that they were not sincerely seeking the truth.

Before you speak, ask yourself: "Am I going to say what is true or what suits me?" God values humble honesty more than an answer that protects our image.
exp.20:28:
This verse says that the first son, when his father asked him to work in the vineyard, answered with a flat refusal. But afterward he changed his mind and did go.

Jesus tells this parable in the temple in Jerusalem to the chief priests and the elders of the people. They had just questioned his authority. With this story he shows them that God does not look only at words, but at what we do. The tax collectors and the prostitutes, who at first said "no" to God, repented when they heard John the Baptist, while the religious leaders appeared obedient but did not believe.

Today, if you have said "no" to God or have turned away from him, it is never too late to change direction. What he values is a repentant heart that obeys.
exp.20:29:
This verse says that the father went to the second son and asked him the same thing: to go and work in the vineyard. This son answered with great respect. But in the end he did not go. His words sounded good, but his actions did not.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with the chief priests and the elders of the people, who doubted his authority. He tells them this parable to show them their situation. The second son represents those who seemed to obey God but did not believe the message of John the Baptist.

Today we can ask ourselves: does my faith stay in nice words, or is it seen in what I do? God values sincere obedience, and we can always repent and return to Him.
exp.20:30:
Jesus asks which of the two sons did what his father wanted. The leaders answer that it was the first, the one who at first refused but later changed his mind and went. Then Jesus tells them that the tax collectors (who collected taxes and were looked down on by the people) and the harlots (women who lived by prostitution) go into the kingdom of God ahead of them, that is, they enter before them.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with the chief priests and the elders of the people, who were questioning his authority. With this parable he shows them that they seemed obedient, but they did not believe the message of John the Baptist. By contrast, many sinners did repent and believe.

For today: God looks not only at what we say, but at what we do. If we have said "no" to God, we can always repent and obey him today.
exp.20:32:
Jesus tells of a man, the owner of a house, who planted a vineyard. He put a fence around it to protect it, dug a winepress (a hollow in the rock where the grapes were trodden to get the juice out), and built a watchtower to keep guard over it. Then he leased it to some tenant farmers and went away to a distant country.

Jesus is speaking in the temple to the chief priests and the elders, who had just questioned his authority. He has just told them that they did not believe John the Baptist. This parable recalls the vineyard of Israel in Isaiah 5, and many understand that the owner represents God and the tenant farmers represent the leaders of the people.

Everything we have comes from God, and we are stewards, not owners. Today we can ask ourselves: am I caring, with gratitude and obedience, for what He has entrusted to me?
exp.20:33:
This verse tells how, when the time of the harvest came, the owner of the vineyard sent his servants to the tenants to receive the share of the fruit that belonged to him. "Tenants" are those who work the land, and here they had rented it from the owner. "Servants" are the owner's workers or messengers.

Jesus is speaking in the temple to the priests and the elders of the people, who doubted his authority. He tells them this parable after speaking about John the Baptist, whom they did not believe. Many understand that the vineyard represents Israel, the owner represents God, and the servants represent the prophets. The tenants would be the leaders who rejected the message.

God has entrusted us with gifts, time, and responsibilities, and he expects us to bear good fruit. Today we can ask ourselves: do I listen humbly when God speaks to me, even when he corrects me?
exp.20:37:
The tenants, seeing the owner's son coming, recognized him as the heir. Instead of respecting him, they planned to kill him so they could keep the inheritance. "Inheritance" means the property that is passed down, and the phrase "come, let us kill him" is what the tenants say to one another.

Jesus tells this parable to the chief priests and the elders of the people, in the temple, a few days before his crucifixion. The owner represents God, the vineyard represents Israel, the servants represent the prophets, and the son represents Jesus himself. Many understand that Jesus is announcing here the rejection he would suffer from his leaders. They themselves pronounce the sentence without realizing it.

For today: it is easy to want to control our lives as if they were our own and not God's. We can ask ourselves whether we are listening to Christ or silencing him to do what suits us. Today is a good day to hand over again what we have.
exp.20:38:
They seized the owner's son, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. "Seized" means they grabbed him, and the phrase about throwing him out means they drove him out of the vineyard. This is the cruelest moment in the parable.

Jesus is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem to the chief priests and the elders of the people. He tells them this parable of the wicked tenants. The vineyard represents Israel, the servants sent are the prophets, and the son is Jesus himself. Many understand that the fact that they threw him out anticipates his death outside the city. The leaders themselves pronounce judgment in the next verse.

For today: God has entrusted us with things that are not ours, such as time, gifts, and family. Ask yourself whether you manage them with gratitude or keep them as if you were the owner. Receive Jesus with humility.
exp.20:44:
It says that the chief priests and the Pharisees heard Jesus' parables and understood that he was speaking about them. The chief priests are the leading priests, the leaders of the temple. To understand here means they grasped the message clearly.

Jesus is in Jerusalem, in the temple, shortly before his arrest. He has just told the parable of the wicked tenants, who mistreat the servants and the son of the owner of the vineyard. Through it he warns the religious leaders that, by rejecting him, they will lose their place of privilege. They understand the message, but instead of repenting, they begin to plan how to trap him.

For today: understanding the truth is not the same as obeying it. When God's Word confronts us, we can harden ourselves or humble ourselves. Let us ask for a heart willing to be corrected, rather than defending ourselves or looking for excuses.
exp.21:1:
Jesus says that the kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepares a wedding feast for his son. This is not a story about politics, but a great celebration full of joy.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, in the last days before his cross, and he addresses the priests and the leaders of the people, who were rejecting him. He tells this parable to show that God invites everyone to his feast, but some of the first guests do not want to come. Many understand the king to represent God and the son to represent Jesus, although the parable does not say so in those words.

For today: God invites us into a relationship with him, and his invitation is a joy, not a burden. Today you can answer him with a grateful heart, and do not let your busy days make you say no.
exp.21:3:
This verse shows the king insisting. Since the invited guests did not want to come, he sends other servants with a more urgent message. The oxen and fattened animals have already been slaughtered, so the wedding feast is ready. All that remains is for the guests to arrive.

Jesus tells this parable in the temple in Jerusalem, and the religious leaders are listening. The king represents God, and the son represents Christ. The repeated invitation shows God's patience, which keeps calling even when people reject him. Many understand it as referring to how Israel received God's prophets and messengers.

For today: God invites us into a relationship with him, and everything is ready through his grace. Let not work or worries make us put off his invitation. Let us respond today with gratitude and simplicity.
exp.21:9:
The king's servants went out into the roads and gathered everyone they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.

Jesus is speaking to the religious leaders in the temple in Jerusalem. He tells this parable about a king who holds a feast for his son. The first invited guests refused to come. Many believe Jesus shows how God's invitation opens up to more people, although interpreters explain the details in different ways. The following verse indicates that how we respond also matters.

For today: God invites everyone, regardless of their past. If you have thought you do not deserve a place, accept his invitation with humility. And if you are already inside, treat others with the same grace.
exp.21:11:
Jesus tells of a king who speaks courteously to a guest. "Friend," he says to him. He asks how he came into the feast without a wedding garment. The man was left with nothing to say, so he was speechless, with no excuse. The wedding garment is the proper clothing for that celebration.

Jesus speaks in a parable about the kingdom of heaven. First, invitations went to those who turned down the feast, and then to everyone, good and bad alike. Many understand the garment as a transformed life, or the righteousness that God gives; interpreters explain it in several ways. What is clear is that being invited is not the same as truly responding.

For today: God invites us with grace, but he expects a sincere heart. Today you can ask him to clothe you with his forgiveness and help you live with humility, without relying on excuses.
exp.21:12:
The king here orders his servants to seize the man who was not wearing wedding clothes, tie his hands and feet, and throw him out, into the darkness. The servants of the king are the attendants who serve him. The outer darkness is a place far from the feast and the light. Weeping and gnashing of teeth expresses pain, anguish, and late regret.

Jesus is telling a parable about the kingdom of heaven, addressed to religious leaders who were rejecting him. The king invites many to his son's wedding, and the guest without the wedding clothes represents someone who accepts the invitation but does not come prepared as he should. Christians understand the wedding clothes in different ways: a transformed life, or the righteousness that God himself gives. There is debate about which emphasis is primary.

For today: God invites us with grace, but he expects a sincere heart. Examine whether your faith is real and not merely a matter of appearance, and receive with humility what Christ offers you.
exp.21:14:
This verse says that the Pharisees withdrew and came together to plan how they might trap Jesus with something he himself said. The verse of the old wording is handled by the verse itself: the Pharisees went away and took counsel together, meaning they made a plan among themselves to catch him in his words, so as to accuse him.

Matthew, who tells the story, has just recorded three parables of Jesus, the last one about the wedding feast. The religious leaders understood that he was speaking about them, and they became angry. Instead of reflecting on it, they looked for a way to make him stumble. Soon they will send their disciples with a question about paying taxes to Caesar, designed as a trap.

For today: when a teaching from God makes us uncomfortable, we can either harden ourselves or allow ourselves to be corrected. Let us ask for a humble heart that listens to the Word in order to change, not in order to defend itself or argue.
exp.21:17:
Jesus recognized the evil intentions of the people speaking to him. So he asked them why they were testing him, calling them hypocrites. Here, "testing" means to put someone to the test or set a trap. "Evil" is wickedness hidden beneath the surface. "Hypocrites" are those who pretend to be something they are not.

The Pharisees sent their disciples along with the Herodians, supporters of Herod's rule. First they flattered him with pleasant words, but their question about paying the tax to Caesar was a trap: if he said yes, he would lose the favor of the people; if he said no, they could accuse him before Rome. Jesus saw their hearts and was not deceived.

For today: God knows the intentions behind our words. Before we ask, praise, or speak with someone, let us examine our hearts and seek to be sincere, without pretending or manipulating.
exp.21:19:
Jesus asks them whose image is on the coin and what the inscription engraved on it says. The image is the likeness of the emperor's face, and the words above it are the title or name the coin carried.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees and some Herodians who wanted to trap him with a question about paying taxes to Caesar. He knew their evil intent. He asks them for a coin, and they themselves bring one out. With this simple question, Jesus leads them to answer in their own words: the coin belongs to Caesar, so they should give back to Caesar what is his.

Today, this scene invites us to ask what our lives bear engraved on them. If the coin carries Caesar's image, the human being carries the image of God, according to Genesis 1:27. Let us fulfill our civic responsibilities, but let us give to God what matters most: the heart and the whole of our life.
exp.21:23:
The Sadducees tell Jesus that Moses taught a rule: if a married man died without having children, his brother was to marry the widow.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that denied the resurrection. They cite the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), but not out of sincere interest. They prepare an exaggerated story of seven brothers to make the idea of life after death look ridiculous and to put Jesus in a difficult position.

We can use the Bible to win arguments instead of seeking the truth. Today the Lord invites us to approach his Word with humility, wanting to know him and not merely to be right.
exp.21:24:
This verse says there were seven brothers among them. The first married and died without children, so he left his wife to his brother. Here "wife" is the word the verse uses.

The Sadducees speak with Jesus. They did not believe in the resurrection, and they bring up an invented or exaggerated case to make that hope look ridiculous. They rely on the law of Moses about levirate marriage, which protected the widow and kept the family name alive. Jesus then answers them that they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

For today: sometimes we use difficult questions to argue, not to seek God. Let us come to Him with humility, and if we do not understand something, let us study His Word, trusting in His power and His goodness.
exp.21:26:
This verse says that the woman, after being widowed seven times, also died at the end. "Last of all" means she outlived the seven brothers. It is the close of a story invented around an extreme case.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They present Jesus with this case, based on the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), to make the idea of returning to life look ridiculous. Jesus answers that their mistake comes from not knowing the Scriptures well or the power of God.

For today: when a hard question seeks to confuse us more than to help us understand, let us return to the Bible and trust that God can do more than our reasoning is able to imagine.
exp.21:28:
Jesus tells his listeners that they are wrong for two reasons: they do not know the Scriptures well, and they do not take into account the power of God.

Those who speak to him are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They brought him the case of a woman who married seven brothers, one after another, to mock that teaching. Jesus answers with firmness, but he points to the root of the problem: they imagined the life to come as a simple copy of this life, and they limited what God can do.

For today: when you have doubts about God or his work, do not rely only on your own ideas. Read the Bible with humility, and remember that God can do more than we imagine.
exp.21:30:
Jesus asks the Sadducees whether they have not read what God himself said about the resurrection of the dead. He reminds them that God spoke, and that those words are written in the Scriptures.

Jesus speaks with the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They had put to him a difficult case about a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus answers that they do not understand the Scriptures or the power of God, and he quotes Exodus 3:6, when God spoke to Moses from the burning bush.

For today: it is not enough to own a Bible; it must be read with humility and with trust in the power of God. If God is still the God of those who died in faith, our hope does not end in the grave.
exp.21:31:
Jesus recalls the words God spoke to Moses: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And he concludes that God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. In other words, these patriarchs, although they died long ago, still live before God.

Jesus is answering the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They had put a difficult question to him about a woman who married several times. Jesus shows them that they understand neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. He uses a text from Exodus, which they did accept, and the crowd was amazed.

For today: if God is the God of the living, our relationship with him does not end at death. We can face the loss of believing loved ones, and our own end, with hope, trusting that God sustains life beyond the grave.
exp.21:32:
When the crowd heard this, they were astonished at his teaching.

This verse tells us that the people who were present, when they heard what Jesus said, were greatly amazed. The word "astonished" means surprised, almost left without words. And "teaching" here means his instruction.

Jesus had just answered the Sadducees, a group that did not believe in the resurrection, who had asked him a question to trap him. He answered them with the Scriptures, reminding them that God presented himself to Moses as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that he is not the God of the dead, but of the living. The crowd, who witnessed everything, was impressed by the clarity and authority of his answer.

For today: approach the Bible with humility and let it teach you, instead of using it to argue. Jesus trusted in the Word of God, and that Word can also surprise you and give you hope.
exp.21:33:
They heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, so the Pharisees came together. Being silenced means being left without an answer, and gathering together means coming to one place with one purpose.

This is Matthew's account. Just before, the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, tried to trap Jesus with a question. He answered them from the Scriptures: God is the God of the living. The Pharisees, rivals of the Sadducees but also opponents of Jesus, now join together to test him. The text that follows shows that one of them tempts him with another question.

For today: be careful about hearing the truth only in order to find a way to win an argument. We can come to Jesus with humility, wanting to learn and to obey, not with a desire to test him or defeat him.
exp.21:36:
Jesus answers with words from the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 6:5). He says that we should love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. That is, with our desires, our whole life, and our thinking. Nothing of ours is left outside that love.

A teacher of the law asked him the question to test him, that is, to trap him with his words. This happened in Jerusalem, when several religious groups wanted to catch Jesus in what he said. He answered clearly: the first and greatest commandment is to love God. Right after, he added that loving our neighbor is like it.

Today, we can begin the day by giving God a moment of prayer and reading his Word. In this way, love for God does not stay as an idea, but guides what we feel, think, and do throughout the day.
exp.21:40:
This verse says that the Pharisees came together in one place, and then Jesus asked them a question. The phrase "while the Pharisees were gathered together" means they were meeting as a group. The question Jesus asks appears in the next verse.

Before this, several religious groups had tried to trap Jesus with difficult questions. A teacher of the law had asked him which commandment was the greatest, and Jesus answered: love God and love your neighbor. Now Jesus takes the initiative and asks the questions himself, to get them thinking about who the Christ, the promised Messiah, really is.

For today: sometimes we know a great deal about religion, but we do not stop to answer the most important question: who is Jesus to me? Today you can take a quiet moment to answer it honestly before God.
exp.22:1:
Jesus says that the scribes and the Pharisees "sit" in Moses' seat. The seat was the chair or place of teaching from which the law of God was explained. The scribes copied and taught the Scriptures, and the Pharisees were a religious group held in high regard. So they had authority to teach the law.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, shortly before his crucifixion, in Jerusalem. He is going to confront the hypocrisy of those leaders. First he acknowledges that they teach the law of Moses, and then he will warn that their deeds do not match their words. Some interpreters see here a respect for their office, others a gentle irony; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Today we can hear the truth of God's Word, even when the one who teaches it is imperfect, but without imitating their bad examples. And let us examine whether we live out what we say we believe.
exp.22:3:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees bind heavy burdens, that is, they impose harsh rules that are hard to keep, and lay them on the shoulders of the people. But they themselves will not lift a finger to move them. In other words, they demand of others what they are not willing to live by or to help carry.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He has just said that the leaders teach from the seat of Moses, but do not practice what they preach. His criticism is not against the Law, but against the hypocrisy and harshness of those who lead.

For today: if you guide or influence others, whether in the church, the home or the workplace, require only what you yourself strive to live, and help with grace anyone who is carrying a heavy load.
exp.22:4:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees do everything they do so that people will see them. Phylacteries were small leather boxes containing verses from the Law, which were tied to the arm and the forehead. The fringes were the tassels on the cloak, which served as a reminder of the commandments. They made them larger to appear more devoted.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. He does not reject the Law or those symbols, which God himself had commanded them to use. He criticizes the hypocrisy of those who teach one thing and live another, seeking applause rather than seeking to please God.

Today we can ask ourselves why we do good: pray, serve, give. Before doing so, ask God for a sincere heart, one that seeks to please Him and not to impress others.
exp.22:8:
Jesus says we should not call anyone on earth "father," because our true Father is one, the one who is in heaven. The verse of this word points to a spiritual authority that deserves supreme honor.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, right after pointing to the scribes and Pharisees. They loved titles, greetings in the marketplaces, and the best seats. Jesus corrects that pride. Some believers understand the command literally, and others as a warning against spiritual vanity. Jesus himself spoke of honoring father and mother.

Today we can respect those who guide us, but without seeking or giving anyone a place that belongs only to God. Let us serve with humility, and not for titles or applause.
exp.22:10:
Jesus says that whoever wants to be the greatest among his followers must be their servant, that is, someone who serves others.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, shortly before he rebukes the scribes and Pharisees. They sought titles, honors and the places of honor. Jesus shows them that in his kingdom greatness is not measured by title, but by humble service. He also teaches that God is the true Father and Christ the true Teacher.

For today: if you have some place of influence, in the family, at work or in the church, ask yourself each day whom you can help. Do one concrete act of service, without seeking applause.
exp.22:13:
Jesus says "Woe" to the scribes and Pharisees, who were teachers of the law and religious leaders. "You devour widows' houses" means that they took advantage of helpless women in order to take their property. "For a pretence make long prayer" means that they prayed at great length to appear pious and to cover over their abuses. For this reason they will receive a more severe judgment.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, in the last period before the cross. He is warning the crowd and his disciples about leaders whose religion was only outward appearance. His "woe" expresses sorrow and judgment. Some ancient manuscripts do not include this verse, and for that reason several translations place it in a note or omit it.

For today: examine whether your life of prayer and faith is accompanied by justice and compassion. God is pleased with the one who cares for the vulnerable, not with the one who only appears to be spiritual.
exp.22:22:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees give a tenth even of the little herbs from the garden: mint, dill, and cumin. But they neglect the most important matters of the law: justice, compassion, and faithfulness to God. He says they should have done the one without leaving the other undone.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, in his last public teaching, to the religious leaders and to the people. He does not condemn tithing; he affirms it. He condemns the hypocrisy of attending to outward details while ignoring fair and merciful treatment of others.

For today: you can be faithful in your religious practices, but ask yourself whether you are also faithful in how you treat people. This week, do one concrete act of justice or compassion toward someone.
exp.22:24:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees take great care to clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but on the inside they are full of extortion (gains taken out of greed) and excess (a lack of self-control, as some other translations put it). "Hypocrites" was the word for those who pretended to be one thing while living as another.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. He is rebuking the religious leaders who kept the outward rules of purity but neglected justice, mercy, and faith. His image of the cup shows that what matters is the heart.

Today we can ask ourselves: am I more concerned with what others see in me, or with what God sees inside? Ask him to cleanse your motives, your way of treating others, and your honesty in the hidden places.
exp.22:25:
Jesus tells the Pharisee to first clean the inside of the cup and the dish, so that the outside will be clean too. "Cup" means a drinking vessel. A "Pharisee" was a religious teacher who was very strict about the rules of purity. The word "blind" points to a person who does not see what truly matters.

Jesus speaks in the temple, in a series of rebukes to the scribes and Pharisees. He charges them with paying close attention to outward religious appearance, while inwardly there was robbery, injustice, and hypocrisy. He uses the image of dishes to speak about the heart and about hidden conduct.

For today: it is not enough to care about how you look to others. Today you can ask God to examine your motives, your thoughts, and your decisions in private. When the heart is renewed with his help, the visible life often reflects it with greater sincerity.
exp.22:26:
He says that the scribes and Pharisees are like whitewashed tombs: on the outside they look beautiful, but inside they are full of dead men's bones and filth. Those called "hypocrites" were people who acted as if they were good but were not. "Scribes" were the teachers of the Law. The woe pronounced on them is a serious warning, mixed with sorrow.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, and he criticizes the religious leaders of his time. Shortly before, he spoke of cleaning the outside of the cup and not the inside. A common explanation is that tombs were whitewashed so that people would see them and not become unclean by touching them. His reproach is that they cared about appearance but not about the heart.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I care more about what others see in me, or about what God sees in me? Let us ask God to cleanse our hearts and make us sincere.
exp.22:27:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees appeared righteous to the people, but inside they were full of hypocrisy and wickedness. "Hypocrisy" is pretending to be good without being good, and "wickedness" is evil or disobedience to God.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, in his last appeal to the religious leaders. He has just compared them to whitewashed tombs: beautiful on the outside, but full of death within. His anger is not mere contempt, but because they cared for appearance and neglected justice, mercy, and faith (Matthew 23:23).

For today: it is not enough to look good at church or before others. Let us ask God to examine our hearts, to cleanse us within, and to let our actions come from a sincere faith.
exp.22:28:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees build tombs for the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous. The word "build" here means that they were constructing or repairing those tombs, and "decorate" means that they were beautifying them. Jesus calls them hypocrites, that is, people who pretend to be something they are not.

Jesus speaks in the temple, in Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. He is denouncing the religious leaders. They honored the dead prophets, but, according to the verses that follow, they said that they would never have killed them. Jesus answers that their attitude shows them to be heirs of those who did.

For today: it is easy to admire the heroes of faith of the past and, at the same time, to resist the voice of God correcting us today. Let us ask God for a humble heart that obeys, not only one that admires.
exp.22:33:
Jesus says that he himself will send to the religious leaders prophets, wise men, and scribes, that is, messengers and teachers of God. He announces that some of them will be killed and crucified, and others will be scourged in the synagogues and pursued from town to town.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. He has just denounced the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and the teachers of the law. They honored the prophets who had died, yet they acted like those who killed them. Jesus shows that God still gives them opportunities, even knowing how they will respond.

For today: God continues to speak to us through his Word and through sincere people, even when his message is uncomfortable. Examine your heart and ask yourself whether you are willing to receive correction with humility, instead of defending yourself or hardening your heart.
exp.22:34:
Jesus says that the responsibility for all the blood of the righteous shed throughout history will fall on those religious leaders. It spans from Abel, the first righteous man killed, to Zechariah, who was put to death between the temple and the altar. The name Zechariah son of Barachias is another form of the name Berechiah. Scholars do not agree on which Zechariah is meant: it could be the one in 2 Chronicles 24, or the prophet Zechariah.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, at the end of a harsh series of warnings. He shows them that by rejecting God's messengers, they are repeating what their ancestors did. Even so, the next passage reveals his grief over Jerusalem.

For today: examine with humility whether, while you criticize the mistakes of the past, your own heart resists the voice of God. Listen to his correction today, before your heart becomes hardened.
exp.23:2:
While Jesus was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him in private. They asked him when these things would happen, what would be the sign of his coming, and what would be the sign of the end of the age.

Jesus had just announced that the temple would be destroyed, and the disciples were shaken. They ask, and he answers by warning them not to be deceived. Many believers understand that the questions combine the destruction of the temple, which took place in the year 70, with the return of Christ, and they debate how the two subjects are related.

For today: before worrying about dates or signs, make sure you are not being deceived. Know well what Jesus taught, read it for yourself, and compare with the Bible whatever others say about the future.
exp.23:5:
Jesus says that his followers will hear of wars and of reports of wars, whether nearby or far away. He asks them not to be frightened or disturbed. He says that these things must happen, but that this is still not the end.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after they asked him about the sign of his coming and the end of the age. Earlier he had warned them against the deceptions of false messiahs. Now he prepares them for hard times and makes clear that wars and crises are not a definite sign. He then calls them the beginning of birth pains. Interpreters differ on how this relates to the year 70 AD and to the future.

When bad news arrives, do not let fear take control of you. Pray, trust that God is still in control, and stay firm in Christ, without being carried away by rumors or alarmist predictions.
exp.23:10:
It says that, before the end, many false prophets will appear, that is, people who speak in God's name without having been sent by Him. Their message will deceive many people.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They asked him about the signs of the end. He warns them of hard times: persecution, betrayal, and the cooling of love. False prophets are part of that trial. Scholars disagree about how much of this refers to Jerusalem in the year 70 and how much to the final time, and some see both.

For today: do not believe something just because it sounds spiritual or because someone famous says it. Compare what you hear with the Scriptures, pray for wisdom, and seek a healthy community of believers. In this way you remain firm in Christ.
exp.23:11:
This verse says that when wickedness grows and becomes common, the love of many people will grow cold. The word "love" here refers to the love the verse speaks of, and "grow cold" means it will lose its warmth, like a flame that goes out little by little.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They asked him about the signs of the end. He warns them about hard times: betrayal, hatred, and false prophets. Then he encourages them to persevere to the end. Interpreters differ on whether this speaks of the years before the fall of Jerusalem, of the final time, or of both.

For today: do not let the hardness of the world make you cold. Guard your love with prayer, with the Word, and with a community of faith, and keep doing good even when others grow weary.
exp.23:13:
Jesus says that the good news of God's kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the earth, as a witness to all nations. The word translated as "nations" here refers to peoples who are not Jews, that is, all the nations of the world. The phrase "then the end will come" means that after this, the final stage of this age will arrive.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when they asked him about the signs of the end. Earlier he spoke of growing wickedness and love growing cold, and he encouraged them to endure. Afterward he speaks of the abomination of desolation and of fleeing from Judea. Christians understand in different ways how these events relate to the year 70 A.D. and to the future.

For today: instead of trying to guess dates, we can live faithfully and share the gospel with love, praying, supporting missionaries, and speaking about Jesus to those around us.
exp.23:16:
He says that whoever is on the roof of his house when that moment comes must not go down to take anything out of the house. In those days houses had flat roofs, and people went up there to rest or pray. The roof is the rooftop, and the instruction is to flee at once, without stopping to grab belongings.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They asked him about the destruction of the temple and the signs of the times. He warns them of a serious danger in Judea, connected with what was said by Daniel. Interpreters disagree: some see it fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, others see it also in a time still to come. In both cases, the message is to act with urgency.

For today: when God shows you clearly that you should obey or move away from a danger, do not delay out of attachment to things. Trust that he cares for you more than your possessions.
exp.23:19:
Jesus advises his disciples to pray that, when they have to flee, it will not be in winter or on the sabbath. "Flight" means escaping from a danger. "Winter" suggests difficult roads, with cold and rain. "Sabbath" is the Jewish day of rest.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, before his death. He warns them of times of great distress in Judea. Many connect this with the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, and others also with future events. As to why he mentions the sabbath, there is no single explanation: it could be because of travel restrictions or because the city gates were closed that day. The text does not make this clear.

For today: Jesus shows us that it is good to pray about specific things, even about details of daily life and about difficult moments that might come. We can bring our fears and plans before God, trusting that he cares for his own.
exp.23:20:
It says that a time of suffering will come, so great as has never been seen since the world existed, and that nothing like it will happen again.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. He answers them about the future of Jerusalem and the end of the age. He announces very hard days, but promises that God will shorten them for the sake of his chosen ones. Christians understand this passage in different ways. Some see it fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, others look for it in the future, and others see both.

For today: Jesus warned of trials so that they would not take us by surprise. We can live with confidence, staying alert, praying, and resting in the knowledge that God cares for his own even in the darkest times.
exp.23:28:
It says that after a time of great suffering there will be huge signs in the sky: the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after they asked him about the end of the age. He uses language similar to that of the prophets of the Old Testament. Some believe it is literal and others that it is symbolic language of judgment. What follows shows that it climaxes with the coming of the Son of Man.

For today: do not live in fear or search for dates. Jesus gave these words so that we would be alert and confident. Do what is right today, love others, and trust that Christ is in control of history.
exp.23:29:
Jesus says that, after a time of great distress, the sign of the Son of man will appear in the sky. All the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see Jesus coming on the clouds of heaven with power and glory. "Mourn" means they will weep or beat their breasts in grief. What exactly the sign is does not become clear; Christians hold several views about it.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about his coming and the end of the age. He uses the language of prophets like Daniel, with images from the heavens, to show that his return will be visible, real, and worldwide.

For today: do not live in fear or try to guess dates. Live with hope and attentiveness, being faithful in everyday life, loving others, and trusting that Christ will keep his promise.
exp.23:37:
It says that before the flood people lived their normal routine: they were eating, drinking, and marrying. The phrase "giving in marriage" means giving a son or daughter in marriage. Everything went on the same way until the day Noah entered the ark.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. He has just told them that no one knows the day or the hour of his coming. He uses Noah as an example: what caught those people off guard was not that they were doing evil things, but that they lived without paying attention to what God was warning. Some understand this as a call to watchfulness, and that is the central idea of the passage.

Eating, working, and building a family are not wrong; they are part of life. But today you might ask yourself: am I so caught up in everyday life that I forget God? Take a moment each day to pray and keep your heart attentive and ready.
exp.23:39:
Jesus says that there will be two people working together in the field, and that one will be "taken" and the other "left." "Taken" means that they are carried away; "left" means that they remain behind. The same applies to the two women grinding grain in the following verse.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, about his coming. He compares that day to the flood: people were living their normal routine and did not notice until judgment arrived. Christians interpret "taken" in different ways: some believe it refers to being caught up to meet Christ, and others to being taken away in judgment, as in the days of Noah. The text does not fully settle the matter.

For today: the point is not to guess dates, but to live each day ready, with sincere faith and faithfulness in ordinary tasks, because Jesus himself said to be watchful.
exp.23:41:
This verse tells us to watch, that is, to stay awake and alert, because no one knows what hour the Lord will return. The word "therefore" shows that this is a conclusion drawn from what came before. The phrase "your Lord" shows that the words are spoken to his followers.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after describing signs and future events. They wanted to know when these things would happen. Jesus does not give them a date, but calls them to live prepared. Christians interpret the details of this passage in different ways, but the call to watchfulness is clear.

For today: do not live in fear or try to guess dates. Live each day faithfully, praying, obeying God, loving others, and doing your work well, like someone who is ready to welcome their Lord.
exp.23:43:
It says we must be prepared, because Jesus, the Son of Man, will return at a moment no one expects. Being ready means being alert and prepared. The phrase at an hour you do not expect means at an unexpected hour.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, in his teaching about the last times. Earlier he gave the example of the homeowner who, if he knew when the thief would come, would stay awake. Then he speaks of the faithful and wise servant, who does his work while his master is away. In this way he teaches that being ready is not fear, but faithfulness day by day.

For today: live each day with integrity and service, as one who knows Christ may return. Do today what you know pleases him: love, forgive, be honest, and fulfill your responsibilities.
exp.23:44:
Jesus asks a question: who is the faithful and wise servant? He is the trusted employee whom his master places in charge of the household. His task is to give food to the family at the proper time, that is, at the right moment. Here "household" means those who live in the house, and "food" is the daily meal.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, teaching about his return. He has just said that no one knows the hour, and he compares his coming to a thief who arrives without warning. For this reason he asks them to be ready. This question shows what being ready looks like: not only waiting, but serving faithfully.

For today: being ready for Christ is not living in fear, but faithfully carrying out what God has entrusted to us. It may be caring for your family, serving in the church, or doing your work well, without waiting for anyone to notice.
exp.23:48:
That evil servant, thinking his master will not come back soon, begins to beat his fellow servants. He also sits down to eat and drink with drunkards, meaning he lives without control and joins those who give themselves over to excess.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after talking about his coming. He tells this parable to show the difference between the faithful servant and the one who abuses his responsibility. Many understand that the master is Christ and the servants are those who have duties among his people; the text gives no further details.

For today: live each day as one who must give account to God, even when it seems he is slow to come. Treat others with respect, especially if you have some authority or responsibility, and take care of your habits in private.
exp.23:50:
This verse says that the master, returning unexpectedly, will punish the wicked servant severely. The phrase about cutting him in pieces is a strong expression; it is understood as a severe punishment, and some think it is figurative language. Then he will be placed with the hypocrites, that is, with those who appear faithful but do not live it out. The weeping and the gnashing of teeth express pain and anguish.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after teaching them about his return. With this parable he calls them to be watchful. The wicked servant thinks his master will be delayed, and so he mistreats others and lives carelessly. The teaching is that no one knows the day or the hour.

For today: live each day with integrity, even when no one sees you. Treat others well, fulfill your responsibilities, and keep your heart ready before God, without putting obedience off until later.
exp.24:2:
This verse says that the foolish virgins took their lamps but did not remember to take extra oil. They looked ready, but they lacked what was needed to wait.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, as he teaches them about his return. He tells this parable to encourage them to be prepared. The virgins represent those who wait for the bridegroom. What the oil exactly symbolizes is interpreted in several ways: genuine faith, the Holy Spirit, or a life truly given over to God.

For today: it is not enough to appear to be a believer on the outside. Spend time praying, reading the Bible, and obeying God, so that your faith is real and ready when you need it most.
exp.24:8:
Here the wise virgins answer the foolish ones who ask them for oil. They say there would not be enough for either group, and they advise them to go to the sellers and buy their own.

Jesus tells this parable about his return and the kingdom of heaven. The wise ones speak because the wait has grown long and the lamps are going out. Many understand the oil as a true and living faith, or a personal relationship with God, though the parable does not explain this precisely. What is clear is that there are personal things no one can lend to another.

For today: do not live off the faith of your parents, your church, or your friends. Cultivate your own relationship with God each day, through prayer and reading his Word, so that you are ready when he comes.
exp.24:14:
A man, before going on a journey, divided his goods among his servants. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, according to each one's ability. The word "ability" here means skill or capacity. A talent was a very large amount of money. After handing them out, the man went far away.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, in his teaching about the last times. Just before this, he asked them to stay alert, because no one knows the day or the hour of his coming. With this parable he shows that waiting is not sitting with folded arms, but faithfully serving with what has been entrusted to us.

For today: God does not ask you for what you do not have, but for faithfulness with what he has given you. Do not compare yourself with others. Ask yourself what abilities, time, or resources you have, and use them today to serve God and others.
exp.24:19:
The verse tells of the servant who had received five talents and came before his master with ten: the five he was given and five more that he gained by working with them. A talent was a very large amount of money. He acknowledges that he received everything from his master.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, shortly before his crucifixion. He tells this parable to teach how to live while awaiting his return. Many understand that the master represents Christ and that we are the servants who trust him. The talents are interpreted as what God entrusts to us: gifts, opportunities, and resources.

For today: think about what God has given you, whether time, abilities, or money, and use it faithfully to serve others, without hiding it out of fear.
exp.24:20:
Here the lord congratulates the servant who received five talents and made them grow. He says "well done, good and faithful servant": he recognizes him as good and worthy of trust. A talent was a large amount of money. The "few things" entrusted to him are not little in themselves, but small compared with what is to come. As a reward, he receives more responsibility and is invited to enter into his lord's joy, that is, to share in his happiness.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the parable of the talents, shortly before his crucifixion. A man goes on a journey and leaves his goods with his servants.
