On his return, he asks them for an account. Many understand that the lord represents Christ and that the parable speaks of how to live while we wait for his return.

For today: God does not ask that all of us have the same thing, but that we be faithful with what he has given us. Think of a gift, a time, or a resource you have, and use it today with consistency to serve others.
exp.24:21:
Here the second servant comes before his master. He says that he received two talents and now brings two more. A "talent" was a very large amount of money in ancient times. "I have gained" the other two in the sense that he made them produce more. His report is simple and honest.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, and he tells this parable to teach how to live while they wait for his return. The master gave each servant an amount according to his ability. This servant received less than the first, but he did the same thing: he worked with what had been entrusted to him. That is why, according to the next verse, he receives the same praise.

God does not ask us to be like others, but to be faithful with what he has given us. Perhaps you have little time, few resources, or simple abilities. Use them today to serve and to love, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.24:22:
He says that the lord praises his servant: he calls him good and faithful. Since he was trustworthy with a few things, he will now give him many things to care for. He invites him to enter the joy of his lord, that is, to share in his master's happiness and celebration. Over a few things means in small matters, and I will make you ruler means he will put him in charge of more.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples, in his teaching about being ready for his return. The lord, who went away on a journey, represents Christ. The servants received talents, which were large sums of money. Here he speaks to the one who doubled what he had received. Many understand that the joy points to communion with Christ in his kingdom.

Today we can be faithful in small things: a job, a family, a hidden service. God does not measure only the results, but the faithfulness with what he has given us.
exp.24:26:
Here the master tells the servant that, if he was so afraid, he should at least have put the money with the bankers, that is, the people who exchanged and kept money safe. In that way, when the master returned, he would have received his money back with interest, a gain on what was lent.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples, speaking about how to live while He is not present and about our accountability before God. The servant did nothing wrong with the money, but he did nothing good with it either: his fear paralyzed him. The master's words are harsh because the servant made excuses instead of acting. Some see in this a warning about judgment; others, a call to faithfulness.

For today: do not let fear stop you. Use simply what God has given you, even if it seems little: your time, your abilities, your kindness. Taking a small step is better than hiding everything away.
exp.24:30:
Jesus says that the Son of Man, a title he uses for himself, will come in great glory and with all the holy angels. Then he will sit on his glorious throne, like a king who is going to rule and judge.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, a few days before his crucifixion. He has just told the parables of the ten virgins and of the talents, which call us to be ready and faithful. This verse opens the scene of the final judgment, where people will be separated like sheep and goats.

We live between two comings of Christ, and that calls us to live with seriousness and hope. Today you might ask yourself: "How can I serve someone in need, as if they were Jesus himself?" And do it with love, without expecting recognition.
exp.24:38:
The righteous keep asking the King when they saw him sick or in prison and went to visit him. The word for "prison" here simply means the jail. The words "or" and "and" in this verse are shown in an older spelling, and they mean the same as "or" and "and" today. They do not remember having done this, because they helped without thinking about receiving a reward.

Jesus tells this parable about the final judgment, when the King separates the people. Here the righteous speak, surprised by what He tells them. In the answer that follows, Jesus explains that what they did for His least brothers, He counts as done for Him. Interpreters debate who these brothers are: for some they are the believers, for others anyone in need.

For today: help those who suffer with simplicity, by visiting someone who is sick, writing to someone who is alone, or accompanying someone who is shut in. Do not expect applause; practical love is precious to God.
exp.24:41:
Here Jesus, as King and Judge, tells those on his left that when he was hungry and thirsty, they gave him no food or drink. The source's quoted forms are rendered as the verse's own wording: the verb for giving is simply "gave" and the verb for feeling hunger is simply "was" hungry, so no separate explanation is needed. Their failure was not helping the one in need.

Jesus is speaking in the parable of the final judgment, when he separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Shortly before, he said that whatever was done to the least of these, his brothers, was done to him. Many understand this to refer to any person in need; others understand it especially to refer to believers who suffer. The condemned are not accused of great crimes, but of not having loved through deeds.

For today: look around you and help someone specific this week. It may be sharing food, doing someone a favor, or accompanying someone who is in need. A simple act, done with love, counts before God.
exp.25:1:
Jesus reminds his disciples that the Passover, the Jewish feast that celebrates Israel's deliverance from Egypt, will take place in two days. He says that the Son of man, a title Jesus uses for himself, is to be betrayed, that is, handed over into the hands of his enemies, to be crucified.

Jesus speaks just after finishing his teaching about the end of the age and judgment. The disciples are with him, and he announces his death to them in advance. Soon after, the religious leaders gather to plan his arrest. Jesus is not caught off guard: he knows what is coming and moves forward with purpose and resolve.

For today: Jesus faced suffering with trust in God's plan. When you go through difficult moments, you can pray and rest in the knowledge that God is still at work, even when not everything is understood.
exp.25:2:
This verse says that the religious leaders of Israel gathered together in the house of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas. There were the chief priests, the teachers of the law (the scribes), and the leaders of the people (the elders). Here "high priest" means the chief priest, and the "courtyard" refers to the open space inside his residence.

Jesus had just told his disciples that in two days he would be handed over to be crucified. While He was announcing this, these leaders were already meeting to plan how to arrest him in secret and kill him. The narrator, Matthew, shows the contrast between God's plan and human wickedness.

For today: even when people with power act unjustly, God remains in control and fulfills his purpose. We can trust Him in the midst of unjust situations, and ask Him to keep us from using religion to defend our own interests.
exp.25:5:
This verse tells us where Jesus was: in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, in the house of a man named Simon the leper. "Leper" probably indicates that Simon had had that disease. The Bible does not explain whether he was healed, or who healed him, so we do not know.

The one telling the story is Matthew. Just before, the religious leaders plan to arrest Jesus secretly and kill him. In the face of that threat, Jesus is calm, in a house where he was welcomed. This place sets the scene for the woman who anoints him with costly perfume.

For today: Jesus sat at the table with people that society regarded with distance. We can ask ourselves whom we are leaving out, and open our table or our friendship to someone who feels lonely or rejected.
exp.25:6:
Matthew tells us that a woman came to Jesus with a jar of alabaster, a fine white stone. Inside was very costly perfume. She poured it on Jesus' head while he was sitting at the table.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. The leaders were planning to arrest him, but they did not want to do it during the feast because they feared the people. The disciples became upset about the expense. Later Jesus says that she prepared him for his burial. Matthew's text does not give her name.

For today: giving Jesus the best of ourselves, with sincere love, is never wasted. Today you might give him time, prayer, or service without seeking applause or worrying about what others think.
exp.25:8:
It says the perfume the woman poured out might have been sold for a great deal of money, and that this money could have been given to the poor. The disciples say this as a complaint.

The disciples speak, annoyed at seeing the woman pour expensive perfume over Jesus' head at the table. They thought it was a waste. Their concern for the poor seems good, but they did not understand what was happening. Jesus defended the woman, since her act of love had a special meaning, and he reminded them that he would not be with them for much longer.

Helping the poor is important, but we should not harshly criticize the sincere love others show toward God. Today we can ask ourselves: what am I giving to Jesus with all my heart, without calculation or complaint?
exp.25:9:
Jesus perceives what his disciples are thinking and saying. He asks them why they are troubling or distressing the woman. He tells them that she has done a good work for him, meaning something beautiful and valuable.

Jesus is in Bethany, and a woman has just poured expensive perfume over his head. The disciples are indignant and see it as a waste, since it could have been sold to help the poor. Jesus defends the woman and explains that she did it with his burial in mind, which was drawing near.

For today: before criticizing another person's act of love, it is wise to pause and ask what is in their heart. A good cause does not always give us reason to look down on someone's sincere devotion to God.
exp.25:10:
This verse says that the poor will always be close to the disciples, but Jesus would not stay with them for long. Jesus is speaking of his coming departure.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Bethany, shortly before his death. A woman poured costly perfume on him, and the disciples were upset because they thought it could be sold to help the poor. Jesus defends the woman and explains that she has done something good, preparing his body for burial. He is not looking down on the poor; the Bible commands us to help them.

For today: serve those in need faithfully, but do not let the unique moments pass to honor Christ and to love those near you, while you still have the opportunity.
exp.25:11:
Jesus says that the woman poured this perfume on his body to prepare it for burial. Her gesture carried a meaning that she perhaps did not fully understand.

Jesus speaks in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. The disciples had become upset, thinking the perfume could have been sold to help the poor. Jesus defends the woman and reminds them that he will soon die. Many understand that she did not know everything this meant, but Jesus did. Shortly afterward, Judas goes out to betray him.

Today we can learn to recognize moments that do not come again. Serving the poor is important, but there are also occasions to express love and gratitude to God without calculation. Ask yourself what you can give Jesus today with a sincere heart, and do not leave it for later.
exp.25:13:
This verse tells us that Judas Iscariot, one of Jesus' twelve disciples, went to the chief priests, that is, the religious leaders of Israel. He was one of those closest to Jesus.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Just before this, a woman had poured perfume on Jesus, and He said she did it to prepare Him for His burial. After that moment, Judas seeks out Jesus' enemies and agrees to hand Him over for thirty pieces of silver. The texts do not fully explain his motives; John mentions his love of money, but not everything is made clear.

We can be close to the things of God and yet drift away in our hearts. Today we can ask God to examine our decisions and keep us faithful to Jesus, without letting money or pride lead us astray.
exp.25:30:
Jesus tells his disciples that this very night they will all be offended because of him. The word he uses here is an older one, and in this verse it means stumbling, doubting, or giving up their faith out of fear or disappointment. He quotes Scripture: God will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.

Jesus speaks after the Last Supper, on the way to the Mount of Olives, shortly before his arrest. He quotes the prophet Zechariah (13:7) and presents himself as the Shepherd. He warns them of their falling away, but right away he promises that he will rise again and wait for them in Galilee. He does not reject them; he is already thinking about gathering them together again.

For today: all of us can fail when the test comes, even while believing we are firm, as Peter did. Instead of trusting in our own strength, let us trust in the Shepherd, who knows us, forgives us, and brings us back together.
exp.25:33:
Jesus tells Peter, very seriously, that this very night, before the cock crows, Peter will deny him three times. "Deny" here means saying that one does not know someone or has nothing to do with them.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after the Last Supper, on the way to the garden of Gethsemane. Peter had just declared that he would never leave him, even if the others did. Jesus knows Peter's heart and warns him, not to humiliate him, but to prepare him. He had already announced earlier that he would meet them again in Galilee, which leaves the door open to restoration.

We can have good intentions and still fail. Rather than trusting too much in our own strength, it is wise to ask God for help every day. And if we fall, Jesus still offers forgiveness and a new beginning.
exp.25:38:
Jesus goes a little way apart from his disciples and bows down to the ground, with his face to the earth. He prays to God, calling him "my Father," and asks that, if it is possible, the cup be taken away from him, an image of the suffering that awaits him. He finishes by surrendering himself: let what God wills be done, not what he himself wants.

Jesus is in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before his arrest. He has just told Peter, James, and John that his soul is deeply sorrowful, even to death. His prayer shows both his real anguish and his complete trust in the Father. Then he finds the disciples asleep.

For today: you can bring your fear and your wish that the pain would pass honestly before God. Then you can end as Jesus did, trusting that the Father's will is good, even when you do not understand it.
exp.25:39:
Jesus returns to where his disciples were and finds them asleep. He speaks to Peter, and really to all of them, with a question that sounds like a gentle rebuke: could you not stay awake with me even one hour?

Jesus is in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before his arrest. He had told them that his soul was very sorrowful, and he asked them to stay with him while he prayed. He speaks to Peter because shortly before this Peter had promised that he would never abandon him. Jesus immediately acknowledges human weakness: the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.

Today, when someone is suffering, sometimes the most valuable thing is simply being present. And in our own weakness, we can ask God for strength to remain alert in prayer.
exp.25:42:
He came back to where his disciples were and found them asleep again. The word "heavy" in the verse means that their eyes were so weighed down with sleep that they could not keep them open.

This happens in the garden of Gethsemane, the night before the crucifixion. Jesus had asked Peter, James, and John to stay awake and pray with him while he endured deep anguish. He himself had said that the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. The disciples wanted to stay with him, but tiredness and sorrow overcame them. Matthew does not present them harshly, but honestly.

For today: recognize your limits without making excuses. If you know that at a certain hour you give in, seek to care for your rest and set aside a specific time to pray. And remember that Jesus continues to treat with patience those who love him, even when they are weak.
exp.25:46:
As Jesus was still speaking with his disciples in Gethsemane, Judas arrived, one of the twelve. He came with a large crowd carrying swords and clubs. These people had been sent by the chief priests (the leaders of the temple) and by the elders of the people (the religious leaders).

The one telling the story is Matthew. Jesus had just prayed in anguish and had said that his hour had come. The leaders wanted to arrest him, and Judas, one of his closest followers, led them to him. Matthew emphasizes that he was "one of the twelve" to show how painful the betrayal was.

For today: Jesus faced this moment with calm, because he had prayed and had surrendered himself to the Father's will. When trials or betrayals come, we can seek God in prayer first, so that he may give us steadiness and peace.
exp.25:50:
This verse tells us that one of the disciples who was with Jesus drew his sword and cut off the ear of a servant of the high priest. The name is not given in this verse, but John 18:10 says it was Peter, and that the servant's name was Malchus.

It is the night of the arrest. Judas has just greeted Jesus with a kiss to betray him, and the crowd has already taken him prisoner. The disciple reacts on instinct, wanting to defend his Master. Jesus stops him right away, and Luke 22:51 tells us that he healed the wounded man.

For today: wanting to defend those we love is natural, but we should not do it with violence or anger. Jesus teaches us to trust God's plan and to respond with peace, even when something seems unjust.
exp.25:52:
Jesus asks whether anyone thinks he could not ask his Father for help. If he did, the Father would send him more than twelve legions of angels. A legion was a large unit of the Roman army, made up of thousands of soldiers; here the word points to an enormous power.

Jesus speaks in the garden of Gethsemane, just as he is being seized. One of his disciples draws a sword to defend him. Jesus stops him and explains that he does not need human defense. He accepts this path because the Scriptures had foretold that he would suffer.

For today: when life hurts or something seems unfair, we do not have to respond with violence or revenge. We can trust God, who is in control, and choose peace and obedience, as Jesus did.
exp.25:53:
Jesus asks: if He defended Himself with force or asked the angels for help, how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled? He says that it must be so, that is, that it is necessary for this to happen. Being fulfilled means coming true.

Jesus speaks with Peter in the garden of Gethsemane, just as they arrive to arrest him. Peter had drawn his sword to defend him. Jesus stops him and reminds him that He is not trapped or weak: He could ask heaven for help. But He chooses to give Himself up because He is following God's plan announced by the prophets. No one knows for certain which passages exactly he is referring to.

For today: when God asks us to go through something difficult, we can trust that He has a purpose. Let us respond with humility and confidence, not with violence or despair.
exp.25:56:
This verse tells that those who had arrested Jesus led him away to Caiaphas, the high priest. There the scribes (teachers of the law) and the elders (leaders of the people) were already gathered.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Jesus had just been arrested in Gethsemane and had said that all this was happening so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled. His disciples had fled. The religious leaders had already met during the night, and the account that follows shows that they were looking for false testimony to condemn him.

For today: Jesus faced injustice and loneliness without running away from his mission. When you are called to suffer for doing what is right, remember that he understands you. You can ask him for courage and faithfulness, even when others leave you alone.
exp.25:57:
It says that Peter was following Jesus, but at a distance, until he reached the courtyard of the high priest's house. The high priest in this case was Caiaphas. The servants were the household attendants and guards. Peter went in and sat down with them, wanting to see how everything would turn out, that is, to find out where it would all end.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Jesus had just been arrested, and the disciples had fled. Peter, though frightened, did not leave altogether: he kept following from a distance. The text does not say exactly what he felt, but it shows a mix of loyalty and fear. Soon after, Peter's denials would come.

For today: following Jesus from a distance can be a step toward falling. When you feel afraid to show your faith, do not pull back; draw near to Jesus in prayer and ask for courage to remain faithful, even in settings where that is not easy.
exp.25:60:
This verse tells what the two false witnesses said at Jesus' trial. They accused him of having said that he could tear down God's temple and rebuild it in three days.

The religious leaders were looking for any pretext to have Jesus condemned to death. The witnesses took some words Jesus had spoken earlier (John 2:19-21) and twisted them. According to John, Jesus was speaking about the temple of his body, which would rise again. They presented it as a threat against the temple in Jerusalem. That is why it was a twisted truth: it had something true in it, but it changed the meaning.

For today: let us guard our words and not repeat what we hear without understanding it well. A phrase taken out of its context can do great harm. Let us seek the whole truth before we speak or judge.
exp.25:64:
Here the high priest tears his clothes and says that Jesus has committed blasphemy, that is, that he has spoken against God in an offensive way. He says there is no longer any need for witnesses, because everyone has just heard his words.

Caiaphas, the high priest, presides over the trial. He had asked Jesus whether he was the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus answered with a reply affirming it and added that they would see him seated at the right hand of God, coming on the clouds. Caiaphas took this as an offense. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief or anger. Christians understand that Jesus was telling the truth about himself.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we listen to Jesus with an open heart or only defend what we already believed. Let us ask for humility to receive his word, even when it confronts us.
exp.25:66:
This verse tells how Jesus was mistreated after being declared guilty. They spat in his face, they struck him with slaps (blows with an open hand), and others hit him with punches, which are blows with a closed fist.

After the high priest, called here the chief priest, tore his clothes and accused Jesus of blasphemy, the religious leaders said that he deserved death. Those who struck him were probably the people who were there at the trial. The text does not give their names. They were mocking Jesus, who had said that he was the Christ.

For today: Jesus endured contempt and pain without returning evil for evil. When someone treats us unjustly or mocks us, we can ask God for patience, not answer with revenge, and remember that Jesus understands our suffering.
exp.25:70:
He says that Peter went out toward the gate, that is, toward the entrance of the courtyard. There another servant girl saw him and told those who were there, "This fellow was also with Jesus of Nazareth."

It is the night of Jesus' arrest. Matthew, the narrator, tells how Peter had stayed close by to see what was happening. He had already denied Jesus once, and now he moves away from the group, perhaps hoping to go unnoticed. But they recognize him again. In this way what Jesus had said about Peter's denials comes true.

For today: when we feel afraid that others will connect us with Jesus, we should not rely only on our own strength. We can pray beforehand, ask for courage, and remember that Christ forgave and restored Peter.
exp.25:72:
After a little while, some of the people standing nearby came up to Peter. They told him that he was surely one of Jesus' followers, because his speech gave him away.

The verse of this verse notes that the way Peter spoke, meaning his accent, made him known. It was his manner of speaking that revealed him.

The people speaking were present in the courtyard of the high priest, where Jesus was being tried. Peter was from Galilee, and many think his regional accent set him apart from the people of Jerusalem. This is a common explanation, though the text itself gives no further detail. Frightened, Peter would deny Jesus a third time.

For today: the way we speak and live ends up showing whom we belong to, even when we try to hide it. If we have failed out of fear, as Peter did, we can weep with repentance and return to Jesus, who forgives and restores.
exp.25:74:
Matthew tells us that Peter remembered what Jesus had said: before the rooster crowed, he would deny him three times. When he realized what he had done, he went out of the place and wept bitterly.

The narrator is Matthew. Jesus had been arrested, and Peter had followed him at a distance into the courtyard of the high priest. There, out of fear, he said three times that he did not know Jesus, even swearing to it. Shortly before, Peter had insisted that he would never deny him. When the rooster crowed, Jesus' word was fulfilled. The text does not explain everything Peter felt, but it shows a sincere grief.

All of us can fail, even after promising faithfulness. When that happens, do not hide it or make excuses. Acknowledge your mistake honestly, weep if you need to, and return to Jesus, who knows our weakness and offers forgiveness.
exp.26:0:
This verse says that at daybreak, the chief priests and the leaders of the people met to decide how to bring about Jesus' death. The "chief priests" were the most important priests; the "elders" were respected leaders of the people. The phrase about handing him over to death means arranging for him to be condemned to die.

Matthew narrates what happened after the night when Jesus was questioned. Here it is the narrator speaking, not a character. The religious leaders wanted to give their decision an appearance of legality, but they needed Roman authority to carry out the sentence, so they would bring Jesus before Pilate, as the account goes on to show.

For today: we must guard our hearts so that neither pride nor fear of losing our position leads us to reject the truth. Let us ask God for humility to listen to Jesus sincerely, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.26:1:
It says that the Jewish leaders bound Jesus and led him away to Pontius Pilate. The governor of Judea was a Roman official, and this is the man the verse names as the governor. To deliver someone here means to hand them over into the power of another authority.

The narrator is Matthew. At dawn, the chief priests and the elders had already decided that Jesus must die. But under Roman rule they needed Pilate's authority to carry out a sentence. That is why they took him to him. Matthew shows that Jesus was not caught by surprise: everything happens with his rejection and his suffering in full view.

For today: Jesus endured injustice without answering with revenge. When someone mistreats you or accuses you without reason, ask God for calm so that you can respond with truth and peace, trusting that he sees everything and does justice.
exp.26:2:
It says that Judas, the disciple who had handed Jesus over, saw that Jesus had been condemned. Then he was overcome with regret and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the leaders of the people. "Chief priests" means the principal priests.

Matthew tells what happened after the Jewish council brought Jesus before Pilate. Judas had accepted that money to betray Jesus (Matthew 26:14-16). Seeing the outcome, he felt the weight of what he had done and tried to undo it. Some understand that his sorrow was only remorse and not a true turning back to God, since it ended in despair.

For today: being sorry for a mistake is not enough; it must be brought to God, who forgives. Do not carry your guilt alone or shut yourself in hopelessness; seek his mercy and the help of trusted people.
exp.26:6:
This verse says that the chief priests, after talking among themselves, used the thirty pieces of silver that Judas returned to buy a piece of land known as the potter's field. That place would serve to bury strangers, that is, outsiders who died far from their own land. Deciding together after deliberation is what the phrase about taking counsel means.

Here the narrator, Matthew, speaks. The religious leaders did not want to keep that money in the temple treasury, because they regarded it as blood money, since it had paid for the betrayal of Jesus. Matthew sees in this the fulfillment of a prophecy; how it relates to the texts of Jeremiah and Zechariah is something scholars explain in several ways.

For today: we can care for our conscience. The priests pretended to be scrupulous about money, yet they had handed over an innocent man. Let us ask God for sincerity, so that we do not guard appearances while neglecting justice.
exp.26:11:
What it says: The religious leaders of the Jews were accusing Jesus before the Roman governor, and Jesus answered nothing. The chief priests were the leading priests, and the elders were respected leaders of the people.

Context: Matthew tells us that Jesus was already standing before Pilate, the governor of Rome. The Jewish leaders wanted him condemned to death. Jesus had only answered the question about being King with a brief reply. His silence recalls the prophecy in Isaiah 53:7 about the servant who does not open his mouth. Many believe Jesus stayed silent because he accepted to give himself up for us.

For today: We do not always have to defend ourselves against every attack or injustice. We can trust God, keep calm, and speak with wisdom when it is necessary.
exp.26:13:
It says that Jesus did not answer Pilate a single word in response to the accusations. Pilate was the governor, the Roman official Pontius Pilate. He was greatly amazed, meaning he was very astonished by that silence.

The chief priests and the elders were accusing Jesus before the Roman governor. Pilate asked him whether he did not hear how many accusations were being made against him, and Jesus did not respond. Many believers see here a fulfillment of Isaiah 53:7, where God's servant stays silent like a sheep before its shearers. Pilate, as a judge, did not expect that silence.

There are moments when we do not need to defend ourselves with many words. When we are unjustly accused, we can trust in God, keep calm, and respond with gentleness, as Jesus did, without letting ourselves be carried away by anger.
exp.26:16:
Pilate gathers the crowd and gives them a choice between two men: Barabbas, a well-known prisoner, or Jesus, who is called Christ, that is, the Messiah.

Pilate is the one speaking; he is the Roman governor. It was the custom at the Passover feast to release a prisoner. The text says that Pilate knew the religious leaders had handed Jesus over out of envy. It seems he hoped the people would choose Jesus. About Barabbas, the text only says he was well known; other gospels give more detail.

All of us face the decision of what to do with Jesus. Pilate tried to hand the decision to the crowd, but no one can avoid answering. Today we can ask ourselves honestly: what place am I giving Jesus in my decisions, and whom am I choosing to follow?
exp.26:19:
This verse tells how the chief priests and leaders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas to be set free and for Jesus to be put to death. "Chief priests" refers to the leading priests; "elders" were respected leaders of the people. The word "persuaded" means they succeeded in convincing the crowd.

Matthew is describing the trial before Pilate. He has just said that Pilate knew they had handed Jesus over out of envy, and Pilate's wife had warned him that Jesus was righteous. Pilate offers the crowd a choice between Barabbas, a well-known prisoner, and Jesus. The leaders influence the people so that they choose wrongly. The text does not describe how they persuaded them.

For today: we should not blindly follow the majority or influential leaders. Before we give an opinion or pass judgment, it is wise to seek the truth, pray, and think for ourselves with humility before God.
exp.26:23:
Pilate sees that he is getting nowhere and that the crowd is growing more agitated instead of calming down. So he takes water and washes his hands in front of everyone. He says that he is innocent of the blood of this righteous man, Jesus, and that they must take responsibility for it.

Pilate was the Roman governor. He had asked what wrong Jesus had done, and no one answered; they only shouted louder. Washing one's hands was a well-known gesture in Jewish tradition for declaring oneself free of guilt (Deuteronomy 21:6-7). Pilate uses it to shift the responsibility off himself, yet he handed Jesus over anyway. The texts show that he knew Jesus was innocent.

For today: it is not enough to declare yourself innocent when we know what is right and fail to act on it. Let us ask God for the courage to defend what is right, even when the pressure of the crowd is strong.
exp.26:24:
The crowd standing before Pilate answers his gesture of washing his hands. They take on responsibility for Jesus' death and say that his blood should fall on them and on their children. "Blood" here means the guilt for a death.

It describes a group of people gathered in Jerusalem, encouraged by the religious leaders, who were demanding crucifixion. Pilate wanted to clear himself of guilt, and the crowd took that weight upon themselves. This verse has been unjustly used to accuse the entire Jewish people of every era. That is a serious error: Jesus himself was Jewish, his first followers were Jewish, and the Bible teaches that he died for the sins of everyone.

For today: never use this text to look down on anyone. Rather, recognize that all of us need the forgiveness Jesus offers, and do not seek to place the blame on others, as Pilate did.
exp.26:25:
This verse tells that Pilate released Barabbas, a well-known prisoner, and ordered Jesus to be whipped. Afterward he handed him over to be crucified. The word for released means that he set him free. Whipping was striking with a lash, a very cruel punishment that usually went along with crucifixion.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Pilate, the Roman governor, had already said that Jesus was innocent, but he gave in to the pressure of the crowd to avoid more trouble. He washed his hands, yet he still gave the order. For Christians, this shows how Jesus took the place of Barabbas, a guilty man.

For today: Jesus bore a punishment he did not deserve, and because of this we can receive forgiveness. This invites us to be thankful and not to be swept along by the pressure of others when we know what is right.
exp.26:30:
This verse tells how the Roman soldiers finished mocking Jesus. They took off the scarlet cloak they had put on him as a joke, returned his own clothes to him, and led him out to be crucified.

It is part of Matthew's account of the suffering of Jesus. The narrator is Matthew, and the soldiers of the governor Pilate had mocked Jesus as the one who claimed to be a king. Without knowing it, they were laughing at the one who truly is King. Matthew shows that Jesus accepted this suffering without defending himself.

For today: when you feel despised or ridiculed for doing what is right, remember that Jesus went through that too, and he understands you. You can bring your pain to him in prayer and ask for strength to respond with patience and without seeking revenge.
exp.26:38:
Those who were passing by insulted Jesus while He was on the cross. The verse says they were speaking to Him with insults and mockery, and they shook their heads as a gesture of scorn and derision.

They were ordinary people who passed near the place of the crucifixion. They mocked Jesus for what He had said about the temple and for claiming to be the Son of God. With their words, and without realizing it, they repeated the kind of mockery that Psalm 22:7 had already foretold. Even so, Jesus did not respond with anger, and He continued on with His surrender for us.

Today, when someone mocks our faith, we can remember that Jesus went through something worse. We can respond with calm and with love, trusting that God sees everything and sustains us.
exp.26:41:
It says that the religious leaders were mocking Jesus on the cross. They acknowledge that He "saved others," but they say He cannot save Himself. They challenge Him to come down from the cross so they can believe in Him.

The chief priests, the scribes, the Pharisees, and the elders are the ones speaking, that is, the leaders of the people. Jesus had already been condemned, and they ridiculed Him in His suffering. They asked for a sign in order to believe, but their hearts were already closed. Without knowing it, they spoke a truth: precisely because He did not save Himself, He was able to save others.

For today: let us not place conditions on God before we believe Him. Jesus stayed on the cross out of love, and that self-giving is the greatest proof of who He is. Let us trust Him even when we do not understand His way.
exp.26:47:
He says that one of those present ran, took a sponge and filled it with vinegar. Then he put it on a reed and brought it to Jesus so that he might drink. The vinegar was a sour, cheap drink, common among the people of that time.

Jesus had just cried out on the cross, quoting Psalm 22:1. Some of the listeners thought he was calling for Elijah. This man acted quickly, perhaps to relieve his thirst, although the others wanted to wait and see whether Elijah would come. Scholars debate whether it was an act of compassion or of mockery. The text does not make this clear.

Even in the midst of pain and others' misunderstanding, Jesus was carrying out his mission for us. Today, a small act of kindness toward someone who suffers, even if imperfect, can be an act of love. Look for someone who is suffering this week and help them with something concrete.
exp.26:52:
It says that some saints who had died came out of their graves after Jesus's resurrection, went into Jerusalem, the holy city, and appeared to many people. "Appeared" means they were seen.

Matthew is the one narrating. He tells what happened when Jesus died: the veil of the temple was torn and the earth shook. The tombs were opened at that moment, but the coming out of the saints happened after Christ's resurrection. Matthew presents it as a sign that Jesus's death overcomes death. The text does not say who they were or what happened to them afterward, so it is not wise to invent details.

For today: the resurrection of Jesus is not just an idea, it is a real hope for those who trust in Him. If you are facing a loss today, you can rest in the knowledge that death does not have the final word.
exp.26:53:
This verse tells that the Roman captain and the soldiers who were guarding Jesus were filled with great fear when they saw the earthquake and everything that was happening. Then they said, "Truly this was the Son of God." A centurion is a Roman officer who commanded about one hundred soldiers. Watching means keeping guard, and feared greatly means they were overcome with a great deal of fear.

The speakers are the centurion along with his soldiers. Jesus had just died, and extraordinary signs took place: the earth shook and tombs were opened. Matthew shows that some non-Jewish men recognized what many Jewish leaders refused to see. We cannot know with certainty what they understood by "Son of God"; some think they meant it in its full sense, while others think it was a more limited confession.

Today we can learn that God can open the eyes of unexpected people. Let us ask to be attentive to his work and respond with humility and sincerity.
exp.26:55:
This verse names some of the women who watched Jesus' crucifixion from a distance: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee's children. According to Matthew, they had followed Jesus from Galilee and had been serving him.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is Matthew who is narrating. After Jesus' death, the centurion acknowledges that he was the Son of God, and Matthew highlights these women as present witnesses. It is often thought that the mother of Zebedee's children is the mother of the apostles James and John, but the text does not give her name. The women will continue to appear at the burial and the resurrection.

Today we can learn from their faithfulness. They did not run away, and they had no answers, but they stayed close. When faith feels confused or painful, staying close to Jesus, praying, serving, and supporting others is also a valuable act.
exp.26:58:
Matthew says that Joseph of Arimathea took the body of Jesus and carefully wrapped it in a clean linen cloth. The word "linen" refers to a cloth made of flax, and "clean" indicates a pure cloth, prepared with respect.

Matthew tells what happened after Jesus died. Pilate had already given permission, and Joseph, a rich man who had been following Jesus, came forward to give him a dignified burial. It was evening, and the day of rest was approaching. The text does not tell us everything he felt; it only shows his brave and respectful action.

For today: serving God and others in difficult moments, when others pull away, is an act of love. You may not be able to solve everything, but you can do with care and reverence what is within your reach.
exp.26:59:
Joseph of Arimathea placed Jesus' body in his own tomb, a new one that he had cut into the rock. Then he rolled a large stone across the entrance to the tomb and went away.

Matthew is the one telling this, and he describes what happened after Jesus' death. Joseph, a rich man and a follower of Jesus, asked Pilate for the body so he could bury it with respect. At that time, a new tomb was sealed with a large stone. Matthew makes clear that Jesus truly died and was buried, which prepares the account of the resurrection.

For today: Joseph used what he had to honor Jesus, even when everything seemed lost. We can serve God with what we have, even in moments of pain or silence, trusting that he continues to work.
exp.26:60:
Matthew says that Mary Magdalene and the other Mary stayed sitting opposite the tomb where they had laid Jesus. The tomb is the place where Jesus was buried. Unlike Joseph of Arimathea, they did not leave; they remained looking at the place, in silence and sorrow.

Matthew, the author, records this right after the death of Jesus and his burial. Joseph of Arimathea had already closed the tomb with a large stone. Matthew mentions these women as witnesses: they saw where Jesus was buried. Later, they will also be the first to go to the empty tomb. Who "the other Mary" was is understood in different ways, but here she is simply presented as a follower of Jesus.

For today: when you feel pain or do not understand what is happening, do not turn away from God. Stay close to Him, even in silence. Faithfulness in dark moments also counts.
exp.26:62:
The chief priests and the Pharisees speak to Pilate. They call him "Sir," out of respect. They say they remember that Jesus, whom they call a deceiver, said while he was still alive that after three days he would rise again.

The ones speaking are the religious leaders who wanted Jesus dead. It was the Sabbath, the day after the day of preparation, which was Friday. They remember Jesus' words better than many of his disciples did. They fear that someone will steal the body and claim he has risen, so they ask for the tomb to be guarded.

For today: we can keep the Word of God in mind and still close our hearts. Let us not only remember what Jesus said, but believe it and follow him with humility.
exp.26:65:
This verse tells us that the religious leaders went to Jesus' tomb and made it secure. That is, they closed it tightly and posted guards over it. To do this, they sealed the stone, meaning they put an official mark on it that would show if anyone had moved it, and they set soldiers on watch.

The ones who speak before this are the chief priests and the Pharisees. They remembered that Jesus had said he would rise on the third day. They feared that his disciples would steal the body and deceive the people. Pilate answered them that they already had a guard and that they could secure the tomb as they wished. The texts do not say exactly how the seal was made, so it is best not to add details.

For today: human plans cannot stop what God has decided to do. If you ever feel that a situation is closed and sealed, trust that God can act even where we see no way out.
exp.27:1:
This verse reports that there was a great earthquake. An angel of the Lord came down from heaven, arrived at the tomb, and rolled away the stone that closed it. Then he sat down on it.

The one telling the story is Matthew, and he recounts the morning of the resurrection. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were going to see the tomb. The angel did not open the tomb so that Jesus could come out; rather, he showed that it was already empty. The guards, out of fear, became like dead men. Matthew thus emphasizes that God acted with power.

When everything seems closed off and without a way out, remember that God can move stones you cannot move. Do what is yours to do with faithfulness, and trust that He is at work even when you cannot see it.
exp.27:2:
This verse describes the angel of the Lord who came down from heaven and rolled back the stone from the tomb. His appearance is his look, his face or figure. He shone like lightning, with a strong and sudden light. His clothing was white as snow, an image of purity and of the heavenly.

Matthew is the one telling the story. The women came to the tomb at dawn on the first day of the week. Before they went in, there was an earthquake, and the angel opened the tomb. The guards were filled with fear and became like dead men. Then the angel calmed the women and told them that Jesus was no longer there. The scene shows that the resurrection is the work of God's power.

For today: when your situation feels sealed shut like a tomb, remember that God can open paths you cannot see. His power is greater than your fear, and so you can trust Him.
exp.27:5:
He is not here, because he has risen, just as Jesus had said. The angel invites the women to look at the empty tomb.

The angel of the Lord speaks to Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, who arrived at the tomb full of sadness and fear. The guards had been left as if dead from fright. The angel calms them and shows them the evidence before sending them to tell the news to the disciples.

For today: the Christian faith does not rest on a vague idea, but on a fact that God fulfilled, just as he promised. When fear or doubt surround you, come honestly to the Scriptures and remember that Jesus keeps his word. And like the women, share with someone the hope you have.
exp.27:10:
It says that, while the women were going to tell the disciples, some of the soldiers from the guard watching the tomb went into the city. They went to the chief priests and told them everything that had happened.

Matthew is the one telling the story. The soldiers had seen the earthquake and the angel at the tomb (verses 2-4). While the women carry the news of the resurrection to the disciples, the guards carry their report to the religious leaders who had posted them there. The text does not say exactly what they said, but the leaders reacted with a plan to keep the matter quiet.

For today: the truth about Christ can reach the ears of people who do not want to believe it. May our response to what God shows us not be to hide it, but to open our hearts with honesty.
exp.27:13:
This verse says that if the governor hears that the soldiers claimed they fell asleep while guarding the tomb, the leaders of the Jews will speak to him and convince him. That way the soldiers will not be in trouble. "Governor" is the word used here, meaning Pontius Pilate.

The chief priests and the elders are the ones speaking. The soldiers had told them what happened at Jesus' tomb. Instead of accepting the truth, the leaders paid them to lie. A soldier found asleep on duty could be punished severely, which is why they promise to protect them.

Today this passage invites us to be honest, even when the truth is uncomfortable. Money and fear can silence or twist the truth, but God's truth does not stop.
exp.27:16:
They say that the disciples, upon seeing Jesus risen on the mountain in Galilee, worshipped him, that is, they bowed before him in reverence. But some doubted. The text does not explain what they doubted, and scholars understand it in several ways: doubts about whether it really was him, or hesitation and bewilderment before something so astonishing.

Matthew is recounting Jesus' meeting with the eleven disciples, just as he had commanded them. Judas was absent, and they were still taking in the resurrection. Right after this, Jesus comes near and gives them the great commission.

For today: you can come to Jesus with faith and doubts at the same time. He does not turn away from those who doubt; he draws near, speaks to them, and gives them a mission. Worship him even with questions.
exp.27:17:
Jesus came near to his disciples and spoke to them. He declared that all authority has been given to him. This authority, a word that means power or rule, extends over heaven and earth, that is, over everything that exists. The wording shows that the Father is the one who gave it to him.

He speaks as the risen Jesus, on a mountain in Galilee, with the eleven disciples. Some worshiped him and others doubted. Before sending them to make disciples of all nations, he affirms who he is and how much he can do. His authority is the foundation of the mission that follows.

For today: when you feel fear or doubt about sharing your faith or about obeying God, remember that you do not depend on your own strength. Jesus has all authority, and he promised to be with you. Take the next step with confidence, supported by him.
exp.26:64:
Pilate answers the chief priests and the Pharisees. He tells them they have a guard and that they should go and make the tomb as secure as they know how. The wording is plain: "make the tomb as secure as you know how" means to secure the tomb as well as they are able.

The religious leaders have just reminded Pilate that Jesus had said he would rise on the third day. They fear that the disciples will steal the body and say he has risen. Pilate does not argue or get more involved: he gives them permission and leaves the task to them. Scholars debate whether that guard was Roman soldiers or temple guards; the text does not make it entirely clear.

For today: human efforts to stop God's plans cannot defeat him. Instead of resisting what God is doing, we can trust in his power and in his word.
exp.13:7:
She asks for the head of John the Baptist on a platter, prompted by her mother beforehand. The phrase "prompted by her mother" tells us she was urged or directed to make this request. The word "here" shows that she wanted it right away, on the spot.

The one speaking is Herodias's daughter, to whom Herod had promised with an oath to give whatever she asked. According to the account, John had rebuked Herod for his marriage to Herodias (Matthew 14:3-4), and she held a grudge against him. So the request comes from her mother's influence. The text does not say what the young woman herself was thinking inside.

For today: be careful with promises made lightly, and with pride before others. Herod knew that what was being asked was wrong, but he gave in to look good. Let us ask God for the courage to do what is right even when others are watching us.
exp.21:8:
This verse says the king sends his servants to the crossroads, the places where streets meet and roads cross outside the city, and tells them to invite to the banquet as many people as they can find. The word translated "crossroads" is the word in the verse itself, so no further comment is needed on it.

Jesus tells this parable to the chief priests and Pharisees in the temple, shortly before his crucifixion. The king represents God, and the first guests refused his call. Many readers understand this to show how Israel rejected the message and how the invitation was opened to all, though there are different ways of interpreting the details.

For today: God invites everyone, regardless of their past. We can share that invitation generously, without deciding who deserves it, and respond ourselves with humility and sincerity.
exp.16:6:
It says that Jesus came close to his disciples, who were lying on the ground in fear, and touched them. Then he said to them, "Get up," and "Do not be afraid." The word "came" means that he drew near to them.

This happens on the mountain of the transfiguration. Peter, James, and John had just seen the glory of Jesus and heard the voice of God the Father from the cloud. That holy moment filled them with awe. Jesus, who speaks here, does not rebuke them but draws near with tenderness. Afterward, they see Jesus alone, just as always.

When God overwhelms us or life frightens us, Jesus does not leave us lying on the ground. He comes near, touches us with his closeness, and invites us to rise. We can trust that his presence is stronger than our fear.
exp.4:0:
When Jesus saw the crowds, He went up on the mountain and sat down. His disciples came to Him. The word "crowds" refers to the large numbers of people gathered around Him, and "came to Him" means that they drew near to Him.

Here the Sermon on the Mount begins. Jesus is the one speaking, and He does so surrounded by people who followed Him because of His healings and teachings. Sitting was the usual posture of a teacher when teaching. The disciples come close to hear Him up close. It is not known with certainty which mountain it was; the text does not say.

For today: Jesus teaches those who come near to Him. We can set aside a moment each day, leave the noise of the crowd behind, and draw near to Jesus with attention to hear His word.
exp.12:35:
Matthew 13:36 tells us that Jesus dismissed the crowds and went into a house. There his disciples came to him and asked him to explain the parable of the weeds in the field. "Dismissed the crowds" means that he sent the people away. The weeds in this parable are the kind that look like wheat.

The ones speaking here are the disciples, who stayed with Jesus. He had been teaching the crowds in parables, and many listened without understanding. The disciples, however, were not content just to hear: they came to him and asked. In this we see that Jesus explained things in private to those who wanted to understand.

For today: when you do not understand something in the Bible, do as the disciples did. Come to Jesus sincerely, ask him for light in prayer, and look for answers in his Word, perhaps together with other believers. Asking humbly is a sign of faith, not of weakness.
exp.4:40:
It says that if someone forces you to carry his load one mile, you should go with him two miles. The word "forces" here means making someone do something against their will. The first sentence of the old wording is not needed for your reading.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. At that time Roman soldiers could force people to carry their baggage for a distance, and the Jews felt this as a humiliation. Jesus teaches us to respond to evil without revenge, with generosity and inner freedom. This connects with his words about loving even your enemy.

Today it can mean that when someone demands a favor from you with a bad attitude, or gives you an unfair task, you do it with a good spirit and even give a little more. It is not allowing yourself to be mistreated without limit, but refusing to repay evil with evil and answering with kindness.
exp.22:21:
And he who swears by heaven swears by God's throne and by the One who sits on it. The "One" refers to God. There is no oath that leaves God out.

Jesus is speaking to the scribes and Pharisees. They taught that some oaths were more binding than others, and so they found ways to avoid keeping what they had promised. Jesus shows them that this trick makes no sense, because everything created belongs to God and is bound to Him. That is why he calls them hypocrites, since they guarded the outward forms but neglected sincerity.

For today: let us be people of our word. We do not need clever phrases or excuses to escape what we have promised. Let us live knowing that God hears every word, and let our "yes" be yes.
exp.12:56:
The people of Nazareth took offense at Jesus. Here "took offense" means they stumbled over him: they could not accept him. Jesus answers with a well-known saying: a prophet is without honor only in his hometown and in his own household. "Honor" means respect or esteem.

Jesus was teaching in the synagogue of his hometown, and his neighbors were amazed at his wisdom. But they had known him since he was a child: they knew who his family was and what his trade was. That is why they found it hard to believe he was more than an ordinary man. The next verse says that Jesus did not do many miracles there because of their unbelief.

Today, familiarity and habit can close our hearts. Let us ask God for humility to hear his Word with fresh eyes, without letting prejudice keep us from receiving what he wants to give us, even through people who are close to us.
exp.7:8:
What it says: The centurion explains that he too lives under authority, since he has people above him. At the same time, he has soldiers under his command. When he tells one, "Go," he goes; and when he tells another, "Come," he comes. He also says that when he tells his servant to do something, the servant does it. "Authority" means the power to give orders and have them obeyed, and "servant" refers to a household worker.

Context: The speaker is a Roman officer, a commander of about a hundred soldiers. His servant was sick, and he came to Jesus. Since he did not feel worthy to have Jesus come into his house, he asked that a single word be enough. He understood that Jesus had authority over the illness, and Jesus marveled at that faith.

For today: Trust that the word of Jesus has real authority, even when you do not see the result right away. Bring your needs to him with humility and rest in the fact that he can act, in his own way and in his own time.
exp.11:49:
Jesus says that whoever does the will of God, his heavenly Father, belongs to his family. The word "whoever" points to anyone who obeys God. So any person who obeys God is, for Jesus, like a brother, a sister, or a mother.

Jesus is speaking while he teaches the people. Someone tells him that his mother and his brothers are outside, looking for him. He answers with a question and points to his disciples. He is not rejecting his family; rather, he shows that true closeness to him is based on obedience to God, not only on ties of blood.

Today we can remember that following Jesus unites us with other believers as a family. One practical way to live this is to draw near to someone in the church, listen to them and help them, and at the same time ask ourselves this week: what does God want me to do today?
exp.17:6:
Jesus says the world will suffer because of "causes of sin," which the Berean Standard Bible calls stumbling blocks: things that lead others into wrong or cause them to lose their faith. He states that these stumbling blocks must come, but he warns sternly against the one through whom they come.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after teaching them about humility and the worth of children. The "little ones who believe in me" are those who are simple and weak in faith. He shows how much he cares for them and how serious it is to make them stumble. This connects with his call to remove from our lives everything that causes us to fall.

Today we can ask ourselves how our words and example affect those who are most fragile in faith. Let us be careful, ask forgiveness when we fail, and try to be support, not a stumbling block, for others.
exp.3:4:
Then the devil takes him to the holy city, which is Jerusalem, and sets him on the highest point of the temple. The highest part and the edge of the building are what is meant here. The words "takes" and "sets" in this verse are simply the ordinary words for carrying and placing him there. The text does not say how the move happened; some understand it as something physical, and others as a spiritual experience.

Matthew speaks of the second temptation in the wilderness. Jesus had just answered with Scripture, and now the devil also quotes a psalm, but he misuses it to push him to test God's care.

For today: it is not enough to quote the Bible; we must understand it as a whole and with humility. Before using a verse to justify a risky decision, ask yourself whether you are trusting God or putting him to the test.
exp.10:4:
Jesus lists what is happening: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor. Each of these works shows that God's power is at work in Him. The healing of leprosy means the lepers are made clean and restored to ordinary life.

John the Baptist was in prison and sent his disciples to ask whether Jesus was the expected Messiah. Jesus does not give a simple "yes," but tells them to report what they see and hear. These works recall what the prophet Isaiah had announced about the time of the Messiah (Isaiah 35:5-6; 61:1). In this way Jesus invites John to recognize the sign.

For today: when doubts arise, you do not have to hide them. Bring them to Jesus with sincerity, and look at what He has done and continues to do, especially His care for the weak and the poor.
exp.14:25:
Jesus says that it is not right to take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs. The word "toss" means to throw it away, and "dogs" here refers to small dogs, the kind kept in the home. The "bread" stands for Jesus' help and blessings, and the "children" are the people of Israel.

Jesus is speaking with a Canaanite woman who asks him to heal her daughter. He had just said that his mission was first toward Israel. Scholars debate the tone of this statement: some see a test of her faith, others an expression of the order of his mission. She is not offended and answers with humility.

For today: when God seems silent or slow to act, we can keep coming to him with humility and trust. Persistent faith does not demand, but it does not give up either.
exp.26:14:
This verse describes a custom: every year, at the feast of Passover, the Roman governor (the governor is Pilate) would release one prisoner, and the crowd would choose which one. The phrase "was the governor's custom" means he regularly did this.

The one telling the story is Matthew. Jesus is already before Pilate, accused by the Jewish leaders, and He remains silent. Pilate is surprised. He appears to be looking for a way out of condemning Him, and so he offers this custom. Outside the Gospels, historians have no clear record of this practice, so we know it only from the biblical accounts.

For today: crowds and pressures often push us to decide wrongly. Before choosing, stop, pray, and ask what is right before God, not what is popular.
exp.17:7:
Jesus says that if your hand or your foot causes you to sin, it is better to cut it off and throw it away. He would rather you enter life crippled or lame than have two hands and two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire. The word "causes you to sin" means something that leads you to stumble or do wrong. A "crippled" or "lame" person is someone whose hand or foot is unable to work or walk as it should.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples about not leading astray the "little ones" who believe in him, and about taking care of themselves. Almost everyone understands that the language is deliberately exaggerated: he is not commanding self-mutilation, but telling us to take sin with complete seriousness.

Today we can ask ourselves what specific thing causes us to fall, such as a friendship, a habit, or content on our phone. With God's help, we must stay away from that without bargaining, even when it costs us.
exp.18:14:
This verse says that Jesus, after placing his hands on the children to bless them, went on from that place. Laying hands on someone was a common gesture of blessing and prayer for them.

Jesus is the one acting here. Some people brought the children to him so that he would pray for them, and the disciples scolded them. Jesus corrected his disciples and said that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who are like these children. This verse closes that scene. Right after, a man comes to ask him how to gain eternal life.

For today: Jesus did not leave until he had first blessed the children. Today we can give the little ones our time, attention, and prayer, and receive their simple trust as an example for our own faith.
exp.10:22:
Jesus says to Capernaum that she was "lifted up to heaven," meaning greatly favored, but that she will be "brought down" to Hades, the place of the dead, a picture of total downfall. He says that if Sodom had seen the miracles done in Capernaum, it would still be standing today.

Jesus speaks to cities of Galilee where he had done many miracles and taught, but the people did not change their lives. Capernaum was like his base in that region. He rebukes them with sadness and firmness, because seeing so much and not repenting brings greater responsibility.

For today: if we have heard the Word many times, it is not enough to admire it. Ask yourself today what truth of Jesus you already know and have not yet obeyed, and take one concrete step to answer him with humility.
exp.14:29:
This verse tells that large crowds came to Jesus bringing their sick: the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others. They laid them at his feet, and Jesus healed them. "Laid them" here means they placed them there, probably in haste and hope.

The one telling the story is Matthew. Jesus had just healed the daughter of a foreign woman because of her great faith. Then he went to the Sea of Galilee and sat down on a mountain. There the people sought him out, and after the healings they praised the God of Israel. This prepares the account of the feeding of the multitude with bread.

For today: just as those people brought their sick to Jesus, you can bring the people you love and their needs to him in prayer. You do not have to fix everything yourself; lay them at his feet and trust his compassion.
exp.11:42:
This verse says that when an evil spirit comes out of a person, it passes through arid, empty places looking for a place to rest, and it does not find one. "Unclean" means impure or evil. The "arid places" are understood as desert sites, lifeless and barren, and some think they symbolize a place without inhabitants where the spirit cannot find a place to settle.

Jesus speaks to scribes and Pharisees who were asking him for a sign, after comparing them with Nineveh and the queen of the South, who did respond to God. With this image, Jesus warns that a superficial cleansing, without a life filled with God, leaves the door open to a greater evil. Interpreters explain in various ways how this applies to that generation.

For today: it is not enough to simply give up a bad habit; the heart must be filled with God. Devote time to his Word, to prayer, and to obeying him, so that no emptiness is left behind.
exp.14:22:
He did not answer her a word. Then his disciples came and urged him, "Send her away, for she keeps crying out after us."

Jesus was in the region of Tyre and Sidon, land of the Gentiles. A Canaanite woman, who was not an Israelite, was pleading with him for her daughter, who was tormented by a demon. The disciples speak here, perhaps annoyed by the noise, or wanting Jesus to help her so that she would leave; the text does not make this clear. Jesus' silence seems to be part of a test or a lesson, and interpreters explain it in several ways.

When it seems that God is silent in response to your prayer, do not lose heart. Keep crying out with humility and faith, like this woman, trusting that He hears and acts in his own time.
exp.12:4:
Some seed fell on rocky ground, where there was little soil on top of the rock. The seed sprang up quickly, because the soil was shallow. "Rocky ground" refers to land full of stones, and "quickly" conveys how fast the plants came up.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd by the sea and teaches in parables, which are simple stories with a deeper message. Later in the chapter (vv. 18-23) he explains that this ground represents the person who receives the word with joy but has no root and falls away when trouble comes.

Faith that grows quickly is not always firm faith. Today we can put down roots by devoting time to prayer, to reading the Bible, and to fellowship with other believers, so that our faith can endure the hard days.
exp.13:1:
Herod tells his servants that Jesus is John the Baptist, who he believes has come back to life after being dead. For that reason, in his view, powers are at work in Jesus. The word "servants" here means attendants or household workers, and "powers" refers to miracles.

The speaker is Herod Antipas, ruler of a region of Jewish territory. He heard about Jesus' reputation and became frightened. He had imprisoned John because John had told him it was not lawful for him to have Herodias, his brother's wife. His fear suggests a guilty conscience. The text does not explain everything he was thinking, but it shows that he could not ignore John or Jesus.

When we ignore or silence the voice of truth, the conscience keeps speaking. Instead of hardening ourselves or inventing explanations, we can listen to God with humility, acknowledge our wrongs, and ask him for forgiveness and change.
exp.10:0:
Matthew 11:1 says that after Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their towns. The verse marks a shift in the story, as Jesus moves from preparing his followers to continuing his own work.

Here the narrator is Matthew. After preparing the twelve for their mission, Jesus does not simply wait around; he carries on with his own work of teaching and announcing the kingdom. Some readers understand "their towns" to mean the towns of Galilee, though the text does not spell this out. The next verse shows John the Baptist, now in prison, beginning to have doubts.

For today: teaching others does not free us from continuing to practice ourselves. Jesus prepared his disciples and still kept serving. If you help others in their faith, keep growing and serving steadily yourself too.
exp.12:24:
This verse tells how, while everyone was asleep, the enemy of the owner of the field came, sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away. The weeds are a plant that, as it grows, looks very much like wheat. "Slipped away" means he left without anyone noticing.

Jesus is speaking to the crowds and tells this parable to explain what the kingdom of heaven is like. It comes right after the parable of the sower. Here he shows that, although God sows good seed, there is also an enemy who works in secret. Later Jesus himself explains the meaning (Matthew 13:36-43).

For today: do not be discouraged if you see good and bad things mixed together in the church or in your own life. Stay alert in prayer, guard your heart, and trust that God will separate everything in his time.
exp.2:6:
John the Baptist sees that many Pharisees and Sadducees are coming to his place of baptism. He says to them, "You brood of vipers," meaning people with a deceitful and dangerous heart. Then he asks who warned them to escape from the coming wrath, that is, from God's judgment.

John speaks, calling the people to repent and confess their sins. Pharisees and Sadducees were influential religious groups. John suspects they seek baptism as a formality, without any real change. That is why, in the verses that follow, he asks for fruit worthy of repentance and warns them that being children of Abraham is not enough.

For today: it is not enough to keep rituals, attend church, or have a good religious reputation. Ask God to examine your heart, and if needed, change one concrete attitude or habit this week as a sign of sincere repentance.
exp.10:10:
Jesus says that, of all the people born up to that time, no one was greater than John the Baptist. But he adds something surprising: the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John. The phrase "born of women" is an old way of saying "all human beings."

Jesus speaks to the crowd, after John's disciples, while John was in prison, asked whether He was the Messiah. Jesus defends John: he was the messenger who prepared the way. Many understand that the difference is not one of personal merit but of privilege: John lived before the cross and the resurrection, and those who are in the kingdom receive what he only announced. Some interpret it in other ways.

For today: do not measure yourself by your achievements or your strength. Your greatness lies in belonging to Christ and his kingdom. Give thanks for that gift and live with humility.
exp.24:34:
Jesus says that he was hungry and you gave him something to eat, he was thirsty and you gave him something to drink, and he was a stranger and you took him in. The word "stranger" here means a foreigner or someone passing through without a home. "You took me in" means they welcomed him and gave him a place to stay.

Jesus speaks as the King who judges the nations at the end of time. He separates the sheep from the goats. He invites the sheep to inherit the kingdom. Their acts of compassion show that their faith is real. In the verses that follow, Jesus explains that what they did for the neediest, they did for him. Some understand that these "brothers" are believers, and others that they are any person in need.

Today you can help a specific person: bring food to a neighbor who is in need, or invite a migrant or someone alone to your table. Do it as if you were doing it for Christ.
exp.25:41:
Jesus goes away a second time to pray in the garden. He calls God "my Father" and speaks to him with confidence. The "cup" is an image of the suffering and judgment he was about to face, and "may Your will be done" means "let what You want be accomplished."

Jesus speaks with his Father shortly before he is arrested. He is deeply distressed, and his disciples, overcome by sleep, cannot keep watch with him. His prayer is sincere: he acknowledges the weight of what is coming, but he leaves the decision in God's hands. Interpreters explain in different ways what exactly the "cup" contains, though all of them connect it with his death.

Today we can speak to God with complete honesty about our fears, and still say, "May Your will be done." Praying this way is not cold resignation, but trust that he is good.
exp.25:37:
Jesus tells his closest friends that his soul is consumed with a sorrow so deep that it nearly takes his life. "Keep watch" means to stay awake and alert. He asks them to remain there and keep him company. "Consumed with sorrow to the point of death" is a way of saying the pain is enormous, so strong that it could cost him his life.

Jesus speaks with Peter, James and John in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before he is arrested. He knows what is coming: the cross. He withdraws a little to pray to the Father, but first he asks his friends to stay with him. It is a deeply human moment for Jesus, showing his anguish without hiding it.

It is healthy to acknowledge our sadness and not pretend that everything is fine. Jesus did not conceal his. He seeks God in prayer and lets trusted people walk with him. Sometimes, being present with someone who is suffering is the best gift we can give.
exp.25:45:
Jesus tells his disciples to get up and go with him. He announces that the one who betrays him is already close by, that is, Judas, who is about to hand him over. The words "Rise" and "See" call attention to what is happening right now.

Jesus speaks in the garden of Gethsemane, after praying three times in anguish. The disciples had fallen asleep. Now Jesus does not run or hide: he goes out to face what is coming. He understands that the hour had arrived to give himself up according to the Father's will. While he is speaking, Judas appears with the crowd.

For today: after prayer, God gives us strength to face hard things without hiding. When something difficult is unavoidable, we can rise with calm, trusting that God remains with us.
exp.24:42:
This verse describes what the King says to those on his left: they did not help people in need. "I was a stranger and you did not take Me in" means he was a foreigner, someone passing through without a home, and they did not welcome him into their homes. "I was naked and you did not clothe Me" means he lacked clothing, and they did not give him anything to wear. He was also sick and in prison, and no one looked after him.

Jesus speaks in the teaching about the final judgment, when he separates the sheep from the goats. He identifies himself with the most vulnerable. According to the verses that follow, ignoring "these least" is ignoring him. Some understand this to refer to anyone in need; others, especially, to the disciples of Jesus. Both views call for compassion.

Today, think of someone close to you who is alone, sick, or lacking something. Call them, visit them, or help with something concrete this week.
exp.17:9:
Jesus warns: "See that you do not look down on any of these little ones." The idea is to regard someone as unimportant or to give them no value. He says that their angels in heaven always see the face of the Father. Many understand from this that God cares very closely for the little ones; the Bible does not explain in detail how these angels work, and Christians have understood this in several ways.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, who had just asked who is the greatest in the kingdom. He set a child in the midst of them and taught them humility. Then he warned against causing others to stumble, and after that he told the parable of the lost sheep, which shows that the Father does not want any one of them to be lost.

Today we can treat with respect and patience those who seem weak or unimportant: children, new believers, humble people. For God, each one is worth a great deal.
exp.20:17:
