This verse tells that Jesus, early in the morning, was returning to Jerusalem from Bethany, and he was hungry. The phrase "as Jesus was returning to the city" means that he was going back to Jerusalem, and "He was hungry" shows that he was fully human, with physical needs like our own.

The account follows the day when Jesus was praised by the children in the temple. He had spent the night in Bethany, a nearby village. Matthew narrates in the third person and sets up the scene of the fig tree, which comes right after. Many understand that fig tree as a sign for Israel, but this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: Jesus knows weariness and hunger, so you can bring him your daily needs with confidence. He does not look at you from afar; he understands what it is to live in a frail body.
exp.16:16:
Jesus answers with grief and firmness: "O unbelieving and perverse generation!" Unbelieving means lacking trust in God, and perverse means turned away from what is right. He asks how long he must remain with them and how long he must put up with them. Then he says, "Bring the boy here to Me."

A desperate father has asked for help for his son, who was suffering dangerous seizures. The disciples had not been able to heal him. Jesus speaks in the plural, so his rebuke reaches the whole crowd, and probably the disciples too, since he later explains to them that they lacked faith (v. 20). It is not an outburst of anger but sorrow over unbelief. Even so, he immediately asks for the boy so that he can heal him.

For today: when our faith fails us or our situation overwhelms us, let us not turn away. Let us bring our burdens to Jesus; He still says, "Bring the boy here to Me."
exp.11:33:
Jesus calls some Pharisees a "brood of vipers," meaning people whose character is harmful, like poisonous snakes. He asks how they can say anything good when they are evil inside. Then he gives the principle: the mouth speaks out of what fills the heart. The "overflow" here means what is full inside and spills out.

Jesus had just healed a man, and the Pharisees were saying he did it by the power of the devil. He answers that a tree is known by its fruit. Their accusing words revealed what was in their hearts. Interpreters debate exactly what the sin against the Holy Spirit is, but the context points to a stubborn rejection of God's work.

For today: if your words come out harsh or bitter, don't stop at only controlling your tongue. Ask God to heal your heart and fill it with his Word and prayer.
exp.11:2:
Jesus answers the Pharisees with a question: "Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry?" With this he leads them to remember a well-known account from the Scriptures.

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees, who were accusing his disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking heads of grain to eat. He relies on 1 Samuel 21, where David and his men, hungry, ate the holy bread of God's house. Jesus shows that human need and mercy matter, and that the Law cannot be understood without them.

Today we can take care that our faith does not become nothing but cold rules. Before judging someone, let us ask whether we are showing mercy, as God desires it, and whether we understand the purpose behind his commands.
exp.18:7:
Jesus answers the Pharisees that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of the people's hearts, not because it was God's plan. "To divorce" here means to send away a wife, or to end the marriage with her. "But it was not this way from the beginning" means that, since creation, God intended marriage to be a lasting union.

Jesus is speaking with some Pharisees who are testing him by asking about divorce. They cite the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 24:1-4). Jesus leads them back to Genesis, to God's original design. According to Jesus, the law of Moses regulated a painful reality; it did not approve it as the ideal.

For today: before asking what is permitted, let us ask what God desires. Let us care for our marriages with humility, forgiveness, and a heart willing to be healed, without becoming hardened.
exp.25:4:
What it says: The religious leaders were planning to arrest Jesus and kill him, but they said they would not do it during the feast. A riot is a violent disturbance. They feared the people would be stirred up if they seized him during those days.

Context: The speakers are the chief priests, the scribes and the elders, gathered in the house of the high priest Caiaphas. The feast was Passover, when Jerusalem filled with pilgrims. They feared losing control and the approval of the people. Even so, the events that follow show that God carried everything out according to his purpose, and that Jesus was handed over during that very Passover.

For today: We can examine our motives. These men cared more about their image and their control than about the truth. Let us ask God for a sincere heart, one that does not act out of fear of what others think.
exp.4:2:
Jesus says that those who are "blessed" are the "poor in spirit," meaning those who recognize that they need God and do not consider themselves self-sufficient or superior. To them belongs the kingdom of heaven, that is, God's rule and blessing. The word "blessed" means fortunate through the grace of God.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, with the crowd nearby, at the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount. With these words he opens his teaching about how those who belong to God live. Some scholars see here humility before God; others add the idea of people who suffer lack. Both ideas can coexist in the text.

Today we can pray with sincerity: "Lord, I need you." Recognizing our limitations, asking for help, and treating others without pride opens the door to God's grace.
exp.11:36:
Jesus says that our words reveal who we are on the inside and will be weighed before God. "Acquitted" means declared innocent or righteous; "condemned" means declared guilty. What we say is not a matter of little importance.

Here Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees, who had just accused him of casting out demons by the power of Satan. He explains to them that the mouth speaks out of what fills the heart. His harsh words showed a closed heart. Many understand that words are evidence of faith or of a hardened heart, not a way of earning salvation by speaking well.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself what is in your heart. Ask God to cleanse it, and try to make your words encourage, tell the truth, and be respectful, especially when you are upset.
exp.26:26:
Then the soldiers of the governor, Pilate, took Jesus into the Praetorium, which was the governor's headquarters, and gathered the whole company of soldiers around Him. The word "company" refers to the cohort, a large group of soldiers. Some scholars think it was not necessarily the six hundred men of a full cohort, but a good number of them.

Matthew is telling what happened right after Pilate released Barabbas, ordered Jesus to be flogged, and handed him over to be crucified. Here it is neither Jesus nor Pilate who speaks, but the narrator describes how the soldiers, following Roman authority, prepare the scene for the mockery that comes in the verses that follow.

For today: Jesus endured humiliation without answering with revenge. When someone treats us with contempt, we can remember that He went through this out of love for us, and ask Him for help to respond with patience.
exp.11:16:
This verse says that what Jesus did, withdrawing from the place, healing everyone, and asking them not to make him known, happened so that a word spoken earlier by the prophet Isaiah would be fulfilled. "Fulfilled" means that it would come to pass. With this, Matthew introduces a quotation from the prophet.

Matthew is the one writing. The Pharisees were already planning to destroy Jesus, and he withdraws calmly, seeking neither fame nor a fight. Matthew sees in that gentle attitude the servant announced in Isaiah 42. Some scholars debate how exactly the word "fulfilled" should be understood here: as a direct fulfillment or as a pattern that repeats. The central point is that Jesus fits that picture.

For today: not everything is resolved by shouting or by winning arguments. Today you can respond to conflict with gentleness, serving and doing good quietly, trusting that God knows how to work.
exp.22:12:
Jesus says "woe to you," an expression of grief and serious warning. He speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, whom he calls "hypocrites," that is, people who pretend to be one thing and live as another. He tells them that they shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces: they do not enter themselves, and they will not let in those who wish to enter.

Jesus is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem, before the crowd and his disciples. Just before this, he taught that the greatest must be a servant and that God humbles the proud. Now he shows the opposite: religious leaders who sought their own image and, through their example and teaching, drew others away from God.

For today: if we teach or guide others, let us examine our hearts. Let our lives be consistent with what we say, so that we help people draw near to God and not stumble.
exp.15:24:
Jesus says that whoever wants to save his life will lose it, while whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. To hold on to your life, that is, to protect and secure it at all costs, is to lose it. But to give it up for Christ's sake is to find it. The word "life" here is the same as "soul," as the following verse shows: it refers to the whole person.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples after announcing that he will suffer and die. Peter had rebuked him, and Jesus answered him firmly. He then explains that following him means denying oneself and taking up the cross. Many understand that he is speaking of total surrender, although this does not always mean physical death.

For today: when you have to choose between your comfort or reputation and being faithful to Jesus, remember that obeying him does not leave you poorer. Ask him for the courage to let go of what binds you, trusting that he takes care of you.
exp.18:27:
Jesus promises his disciples that, because they have followed him, they will sit on twelve thrones. The phrase "the renewal of all things" points to a new beginning, when everything is made new. "Judging" here can be understood as ruling or governing. "You" is addressed to the whole group of followers. The twelve tribes of Israel are the people of God.

Peter has just asked what they will receive, since they left everything behind. A rich young man had gone away sad because he would not give up his riches. Jesus answers with a promise. Scholars disagree about how it will be fulfilled: some think of the future kingdom, while others also see a spiritual meaning for the Church.

For today: following Jesus has a cost, but God forgets nothing. Serve with confidence, without seeking applause, knowing that he rewards in his own way and in his own time.
exp.24:11:
When the bridegroom hears the virgins who arrived late, he answers them firmly: "Truly I tell you, I do not know you." The door was already shut, and he does not recognize them as part of the feast.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in the parable of the ten virgins. The bridegroom represents Christ, and the story teaches us to be ready for his coming. Some of the virgins did not prepare in time. That serious statement shows that it is not enough to appear ready; one must live with a real and steady faith. Commentators explain the oil in different ways, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our relationship with God is genuine or merely a matter of habit. Set aside time each day to pray, read his Word, and obey him, so that you live ready and at peace.
exp.12:20:
He has no root in himself, so his faith lasts only for a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away, that is, he stumbles and gives up his faith. "Quickly" means right away.

Jesus speaks to the crowds and then explains the parable of the sower to his disciples. The seed is the word of the kingdom, and the different kinds of ground are the ways people respond. Here he refers to the rocky ground: a real initial joy, but without depth. Some debate whether this describes someone who never truly believed; the text only notes that it did not produce lasting fruit.

For today: it is not enough to be moved emotionally on a Sunday. Put down roots through daily prayer, Bible reading, and friendship with other believers, so that when trials come, your faith stays firm.
exp.8:6:
This verse says that the paralyzed man obeyed Jesus at once: he got up and went home. The verse reads "the man got up and went home," so the sentence about the old spelling and its meaning has been removed, since it refers to wording the reader never sees.

This verse closes a scene in Capernaum. Some men had brought a paralyzed man to Jesus, and Jesus first told him that his sins were forgiven. Some teachers of the law thought this was blasphemy. Jesus then showed that he has authority to forgive sins, and he commanded the man to rise. The verse records the man's response. Afterward, the crowd glorified God.

When Jesus speaks to us through his Word, faith shows itself in obedience. Today you can take a concrete step of trust in what he has already told you, without waiting to feel ready.
exp.16:0:
Six days after an important moment, Jesus took three of his disciples, Peter, James, and John the brother of James, and led them up a high mountain, away from the others.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. The six days come after Peter confessed that Jesus is the Christ, and after Jesus announced his death (Matthew 16). The text does not say which mountain it was; some think of Hermon or Tabor, but this is uncertain. What follows is the transfiguration, where the disciples see the glory of Jesus.

For today: Jesus invites his own to withdraw with him. Look for a quiet moment each day, without noise or hurry, to listen to him in prayer and in his Word. There faith is strengthened for difficult times.
exp.24:28:
This verse says that to the one who has something and uses it well, more will be given, and that from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away. The phrase "to everyone who has" is kept as it is in the Berean Standard Bible, which reads "For everyone who has will be given more." "Usury" means interest or profit. A "talent" was a large sum of money.

Jesus speaks in the parable of the talents. A master, who is going on a journey, entrusts his money to his servants. Two of them put it to work and make it grow, but the third hides it out of fear. Jesus teaches that God expects us to be faithful with what he gives us, while we wait for the day when the Son of Man will come. Whoever does not use what he has, out of fear or laziness, loses the opportunity. Some see here gifts and opportunities; others see faith itself.

Today, ask yourself what God has given you: time, abilities, possessions, affection. Do not keep it locked away out of fear. This week, begin to use one specific thing to serve someone.
exp.13:25:
This verse says that the disciples saw Jesus walking on the sea and were terrified. They thought it was a ghost and cried out in fear. "Terrified" means that they were filled with fright. "The sea" is the lake of Galilee in this case. "Cried out" means that they shouted.

The one telling the account is Matthew. It was early in the morning, since the fourth watch was the last shift of the night, roughly between three and six o'clock. The disciples were in the boat, battered by the waves and with the wind against them. They were tired and afraid, and they did not expect to see Jesus coming in that way. That is why they did not recognize him.

Sometimes Jesus draws near in the middle of our storm and we do not recognize him, because we were expecting a different kind of help. When you are afraid, pause and listen for his voice. You can pray quietly, asking him to help you see him present in your difficulty.
exp.23:33:
Jesus says with complete seriousness that "this generation" will not pass away until "all these things" have happened. Your verse uses "will not pass away" and "have happened," which convey the same firm promise he had been making about what was coming.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the destruction of the temple and the signs of the end. He has just spoken about the fig tree: just as its leaves announce that summer is near, certain events announce that something is close at hand. Scholars disagree about what "this generation" means: Jesus' contemporaries, the Jewish people in general, or the generation that would see the signs. And about "all these things": the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, or the final return of Christ, or both.

Although we do not have all the answers, the next verse guides us: no one knows the day or the hour. Instead of calculating dates, we can live awake, faithful, and confident that the words of Jesus do not fail.
exp.17:14:
Jesus says that if a brother sins against you, you should go and confront him privately. To "confront" here means to point out the wrong clearly and with a good purpose. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over: that is, you have restored the relationship and helped him return to the right path.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Just before this, he told the parable of the lost sheep, where God does not want even one of these little ones to be lost. For that reason, correcting a brother is not meant to win an argument, but to rescue a person who is precious to God.

If someone hurts you, do not talk about it with others or hold on to resentment. Pray first, and then speak with that person in private, with humility and respect. Ask yourself: "Am I seeking to win back my brother, or only to vent my feelings?"
exp.12:55:
It says that the people of Nazareth knew all of Jesus' family. His sisters lived there, among them. That is why they ask where Jesus got that wisdom and those miracles. The phrase "this man" sounds dismissive: they speak of Him with contempt, not with respect.

The speakers are Jesus' neighbors in his hometown, who hear him teach in the synagogue. They are amazed, but they do not believe. They see him only as the carpenter's son, someone ordinary and familiar. Their familiarity keeps them from seeing who he really is. So they are "offended," that is, they stumble over him and reject him. The texts do not explain here in detail the relationship of the "brothers"; some Christian traditions understand them in different ways.

Today we can fall into the same thing: hearing Jesus so many times that we stop being amazed. Ask God for a humble and open heart, and read his Word as if it were new.
exp.18:0:
This verse marks a change of place. When Jesus had finished teaching, he left Galilee and went into the region of Judea, on the far side of the Jordan River. "Happen" means to take place, and "borders" means the territory or limits of a region. The "crowds" are the great numbers of people.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. He has just finished a block of Jesus' teachings, and now the journey toward Jerusalem begins, where Jesus will face the cross. The verses that follow show that many people followed him and that the Pharisees came to set a trap for him with a question about divorce. Some scholars understand the place as Perea, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: Jesus keeps on his way and serves the people even when there is opposition. We can do the same: keep loving and helping faithfully, even when someone tries to confuse us or put us to the test.
exp.18:2:
The Pharisees came to Jesus to test him. They asked whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason. "Testing him" here means trying to catch him out, with the intention of setting a trap.

Jesus had just arrived in Judea, on the other side of the Jordan, and large crowds were following him. The Pharisees were religious teachers who often questioned him. At that time there was debate about which reasons justified divorce, and some understood the law of Moses very broadly. They probably wanted Jesus to take a side in that debate. He, however, led them back to what God said from the beginning.

For today: before looking for what is allowed, ask yourself what God desires. Guard your marriage and your promises with that heart, not with excuses.
exp.25:24:
Judas, the one who was going to betray Jesus, asks him: "Surely not I, Rabbi?" Jesus answers him: "You have said it yourself." That answer was a way of saying "yes, just as you say." Here "betray" means handing Jesus over to his enemies. Notice that Judas calls him "Rabbi," while the other disciples had called him "Lord."

We are at the Passover supper, the Last Supper. Jesus has just said that one of the twelve would betray him, and the disciples were filled with sorrow. Jesus speaks calmly, knowing what is coming and that this had been foretold in the Scriptures. Even so, he makes clear that betrayal is a serious responsibility for the one who commits it. Jesus does not expose him harshly, but he makes the truth plain to him.

For today: God knows our heart even when we appear to be something else. We can speak honestly before him, acknowledge our faults, and turn back to him while there is still time.
exp.22:7:
Jesus tells his disciples not to be called "Rabbi," a word meaning "my teacher" that was a title of respect. The reason is that they have one Teacher, and all of them are brothers, equal in standing before him.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, shortly before his arrest, while he criticizes the scribes and Pharisees. They loved the best seats, the greetings in the marketplaces, and titles of honor. Jesus does not condemn teaching or respecting others, but the pride of seeking prestige. Some scholars debate how literal the command about titles is.

Today we can serve without seeking applause or rank. If you hold a position or teach in the church, treat others as brothers and sisters, and let the recognition belong to Christ.
exp.25:47:
Judas, the one handing Jesus over, had set up a signal with the crowd that had come to arrest him. The man he kissed would be Jesus, and they were to take hold of him. It was night, and the kiss would help them single him out from among the disciples.

The writer is Matthew, and he tells what happened in the garden of Gethsemane. Judas, one of the twelve, arrived with an armed crowd sent by the religious leaders. A kiss was a familiar greeting between a teacher and a disciple, but Judas used it to betray. Jesus already knew what would happen and, even so, called him "friend."

For today: we should make sure that our gestures of affection and faith are sincere. It is possible to appear close to God or to others while the heart is far away. Let us ask God for an honest heart, one that does not use lovely words to hide bad intentions.
exp.4:27:
Jesus says that it is not enough to avoid the act of adultery. To look at a woman "to lust after her" means to fix your gaze with the desire to possess her; it is not a passing glance, but deliberately feeding that desire. According to Jesus, this has already committed adultery "in his heart."

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He cites the commandment against adultery and shows that God looks beyond actions to the intentions of the heart. His strong words about the eye and the hand, which follow in the text, show how seriously sin must be taken. Interpreters debate whether they are an intentional exaggeration meant to teach, but all agree that they warn against tolerating sin.

Today, be careful about what you look at and what you think about. If something feeds your desire in a harmful way, step away from it and ask God for a pure heart.
exp.18:24:
The verse tells us that the disciples, on hearing Jesus, were greatly astonished and asked, "Who then can be saved?" The word "astonished" means they were deeply struck by what they heard. Their question shows the weight of the moment: if even a rich man cannot enter the kingdom, who will be able to be saved?

Jesus had just spoken about the rich young man who was not willing to give up his possessions to follow him. He said that it is very hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. In that time, many people saw wealth as a sign of God's blessing, so the disciples' reaction is understandable. Jesus answers them that it is impossible for men, but with God all things are possible.

No one is saved by their money, their merits, or their effort. Today we can stop trusting in what we have or what we do, and rest in the grace of God, who is able to save us.
exp.15:21:
Peter takes Jesus aside and begins to rebuke him firmly. The words "Far be it from you, Lord" mean "far from you be this, Lord." The words "This shall never happen to you" mean that Peter rejects the idea that Jesus should suffer and die.

Shortly before, Peter had confessed that Jesus was the Christ. Then Jesus begins to explain that he must suffer, die, and rise again. Peter speaks out of affection, but he thinks like the people of his time, who expected a Messiah without suffering. That is why Jesus rebukes him so strongly in the next verse: Peter, without realizing it, was standing in the way of God's plan.

We can want what is good and still go wrong if we act on human ideas. Before we counsel God or demand that he spare us all pain, let us ask him to teach us to understand his ways, even when they include self-denial and sacrifice.
exp.7:6:
Jesus responds with a direct promise: "I will go and heal him." The word "servant" here means a young servant or attendant, and "heal him" is the sense of the verse above. Jesus does not hesitate or set conditions; he offers to go personally to the sick man's house.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum to a centurion, a Roman officer in command of about a hundred soldiers. This man was not a Jew, yet he came to Jesus with humility to ask for help for his servant, who was paralyzed and suffering greatly. Some scholars note that the sentence could also be read as a question, but most readings understand it as a promise. Afterward, the centurion shows remarkable faith by saying that a word from Jesus is enough.

For today: when someone you love suffers, bring them to Jesus with confidence and humility. He cares for those who suffer, including those others overlook, and he wants to hear from you.
exp.14:28:
Jesus left the place where he had been and walked along the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Then he went up on a mountain and sat down there.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Jesus has come from the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed the daughter of the woman who showed great faith. Now he returns to the area of the lake. Matthew does not explain why he chose that mountain, but in the verses that follow, great crowds come with their sick, and Jesus heals them.

For today: Jesus was always available to anyone who sought him. If you feel tired or burdened, you can come to him in prayer with confidence, and also bring to him the people you love, as those did who brought their sick and laid them at his feet.
exp.14:27:
Jesus tells the woman that her faith is great and that her request is granted. From that very moment, her daughter was healed. The phrase "let it be done for you as you desire" refers to what she had asked for.

He speaks with a Canaanite woman, who was not Jewish and who was pleading for her daughter, who was tormented by a demon. Jesus had tested her persistence with the image of "little dogs" and the bread. She was not offended but answered with humility and trust in the Lord's goodness. Some think Jesus wanted to show the disciples her faith.

Today we can come to God with humility and perseverance, without giving up when the answer seems slow in coming. He delights in simple faith that trusts in his goodness and keeps crying out.
exp.20:7:
This verse tells that a massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road where Jesus was passing. Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road too. (Rewritten: "a massive crowd" refers to the large gathering of people, and "spread" means they laid their cloaks and branches down on the road.)

It is the entry of Jesus into Jerusalem, riding on a donkey with its colt, a few days before his crucifixion. Matthew is the one who narrates it. Spreading cloaks was a way of honoring a king, and the people received him as the Son of David, the expected Messiah. Matthew connects this with Zechariah's prophecy about a humble king who arrives on a donkey.

For today: honoring Jesus costs something. The people gave their cloaks, which were valuable to them. We can ask ourselves what we are sincerely offering to Jesus: time, pride, comfort, or personal plans.
exp.23:38:
This verse says that the people in Noah's time went on with their normal lives and were not aware of what was coming, until the flood arrived and swept away everyone who was outside the ark. Jesus says that his coming will be the same. The word "oblivious" here means "unaware" or "not paying attention." "Swept away" means that the flood carried them off.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the signs of his coming and of the end of the age. He explains that he will come suddenly, when many do not expect him. His point is not that eating or marrying is wrong, but that the people were living without paying attention.

For today: live with your eyes open and your heart ready. Work, love, and enjoy your family, but do not let everyday life distract you from God. Take a moment today to pray and place your life in his hands.
exp.21:21:
This verse tells us that those who heard Jesus' answer were amazed. The phrase "they were amazed" means they were filled with wonder and surprise. And "left him and went away" means they walked away from him and left him alone, without saying anything more.

The ones speaking here are some disciples of the Pharisees together with some Herodians. They had tried to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to Caesar. Jesus asked them for a coin, pointed out the image on it, and gave them a wise answer that left them with nothing to accuse him of.

For today: we can fulfill our responsibilities to the authorities and, at the same time, give God first place in our lives. Let us ask him for wisdom to answer with calm and truth when someone questions or pressures us.
exp.0:13:
This verse continues the list of Jesus' ancestors. It says that Azor was the father of Zadok, Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud. Each name is the father of the next, so the list moves forward one generation at a time.

Matthew writes this Gospel, probably with Jewish readers in mind, and opens with the genealogy of Jesus. These names appear only here, and we know almost nothing about these people. Matthew shows that Jesus comes from the line of David and Abraham, and that God's promises are fulfilled across generations. Some scholars think Matthew summarized the list.

For today: God also works through unknown people and ordinary lives. Your faithfulness each day, even when no one notices it, can be part of what God is doing.
exp.16:3:
Peter sees Jesus shining like the sun, standing beside Moses and Elijah, and suggests they stay there. He offers to put up three shelters, simple huts made of branches. The words "It is good for us to be here" express how wonderful it is that they are there.

Peter speaks in the middle of something astonishing. Moses represents the Law and Elijah the prophets. Some think Peter wanted to make the moment last, or that he was placing Jesus on the same level as them. Mark 9:6 says he did not know what to say, because they were very frightened. Then the Father speaks from the cloud and says: "This is my beloved Son. Listen to him."

For today: moments of peace or closeness with God are a gift, but they are not meant for us to stay in. God strengthens us to return to daily life. And in every situation, the priority is to listen to Jesus.
exp.19:12:
Here the owner of the vineyard answers one of the workers who was complaining. "Friend" is a courteous way of addressing him, not one spoken in anger. The owner says he is not being unfair to him, and he reminds him that they had agreed on one denarius, a day's wage. The worker received exactly the payment they had agreed on.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The workers from the first shift become angry because those who arrived at the end received the same pay as they did. The owner did not take anything from them; he simply chose to be generous to others. Many understand that the parable speaks of God's grace, which is not earned by merit.

For today: when you see God blessing others, even those who came to faith late, rejoice instead of comparing yourself. Give thanks for what God has given you and celebrate his goodness toward others.
exp.25:49:
Jesus speaks to Judas in a kind tone: "Friend." Then he tells him to do what he came for, and right away the men with him step forward and seize Jesus, arresting him.

Jesus is in the garden of Gethsemane. Judas has just greeted him with a kiss, which was the agreed sign to identify him before the crowd. Jesus knows what is coming and does not run away. Some understand his words as an invitation for Judas to reflect; others see them as a way of showing Judas that Jesus knows about the betrayal.

For today: even when someone betrays or hurts us, we can respond with self-control and without hatred, trusting in God. Jesus shows us that it is possible to keep calm and kindness in the middle of injustice.
exp.4:41:
Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Just before this, he has talked about not repaying evil with evil, giving up one's coat, and walking the second mile. He wants to show a righteousness that goes deeper than outward obedience, one that comes from a heart like God's. Right after this, he moves on to love for enemies. Many understand this as describing a generous attitude, not a rule that obliges us to give everything to anyone without wisdom.

Today we can ask ourselves: whom can I help this week? Perhaps with money, time, or a tool. Let us do it with joy and good judgment, seeking the good of the person.
exp.26:57:
This verse tells that Joseph of Arimathea went to Pilate, the Roman governor, and asked for the body of Jesus. Pilate ordered that it be given to him. The phrase "to ask for" describes a request made directly to the governor, and "ordered" means that Pilate gave a clear instruction for the body to be handed over.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had already died on the cross, and his closest disciples were hidden or far away. Joseph, a wealthy man who also followed Jesus, took a brave step. Asking for the body of a condemned man could bring him trouble, yet in this way Jesus received a dignified burial. The Gospels do not explain all of his motives.

For today: sometimes God invites us to serve in a concrete way when others remain silent. Perhaps you cannot do something great, but you can do a simple and courageous act of love, even if it costs time, money, or comfort.
exp.12:26:
The owner's servants come to him in surprise and ask: if he sowed good seed in the field, where did the weeds come from? The note about the words "seed" and "tares" is not needed here, since the verse says "good seed" and "weeds." The weeds in this parable are a plant that looks like wheat while it grows.

Jesus tells this parable to the crowds to explain what the kingdom of heaven is like. He himself interprets it later (Matthew 13:36-43): the sower is the Son of Man, the field is the world, the wheat is the children of the kingdom, and the enemy is the devil. The servants' question shows their bewilderment at the presence of evil.

When you see bad things in the world or in the church, do not lose faith by thinking God made a mistake. There is a real enemy, but God is patient and has the last word. Trust his timing and keep bearing good fruit.
exp.6:2:
Jesus asks a question to get us thinking. The speck is a very small particle, like a bit of straw or a grain of dust. The beam is a large timber from a building. He deliberately exaggerates: we notice the small fault in another person, but we miss the huge error we have ourselves.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples and the crowd. Shortly before, he said that we will be judged by the same standard we use on others. Here he corrects the habit of criticizing harshly without looking at one's own heart. Then he calls the one who acts this way a hypocrite, and asks him to begin with himself.

For today: before correcting or criticizing someone, take a moment to pray and ask God: "What in me needs to be put right?" Then, if it is necessary, speak with humility and kindness.
exp.23:49:
This verse says that the master of that wicked servant will arrive unexpectedly, on a day and at an hour the servant does not anticipate. "Master" here means the owner of the household. The phrase warns that the return comes when one least expects it.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he teaches them about the end of the age. He tells this parable to contrast the faithful servant with the wicked one, who takes advantage of the master's delay to mistreat others and live without restraint. Many understand the master to represent Christ at his return.

For today: live each day as if you were accountable to God, treating others well and faithfully carrying out what has been entrusted to you, without putting off obedience or believing there will always be more time.
exp.0:15:
This verse closes the list of Jesus' ancestors. It says that Jacob was the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary. Notice the change: it does not say that Joseph was the father of Jesus, but that Jesus was born of Mary, the woman Joseph was married to. The word "Christ" means "the Anointed One," the promised Messiah.

The one speaking is Matthew, who writes mainly for Jewish readers. His genealogy shows that Jesus comes from the line of Abraham and David, as the Scriptures promised. The change in wording at the end prepares the next account, where Jesus is conceived by the Holy Spirit. Some scholars think this list follows Joseph's legal line; others understand it in different ways.

God works in real history, with real families and ordinary names. If you feel small or unimportant today, remember that God keeps his promises through ordinary people, and he can also work in your life.
exp.2:4:
Many people were going out to meet John the Baptist. They came from Jerusalem, from all of Judea, and from the whole region around the Jordan. The phrase "went out to him" means they were heading toward him. The words "the region around the Jordan" refer to the areas along the river. Matthew says "all" to show that a large crowd came, not necessarily every single person.

Matthew has just presented John as the voice preparing the way of the Lord, according to Isaiah. His plain clothing and his desert food showed a simple, disciplined life. The people went to hear him and, according to the next verse, to be baptized while confessing their sins.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we hunger to come close to God with humility. Preparing the way of the Lord can begin with something concrete: acknowledging a sin before Him, asking for forgiveness, and taking a step of change.
exp.19:16:
As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside from the crowd to speak with them in private. The phrase "going up" is used because Jerusalem sits on high ground.

The one telling this account is Matthew, who recounts what Jesus did. Just before, Jesus had told the parable of the workers in the vineyard, where he taught that God is generous and that the last can be first. Now he changes the subject and prepares his closest friends for what is coming: his suffering, his death, and his resurrection in Jerusalem.

For today: Jesus did not hide the hard things from his disciples. We can draw near to God in private, listen to his voice with sincerity, and trust that he prepares us even for the difficult moments, without ceasing to walk with us.
exp.24:35:
This verse says that the King recognizes three acts of kindness: clothing the person who was naked, looking after the sick, and visiting the one who was in prison. "I was naked and you clothed Me" means that they gave him clothes. "You visited Me" means that they went to see him in prison, not that they stayed far away.

Jesus speaks as King in the parable of the judgment of the nations, at the end of his teaching about the last times. He separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Acts of mercy show a living faith. He identifies himself with the needy: what is done for them is done for him. Some understand "My brothers" to refer to his disciples, and others to all the needy.

Today we can notice someone who is sick, alone, or in trouble, and reach out with a visit, a phone call, or concrete help this week.
exp.11:35:
He says that Jesus gives a serious warning: every careless word people speak will have to be answered for before God on the day of judgment. The word "careless" means words that are empty, without benefit, or without truth. "Give account" means to answer for something, the way someone reports back on what they have done.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees, who had just accused him of casting out demons by the power of the devil. He shows them that their evil words came from a hardened heart. For that reason he connects words with the heart: what we say reveals what we carry inside. Interpreters debate how broad the meaning of "careless" is, but all agree that words matter a great deal.

Today, before you speak or write on social media, pause and ask yourself: "Is this true, does it build up, and does it honor God?" Ask him to cleanse your heart.
exp.24:29:
This verse says that the servant who is "worthless," the one who did nothing with what his master entrusted to him, is thrown into "the outer darkness." That darkness is a place far from the light and from the master's feast. "Weeping" means crying, and "gnashing of teeth" expresses pain, anguish, or rage. The command to throw him out means "throw him out."

Jesus speaks to his disciples shortly before his death and tells the parable of the talents. A man leaves his goods with his servants and goes away. When he returns, he rewards those who worked, but the one who hid his talent out of fear is judged. Jesus teaches them to be ready for his return. Interpreters debate how far this applies to believers and how far to false followers.

For today: do not hide out of fear what God has given you, whether time, abilities, or money. Use it with faith to serve others.
exp.19:3:
This verse says that the owner of the vineyard found some men who had no work and invited them to work in his vineyard. He did not set an exact wage for them, but promised to pay them whatever is right, that is, whatever is fair. They agreed and went. The word "you" in the verse is plural, meaning "all of you," and a "vineyard" is a piece of land where grapes are grown.

Jesus tells this parable to explain what the kingdom of heaven is like. It comes after Peter asked what the disciples would receive for having left everything. The owner represents God, who calls people at different times. Interpreters explain in various ways who the workers are, but all agree that God is generous.

For today: God invites us to serve him no matter how long we have been waiting. Trust that his dealings will be fair, and answer his call promptly, without putting it off.
exp.11:27:
Jesus says that he drives out demons by the Spirit of God, and that because of this the kingdom of God has already come upon them. The phrase "drive out" means to force out. "Has come upon you" means that it is present and within reach, not only far away.

Jesus is speaking to some Pharisees who accused him of driving out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of the demons. He answers with reason: a divided kingdom cannot stand. His power comes from God, and the freeing of those who were held by demons shows that God is at work and that Satan is being overcome, as the picture of the strong man being bound explains.

For today: do not close your eyes to the work of God out of pride or prejudice. Recognize with humility where God is freeing and healing, and stand on the side of Jesus, trusting that his kingdom is stronger than any evil.
exp.17:18:
Jesus says that if two people on earth agree about something they ask for, his Father in heaven will grant it. The phrase "if two of you agree" here means "if two of you come to an agreement," and "anything you ask for" refers to what the two of them request together.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples about how to deal with sin among fellow believers. Just before this, he explained how to seek reconciliation, and then Peter asks how many times he must forgive. For this reason, many understand this promise to refer to the prayer of a community that seeks restoration and justice according to God's will. It is not a guarantee of receiving anything one desires.

For today: when there is a conflict or a difficult decision in your family or church, seek out someone you trust and pray together with humility, asking for wisdom, peace, and reconciliation.
exp.4:37:
Jesus recalls what the people had heard from long ago: "Eye for eye and tooth for tooth." The words "you have heard" and "it has been said" point back to a saying from the law of Moses (Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20).

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and the crowd. That law set a limit on revenge: the punishment was not to be greater than the harm, and it was carried out through the judges. Now Jesus is going to show a deeper way, the way of the heart. With the words "But I say to you" he begins to explain this in the verses that follow.

For today: when someone wrongs you, before you pay them back with harsh words or cold silence, stop and pray. Ask God for help to respond with patience and with good.
exp.9:12:
If the home is worthy, the peace you wish on it will rest there. If it is not, that peace is not lost. It will return to you, meaning it comes back to those who offered it.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to announce that the kingdom of heaven is near. He gives them practical instructions: look for homes ready to welcome them, and greet them with peace, the common greeting of the time, which here also carries a blessing. Interpreters explain in various ways how that peace "returns," but they all agree that it is not wasted.

For today: offer your kindness and your peace to everyone, without fear of rejection. If someone does not receive it, do not carry guilt or bitterness. Your peace stays with you.
exp.6:27:
This verse says that when Jesus finished speaking, the crowds were astonished at his teaching. The phrase "the crowds were astonished" describes people who were filled with wonder and deeply impressed by what they had heard.

It is the closing of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). Matthew, who writes the account, tells how the crowd reacted after Jesus spoke about the house built on the rock and the house built on the sand. The next verse explains the reason for their amazement: Jesus taught with authority, not like the scribes, who usually relied on the opinions of other teachers.

For today: admiring the words of Jesus is not enough. Ask yourself what teaching of his you can put into practice this week, however small it may be, so that your life has a firm foundation.
exp.8:34:
This verse sums up what Jesus was doing: he went through all the towns and villages. The word for "went through" means that he traveled from place to place. He taught in their synagogues, the places where Jewish people gathered to hear the Scriptures. He preached the good news of the kingdom, and he healed every disease and sickness among the people.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Before this, the crowd was amazed to see a man who could not speak begin to speak, while the Pharisees accused Jesus of acting by the power of evil. This summary shows that Jesus kept serving, without stopping because of the criticism. What follows explains the reason: when he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them.

For today: Jesus taught, and he also cared for people. We can imitate him by attending both the need of the soul and the need of the body, with a word of hope and concrete help for those near us.
exp.15:13:
The disciples answer Jesus' question about what people think of him. They say some believe he is John the Baptist, others that he is Elijah, and others that he is Jeremiah or one of the prophets. The word "or" here is simply the ordinary modern English "or."

Jesus is near Caesarea Philippi and asks who people say the Son of Man is. The disciples report the opinions of the crowd. All of them are respectful, since they compare Jesus with great servants of God, but they fall short. None of them recognizes him as the Messiah. This prepares the next question, which is more personal: "But who do you say that I am?" and Peter's answer.

Today too there are many good opinions about Jesus: a great teacher, a righteous man, a prophet. But it is not enough to repeat what others say. Take a moment to answer honestly: who is Jesus to you?
exp.17:26:
This verse tells us that the king, seeing the servant on his knees, had compassion on him. He did not only give him more time, as the servant asked: he forgave the debt completely and let him go free. Having compassion means that he felt pity and tenderness for him. To release him means that he set him free.

Jesus tells this parable in answer to Peter, who asked him how many times he should forgive his brother. The king represents God, and the servant represents each one of us. The debt was enormous (the text before this speaks of ten thousand talents), impossible to pay. What follows shows that this servant did not know how to forgive another.

For today: when it is hard for you to forgive someone, remember how much you have received from God. Ask him to help you offer that same compassion to others, even if it is only little by little.
exp.23:15:
Jesus says that when a certain sign appears, the people living in Judea should flee to the mountains. The phrase "flee to the mountains" is an order to escape quickly, without stopping to wait.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the destruction of the temple and about the end. He mentions the "abomination of desolation" that Daniel had announced. Many believe it was fulfilled in part with the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70; others also see a future fulfillment. Christians interpret it in several ways. What is clear is that Jesus gives a warning in order to care for his own.

For today: when God shows you a danger, do not ignore it or put it off. Act with wisdom and obedience, trusting that he takes care of you.
exp.13:26:
This verse tells us that Jesus spoke up at once to his disciples to calm them. "But Jesus spoke up at once" means he answered them right away, in that very moment. "Take courage" means "take heart" or "calm down." With "It is I" he identifies himself: "It is I. Do not be afraid."

The disciples were in the boat, in the early morning (the fourth watch was between three and six in the morning, by the Roman way of counting). They saw someone walking on the sea and thought it was a ghost. They cried out in fear. Jesus, who is the one speaking, answers them to reassure them with his voice and his presence.

For today: when fear or confusion comes, we can remember that Jesus draws near in the middle of the storm. Before everything is resolved, listen for his voice in the Bible and in prayer: "It is I. Do not be afraid."
exp.25:29:
After the Passover meal, Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn and then went out toward the Mount of Olives, a hill near Jerusalem.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Jesus had just instituted the Lord's Supper and had spoken of his blood being poured out. Many scholars think the hymn was the Hallel Psalms (Psalms 113 to 118), which were sung at Passover, though the text does not say so with certainty. Even knowing that suffering was coming, Jesus sings and moves forward. Right after this, he tells them that all of them will fall away from him.

For today: when difficult moments come, we can pray and praise God, trusting that he remains in control, just as Jesus did before the cross.
exp.12:39:
Jesus says that, just as the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so it will be at the end of the age. "Collected" here means gathered together.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, at home, after telling the parable of the wheat and the weeds. They asked him to explain it to them. He teaches that good and evil live side by side for now, but God, not us, will make the separation in the end, through his angels. Christians understand this judgment in different ways in the details, but all recognize that God is just.

For today: do not lose heart or become bitter because evil seems to prosper. Trust that God will judge with justice. In the meantime, live with humility, leave the final judgment in his hands, and strive to bear good fruit every day.
exp.19:21:
Jesus answers the mother and her two sons, James and John: "You do not know what you are asking." He asks them, "Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?" They answer, "We can." In that time, the cup is an image of the suffering and self-giving that Jesus would face.

The mother of Zebedee's sons asked for the places of greatest honor in Jesus' kingdom. Shortly before, he had announced that he would be handed over and crucified. They were thinking of glory; Jesus was speaking of the cross. The other ten disciples became angry, and that shows that all of them struggled with the desire for greatness.

Before asking God for position, success, or recognition, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are willing to follow Jesus also in service, humility, and hardship. Following him costs something, and his way passes through self-giving, not applause.
exp.24:27:
This verse is a command from the master in the parable to his helpers. He tells them to take the talent away from the servant and give it to the one who already has ten. A talent was a large amount of money. The phrase "take the talent" sets out the first action, and "give it" sets out the second.

Jesus is speaking, telling the parable of the talents. Each servant received money to manage while his master was away traveling. This servant hid it out of fear and did nothing with it. The master calls him "wicked" and "lazy" because he did not even try. Some understand that the master represents Christ and that the parable is about being prepared for his return.

Today we can ask ourselves what gifts, time, or resources God has entrusted to us, and begin to use them to serve others, even if they are few and we feel afraid.
exp.4:28:
It says that if your right eye causes you to sin (a "cause of stumbling" means something that makes you trip), you should gouge it out and throw it away. It is better to lose one part of your body than to have your whole body thrown into hell (in Greek, "Gehenna").

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just said that sin begins in the heart, not only in actions, and that looking in order to desire is already adultery in the heart. Almost everyone understands that he uses exaggeration on purpose, since gouging out an eye would not end desire in the heart. He wants to show how seriously sin must be taken.

For today: identify what makes you stumble, whether a website, an app, or a friendship, and make a concrete decision to step away from it. Ask God for the strength to do it.
exp.21:35:
An expert in the law of Moses comes up to Jesus and calls him "Teacher." He asks which commandment is the greatest one, meaning the most important in all the law. The word "tempting" means that he was testing him, and "together" means that they came together with the same purpose.

The Pharisees had just heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, another religious group. Then they gathered together, and one of them asked him this question. The teachers of the law argued a great deal about which commandment carried the most weight. That is why the question could have been a test, and the Bible does not say for certain what exactly he was looking for. Jesus answers plainly: love God.

For today: before you fill your life with religious tasks, ask yourself what place God holds in your heart. Spend a few minutes each day talking with him and thanking him, because love for God is the foundation of everything else.
exp.18:23:
Jesus says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. It is a deliberately exaggerated image meant to show something that is nearly impossible.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after a rich young man has walked away sad, because he was unwilling to give up his possessions to follow him. The disciples are alarmed and ask who then can be saved. Jesus answers that with men it is impossible, but with God all things are possible. Some have proposed explanations about a gate called the "eye of the needle," but there is no solid evidence for that.

Today, examine which thing is hardest for you to let go of: money, security, or comfort. Hand it over to God in prayer, trusting that salvation is the work of his grace, not of your own strength.
exp.23:40:
It says that two women will be working side by side, grinding grain at a hand mill, something very common in that time. Suddenly one will be taken and the other left. The word "mill" refers to a small grinding stone, and "taken" means being carried away or set apart. This is understood in two ways: some think being taken means being gathered up to be with Christ, and others think it means being carried off in judgment, as in the days of the flood.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. He explains how his coming will be and compares that moment with the days of Noah, when people lived normally and did not notice what was coming. That is why he immediately tells them to keep watch.

For today: do not put off spiritual preparation until later. As you go about your daily tasks, live with faith, prayer, and obedience, ready to meet the Lord at any moment.
exp.14:37:
This verse says that those who ate were four thousand men, and that there were also women and children in addition. That is, the real crowd was considerably larger, although the text does not give an exact number. The word "besides" here means "not counting" or "in addition to." The leftover pieces are the scraps that were left over, and the baskets were large hampers.

It is the narrator, Matthew, who speaks. Jesus had just healed many sick people and felt compassion because the crowd had been with him for three days and had nothing to eat. With seven loaves and a few small fish he fed them. Many scholars see here a second miracle of multiplication, distinct from the one with the five thousand, and there are also those who debate this.

Jesus pays attention to the concrete needs of people, even to those that others overlook, such as women and children. Today we can imitate him: look at the people near us, notice what they lack, and offer the little we have, trusting that God can multiply it.
exp.5:13:
This verse says that if we forgive the people who have offended us, our Father in heaven will also forgive us. The word "forgive" and the word "you" here are the plain verb and pronoun you see in the verse above, and "offenses" are the wrongs or harms that others do to us.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples. He has just given them the Lord's Prayer, where we ask for forgiveness in the same measure that we forgive others. With this verse and the next, he explains that request: the forgiveness we receive from God and the forgiveness we give are joined together. Some scholars understand this as a sign of a truly changed heart, not as a way of earning forgiveness.

Today, think of someone who hurt you and bring that wound to God in prayer. Ask him for help in letting go of resentment, even if it happens little by little, and for the courage to take the first step toward peace.
exp.7:25:
Jesus asks his disciples why they are so afraid, and he calls them "you of little faith." Then he gets up, speaks to the winds and the sea, and it becomes perfectly calm.

Jesus is in a boat with his disciples when a violent storm comes up. Frightened, they wake him and ask for help. He corrects them gently, but he also shows his power. The disciples are amazed and ask themselves who this man really is, the one whom even the wind and the sea obey.

When your storms come, whether they involve your health, your money, or your family, remember that Jesus is with you in the boat. You can bring him your fear honestly, as the disciples did, and trust that he is in control, even though he does not always calm everything right away.
exp.24:17:
This verse says that the servant who received one talent did not use it. He went off, dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master's money. A talent was a large amount of money. To dig a hole and hide the money means he buried it and kept it out of sight.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and tells this parable to teach them how to live while they wait for his return. The master entrusts his goods to his servants, and each one receives according to his ability. The first two put what they received to work; this third servant decides to keep it safe, without risking anything. The verses that follow show that there will be a reckoning.

For today: God has entrusted us with gifts, time, and opportunities, and they are not meant to be hidden out of fear or comfort. Think of something small that God gave you and use it this week to serve someone.
exp.5:3:
Jesus says that giving to the poor should be done in secret. The reason is that God, the Father, sees what no one else sees, and he himself will take care of the reward. The phrase "will reward you" speaks of God responding to what is done with a sincere heart. Some English translations add the word "openly" to the reward, but some scholars doubt that this part was in the earliest manuscripts.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Just before this verse, he criticizes the hypocrites, people who gave in order to be admired. Blowing a trumpet was a way of drawing attention. Jesus wants his generosity to come from love and not from applause.

Today, try to help someone without telling anyone or posting about it, simply because God sees it and cares.
exp.17:25:
The servant falls on his knees before his master. He kneels low in deep respect and begs, "Have patience with me," meaning give me time, and he promises to pay back everything.

Jesus tells this parable in answer to Peter, who asked how many times he should forgive his brother. The debt of ten thousand talents was enormous, impossible to repay in a lifetime. So the servant's promise sounds sincere, but unrealistic. Even so, the master forgives him completely.

For today: recognize how much you have received from God's forgiveness, something you could never repay. That gratitude helps you forgive the person who offended you, even when it is hard. Ask yourself today: whose debt should I release from my heart?
exp.25:18:
This verse says that the disciples did exactly what Jesus had directed them to do. The word "prepared" in the verse means they got things ready. They prepared the Passover meal, the special feast the Jews celebrated every year.

The author, Matthew, recounts what happened a few hours before the Last Supper. The disciples had asked where to prepare the meal, and Jesus gave them clear instructions: go into the city, find a certain man, and tell him that his time was near. Jesus knew what was coming, and the disciples trusted his word, even though they did not understand everything.

For today: obeying God often means taking the next simple step, even when we cannot see the whole picture. The disciples did not have all the answers, but they did what they were asked. We can trust Jesus and obey him in the small things of each day.
exp.21:10:
In this verse, the king comes in to look over the guests, and there he spots a man who is not dressed in wedding clothes. The guests are the people who were invited to the celebration, and wedding clothes are the proper dress for that occasion.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The guests who were first invited refused to come, so the king invited everyone he could find, both good and bad. Some readers take the garment to represent the righteousness God gives, and others take it to represent a life changed by Him. Either way, the invitation is free and generous, but the king expects a sincere response. The parable does not explain its symbols, so this cannot be known with complete certainty.

For today: accepting God's invitation is not just showing up at the feast. We can ask ourselves honestly whether we come trusting in His grace and willing to let Him change us, rather than presenting ourselves on our own terms.
exp.27:9:
The risen Jesus meets the women who had come away from the tomb and says to them, "Do not be afraid." He asks them to go and tell his brothers to go to Galilee, where they will see him.

Jesus, just risen, speaks to the women who had gone to the tomb. They felt fear and great joy at the same time. Jesus calms them and gives them a mission. It is striking that he calls them to carry the message to the disciples, whom he calls "my brothers," even though they had abandoned him.

For today: when you feel fear or doubt, remember that Jesus lives and speaks to you with tenderness. He also entrusts you with sharing the good news with others, even if you feel small or afraid.
exp.22:36:
Jesus speaks with sorrow to Jerusalem. He reminds the city that it has killed the prophets and stoned those sent to it. He says that many times he longed to gather its people together, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but they were unwilling.

Jesus speaks in the temple, at the end of his warnings to the Pharisees and the teachers of the law. His tone is not one of hatred but of grief. He announces a judgment that is near, yet before that he shows a heart that longed to protect them. Some understand the "desolate house" as the temple; others understand it as the whole people.

For today: God invites us tenderly to take refuge in him, but he respects our decision. Today we can set aside pride, listen to his correction, and come to him instead of running away.
exp.20:20:
Jesus responds to his disciples' question about the withered fig tree. He tells them that if they have faith and do not doubt, they will be able to do the same and even more: they could say to a mountain, "Be lifted up and thrown into the sea," and it will happen. "Doubt" here means hesitating, not trusting. The phrase "the sea" in the verse refers to the sea.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the way to Jerusalem, one day after cursing the fig tree, which had leaves but no fruit. They are amazed. He uses the moment to teach them about faith. Saying that a mountain can be moved is probably an expression for what seems impossible. Some also see here a warning against religious appearance without fruit.

Today we can bring to God with confidence what seems impossible to us, praying without doubting his power. But faith is not forcing God to do our will; it is trusting him and asking according to his heart.
exp.12:47:
It says that when the net was full of fish, the fishermen pulled it ashore. Then they sat down and sorted the fish: they put the good ones into containers and threw the bad ones away. The word "sorted" here captures the sense of separating the catch into two groups.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in a series of parables about the kingdom of heaven. The net cast into the sea catches all kinds of fish, and the separation comes only at the end. With this image, Jesus explains in the verses that follow that at the end of the age the angels will separate the wicked from the righteous. It is a serious warning, but also a promise of justice.

For today: it is not your place to judge who belongs to God and who does not. Devote yourself to living with sincerity, to following Christ wholeheartedly, and to trusting that God will do justice in his time.
exp.27:11:
This verse tells us that the chief priests met with the elders, made a plan, and gave a large sum of money to the soldiers who had been guarding the tomb. "Formed a plan" means they discussed the matter among themselves and agreed on what to do. "The soldiers" refers to the guard who had been watching over the tomb.

Matthew recounts what happened after the guards reported what had taken place at the tomb. The chief priests and the elders, instead of investigating whether Jesus had risen, chose to keep the news quiet. They gave the guards money and a false account of events, which Matthew describes in the verses that follow.

For today: when faced with the truth of God, we can respond with openness or with resistance. This passage invites us not to use money, power, or pride to cover up what we know to be true, but to seek with honesty and humility.
exp.21:42:
Jesus answers the Pharisees with another question. He asks how it is possible that David, speaking by the Spirit, calls the Christ "Lord." The words "in the Spirit" mean that David was speaking under the inspiration of God. The sentence continues in the following verse, where Psalm 110 is quoted.

Jesus is in the temple in Jerusalem, and the Pharisees, who wanted to trap him with questions, have just said that the Christ is the son of David. That was true, but incomplete. Jesus does not correct them with anger; he invites them to think more deeply. A father would not normally call his descendant "Lord," so the Messiah had to be more than a simple human heir.

For today: it is not enough to know correct facts about Jesus. We can ask ourselves whether we truly acknowledge him as Lord of our lives, and not merely as an admirable figure in history.
exp.4:32:
Jesus recalls what was taught to the people long ago: do not break an oath, and keep before the Lord the vows you have made. Saying "do not break your oath" means not lying and not failing to keep a promise you have sworn to. In this explanation, "fulfill" is the word that carries the sense of keeping your promise.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. This teaching sums up commands from the law, such as Leviticus 19:12 and Numbers 30:2. He shows that God looks for a sincere heart, not merely the outward keeping of rules. Then, in the verse that follows, he will go even further.

For today: try to be a person of your word. Before promising something, think it through carefully, and if you promise, keep it. Let your "yes" be yes and your "no" be no, so that others can trust you.
exp.23:6:
It says there will be conflicts between nations and kingdoms, and also suffering in nature and in society. "Famines" are shortages of food, "earthquakes in various places" means ground tremors in different regions, and the general sense is that such troubles will break out in many parts of the world.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the signs of the end. He warns them that these things will happen, but that they are not yet the end: they are the "beginning of sorrows," like the start of labor pains. Some interpret them as events close to the fall of Jerusalem, others as signs that repeat until his return.

When the news frightens us, let us not panic or let ourselves be deceived by those who claim to know the date. Let us trust in Christ, pray, and keep serving with love those who suffer.
exp.20:12:
Jesus speaks firmly in the temple. He quotes the Scripture: "My house will be called a house of prayer." Then he confronts those who were making it a place for profit: "you" are making it "a den of robbers," that is, a hideout where people gather to take advantage of others.

Jesus has just entered Jerusalem and driven out those who were selling and buying in the temple. His quotation combines words from Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. Scholars explain the rebuke in different ways: some see abuse in the prices, others a place that no longer served to worship God. What is clear is that the temple had lost its purpose. Right afterward, Jesus heals the blind and the lame right there in the temple.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our lives and our churches are places of prayer and of encounter with God, or whether self-interest has taken its place. Take a sincere moment today to pray.
exp.11:1:
The Pharisees saw that Jesus' disciples were picking heads of grain and eating them on the Sabbath day. So they said to Jesus that his disciples were doing something unlawful. The word "unlawful" means not permitted by the law. "Sabbath" is Israel's weekly day of rest.

The ones speaking are the Pharisees, a religious group very strict about the law and its traditions. The disciples were hungry, and taking grain while passing through a field was permitted by the law (Deuteronomy 23:25). The Pharisees probably considered it harvest "work" on the Sabbath. What they accuse them of seems to come from their interpretation of the law, not from a clear command. Jesus will answer them with the example of David.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we judge others by rules that we ourselves have added. God calls us to obey him with a merciful heart, not only to watch over others.
exp.19:30:
This verse says the crowd scolded the two blind men to make them be quiet. Here the word "admonished" means to warn or reprimand them firmly. But instead of falling silent, they cried out all the louder: "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!" "Mercy" is compassion and help for someone who cannot manage on their own.

Jesus was leaving Jericho with a large crowd following Him. The two blind men, sitting by the road, heard that He was passing by. They called Him "Son of David," a title that recognized Jesus as the promised Messiah. The people probably regarded them as a nuisance, but they did not want to lose this opportunity.

For today: when others discourage you or you feel that your need is an inconvenience, do not stop praying. Keep asking with humility and faith, for Jesus stops to listen to those who trust in Him.
exp.4:39:
If someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, this verse says you should also let them have your cloak. The tunic is the undergarment worn next to the body, and the cloak is the larger outer garment worn over it. To sue someone means to take them to court. The cloak was also the large outer garment that served as a blanket at night.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just cited the law of "an eye for an eye," which limited revenge and sought justice. Now he shows a deeper way: to respond to wrong without revenge and with generosity. Many understand this as teaching about the heart, not as a rule to be applied literally in every case.

For today: when someone treats you unfairly over something material, ask yourself whether it is worth fighting over. Consider yielding or giving more, and respond with peace and kindness, asking God for wisdom.
exp.9:29:
Jesus says that God knows even the smallest details of our lives: even the very hairs of our head are numbered, meaning God knows each one individually. It is a way of speaking that shows how much he cares for each person.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples before sending them out to proclaim the kingdom of God. He warns them that there will be rejection and persecution. That is why he asks them not to fear other people. He compares the sparrows, which are worth very little, with them, who are worth far more to the Father. In this way he encourages them to trust and to remain faithful when they confess him.

When you feel afraid or think no one sees your struggles, remember that God knows you and cares for you. Bring that specific worry to him in prayer today and take a step of faith with confidence.
exp.25:34:
Peter assures Jesus that even if he has to die with Him, he will never deny Him. To deny someone means to disown them, or to say that you do not know them. The other disciples say the same thing.

Jesus has just announced that all of them would abandon Him, and that Peter would deny Him three times that very night. Peter answers with great sincerity and courage, but without realizing his own weakness. Shortly afterward, in Gethsemane, Jesus is troubled and prays, while the disciples fall asleep.

For today: wanting to be faithful is not enough if we trust only in our own strength. Let us be humble, recognize our weakness, and ask God for help each day. And if we fail, let us remember that Jesus knows our frailty and offers forgiveness and restoration.
exp.25:44:
Jesus returns for the third time and finds his disciples asleep. He says to them, "Are you still sleeping and resting?" and announces that the hour is near. The phrase "Then He returned to the disciples and said" carries the same sense as "he goes back to the disciples and speaks to them." "Betrayed" means handed over and placed in the power of others. "Sinners" here refers to men who will act against him.

Jesus is in Gethsemane, praying in anguish before the cross. He had asked his friends to keep watch with him, but exhaustion overcame them. Some believe his words are a gentle rebuke; others take them to mean that there is no longer time for watching. Soon Judas arrives with the crowd, and Jesus rises to face them calmly.

There are times when we fail out of weakness, but Jesus does not abandon us. Today you can pray sincerely and ask him for strength, knowing that he understands you and receives you with patience.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the Holy Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, and there the devil put him to the test. The word that appears here means tested or put to the test, with the intention of making him fall.

This is Matthew's account, and it is not Jesus speaking but the narrator. This happens right after Jesus' baptism, when the Father called him his beloved Son. It follows a fast of forty days, and the tempter begins with the words "If you are the Son of God." Matthew shows that this testing was not an accident, but part of the path God allowed for Jesus.

For today: trials do not always mean that God has moved away from us. Jesus went through them and understands us. When they come, we can seek God, remember who we are in him, and trust his Word, as Jesus did.
exp.6:19:
Jesus says that people are recognized by the fruit they produce, that is, by what they do and how they live. The word "recognize" here means you will be able to discern, or see for yourself, what someone is really like.

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount. Just before this, he warned about false prophets who look like sheep but are wolves on the inside. He gives his listeners a way to tell them apart: not by their pleasant words or their appearance, but by their steady conduct.
