He then makes clear that saying "Lord, Lord" is not enough; what matters is doing the will of the Father.

For today: before trusting a leader or teacher, watch their life over time, their humility, their honesty, and their love. And do the same with your own life, asking God to produce good fruit in you.
exp.1:6:
Then this verse tells how Herod secretly called the wise men and carefully learned from them the exact time the star had appeared. The phrase "the exact time" is the detail to note, since Herod wanted precise information about when the sign first appeared.

Herod was the king of Judea, and he felt threatened, because the wise men were seeking the newborn one who had been born king of the Jews. He had already consulted the chief priests and scribes, who pointed him to Bethlehem according to the prophecy. Now he wanted to know roughly how old the child was. The text does not say why he acted in secret, but it fits with the deceitful plan we see afterward.

For today: there are people who speak of God with kind words, but their hearts are not sincere. Let us examine our intentions before the Lord. Let us seek Christ in order to worship him truly, not to use him or to protect our own power or comfort.
exp.25:14:
Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples, goes to the chief priests and asks what they will pay him if he hands Jesus over to them. They agree on thirty pieces of silver. The question "What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?" shows that Judas is the one who makes the offer, and that he is setting the terms. The text does not say more about the exact value of the silver coins.

Judas speaks here, and shortly before this a woman had anointed Jesus with costly perfume. The contrast is strong: she gives the best she has, and he offers to sell his Master. The text does not explain all of his motives. Some think of money, and others of disappointment or disillusionment; the Bible does not make this entirely clear. What is certain is that from that moment Judas looked for an opportunity to betray him.

For today: examine what things might draw you away from Jesus, such as money or ambition. Ask God for a faithful and grateful heart, one that values Christ above any gain.
exp.4:12:
Jesus says to his disciples: "You are the salt of the earth." But if salt loses its savor, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, right after the Beatitudes, where he also spoke about persecution. He tells his followers that they have an important role in the world. Salt gave flavor and helped preserve food. Some scholars think Jesus means that his disciples have a good influence on society. The details of how salt could lose its taste are explained in several ways.

For today: live your faith with simplicity and love, in your work and in your family. Do not hide it or water it down out of fear of what others will say. In this way your life will be a blessing to others.
exp.21:22:
That same day, some Sadducees came to Jesus. The Sadducees were a religious group who taught that there is no resurrection. "That same day" means on that very day, and "came to Jesus" means they approached him in order to question him.

Earlier, the Pharisees had tried to trap Jesus with the question about paying taxes to Caesar, and he silenced them. Now the Sadducees, another rival group, come with another difficult question. Matthew is the one telling the story, and his purpose seems to be to show that the leaders wanted to test him, even though they did not agree with one another.

For today: when someone asks you questions with bad intentions, do not be anxious. Seek the truth in God's Word and answer with calm and humility, as Jesus did.
exp.19:20:
Jesus asks a woman what she wants, and she requests that in his kingdom one of her two sons may sit at his right hand and the other at his left. The words "at your right hand" and "at your left" point to the places of greatest honor beside a king.

The woman is the mother of James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Jesus had just announced that he would be handed over, flogged, crucified, and raised again. She seems to be thinking of a kingdom that would come right away, and she wants to secure a good place for her sons. In the parallel account in Mark, the sons themselves make the request, so it is likely that both were involved.

Today we can bring our requests to God with confidence, but it is good to examine our desires. Jesus speaks of serving and suffering, not of gaining status. Before asking for places of honor, let us ask ourselves whether we are willing to follow him in humility and self-giving.
exp.0:11:
It says that, after the exile to Babylon, Jeconiah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel. "Exile" means being forcibly carried away from your homeland, and "the father of" simply names a direct parent-child link in the family line.

Matthew writes this genealogy to show that Jesus is a descendant of Abraham and of David, the promised Messiah. This verse marks the passage through the exile, the darkest moment in Israel's history. Some lists in the Old Testament give Zerubbabel a different family relationship, and scholars explain this in several ways. Even so, the royal line continues.

For today: even in times of defeat or exile, God does not abandon his promises. If you are going through a dark season today, trust that he is still at work and carrying his plan forward.
exp.23:14:
Jesus says that when you see "the abomination of desolation," spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place, you will know what he means. An "abomination" is something detestable that defiles what is sacred; "desolation" means destruction or ruin. The words "let the reader understand" invite the reader to pay close attention and grasp the meaning.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when they ask him about the destruction of the temple and the end. He uses this sign as a warning to flee, as the verses that follow show. Christians understand it in different ways: some see it fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, others in an event still in the future, and others in both senses.

For today: Jesus wants us to be watchful and to read the Bible with care. We can set aside time regularly to study it with humility, so that we act with wisdom and not with fear.
exp.6:1:
This verse says that the way we treat others is the way we will be treated. If we judge harshly, we will receive harshness; if we are merciful, we will receive mercy. A "measure" is like a rod or a scale: the same measure you use with others will be used on you. The phrase "it will be measured to you" means that it will be measured back to you. Some understand that this refers to people, and others to God; the text allows both ideas.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples and the crowd. After this verse he uses the image of the speck and the beam: he warns against the hypocrisy of correcting small faults in others while ignoring greater faults of our own.

For today: before criticizing someone, stop and ask yourself what is in your own heart. Then treat that person with the patience and grace you would also want to receive.
exp.12:42:
Jesus says that the righteous, that is, those who belong to God and live in his favor, will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. "Shine" means to give off a bright light. At the end, "He who has ears, let him hear" is a call to pay attention with the heart, not only to listen with the ears.

Jesus is explaining the parable of the wheat and the weeds to his disciples. Earlier he spoke about judgment on those who do evil, and now he shows the other side: the glory of the righteous. Afterward he will go on with parables about the value of the kingdom. Many understand this light as referring to future glory, although the text gives no further details.

Today, this promise encourages us when living by faith seems hard or little seen. We can follow Christ with patience, knowing that God sees what we do and that our hope is not in vain.
exp.8:2:
Here, some of the scribes, who were teachers of the law, said to themselves that Jesus was speaking blasphemy. They did not say it out loud. They kept it in their thoughts. To blaspheme means to speak against God or to claim for yourself what belongs only to Him.

Jesus had just told the paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven. For the scribes, only God could forgive sins, so they believed Jesus was putting himself in God's place. Jesus knew what they were thinking, and he confronted them, then healed the man to show his authority.

For today: let us be careful about what we think in our hearts, because God sees it. And when something about Jesus makes us uncomfortable or we don't understand it, instead of judging in silence, we can come to him with humility and ask what he wants to teach us.
exp.26:33:
They offered Jesus, now at Golgotha, wine mixed with gall. Gall was something bitter, and the wine was sour. Jesus tasted it, but he refused to drink it.

Matthew, who narrates, recounts the moment just before the crucifixion. Some think the mixture was meant to ease the pain, and others see an echo of Psalm 69:21, which speaks of gall and vinegar. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact purpose. What is clear is that Jesus refused the relief and faced the cross with full awareness.

For today: Jesus chose the difficult path out of love for us. When we face trials, we can remember that he knows pain and walks with us. We can ask him for strength to remain faithful, without seeking shortcuts that would lead us away from what God asks of us.
exp.3:7:
This verse tells us that the devil takes Jesus once more, this time to a very high mountain. From there he shows him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. The word "took" in the verse above is the same action this comment describes, and "glory" here refers to their wealth, power, and beauty.

This is the third temptation in the wilderness, after Jesus had fasted for forty days. The devil is the one acting here, and he seeks to turn Jesus away from the mission the Father gave him. The texts do not explain how Jesus saw all the kingdoms; some believe it was a vision and others believe it was something real. What is certain is that the devil offers him a shortcut without the cross, and Jesus rejects it with Scripture.

For today: often what tempts us looks bright and easy. Before choosing, ask yourself whether that path honors God. Keeping his Word in your heart helps you say no.
exp.26:3:
Judas confesses to the religious leaders: "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." They answer him coldly: "What is that to us?" and then, "You bear the responsibility." The question "What is that to us?" means "what does it matter to us?", and the reply places the burden of the matter squarely on Judas himself.

Judas speaks after seeing that Jesus has been condemned. He repented and returned the thirty pieces of silver. The priests and elders, who had paid him to hand Jesus over, now do not want to carry any guilt. Judas acknowledges that Jesus is innocent, but his remorse leads him to despair rather than to seeking forgiveness. Some interpreters distinguish between this kind of repentance and the repentance that leads to God.

For today: when you recognize a mistake, do not carry it alone or sink into guilt. Bring your sin to God, who forgives, and also seek the support of people who will walk alongside you with compassion.
exp.16:24:
Peter answered "Yes" when the tax collectors asked whether Jesus paid the temple tax. When Peter entered the house, Jesus spoke first and asked what he thought: do the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes from their own sons, or from others outside the family? The question points to the answer Peter would give.

Jesus speaks with Peter in Capernaum. Shortly before, he had announced his death, and the disciples were saddened. The tax collectors asked about the two drachmas, a tax for the temple. Jesus uses a simple question to show that he, as the Son, was not obligated, yet he paid it so as not to cause offense.

For today: sometimes we have a right to something, but we can give it up out of love, so as not to become a stumbling block to others. Ask yourself in what situation you can act with humility and a good witness, without losing the truth.
exp.13:0:
It tells that Herod, called "the tetrarch" (a ruler over a fourth part of a territory, under Roman power), heard the reports about Jesus. The "reports" were what people were saying about Him: His teachings and miracles.

Here the narrator, Matthew, speaks. This Herod is Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee. The verses that follow show his reaction: his conscience troubled him, and he thought Jesus was John the Baptist risen from the dead, the man he had ordered imprisoned. Matthew wants to show that news of Jesus reached the palaces, and that a guilty heart can hear about Christ and be afraid, without coming to believe.

For today: it is not enough to hear about Jesus or to hold opinions about Him. Herod listened, but he did not repent. Today we can ask ourselves whether we respond to Jesus with humility and obedience, or only with curiosity or fear.
exp.8:5:
Jesus says that he wants people to know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. Then he speaks to the paralyzed man: "Get up, pick up your mat, and go home." The word "authority" shows that Jesus has real right and power to act here on earth. The "mat" was a simple bed that could be carried, and "go home" means return to your house.

Jesus speaks with some teachers of the law who were accusing him in their hearts of blasphemy, because he had told the sick man that his sins were forgiven. To show that his word has authority, he healed the man in front of everyone. "Son of Man" was a title Jesus used for himself; some connect it with Daniel 7.

Today we can come to Jesus with confidence, knowing that he can heal the deepest part of the heart. If you carry guilt, bring it to him, believe him, and rise up to walk in a new life.
exp.17:4:
Whoever welcomes a child like this in Jesus' name is, in fact, welcoming Jesus himself. The phrase "such a child" means a child like the one Jesus has just placed in front of them.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, who had asked him who was the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. He places a child in their midst and teaches that greatness is measured by humility and simplicity, not by prestige. Many understand that "child" also includes believers who are simple and humble. The verses that follow firmly warn against harming them.

For today: value and treat with respect those whom people often overlook, such as children, the weak, or those newly arrived in the faith. Give them your time, listen to them, and care for them, for in this way you serve Christ himself.
exp.10:14:
Jesus says that whoever has ears should hear. The word "hear" is an invitation to listen with attention. It is not only about hearing sounds, but about understanding and obeying what He has just said.

Jesus is speaking to the people about John the Baptist. He has just said that John fulfills what the prophets foretold, and that he is the one who was to come as the great prophet. But He adds, "if you are willing to receive it," because accepting it requires an open heart. Then Jesus laments that that generation did not respond either to John or to Him. Some interpret the reference to the prophet as a role John played, not as meaning that John was that prophet in person.

Today, listen to the Word of God with humility, without excuses or prejudice. Before reading the Bible, ask God for a heart ready to receive and put into practice what He shows you.
exp.22:15:
Jesus calls the teachers of the law "blind guides" because they taught people how to keep their promises. They said that swearing "by the temple" meant nothing, but swearing "by the gold of the temple" bound a person to keep the oath. Your verse uses the word "swear" for making a solemn promise, and the words "bound by his oath" mean that the person must keep what they promised.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem and addresses the scribes and Pharisees with a series of solemn warnings, one after another. He rebukes them because they placed more value on the gold than on the holy place that gave the gold its worth. Their way of teaching made room for excuses not to keep one's given word.

For today: let us be people of our word. Let us not look for clever phrases or excuses to escape what we have promised. Let our "yes" be yes and our "no" be no, and let us value what pleases God more than what suits us.
exp.15:6:
The disciples were talking together quietly, each one turning the matter over in their own mind, and they thought Jesus was speaking about bread. They believed he was rebuking them for not bringing any.

Jesus had just warned them to beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He was speaking figuratively: he meant a teaching that spreads and influences. The disciples took him literally, because they were keenly aware that they had no bread with them. Afterward Jesus reminded them of how he had multiplied the loaves.

Today we too can misunderstand what God is telling us when we are preoccupied with our own needs. Before we worry, it is good to remember how God has cared for us and to ask him to help us hear his voice clearly.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that Jesus moved to Capernaum "to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah," that is, so that something Isaiah had said long before would come true. It is a phrase that prepares the quotation that follows right after it.

The one speaking here is Matthew, the author of the gospel. He writes mainly for Jewish readers and wants to show that the life of Jesus matches the Scriptures. Jesus went to Galilee after learning that John had been arrested, and Matthew sees in that place, a region mixed with peoples from other nations, the fulfillment of the prophecy in Isaiah 9:1-2.

For today: God does not act by chance. Even difficult changes, such as moving or starting over, can be part of a greater plan. Trust that God can bring light into dark places, and offer yourself to be part of that light.
exp.24:9:
It says that while the foolish virgins were on their way to buy oil, the bridegroom arrived. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding banquet, and the door was shut. The word "foolish" here means lacking good sense.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, and he tells this parable to encourage them to be ready for his return. The bridegroom is delayed, and that tests everyone. Many understand the oil as a true, personal faith, although it is interpreted in several ways. The central teaching is clear: one must be prepared.

For today: do not leave your relationship with God for later. Nurture your faith every day with prayer, the Word, and obedience, because the preparation of the heart cannot be borrowed from someone else at the last moment.
exp.12:11:
Jesus says that whoever has will be given more, and they will have an abundance. But whoever does not have, even what they have will be taken away from them.

The idea is not about money, but about what each person does with what God makes known to them.

Jesus is answering his disciples, who ask him why he teaches in parables. He tells them they have been given the privilege of understanding the secrets of the kingdom of heaven. Many others hear, but they do not want to understand or are not able to. Jesus follows the line of what the prophet Isaiah said about a people with a closed heart.

For today: if you receive with humility what God shows you in his Word and put it into practice, your understanding will grow. If you ignore it, it grows cold. Read a passage today and do one concrete thing it teaches you.
exp.3:10:
What it says: After the third temptation, the devil left Jesus. Right away, angels came and began to care for him. The phrase "they ministered to him" means that they took care of him and gave him what he needed. The Bible does not detail how they did this; some think they strengthened him or gave him food, but the text does not say so.

Context: Matthew tells what happened after Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness. Satan offered him all the kingdoms if he would worship him, and Jesus answered with the Scriptures: only God is to be worshiped and served. By resisting, Jesus showed his faithfulness to the Father. Then Matthew moves on to the beginning of his ministry in Galilee.

For today: Trials come to an end, and God does not abandon the one who is faithful to him. When you face a temptation, answer with the Word of God and trust that he will care for you after the struggle.
exp.12:2:
Jesus taught the crowd many things using parables, which are simple stories drawn from everyday life. He begins with a farmer who went out to sow his seed. The crowd gathered around him, and the lake is the sea of Galilee, so the scene takes place on the water's edge.

Jesus is speaking to a large crowd beside the sea of Galilee. So that everyone could hear him, he got into a boat and taught from there. He used the image of a farmer sowing seed, something very familiar to people who lived in the countryside. Later he explains that parables help those who want to listen, while others pay no attention.

For today: hearing the Word of God is not only hearing it, but preparing ourselves to receive it. We can set aside a quiet moment each day to read the Bible, think about it, and ask God for a heart ready to obey.
exp.7:17:
Matthew 8:18 says that when Jesus saw a large crowd around him, he gave orders to cross to the other side of the sea. That sea is the Sea of Galilee, a lake. The verse means he instructed his disciples to cross by boat.

The account follows a very busy evening, when Jesus healed the sick and freed those tormented by demons. Matthew connects it with Isaiah's prophecy about the servant who bears our infirmities. After so much service, Jesus decides to withdraw from the crowd. Some think he was seeking rest; the text does not say so clearly. Soon a scribe appears who wants to follow him, and Jesus speaks to him about the cost of being his disciple.

For today: Jesus served with devotion, but he also knew how to stop and move according to the Father's guidance. Learn to listen to God so you know when to serve and when to withdraw, without being carried along only by the crowds or by the rush.
exp.21:39:
Jesus says that all the law of Moses and the writings of the prophets rest on two commandments: to love God and to love your neighbor. The word "rest" here is like a picture hanging from a nail: everything else is held up by these two loves. "Neighbor" means the person near us.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, in the temple. An expert in the law asked him which commandment was the greatest, and some Pharisees were trying to test him. Jesus does not invent something new; he joins two texts that were already in the Scriptures (Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18) and shows that the heart of the law is love.

For today: before keeping a rule or making a decision, ask yourself whether what you are about to do shows love for God, and respect and kindness toward the person beside you.
exp.8:20:
This verse shows us what the woman was thinking inwardly. "She said to herself" means that she was speaking in her own mind, without anyone else hearing her. She believed that if she could only touch Jesus' cloak, she would be healed of her illness.

Matthew tells us what she was thinking as she came up to Jesus from behind, when he was on his way to the house of an important man. She had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. Jesus turned, looked at her, and told her that her faith had healed her. Some explain that she approached in this way out of shame or fear; the Bible does not say so clearly.

Today, even if your faith is small or timid, you can come to Jesus just as you are. Speak simply to him about what weighs on you, and trust that he sees you and hears you.
exp.17:33:
This verse says that the king in the parable was angry with the servant who would not forgive. In anger, he turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, and he kept him there until he should repay all that he owed, that is, until the whole debt was paid.

Jesus tells this parable in answer to Peter, who asked how many times he must forgive his brother. One servant owed an enormous amount, and the king forgave it. But that same servant had no compassion on a fellow servant who owed him very little. Jesus ends by saying that the heavenly Father will act the same way toward anyone who does not forgive from the heart. Some understand this as a serious warning; others see it as a teaching about how impossible it is to receive grace and yet refuse it to others.

Today: think of someone who offended you and remember how much you have received from God. Ask him for help to forgive that person from the heart, even if it happens step by step.
exp.24:43:
The people on the left are surprised and ask the King: "Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick, or in prison, and not help you?" The word "stranger" here means a foreigner or a homeless person.

Jesus is speaking in the parable of the judgment of the nations, at the end of his teaching to the disciples. The King separates the sheep from the goats. These people did not deny loving God; they simply did not recognize Christ in those who were in need. Jesus says that what they did not do for "one of the least of these," they did not do for him. Some understand this to refer to any person in need, and others to believers in particular.

Today, let us not wait for great occasions. This week, look for someone close to you who is alone or in need, and help them in a concrete way: a visit, a meal, a phone call.
exp.27:15:
This verse says that the eleven disciples, that is, the apostles without Judas, went to Galilee. There they reached the mountain that Jesus had pointed out to them. The word "meanwhile" here signals that this happened at the same time as the events just before it, and "designated" means that Jesus had chosen that place for them.

Matthew records this after the resurrection. Earlier, Jesus had told them that they would see him in Galilee (Matthew 26:32; 28:7, 10). While the religious leaders were paying the soldiers to spread lies, the disciples simply obeyed. The text does not say which mountain it was, so we cannot know with certainty which one it was.

For today: obey Jesus even when we do not understand everything. The disciples went, even with fear and doubts, and there they received the greatest mission of all. Take the step of obedience that is clear to you today, and let God meet you along the way.
exp.10:28:
Jesus invites people to take his yoke, which was a wooden piece that joined two animals so they could work together. To take his yoke is like saying: "Walk with me and be my disciples." He also says "learn from me." He is gentle and humble in heart, that is, kind and free of pride. And he promises rest for the soul.

Jesus speaks to people who are tired and burdened, perhaps by the religious demands of his time or by the weight of life. Just before this, he says that only he reveals the Father. His invitation is to know God through him, not to carry a heavy list of rules.

Today, when you feel worn out by the pressure to prove your worth, stop and go to Jesus in prayer. Read the Gospels and notice how he treats people. Learn from his patience and humility, and place in his hands what you cannot carry alone.
exp.12:33:
He says that on that occasion Jesus taught the crowds using only parables, that is, simple stories taken from everyday life. The word "crowds" in the verse above refers to the large groups of people who had gathered around him.

Jesus speaks to the crowd beside the sea, and he has just told the parables of the mustard seed and the yeast. Matthew explains that this fulfills what was spoken by the prophet: Jesus would open his mouth in parables. Then he leaves the crowd and explains the meaning to his disciples at home. Interpreters debate why he used parables: some think it was to reveal truth, and others think it was also to hide it from those with closed hearts.

For today: do not be content with hearing Bible stories or teachings from a distance. Like the disciples, draw near to Jesus in prayer and ask him to explain his Word to you clearly.
exp.22:23:
Jesus calls the religious leaders "blind guides." The verse's word "strain" means to filter out. They would filter wine to remove a tiny gnat, yet they would swallow a camel, which is enormous. This is an exaggeration to show that they guarded small details while neglecting what mattered most.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees in his series of warnings in the temple. He had just said that they tithed even mint, dill, and cumin but set aside justice, mercy, and faithfulness. A gnat and a camel were both unclean animals according to the law, so the image also speaks of caring for outward religious appearance.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I worry more about small rules than about being just, compassionate, and faithful? Before judging the small details in others, let us ask God to first put our own hearts in order.
exp.20:36:
He says that after sending several servants who were mistreated, the owner of the vineyard finally sent his own son. He thought they would respect him. The verse of the wording: "finally" points to the last step in a series of sendings, and "respect" means to treat him with honor and regard.

Jesus tells this parable in Jerusalem, speaking to the priests and elders of the people. The owner represents God, the vineyard represents Israel, the servants represent the prophets, and the son, according to most interpreters, represents Jesus himself. With this he shows them that God was patient, but they kept rejecting his message.

For today: God speaks to us with patience, and his clearest message is Jesus. We can ask ourselves whether we listen to him with respect or whether we make excuses not to obey him. Today you can read a passage from the Gospels with attention and with a willing heart.
exp.0:16:
Jesus's family line in this verse is divided into three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, and from that exile until the Christ. The exile was the time when the people were taken away as captives to Babylon.

Matthew, writing for Jewish readers, summarizes the history of Israel this way to show that Jesus is the promised Messiah. Abraham and David represent God's promises. Many believe the number fourteen has a symbolic meaning, since the name of David in Hebrew adds up to fourteen, though this is understood in various ways. Matthew also leaves out some names, which was common in ancient genealogies.

God does not improvise or forget his promises. Even in times of exile and silence, he kept working. If today you feel that your situation is dragging on or makes no sense, trust that God works with patience and fulfills what he says.
exp.11:47:
Jesus answers the person who told him that his family was looking for him. Instead of going out right away, he asks a question: "Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?" The crowd around him was a large group of people, and his mother and brothers wanted to speak with him.

Jesus is teaching the crowd when he is told that his mother and brothers are waiting outside. With his question he does not look down on his family; rather, he is setting up a lesson. In the verses that follow he points to his disciples and explains that his true family is those who do the will of his heavenly Father.

For today: faith unites us as a family in Christ. This week, reach out to someone in your church, and look for a concrete way to obey God alongside that person, helping or encouraging them.
exp.24:45:
This verse closes the scene of the final judgment. It says that some will go away into a punishment that does not end, and that the righteous will go into a life that does not end either.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the last days before his cross. He has just described how the King separates people according to how they treated the needy, whom he calls his brothers. Christians understand the details of this punishment in different ways, but all of them see here a serious warning.

For today: this week, notice one person near you who is suffering, such as a lonely neighbor, a sick person, or someone who is hungry. Help them with one concrete act, knowing that Jesus counts that care as done to him.
exp.17:11:
Jesus asks a simple question: if a man has a hundred sheep and one of them wanders off and gets lost, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost?

The phrase "goes astray" means that the sheep has wandered off the path and is lost.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He has just warned them not to look down on the little ones, meaning the humble and simple people who believe in him. With this parable he shows that God cares about every person, and that he does not want any of them to be lost.

For today: if someone has drifted away from the faith or from the church, do not judge them or forget them. Pray for that person, seek them out with affection, and remind them that God still values them.
exp.17:31:
The verse tells us that the king calls the servant back, the one he had forgiven. He calls him a wicked servant because, after receiving an enormous pardon, he refused to forgive a small debt. The words "I forgave all your debt because you begged me" mean that the servant pleaded for mercy, and the king granted it.

Jesus tells this parable after Peter asked him how many times he should forgive his brother. The king represents God, and the servant represents each of us. The other servants were grieved when they saw the injustice and told the king about it. Jesus wants to show that the forgiveness God gives us should shape the way we treat others.

Today we can remember how much we have received from God's grace before refusing forgiveness to someone. If there is an offense that you find hard to let go of, ask God for help to forgive, just as He forgave you.
exp.7:33:
This verse says that the whole town went out to meet Jesus. But when they saw Him, instead of welcoming Him, they begged Him to leave their region. The word "region" refers to the territory around the town, and "begged" means they kept pleading with Him.

Jesus had just set free two men controlled by demons in the region of the Gadarenes, and the demons entered a herd of pigs that rushed into the sea. The herdsmen told everything in the town. The text does not explain why they asked Him to leave; it could be fear, or the financial loss of the pigs, or both. Here the narrator is Matthew.

For today: sometimes we prefer comfort to the changes Jesus brings. Ask yourself honestly whether there is something you are afraid to let go of. Invite Him in, even though His presence may disturb what you have arranged.
exp.13:18:
Here Jesus directs the crowd to sit down on the grass. He takes the five loaves and the two fish, looks up to heaven, and speaks a blessing. "Blessed" here means that he gave thanks and praised God for the food. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.

The account takes place with Jesus and his disciples before a large crowd, at the end of the day, in a remote place. The disciples told him they had only five loaves and two fish, far too little for so many people. Jesus asked them to bring the food to him. He did not leave them to solve the problem alone; he included them in the miracle, since it was they who passed out the food.

For today: God can use what little we have if we offer it to him in trust. We do not have to wait until we have plenty. We can give thanks, offer what is in our hands, and serve others.
exp.6:6:
Jesus invites us to ask, seek, and knock. The three actions build in intensity: asking is expressing a need, seeking is putting in effort, and knocking is persisting at a door. The promise is that God responds. "It will be given to you" and "the door will be opened to you" are ways of saying that God himself gives and opens.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, addressing his disciples and the crowd. He has just spoken about not judging others with hypocrisy and about having discernment. Then he uses the example of a father who gives bread to his son. In this way he teaches that God is a good Father. Many understand that what God gives is what is good for us, not always what we imagine.

Today, we can bring every need to God with confidence, pray with persistence, and trust in his fatherly care, even when the answer takes time or is different.
exp.0:19:
But while Joseph was thinking about these things, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. The angel called him "son of David," reminding him of his royal family line, and told him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife. The angel explained that the child she was carrying was from the Holy Spirit. The word "take" here means bringing her into his home and marrying her.

Matthew tells us that Joseph and Mary were betrothed, a very serious commitment in that culture. When Joseph learned of the pregnancy, being a righteous man, he wanted to act without shaming her. The angel speaks on God's behalf to calm his fear and make clear to him what was happening.

For today: when you are afraid before a difficult decision, ask God for direction and listen to his Word before you act. He can give you clarity and courage to obey, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.15:1:
Jesus tells the Pharisees and Sadducees that when evening comes, they say, "The weather will be fair, for the sky is red."

Jesus speaks to religious leaders who were normally at odds with one another, but who now join together to test him. They ask him for a sign from heaven, even though they had already seen his miracles. He shows them that they know how to read the weather, but they are unwilling to recognize what God is doing right in front of them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are asking God for more proof when he has already shown us enough. Take a moment to remember how God has worked in your life and in his Word, and respond with trust and obedience.
exp.7:13:
Jesus came to the house of Peter and saw his mother-in-law sick in bed with a fever. Matthew is the one telling the story. Jesus has just healed the servant of a Roman centurion, a foreigner who trusted in his word. Now Jesus enters an ordinary home, the house of one of his disciples. Matthew shows that Jesus cares for those who are far away just as much as for those who are near. He does not say anyone asked him to do this; Jesus sees the need and acts.

For today: Jesus is interested in your home and your everyday problems, not only in what is "spiritual." Bring to him in prayer the illness, the exhaustion, or the worry in your family, trusting that he already sees them.
exp.8:3:
Jesus knows what the scribes are thinking, even though they have said nothing out loud. He asks them why they harbor evil in their hearts. The word "harbor" means that they were holding on to malice or accusation, not sincerely searching for the truth.

Some friends bring a paralyzed man to Jesus, and Jesus forgives the man's sins. Some scribes, experts in the law of Moses, think that Jesus is blaspheming, because only God can forgive sins. Jesus speaks to them to show that he knows their inner thoughts, and then he heals the man to prove his authority.

For today: God knows what we think, even what we keep silent. Instead of hiding doubts or judgments, we can bring them to him with honesty and ask him for a humble heart, willing to recognize what Jesus does.
exp.25:73:
This verse tells that Peter, for the third time, denied Jesus. "Cursing" means calling down curses on oneself, and "swearing" means making a strong promise or declaration that something is true. Peter said he did not know the man, and immediately a rooster crowed.

Peter was in the courtyard of the high priest while Jesus was being questioned. Some people noticed his accent and pointed him out as a follower of Jesus. He was afraid. Earlier, Jesus had told him that he would deny Him three times before the rooster crowed. The crowing of the rooster reminded him of that warning, and he went out and wept bitterly.

All of us can fail when we feel pressure or fear. Instead of trusting in our own strength, it is wise to pray and depend on God. And if we do fail, Peter's sincere repentance shows us that we can return to Jesus with humility.
exp.5:10:
This verse is a simple request: "Give us this day our daily bread." "Daily" means "for each day." "Bread" stands for food and, by extension, whatever is needed to live. The Greek word translated this way is rare, and some understand it as "bread for today" or "bread for tomorrow." Even so, the general idea is clear: asking for what is necessary for each day.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the Sermon on the Mount. He teaches them how to pray, and before asking for our needs, the prayer puts God first: his name, his kingdom, and his will. Then it continues with forgiveness and protection from evil.

For today: ask God with confidence for what you need today, without worrying about the whole future. And give thanks for what he already gives you, remembering that your "our" includes those who have less.
exp.13:23:
The boat carrying the disciples was by now far from land, out in the middle of the lake, and the waves were beating against it hard. The wind was blowing against them, so they could not make progress. "Buffeted by the waves" means shaken and battered by the waves. "The sea" here is the Sea of Galilee.

The one telling the story is Matthew. Jesus himself had told the disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him, while he sent the crowds away and went up the mountain alone to pray. In other words, they were in the storm because they had obeyed. Jesus was not with them at that moment, but he had not forgotten them; in the next verse he goes out to them.

Obeying God does not always keep us from storms. When you face a headwind, do not think that God has abandoned you. Keep trusting, keep praying, and remember that Jesus knows where you are and comes to meet you.
exp.20:35:
It says the owner of the vineyard sent other servants again, more than the first group, but the tenants did the same to them. The violence did not stop; it was repeated.

Jesus is speaking in the temple to the priests and elders of the people. He tells this parable of the vineyard to show how Israel had treated the prophets that God sent. Many understand that the owner represents God and the son, who comes later, represents Jesus himself. It also shows God's patience.

For today: God is patient and calls us many times to return to Him. Think about whether there is some voice He has sent you, such as a piece of advice, a passage, or a person, that you have ignored. Today you can listen to it with humility and respond.
exp.12:8:
Jesus says: "He who has ears, let him hear." We all have ears, so he is not speaking only of physical hearing. It is an invitation to listen carefully, with a desire to understand and to obey. The word "hear" works like a kind and firm command: pay attention!

Jesus is teaching a crowd beside the sea, and he has just told the parable of the sower. That story is about seeds that fall on different kinds of ground, and about how people receive his message in very different ways. With this sentence, Jesus calls each listener to think about what kind of ground he or she is. Shortly afterward, the disciples ask him why he teaches in parables.

Today we can read the Bible or listen to a sermon with a ready heart, not in a hurry or distracted. Before you begin, pray: "Speak, Lord, I want to hear and obey." Then put into practice one concrete thing you have learned.
exp.20:15:
The religious leaders ask Jesus whether he hears what the children are saying in the temple: they are calling him "Son of David," that is, the promised Messiah. Jesus answers that he does hear, and he reminds them of words from Scripture (Psalm 8:2): God has ordained praise through the mouths of children and infants, bringing it to completion through those who are still young.

The ones speaking are the chief priests and the scribes, angry because Jesus had just healed the blind and the lame in the temple, and the children were praising him for it. Jesus does not silence them. He answers from the same Scriptures the leaders claimed to know, and so he leaves them without a reply: they had seen the wonders, but did not recognize who was doing them.

Today we can praise God simply and sincerely, without thinking that we must be wise or important. We can also ask ourselves whether our pride keeps us from seeing what God is doing.
exp.10:19:
Then Jesus began to denounce the cities where most of his miracles had been performed, because they did not repent. "Denounce" means to speak out strongly against something and call it wrong. To "repent" means truly turning back to God, not merely feeling sorry.

Jesus is the one speaking. He has just pointed out that the people rejected both John the Baptist and him, always with some excuse. Now he speaks of cities in Galilee, such as Chorazin and Bethsaida, which saw his miracles up close. What they had seen was great, and so their responsibility was greater. His denunciation does not come from contempt, but from the fact that he was expecting a response.

For today: seeing God's work and hearing his Word is not enough; he expects us to respond. Today you can ask yourself, "Is there something God has shown me that I keep putting off changing?" Give yourself an honest answer, with humility.
exp.24:12:
Jesus says: "Therefore keep watch," which means to stay awake and alert, and the word "therefore" connects this teaching to the parable of the ten virgins that comes just before it. No one knows the day or the hour when the Son of man, that is, Jesus himself, will come back. The teaching is to always live prepared.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he teaches them about the last times. In the parable, five of the virgins did not bring extra oil and were left outside the feast. Some believe the oil represents a living and true faith, although the text does not explain this exactly.

Today we can live each day with a sincere faith and not leave for later what is important: praying, forgiving, obeying God, and serving others. It is not about living in fear, but about having a heart ready to meet Jesus.
exp.16:23:
This verse tells us that Jesus and his disciples arrived in Capernaum. There, the collectors of the two-drachma tax came to Peter. This was a small yearly payment made for the temple. They asked him whether his Teacher pays it.

The ones asking are the tax collectors, who speak to Peter. Jesus had just announced his death and resurrection, and the disciples were very sad. Afterward Jesus teaches Peter that, being the Son of God, he had no obligation to pay, yet he decides to pay anyway so as not to cause offense (as the following verses explain).

For today: sometimes we have a right to something, but we can give it up with humility so as not to offend or hinder others. Love is sometimes worth more than defending our rights.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, is by no means least among the rulers of Judah, because out of it will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of God's people Israel. The word "shepherd" points to someone who feeds and cares for his flock, just as a shepherd looks after his sheep.

The chief priests and the scribes say this when King Herod asks them where the Christ was to be born. They quote a prophecy from Micah 5:2. The wise men were seeking the newborn king, and Herod felt threatened.

For today: God often works in places and people that the world considers small. Do not be discouraged if you feel unimportant; God can use your life. And do not limit yourself to knowing the Bible: respond to it with faith, not with indifference or fear.
exp.20:13:
This verse tells that, after Jesus cleared the temple, blind and lame people came to him there, and he healed them. The word "á" is an old way of writing "a," so it is not needed here. Healed means that he cured them.

Jesus had just driven out those who were doing business in the temple, saying it was a house of prayer. Now that same place is filled with needy people who come to him. Matthew is the one who tells the story. Some interpreters see a contrast here: the merchants were looking for profit, but the sick were looking for help. The religious leaders, on the other hand, were upset when they saw these wonders.

For today: God invites us to come to him just as we are, with our weaknesses and needs. We can bring to him in prayer whatever hurts us, without pretending to have everything in order.
exp.24:15:
The servant who had received five talents went at once and put that money to work, and he gained five more. A talent was a large sum of money, not a small coin.

Jesus spoke this parable to his disciples shortly before his crucifixion. Through it he taught them how to live while they waited for his return. The man who goes on a journey represents Christ, and the servants are those who belong to him. To each one something is entrusted according to his ability, and faithfulness is expected, not equal results.

For today: God has entrusted you with gifts, time, and resources. Do not compare yourself with others or wait for the perfect moment. Begin today to faithfully use what you have to serve others and honor God.
exp.14:2:
Jesus answers the Pharisees with a question of his own. The word "break" means to violate or disobey. "Tradition" refers to customs handed down from one generation to the next. Jesus points out that while they accuse his disciples of breaking a human custom, they themselves set aside a command of God in order to keep their own traditions.

Jesus is the speaker. Some scribes and Pharisees who came from Jerusalem question him because his disciples do not wash their hands before eating, following the tradition of the elders. Jesus does not respond by defending himself; instead he shows them that they fail to honor their parents, something God had clearly commanded.

For today: consider whether any custom, habit, or way of doing things in your church or family leads you to neglect what God clearly asks, such as loving and caring for your parents.
exp.11:4:
Jesus asks whether they have not read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent. "Break" here means treating as ordinary something that is holy; he says it with irony, since in reality they were carrying out their service. "Innocent" means they are not guilty.

Jesus is speaking with the Pharisees, who accused his disciples of picking heads of grain on the Sabbath because they were hungry. He gives them examples from Scripture: David and the priests. If serving God allowed those exceptions, then all the more could someone "greater than the temple" do so, that is, he himself. Then he quotes Hosea 6:6: God desires mercy.

For today: before judging someone by a religious rule, ask yourself whether you are showing mercy. Obeying God should never make us hard toward people in need.
exp.21:6:
The king became angry when he learned that the guests he had invited had killed his servants. So he sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city.

Jesus is speaking in a parable about the kingdom of heaven, addressed to the religious leaders who were rejecting him. The king represents God, and the guests who scorn the wedding feast represent those who reject his call. Many scholars see here a possible reference to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70 A.D., although some interpret it in other ways.

For today: God's invitation is a gift, not a minor matter. Let us not put it off because we are busy. Let us respond today with humility and gratitude, giving Him the first place.
exp.27:0:
After the sabbath had passed, as the first day of the week (our Sunday) was just beginning to dawn, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb where Jesus had been laid. The timing marks the close of the sabbath and the start of a new day.

This is the opening of the resurrection account in Matthew. The narrator introduces two faithful women who had followed Jesus to his burial. They went to see the tomb, perhaps with grief and without expecting what would come next. The verses that follow show that God acted in a powerful way.

For today: although sometimes all we can do is go to see the tomb, that is, draw near to God with sadness or doubts, it is worth staying present and faithful. God often surprises us just when we keep seeking him.
exp.4:30:
Here Jesus recalls a well-known teaching: "Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce." To "divorce" means to send a wife away from the marriage. The phrase "it has also been said" means "it was taught" or "it was commanded." This comes from the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 24:1).

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, and in this part he shows that the law goes beyond the outward act. Many people treated the written certificate as an easy permission to send a wife away. In the verses that follow, Jesus corrects that idea and defends the seriousness of marriage. Scholars discuss how to apply the words "cause of unchastity," but the emphasis is clear.

For today: treat your marriage, or your promises, as something sacred, not as a deal that is broken for convenience. Speak, forgive, and seek help in time.
exp.5:33:
Jesus says not to worry about tomorrow. "Worry" means being filled with anxiety or concern. "Trouble" refers to the problems and burdens that weigh on us. Each day already brings enough of its own, so there is no need to add the troubles of the future.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Shortly before, he explained that God takes care of the birds and the flowers, and that the Father knows what they need. The Gentiles, who did not know God, lived anxious about food and clothing. Jesus invites his listeners to put the kingdom of God first and to trust in his care.

Today you can apply it this way: when worry about what will happen tomorrow comes to you, take a brief moment to pray, entrusting that concern to God. Then calmly do what is yours to do today. Planning with wisdom is good; living in anxiety is not.
exp.8:21:
Jesus turned around and saw the woman. He said to her, "Take courage, daughter; your faith has healed you." The phrase "take courage" means to be encouraged and not afraid. "Healed" here means she was made well and free from her sickness. The word "daughter" is spoken here as a term of affection. From that very hour she was healed.

Jesus is speaking as he goes on the way to the house of an important man whose daughter had died. A woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the edge of his cloak, believing that she would be healed. Jesus did not let her slip away unseen: he looked at her and called her "daughter," with tenderness.

Today we too can come to Jesus with our need, even when our faith is small or timid. He sees us, receives us with kindness, and invites us to trust. Tell him today, honestly, what weighs on you.
exp.1:12:
After the wise men had gone, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream. The angel said, "Get up! Take the Child and His mother and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, for Herod is going to search for the Child to kill Him."

The one speaking is the angel, a messenger from God. Herod was the king who ruled the region and felt threatened by the birth of one called king of the Jews. God protects Jesus by warning Joseph, who had already received other instructions in dreams. Matthew later connects this journey to the prophecy of Hosea, saying: "Out of Egypt I called My Son."

For today: Joseph obeyed at once, by night, and without knowing the future. We can learn to trust God's guidance, taking the next step we know He asks of us, even when we do not understand the whole path.
exp.25:32:
Peter answers Jesus with great confidence. He says that even if all the others fall away because of Jesus, he never will. The word "fall away" here does not refer to a public scandal, but to stumbling or failing in faith.

Jesus has just announced that all the disciples will forsake him that very night, quoting a prophecy about the shepherd and the scattered sheep (Zechariah 13:7). He also promises that after he rises, he will go ahead of them to Galilee. Peter, with a good heart but trusting in his own strength, does not accept that this could include him.

For today: loving Jesus truly takes more than good intentions. Let us be humble, recognize our weakness, and ask him for help every day, because he sustains us even when we fail.
exp.22:38:
Jesus tells the people that from that moment they will not see him again until they say, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." That phrase comes from Psalm 118:26 and was a greeting of praise for the Messiah. "I tell you" is a plain way of saying that Jesus is speaking directly and clearly to them, and "you will not see me" means they will no longer have him among them in the same way.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, at the end of his public teaching, after rebuking the religious leaders. With sorrow, he mourns that the city rejected the prophets and also him. Christians interpret this "until you say" in different ways: as a reference to his return, or to a future acknowledgment by Israel. Not everyone agrees.

For today: Jesus speaks with pain, not coldness. He desires to draw near to us. Today we can respond to him with humility, welcoming him and saying, "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord."
exp.20:31:
Jesus says that John the Baptist came showing the right way to live before God, but the religious leaders did not believe him. By contrast, the tax collectors (despised by the people) and the prostitutes (women who sold their bodies) did believe him. Even after seeing that change, the leaders did not repent and believe him. Here, "repent" means changing one's attitude and turning to God.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with the chief priests and the elders, who were questioning his authority. He has just told the parable of the two sons: one said no but went, the other said yes and did not go. With it he shows them that talking about religion is not enough if it is not followed by obedience.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we answer God only with words or with real obedience. It is never too late to change direction, even when others judge us or we ourselves feel far away.
exp.12:5:
What it says: When the sun rose, the heat scorched the young plants. They withered because they had no root. The plants sprang up quickly, but they could not endure the heat.

Context: Jesus is speaking to a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. He teaches with the parable of the sower, a simple story to explain how people receive his message. Later in this same chapter, Jesus explains that this seed represents the person who receives the word with joy but does not let it take root, and when difficulties or persecution come, turns away.

For today: A faith with roots is formed little by little. Set aside time each day to read the Bible, pray, and spend time with other believers. That way, when trials come, your faith will have something to hold on to.
exp.9:6:
Jesus tells his disciples that, as they go along the road, they are to announce a message: "The kingdom of heaven is near." That is, the rule and reign of God are close at hand, they are becoming present. The word "preach" means to proclaim or announce aloud, and "as you go" reminds us that this message is carried out by moving forward, not by waiting while sitting still.

Jesus speaks to the twelve apostles just as he sends them out for the first time. He sends them first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, his own people. His message is the same one Jesus had been preaching, and the healings that follow showed that this kingdom was truly drawing near.

Today we can share God's hope with simplicity, without forcing anything on anyone. With kind words and acts of kindness, we can tell someone close to us that God is not far away and that his love is within their reach.
exp.13:17:
Jesus asks his disciples to bring him the five loaves and the two fish. "Bring them here to Me" is a plain request to hand over what they have. He is not asking for more food or for a human solution: he asks for the little they have.

Jesus is in a remote place, with a crowd that followed him until evening. The disciples wanted to send the people away so they could find food, but Jesus told them to give the people something to eat themselves. They answered that they had only five loaves and two fish. Then Jesus speaks these words and takes control of the situation.

For today: when you feel that what you have is too little for a great need, do not hide it. Hand it over to Jesus with confidence. He can take the small, bless it, and use it to help many.
exp.23:4:
Jesus says that many will come using his name, claiming, "I am the Christ," that is, the promised Messiah. And they will deceive many people. The word "deceive" means to make people believe something false. The claim "I am the Christ" is the claim itself, so the meaning is that these people will say they are the Messiah.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They asked him when these things would happen and what the sign of his coming would be. Before speaking of wars or earthquakes, Jesus begins with a warning: be careful about deceptions. Interpreters differ on how this is fulfilled, whether in the past, in the present, or in both, but the warning is clear.

For today: do not believe everything someone says in Jesus' name. Know the Bible well, compare what you hear with what Jesus taught, and ask God for wisdom to discern the truth.
exp.24:3:
This verse says that the five wise young women, besides carrying their lamps lit, also took extra oil in flasks. "Wise" means sensible, people who think about the future. The "foolish" ones of the previous verse are the ones who did not prepare.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples, in his teaching about the last times, to encourage them to be ready for his return. The bridegroom represents Christ. Many believe the oil symbolizes genuine faith or a prepared life, although the text does not explain this exactly, and there are different interpretations.

For today: true faith is not improvised at the last moment. Look after your relationship with God every day, with prayer, with his Word and with simple obedience, so that when a trial or a surprise comes, your heart is already prepared.
exp.14:7:
This explanation says that many people speak respectfully about God and use words of honor, but inwardly their hearts are far from Him. "Honor Me with their lips" means they praise Him with their mouths, while their love and obedience are not sincere. The word "but" in the verse marks the contrast between the outward words and the inward heart.

Jesus is speaking to the scribes and Pharisees, who had criticized Him for not following their traditions. He answers that they themselves were disobeying a command of God, to honor father and mother, by using religious excuses to avoid helping them. He quotes the prophet Isaiah (29:13) to show that this hypocrisy was not new.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: do my prayers, songs, and words in church match my obedience in everyday life? For example, do I treat my family well and act fairly at work? God looks for a sincere heart, not just good words.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that the meek are happy, that is, people who are humble and gentle in character, who are neither violent nor proud. They "will inherit the earth," that is, they will receive it as an inheritance, as a gift passed down to them. "Blessed" means happy, favored.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples and the crowd. Here he takes up the idea of Psalm 37:11, where the meek inherit the land. Some understand this promise as the kingdom of God and the new creation; others see it as a blessing that is also present now. Jesus shows that his kingdom works the opposite way from the world: the humble are the ones who are favored.

Today, when you get angry in an argument, try to respond with calm and without offending. Being meek is not being weak, but keeping your strength under control, trusting that God takes care of you.
exp.12:31:
Jesus says that the mustard seed is the smallest of all seeds, yet when it grows it becomes the largest of the garden plants. It grows into something like a tree, and the birds of the air come and nest in its branches. "Seeds" refers to the small grains that plants grow from.

Jesus is teaching the crowds with parables, which are simple stories with a spiritual message. He has just spoken about the wheat and the weeds, and now he shows another aspect of the kingdom of God: it begins small and almost unnoticed, but it grows greatly. Some see in the birds an image of the peoples who find shelter in the kingdom; others interpret it in different ways.

For today: do not despise small beginnings. A prayer, an act of kindness, or a word of faith planted with patience can grow more than you imagine. Trust that God gives the growth.
exp.18:25:
Jesus looked directly at his disciples and spoke to them plainly: with human ability, salvation is impossible, but all things are possible with God.

Jesus had just spoken with a rich young man who was unwilling to give up his possessions to follow him. Then he said it is very hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. The disciples were startled and asked, "Who then can be saved?" Jesus answers that salvation does not depend on what human beings accomplish, but on what God does.

Today, this invites us to stop trusting in our merits, money, or strength to be accepted by God. If you feel unable to change, pray with humility and ask God to do in you what you cannot do.
exp.13:8:
This verse says that King Herod was grieved when the girl asked for the head of John the Baptist. But because of his oaths and the guests who were sitting with him at the table, he ordered that her wish be granted. The phrase "he ordered that her wish be granted" means that he gave the command to hand over what she had asked for.

Matthew's account tells what happened at Herod's birthday. His niece or stepdaughter danced, and he promised to give her whatever she asked. Her mother, Herodias, was resentful toward John, because he had said it was not lawful for Herod to live with her. Herod felt sorrow, but he did not act with courage to correct his mistake.

Today it teaches us to think before we promise something lightly. It also reminds us that fear of looking bad before others can lead us to do harm. It is better to obey God and our conscience, even when it costs us.
exp.13:22:
This verse tells how Jesus dismissed the crowd and went up on a mountain by himself to pray. The words "after he had dismissed them" mean the crowd had already gone home. "By himself" means alone, apart from others. When evening came, Jesus was still there, alone.

This is an account from the Gospel of Matthew. Jesus had just fed about five thousand men, besides women and children. Then he sent his disciples ahead of him in the boat. After a day of giving himself fully to the people, Jesus looks for a quiet moment to be with the Father. Meanwhile, the disciples were going to face a storm.

For today: after days full of work or of people, look for a little time alone with God. Even ten minutes without a phone or noise, speaking to him honestly, renews you and prepares you for whatever comes.
exp.17:27:
The servant who had just been forgiven went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He grabbed him and began to choke him, demanding, "Pay back what you owe me." The word for fellow servant means a co-worker, and "grabbed" shows he seized him with force. A denarius was roughly the pay for one day's work.

Jesus tells this parable in answer to Peter, who asked how many times he should forgive his brother. A king had forgiven this servant an enormous debt (ten thousand talents, according to verse 24). Jesus shows the contrast between that immense debt and the small one the servant demands repayment of.

For today: when it is hard for us to forgive someone, let us remember how much we have received from God. His mercy toward us moves us to be merciful to others.
exp.19:31:
This verse tells that Jesus stopped when he heard the cries of two blind men. He called them and asked them a question: "What do you want Me to do for you?" The question asks what they want, and it shows that Jesus stopped in the middle of his journey to attend to them.

Jesus was on his way, surrounded by a crowd, and the two blind men kept pleading for mercy, even though the people tried to silence them. They called him "Son of David," a title that expressed hope in the Messiah. Jesus did not ignore their cry; he attended to them personally. Although their need seemed obvious, he invited them to express it in their own words.

For today: God invites us to speak to him honestly about what we need, even though he already knows it. When others tell you to be quiet or that your problem does not matter, keep crying out to Jesus. He stops to listen to you.
exp.25:67:
This verse shows the mockery directed at Jesus. Those who guarded him blindfolded his face (according to Luke 22:64), struck him, and said: "Prophesy to us, Christ! Who hit you?" Here "prophesy" means to guess. "Hit" means struck.

The people speaking are those gathered around Jesus in the house of the high priest Caiaphas, after the council had declared him deserving of death. They mocked his claim to be the Christ, the Messiah. Without realizing it, they fulfilled what was foretold about the suffering servant in Isaiah 50:6. Jesus remained silent and did not respond with revenge.

For today: when someone mocks your faith or mistreats you, remember that Jesus went through this first. You can respond with calm and trust in God, without returning evil for evil.
exp.7:23:
Suddenly a violent storm came up on the sea, so strong that the waves swept over the boat. Yet Jesus was sleeping.

The storm is described simply as a violent storm striking the sea, and the sea here is the Sea of Galilee. The verse does not give a separate description of the waves beyond their covering the boat.

Matthew tells this right after Jesus called his disciples to follow him without excuses. They obeyed and got into the boat with him. The writer shows that following Jesus does not spare anyone from storms. It also reveals his human tiredness, since he sleeps, and later his authority in calming the sea.

Today we can remember that going through a storm does not mean God has left us or that we took the wrong road. When you feel fear, do as the disciples did: come to Jesus with a sincere and simple prayer, even when it seems to you that he is sleeping.
exp.24:44:
Here Jesus answers those who asked when they saw him in need and did not help him. He says that what they failed to do for "one of the least of these," that is, for humble and needy people, they failed to do for him. The reader sees "the least of these," and the verse of this phrase is that it refers to humble and needy people. The phrase "truly I tell you" means "I assure you." The phrase "whatever you did not do" means "every time you did not do it."

Jesus speaks as King and Judge at the end of the parable of the sheep and the goats. He explains to them that how we treat the needy reveals what is in the heart. Some understand "the least" to be anyone in need; others, especially the disciples of Jesus. The passage serves both readings.

Today, do not wait for a great occasion to serve. Look this week at someone close to you who is suffering, such as a sick person, a lonely one, or a poor one, and help them in a concrete way with a visit, a meal, or some company.
exp.14:36:
This verse says that all the people ate and were satisfied. Afterward, the disciples picked up the pieces that were left over and filled seven baskets. "Were satisfied" means they ate until they had all they needed.

Jesus was in Galilee, near the lake, and he had compassion on a crowd that had been with him for three days and had nothing to eat. With seven loaves and a few fish, he gave thanks, broke the food, and gave it to his disciples to distribute. Matthew tells of the miracle and shows Jesus' care for the people.

For today: God pays attention to our real needs and is generous. You can offer him what little you have, even when it seems insufficient, and trust that he knows how to use it. You can also be a channel that passes his kindness on to others.
exp.18:20:
Jesus tells the young man: if you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then he adds: come and follow me. The word "perfect" here carries the sense of being complete in following God, and the verse does not need to dwell on it further.

Jesus speaks with a rich young man who said he had kept the commandments and asked what he still lacked. Jesus touches on what ruled his heart: his possessions. The young man went away sad. This is not understood as a rule for everyone, but as a call to that particular man, who revealed his attachment to money.

Ask yourself honestly: is there something you find so hard to let go of that it keeps you from following Jesus? Offer it to God in prayer, and take one concrete step of generosity this week.
exp.18:16:
Jesus responds to a man who called him "Good Teacher." He asks why he calls him good, and says that there is only One who is good. Then he tells him that if he wants to enter life, he should keep the commandments.

A man comes to Jesus with a sincere question: what good must he do to have eternal life? Jesus leads him to think of God as the measure of what is good, not of human praise. He does not deny his own goodness; many understand that he invites him to reflect on what he is saying. Then he points him to the commandments, which the man knew well.

Before seeking religious achievements, look to God as the source of all good. Ask yourself today whether your obedience comes from loving him or from wanting to show off your own goodness.
exp.9:24:
Jesus says that it is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher, and a servant like his master. He then adds that if the head of the house has been called Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household will be treated the same way.

Beelzebul was a name used to refer to the prince of the demons. Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to preach throughout Israel. He warns them that there will be rejection and persecution. The Pharisees had already accused Jesus of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul (Matthew 9:34). So he tells them not to be surprised if they are treated the same way.

For today: if you follow Jesus and someone despises you or mocks you for your faith, do not lose heart or think that something is wrong. Remember that your Teacher went through this first, and trust that he walks with you.
exp.18:1:
Large crowds followed Jesus, and He healed them there. The phrase "large crowds" refers to many people gathering around Him. "He healed them" means that He cured the sick who came to Him.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just left Galilee and had arrived in the region of Judea, on the other side of the Jordan River. Even while travelling, people sought Him out. Matthew shows that Jesus met people's needs with compassion. Soon the Pharisees arrive with a question meant to test Him, but before that debate, the text shows us Jesus healing.

For today: Jesus did not stop serving others even though He was tired from the journey, and a difficult argument was soon to come. We can ask Him to make us attentive to whoever today needs help, a visit, or a prayer.
exp.22:17:
Jesus quotes what some teachers were saying: if someone swore by the altar, the oath meant nothing, but if someone swore by the gift placed on the altar, the person was bound by the oath. The phrase "bound by his oath" means that he was held responsible for what he had promised to do.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees in the temple in Jerusalem, in his strong rebuke in Matthew 23. He calls them "blind guides" because they invented rules that let people make solemn promises while leaving ways to avoid keeping them. He shows that the altar is more important than the gift, because it is the altar that makes the gift holy.

For today: be a person of your word. Do not use clever phrases or excuses to escape your promises; tell the truth and keep what you say, because God sees the heart.
exp.26:56:
When evening came, a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph appeared. The verse says he was himself a disciple of Jesus.

Matthew is the one telling the story, relating what happened after Jesus died on the cross. Up to this point, only the women watching from a distance had been mentioned. Now Joseph comes forward, approaching Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus so he could give it a dignified burial. The Gospels do not explain all of his reasons, but his action shows courage and affection.

For today: God can use what we have, whether money, influence, or time, to serve Christ, even when others step away. We should not wait for the perfect moment to show our faith through concrete actions.
exp.7:11:
It says that the "sons of the kingdom," meaning those who believed they were secure heirs of God's kingdom, will be thrown into the "outer darkness." There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there, a way of expressing deep pain and anguish. The word "thrown" conveys forceful removal, and "weeping" is the same as "crying."

Jesus speaks to those who were following him, after marveling at the faith of a Roman centurion, a foreigner. With this he warns that belonging to the people of Israel does not guarantee entry into the kingdom; faith is what matters. Some understand "sons of the kingdom" to mean the Israelites who rejected Jesus.

For today: let us not trust in our family, church, or tradition as if that would save us. Let us examine whether we truly trust in Christ, with a simple and sincere faith like that of the centurion.
exp.0:14:
Eliud was the father of Eleazar, Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob. It is part of a family list. In this list, "father of" means a direct son, though in Bible genealogies a name can sometimes stand for several generations.

Matthew, the author of the gospel, opens his book with Jesus' genealogy. He wants to show his readers, who were largely Jewish, that Jesus comes from the line of Abraham and David. These names from the period after the exile are little known, and the Bible tells us nothing more about them. This list ends with Jacob, the father of Joseph.
