For today: God works through ordinary and unknown people. Even though no one may remember your name, your faithfulness can be part of what God is doing in your family and in the generations to come.
exp.9:37:
Jesus says that anyone who does not take up their cross and follow him is not worthy of him. To "follow" him means to walk behind him as a disciple does. To be "worthy" of him means to be someone who measures up to being his disciple.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles before sending them out to preach. He warns them that following him can bring rejection, even from one's own family. In that time the cross was known as an instrument of execution, so he was speaking of being willing to suffer and to give oneself completely. Some understand that Jesus had not yet spoken of his own cross, and so his hearers would grasp the image of public condemnation.

Today, following Jesus may cost us comfort, approval, or time. Ask him today to help you obey him in one specific thing, even if others do not understand it.
exp.9:33:
Jesus says that he did not come to bring an easy and comfortable peace to the earth, but a sword. The word for "bring" here means "bring" or "put" in the sense of setting something in place. The sword is a picture of division, not an invitation to violence.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles, whom he is sending out to preach. He warns them that following him will have a cost. Earlier he asked them to confess him openly, and now he explains that his message will divide even families, because some will accept it and others will not. His ultimate goal is indeed peace with God, but the road to it passes through difficult choices.

For today: if following Christ brings you tension or rejection, even within your family, do not be discouraged or think that something has gone wrong. Remain faithful with humility and love, without seeking quarrels, and trust that He sustains you.
exp.3:8:
Here the devil says to Jesus: "All this I will give You if You will fall down and worship me." Bowing down to the ground in worship is what the word "fall down" describes: lying face down or bowed low as a sign of honor and devotion.

This is the third temptation in the desert. Satan shows Jesus the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and offers him a shortcut: power and honor without going through the cross. Jesus does not argue about the offer; he answers with Scripture (Deuteronomy 6:13) and tells him to leave. Afterward, angels came and ministered to him.

For today: temptation often comes as a shortcut that promises success, money, or approval, but in exchange asks us to put something above God. Before you choose, ask yourself: whom am I serving with this decision? Answer as Jesus did, with the Word of God in your heart.
exp.22:6:
The scribes and Pharisees, Jesus says, love to be greeted with respect in the marketplaces, that is, in the public places where people gather. They also love the title "Rabbi," which means "my teacher." The greetings are the words people say when they meet and welcome one another.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, shortly before his arrest. He criticizes the teachers of the law because they performed their religious duties so that they would be seen and admired. He does not reject the teaching of the law, but the vanity and hypocrisy of those who sought honor for themselves. Then he reminds his followers that only Christ is their Teacher and that all of them are brothers.

Today we can ask ourselves why we serve: do we seek applause, or do we seek to please God? If we teach, help, or lead, let us do it with humility, treating others as brothers and not as people beneath us.
exp.24:18:
After a long time, the master of those servants returns and settles accounts with them. That is what this verse tells us: a long period passes, and then the master comes back to review what each servant has done with what he was given. "Settling accounts" means he looks over how each one handled the money entrusted to him.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in the parable of the talents, shortly before his death. He is teaching them how to live while they wait for his return. The master in the story goes away on a journey and entrusts his property to his servants. Many understand the master to represent Jesus, and the "long time" reminds us that his return could be delayed. This interpretation is the most common among Christians.

God has entrusted us with time, gifts, and opportunities. We do not know when he will call us to account, so today we can use what we have faithfully, serving others without being overcome by fear or laziness.
exp.26:35:
This verse says that the Roman soldiers sat down near the cross and kept watch over Jesus. The phrase "kept watch" here means making sure no one took him down or interfered. After crucifying him and dividing his clothing among themselves, they stayed there as if on a guard shift.

It is Matthew who tells the story, as a witness to what his Gospel records. He describes a routine scene for the soldiers: carrying out the execution, dividing the clothing, and keeping watch. Matthew has already shown that what the prophet said was being fulfilled (Psalm 22:18). While the soldiers were only doing a job, without realizing it a greater plan was being fulfilled.

Today we can notice that while some looked on the suffering of Jesus with indifference, he was giving his life for everyone. Let us ask God for an attentive heart, one that does not become used to what is sacred or look at it coldly, but with gratitude and reverence.
exp.25:58:
This verse says that the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were looking for false testimony against Jesus. Their goal was to have him put to death. "Chief priests" refers to the leading priests, and the Sanhedrin was the high council of Israel's leaders.

Matthew tells us what happened after Jesus was arrested and taken to the house of the high priest Caiaphas. No one speaks in this passage; it is the narrator who describes the scene. The leaders had already settled on the outcome and only wanted to give their decision the appearance of justice. Meanwhile, Peter followed at a distance, afraid.

Today it reminds us that it is dangerous to look for reasons to justify what we have already decided in our hearts. Let us ask God for honesty to hear the truth, even when it makes us uncomfortable, and for the discipline never to speak against anyone without evidence.
exp.12:51:
Jesus says that every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven, that is, a teacher of the Law who has been taught about what God is doing in his kingdom, is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples after seven parables about the kingdom. He asks them whether they have understood, and they say yes. Then he shows them that whoever understands these teachings should share them. Many think the old is the Law and the Prophets, and the new is the teaching of Jesus, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: when you teach or advise others, bring together the Scripture you have received from long ago with what Christ is showing you now, without despising either one.
exp.12:16:
Jesus says that many prophets and righteous people of earlier times longed to see and hear what his disciples were seeing and hearing, but they did not manage to. "Truly" is the word Jesus uses to introduce what he is about to say. "Longed" means they wanted it eagerly.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, after explaining why he teaches in parables. Many who listened to him did not understand, because their hearts had grown hardened. By contrast, the disciples did see who he was and what he was doing. The ancient prophets had announced the Messiah, but they lived before his coming.

For today: let us not take for granted the privilege of having the Bible and knowing Christ. What many longed for across the centuries is within our reach today. We can give thanks to God and read his Word with an attentive heart, ready to obey.
exp.12:25:
It says that when the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the weeds also appeared. "Wheat" here is the grain plant, and "bore grain" means that it produced the crop. The weeds are plants that, at first, look very much like wheat.

Jesus is teaching the crowd with parables about the kingdom of heaven. He tells that an enemy secretly sowed weeds among the wheat, at night. Until the plants matured, no one noticed the difference. With this Jesus explains that good and evil can live together in the world for a time.

For today: do not become discouraged or scandalized if you see bad things mixed with good, even near the church. Keep bearing good fruit, ask for discernment, and trust that God will know how to separate everything in its proper time.
exp.12:41:
In the final days of the age, the angels will throw the wicked into the fiery furnace. There, there will be weeping, meaning crying, and gnashing of teeth, an expression of pain, anguish, or rage. The "stumbling blocks" mentioned in the previous verse refer to whatever causes others to fall.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and explains the parable of the wheat and the weeds. The field is the world, and the wheat and the weeds grow side by side until the harvest. Jesus teaches that God will judge at the end, not us. Many understand the fire as an image of God's judgment, and Christians debate how to interpret it exactly.

Today, this text invites us to live with seriousness before God, without judging others as if that task belonged to us. We can ask him to examine our hearts and trust that he will do justice.
exp.22:11:
It says that whoever exalts himself, that is, places himself above others and seeks to be admired, will be humbled. On the other hand, whoever humbles himself, that is, places himself simply at the service of others, will be exalted. The word "exalt" means to raise up or make great; "humbled" means to be brought low.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, shortly before his arrest. He has just pointed to the scribes and Pharisees, who loved the first seats and honorable titles. He teaches that in his kingdom greatness is measured by service, not by prestige.

Today we can ask ourselves where we seek recognition. One practical way is to do a simple act of service this week, without anyone knowing or applauding it, and to let God be the one who honors us in his time.
exp.3:14:
This verse names the places in northern Israel where Jesus began his ministry. Zebulun and Naphtali were ancient tribes of Israel. The phrase "Way of the Sea" refers to the route near the Sea of Galilee, and "beyond the Jordan" indicates the area next to the river. "Galilee of the Gentiles" means that many non-Jews lived there.

Matthew, the author, explains that Jesus left Nazareth and went to live in Capernaum. For Matthew, this fulfills what Isaiah said (Isaiah 9:1-2). That region had been looked down upon, but God chose it to show the light of Christ first. Scholars agree on the general sense, though they debate exactly how Matthew applies the prophecy.

For today: God does not despise the places or the people that others ignore. If you feel small or far from everything, Jesus can draw near to your life. And you too can carry his light to those others pass over.
exp.18:26:
Peter tells Jesus that they have left everything to follow him, and asks what they will get in return. In the Berean Standard Bible, the word "then" in his question means "so" or "as a result." It is a sincere and direct question.

Peter speaks on behalf of the disciples. They had just seen a rich young man walk away sad because he would not give up his possessions, and they had heard Jesus say that it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom. Peter compares their situation with that of the young man. Jesus does not rebuke him but answers with promises: a place of honor in his kingdom and a reward greater than everything they have left behind, together with eternal life. Some interpret the "twelve thrones" literally and others symbolically.

Today we can speak to God honestly about what it costs us to follow him. He sees every sacrifice and does not remain in debt. Let us follow Christ trusting in his generosity, not only for what we will receive.
exp.21:38:
It says the second most important commandment is like the first: loving others as we love ourselves. "Neighbor" here means the person who is near you or whom you meet along your way. "Like" means similar or of the same kind.

Jesus is speaking with an expert in the law, sent by the Pharisees to test him. They ask him which commandment is the greatest. Jesus answers with love for God and then adds love for your neighbor. He says that all the law and the prophets depend on these two, meaning that everything God asked for in the Scriptures is summed up in love.

Today we can put this into practice with something simple: think of someone close to you who is going through a hard time, and call them, listen to them, or help them with something specific. In this way you treat others with the same care you would want to receive.
exp.21:4:
This verse says that the guests invited to the wedding feast paid no attention to the king's invitation. "Paid no attention" means that they did not take it seriously. Each one went away to his own concerns: one to his field and another to his business.

Jesus is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem, in front of the religious leaders. He tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The king represents God, and the guests who refuse represent, according to many interpreters, the people who did not receive God's call. Jesus shows that ignoring the invitation has serious consequences.

For today: good things, such as work and projects, can take the place that belongs to God. Today you can set aside a specific time to pray and read the Bible, before your daily responsibilities fill up the whole day.
exp.22:20:
Matthew 23:21 says that whoever swears by the temple is swearing not only by a building but also by God, who dwells there. The verse speaks of swearing "by the temple" and "by the One who dwells in it," so the point is that the oath reaches all the way to God.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees. They taught that swearing by the temple or the altar did not bind as much as swearing by the gold of the temple or by the offering. Jesus calls them fools and blind because they gave more value to things than to God, who is the one who gives those things their true worth. In this way they could use solemn words and still avoid keeping what they had promised.

Today, we can be people whose word is clear and sincere. There is no need to look for clever phrases to escape a commitment. If we say "yes," we should keep our word, remembering that God knows everything we promise.
exp.11:44:
It says the unclean spirit returns and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself. All of them go in and live in that person, and his final condition becomes worse than the first. The verse says "so will it be," which means "it will happen the same way," and "that man" refers to that person. Jesus says the same thing will happen to "this wicked generation."

Jesus speaks to some scribes and Pharisees who were asking him for a sign, after they had accused him of casting out demons by the power of Satan. He warns them that a surface-level cleansing, without a true surrender to God, leaves the house empty and exposed. Some understand that "seven" speaks of a very serious condition, rather than an exact number.

For today: it is not enough to simply drop a bad habit; life must be filled with Christ, his Word, prayer, and fellowship with other believers. Give your heart to him completely today.
exp.24:36:
Here the righteous, surprised, ask the King: "Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you something to drink?" Their question shows that they had no idea they had been serving him at all. Their help was simple and practical, the kind of care that keeps a person alive and comfortable.

Jesus tells this parable about the final judgment. The King has just praised those who helped him. They do not remember having done it, which suggests they served simply, without seeking reward or recognition. Later, the King explains that what they did for the least of these, they did for him. Some scholars understand these "least" to be anyone in need, and others take them to be especially the followers of Christ. Both ideas are debated.

Today we can notice someone close to us who is in need, such as a neighbor, a coworker, or a relative, and help them in a concrete way this week, without expecting anything in return.
exp.16:15:
This is a desperate father speaking to Jesus. He tells him that he brought his sick son to the disciples, but they could not heal him. "Brought" means he took the boy to them in person, and "heal" means to restore him to health. The boy's illness involved seizures, and the account goes on to name a demon as the cause.

The one speaking is this father, who kneels before Jesus and asks for mercy. Jesus had gone up the mountain with three disciples, and the other nine stayed below. Their lack of power leads Jesus to speak of their little faith. Then he heals the boy.

For today: when your own strength or the strength of others is not enough, do not stay silent. Bring your need directly to Jesus, as this father did, with humility and trust.
exp.23:42:
Jesus says that if the owner of a house had known in which watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into, that is, have a hole dug through the wall to get in. Keeping watch means staying awake and alert. The word "But" at the start of the verse is there to draw attention to what comes next. Being prepared means being ready.

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he explains future events and his coming. He uses this comparison to show that no one knows the exact moment of his return. For that reason, the task is not to work out dates, but to live ready.

For today: do not live in fear or making calculations, but with a simple and steady faith. Today you can put your unfinished affairs in order, ask someone for forgiveness, pray, and faithfully carry out what God has entrusted to you.
exp.5:17:
This verse says that fasting should not be done so that people see us and admire us, but for God, who is present even when no one else notices. "Not obvious to men" means not being visible to others. "Secret" is what is done in private. God sees what is done in secret and promises to reward it.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Earlier he has spoken about giving to the needy and prayer. Now he teaches that fasting, like those practices, should come from a sincere heart and not from the pursuit of applause, as the hypocrites did.

Today, when we pray, help others, or serve, let us ask ourselves: "Am I doing this for God or so that people will see me?" Let us do something good without telling anyone, trusting that God sees it.
exp.16:21:
Jesus is with his disciples in Galilee, and he tells them that the Son of Man, a title he uses for himself, is about to be delivered into the hands of men. "Is about to be delivered" means that he will soon be placed in the power of other people, who will treat him badly.

Jesus has just healed a boy and taught the disciples about faith and prayer. Now he is preparing them for what is coming. From the next verse we see that he is speaking of his death and resurrection. The disciples become deeply sad, because they do not yet understand the whole plan of God.

God is not caught off guard by suffering. Jesus saw it coming and went forward with confidence. When you go through hard moments, remember that God is still at work even in what you do not understand, and pray asking him for the faith to trust in him.
exp.25:40:
Jesus tells his disciples to stay awake and alert, and to pray so that they do not enter into temptation. The verse notes that the spirit is "willing," that is, eager and well-intentioned, but the body is "weak," that is, frail and prone to fail.

Jesus speaks in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before he is arrested. He himself is troubled and prays to the Father. He returns and finds his friends asleep, though they had promised to be faithful to him. He speaks to them with tenderness, not only with rebuke: he acknowledges that they want to obey, but they are fragile.

For today: do not rely only on your good intentions. When you face a trial, set aside a moment each day to pray and ask God for strength, and stay alert to the situations where you tend to fail.
exp.12:15:
Jesus says that the eyes and ears of his disciples are blessed, that is, very happy and favored by God, because they see and hear. The word "because" in this verse gives the reason for the blessing. Here, seeing and hearing mean more than using the senses. They mean understanding what God is showing.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the parable of the sower to the crowd. They asked him why he taught in parables. He explains that many hear without understanding, as Isaiah had said, but the disciples have been given understanding. Then he tells them that many prophets and righteous people longed to see what they were seeing.

For today: value the privilege of knowing Christ and his word. Read the Bible with gratitude and a willing heart, asking God to help you understand and obey what you hear.
exp.5:9:
This verse is part of the prayer that Jesus taught. It asks that the kingdom of God come, that is, that his rule and authority be made present. It also asks that your will be done on earth, just as it already is done in heaven. The word "come" expresses a desire and a request.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the Sermon on the Mount. Shortly before, he warned them not to pray with empty words like others do, because the Father already knows what they need. Then he gives them this model of prayer, which begins by honoring God before asking for our needs.

For today: before asking God for things, try to tell him sincerely, "Your will be done." Then look for one concrete decision this week, in your work or your family, and hand it over to him, willing to obey.
exp.1:13:
Joseph woke up from the sleep in which the angel had spoken to him, and at once he got up, took the Child and His mother, and left that very night for Egypt.

The one telling the story is Matthew. He explains that God warned Joseph in a dream that King Herod wanted to kill the child. Joseph does not argue or wait; he obeys right away. Later, Matthew connects this journey with the prophecy of Hosea: "Out of Egypt I called my Son." Scholars have understood in various ways how that prophecy relates to Jesus, but Matthew sees it as a fulfillment.

For today: when we sense that God is pointing us toward a right step, even if it is uncomfortable or uncertain, we can obey without delay and trust that He cares for us along the way.
exp.17:21:
Jesus answers Peter that he should not forgive only seven times, but seventy-seven times. The reader sees the verse's own wording: not just seven times, but seventy-seven times. The point is that forgiveness should have no limit that can be counted.

Peter had asked Jesus how many times he had to forgive a brother who wronged him, and he himself suggested seven, which already seemed a generous number. Jesus speaks here with his disciples about how to treat one another within the community. Forgiveness is not kept in a ledger. Right after this, Jesus tells the parable of the servant who owed an enormous debt.

For today: when someone offends you again and again, do not keep count of the times. Ask God for help to let go of resentment, remembering how much He has forgiven you.
exp.22:0:
Here Matthew presents the beginning of a teaching of Jesus. He speaks to the crowds and also to his disciples. The word "spoke" is simple; it means just what it says.

Jesus is in Jerusalem, in the final days before his cross. Shortly before, the religious leaders had tested him with questions. Now Jesus addresses everyone who is listening, not only his close followers, to warn them about the example of the scribes and Pharisees, who taught the law but did not live it from the heart.

Today we might ask ourselves: does what I say with my mouth match what I do? Jesus invites us to listen carefully to the truth of God, but also to live it with sincerity, without pretending to be what we are not.
exp.26:51:
It says that, when Jesus died, the tombs broke open and many believers who had already died ("fallen asleep," a way of speaking about death) were raised. "Saints" here means people who are faithful to God. The next verse clarifies that they came out of the tombs after Jesus' resurrection and appeared to many in Jerusalem.

Matthew, the narrator, recounts signs that accompanied the death of Jesus: the temple veil torn, the earthquake, the rocks split. They show that something great was happening. Interpreters debate details, such as who those saints were or what happened to them afterward, because the text does not say. The centurion and the soldiers, seeing everything, recognized Jesus as the Son of God.

For today: the death of Jesus opens real hope. If death did not have the last word that day, it will not have the last word in your life either. Trust in Christ when you face losses.
exp.11:13:
The verse says that the Pharisees went out of the synagogue and plotted together to kill Jesus. The word "plotted" means they made a plan among themselves, and "how they might kill Jesus" means how they could bring his life to an end.

Jesus had just healed a man's withered hand on the Sabbath. The Pharisees guarded the law of rest very closely and thought that healing on that day was forbidden work. Jesus had explained that doing good on the Sabbath is lawful, that is, permitted. Instead of rejoicing at the miracle, they were filled with anger and rejection. The text does not say everything that was in their hearts, but it shows that their hardness went very far.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we defend our customs more than love for our neighbor. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that rejoices when someone receives help, even when it is not what we expected.
exp.15:16:
Jesus tells Peter that he is "blessed," meaning happy and favored by God. He explains that this insight did not come from "flesh and blood," meaning it did not come from other people or from human reasoning. It was revealed by his Father in heaven. The name "Simon son of Jonah" identifies Peter by his father.

Jesus asks his disciples who they believe he is. Peter answers that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Jesus recognizes that this conviction is a gift from God. He then goes on to speak about the church, and Christians have interpreted in several different ways what the rock refers to.

Recognizing who Jesus is is not only an achievement of intelligence but a gift from God. We can thank him for the faith we have and ask him to keep showing us Christ with greater clarity, with humility and gratitude.
exp.17:17:
Jesus says that whatever his disciples forbid on earth will be forbidden in heaven, and whatever they permit on earth will be permitted in heaven. To forbid is to bind; to permit is to loose.

Jesus speaks to his disciples about how to deal with a brother who sins. First the matter is taken up privately, then with witnesses, and finally with the church. Here Jesus gives the community authority to decide in these cases. Some understand these to be decisions about discipline; others understand them as teaching with authority what God permits or forbids. The verses that follow speak of unity and prayer.

For today: when you have a conflict with someone, act with humility, seek wise counsel, and aim for restoration, not victory. God honors those who seek his will together.
exp.6:14:
Jesus tells us to beware of false prophets. "Beware" means "be on guard" or "stay alert." They come to you in sheep's clothing, that is, they seem gentle and harmless, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves, that is, fierce creatures who want to devour and take advantage of others.

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount, and he has just invited people to enter through the narrow gate, the hard road that leads to life. Now he warns that there will be voices that draw people away from that road. He right away gives a way to recognize them: by their fruits, that is, by their conduct and the results of their life and teaching.

Today, do not let yourself be impressed only by beautiful words or a good image. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and observe the character of the person teaching: whether there is humility, truth and love, or only self-interest.
exp.11:22:
This verse tells us that the crowds were astounded by what Jesus had done. They asked, "Could this be the Son of David?", meaning the promised Messiah, a descendant of King David. The word "astounded" means very surprised, and "crowds" here means the large groups of ordinary people gathered around him.

The speakers are the crowds. They had just seen Jesus heal a man who was possessed, blind, and mute, and the man then spoke and could see. Their question shows a hopeful doubt: they do not claim that he is the Messiah, but they suspect it. Right after this, the Pharisees react with rejection and accuse him of acting by the power of Beelzebub.

For today: when we see the works of God, we can be amazed and also ask sincerely who Jesus is. Let us not allow prejudice to put out that question; let us seek answers by reading the Gospels with an open heart.
exp.7:30:
The demons make a specific request of Jesus: if he is going to drive them out of the two men, let them enter a herd of pigs that was nearby. A "herd" here means a group of animals feeding together. The request conveys that they begged him, insisting on it.

The ones speaking are the evil spirits that had been tormenting two men in the region of the Gadarenes. They had already recognized Jesus as the Son of God and feared his judgment. Their request shows that they cannot act on their own: they need Jesus' permission. He tells them "Go," and they obey. Some wonder why Jesus allowed this; the text does not explain it, so it is best not to invent reasons.

For today: no power of evil stands above the authority of Christ. If something frightens or oppresses you, you can come to Jesus with confidence, because He has the final word.
exp.7:32:
The men who were tending the pigs ran off. When they reached the town, they reported everything that had happened, including the account of the two men who were held by demons. The people here are the herdsmen, the ones who look after the pigs, and the men are described as demon-possessed, meaning they were under the control of evil spirits.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is Matthew who narrates. Jesus had just set these men free, and the demons went into the pigs, which rushed into the sea and drowned. The herdsmen, frightened, carried the news. Afterward, the people of the town asked Jesus to leave. The text tells us what they asked, but it does not say with certainty everything they felt; it may have been fear or the loss of their livestock.

For today: when Jesus acts, not everyone responds in the same way. Let us ask Him to give us an open heart to value what He does, even when it disturbs us or changes our plans.
exp.25:16:
This verse tells us that, on the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus and asked where he wanted them to prepare the Passover meal. The word for "prepare" here means to get something ready or arrange it. The Passover was the meal by which the Jewish people remembered their deliverance from Egypt.

The ones speaking are the disciples, who want to serve their Master. Shortly before this, Judas had agreed to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver. While some prepare the supper simply, another is preparing the betrayal. Jesus, according to the account, already knew what was coming, and his reply shows that he was in control of the situation.

For today: ask Jesus how he wants you to serve him. The disciples did not decide on their own; they asked and they obeyed. Seek his direction in prayer and faithfully do what he shows you, even in small things.
exp.23:46:
It says that the master will reward the faithful servant. The phrase "Truly I tell you" is a solemn way of saying "I assure you." The words about putting him in charge of all the master's possessions mean that the master will give him responsibility over everything he owns. The servant who was faithful with a little is given a much greater responsibility.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he teaches them about the end of the age and his return. With this parable he encourages them to live faithfully while they wait. The faithful and wise servant contrasts with the wicked servant who appears afterward, who abuses others because he thinks his master will be delayed.

For today: be faithful in what God has entrusted to you, whether it is your family, your work, or your service in the church, even when no one sees you. God notices steadiness in small things, and you do not need to know when Christ will return in order to live with responsibility and love each day.
exp.16:14:
A father kneels before Jesus and says, "Lord, have mercy on my son." He tells Jesus that his son has seizures and is suffering terribly. Many believe these seizures are epilepsy. The son often falls into the fire or into the water, so his life is in danger.

It is a desperate father who speaks. Jesus has just come down from the mountain of the transfiguration and meets the crowd. Later the man explains that the disciples could not heal the boy. That is why he goes directly to Jesus, with humility and imperfect faith.

For today: when the pain of a child, or of someone you love, overwhelms you, do not wait until everything is in order. Come before Jesus, kneel in prayer, and ask him for mercy simply, as this father did.
exp.19:14:
The owner of the vineyard says he has the right to do as he pleases with his own money. He asks, "Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine?" In other words: isn't he free to use what belongs to him as he chooses? Then he asks, "Or are you envious because I am generous?" In the speech of the time, an envious eye pointed to envy or meanness. Put simply: are you bothered that I am generous?

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The owner hires workers at different hours, and at the end he pays everyone the same amount. The first ones complain. Here the owner answers one of them: he had agreed on a denarius with him and he gave him what he agreed. Jesus teaches that God's grace is generous and is not earned by comparison. Some understand that he is speaking also of Jews and Gentiles; the text does not make this clear.

Today, when someone receives a blessing or forgiveness that seems undeserved to you, rejoice with them instead of comparing. Also be thankful for what God has given you.
exp.18:22:
Jesus tells his disciples, with great seriousness, that it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. His words "Truly I tell you" mean "I assure you," and "hard" means it takes great difficulty, not that it is impossible.

Jesus has just spoken with a rich young man who wanted eternal life. When Jesus asked him to give up his possessions and follow him, the young man went away sad, because his possessions weighed more heavily on him than his desire to follow Christ. The disciples are astonished, and Jesus teaches them that only God can save.

For today: consider what you would find hard to let go of if God asked it of you, whether money, comfort or security. Ask God that your heart depend on Him and not on what you have.
exp.21:20:
He asks them whose image is on the coin, and they answer, "Caesar's." Then Jesus tells them to give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.

Jesus was speaking with Pharisees and others who wanted to trap him with a difficult question: whether it was right to pay taxes to Caesar. If he said no, they could accuse him before Rome; if he said yes, he would lose the support of the people. His answer left them amazed. Some understand that the coin bore Caesar's image, and that human beings bear the image of God, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: fulfill your responsibilities as a citizen, but remember that your whole life belongs to God. Ask yourself each day what you are giving to Him: your time, your heart, your obedience.
exp.26:4:
He threw the thirty pieces of silver down in the temple, left that place, and went off and hanged himself. The word "departed" in the older text means he withdrew or went away, and the word "went" is simply "went." The phrase "hanged himself" means he took his own life by hanging.

Matthew, the author, tells what happened after Jesus was condemned. Judas felt remorse and went to the religious leaders to confess that he had betrayed an innocent man. They turned him away coldly, saying, "See to it yourself." Without help, Judas was left weighed down by guilt. What follows in the account, the purchase of the field, shows that this silver had a place in God's plan. The book of Acts gives other details about his death, and scholars explain them in different ways.

For today: remorse alone does not heal. If we fail, we should not withdraw alone; let us bring our guilt to God, who forgives, and seek help from trustworthy people.
exp.13:4:
This verse says that Herod wanted to kill John the Baptist, but he was afraid of how the people would react. The crowd regarded John as a prophet, that is, as a man sent by God. The word "but" in the verse is the connecting word that introduces this contrast, and the phrase "because they regarded John as a prophet" simply means that the people saw him as a prophet.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is explaining why John was in prison: he had told Herod that it was not lawful for him to have Herodias, who had been the wife of his brother. Herod was angry, but he did not dare to kill him because of his fear of the people. Shortly afterward, at the birthday feast, that fear would give way to a promise made under oath.

For today: sometimes we fear the opinion of people more than we fear God, and that leads us to decide wrongly. Let us ask for the courage to do what is right, even when it costs us.
exp.22:37:
Jesus says that their "house" is left to them "desolate," meaning empty and abandoned. The phrase "left to you" means that they are left alone, without the protective presence of God. There are several interpretations of "house": it may refer to the temple, to the city of Jerusalem, or to the whole nation.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees and to the people in Jerusalem, at the end of his public teaching. He has just lamented that they rejected the prophets and rejected him too, even though he wanted to care for them the way a hen gathers her chicks. His grief is real, not merely anger. Yet he leaves open a hope: someday they will say, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

Rejecting God's invitation has serious consequences, but his heart remains tender. Today we can examine whether we are letting Jesus into our lives, and respond to him with humility before we harden ourselves.
exp.12:7:
Another part of the seed fell on good soil and produced a crop, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another thirtyfold.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. He tells the parable of the sower. Afterward he explains that the seed is the word of the kingdom and that the different kinds of soil are different ways of receiving it. The good soil represents the one who hears the word, understands it, and bears fruit.

For today: it is not enough to hear the word of God; you must let it take root. This week, read a Bible passage slowly, ask God to help you understand it, and decide on one concrete step to put it into practice. Fruit is not measured by comparison: God rejoices over every life that grows.
exp.22:30:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees, by their own words, show themselves to be the sons of those who murdered the prophets. The phrase "you testify against yourselves" means that they themselves admit it. "Sons" can be understood as descendants, but also as those who follow the same character.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, in his strong rebuke of the religious leaders. They honored the dead prophets by building their tombs and claimed that they themselves would never have killed them. Jesus shows them that their hearts were the same as those of their ancestors. Some understand that he was already foretelling the rejection he himself would suffer.

For today: it is easy to admire the heroes of the faith and to criticize the mistakes of the past. Let us ask God to examine us, so that we obey his Word today, even when it makes us uncomfortable or corrects us.
exp.14:9:
Jesus gathers the crowd and says to them, "Listen and understand." The wording of the verse is plain: Jesus called the crowd to himself, meaning he invited them to come close to him, and the crowd is the ordinary people gathered there. Jesus asks for more than listening; he wants them to grasp what he is saying.

Jesus speaks this after confronting the Pharisees and scribes, who objected because his disciples did not wash their hands before eating, according to tradition. He answered that they honored God with their lips while their hearts were far from him. Now he turns to the common people to teach them what truly matters to God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith is only custom and outward appearance, or whether it comes from the heart. Before we speak or act, it is good to listen carefully to Jesus and ask him for understanding so that we may live a sincere faith.
exp.26:7:
This verse says that the field bought with the thirty pieces of silver received a name: "the Field of Blood." That name has been used ever since, up to the time Matthew wrote. The phrase "That is why" means "for this reason," and "has been called" means that is what people named it.

The speaker here is Matthew, the narrator. The chief priests did not want to keep that money in the temple treasury, because it was payment for the death of Jesus, who had been handed over earlier by Judas. With it they bought a piece of land to bury foreigners. Matthew sees in this the fulfillment of a prophecy, which he cites as coming from Jeremiah; scholars explain that citation in several ways, because it also resembles Zechariah.

For today: let us care for our conscience. The priests pretended purity with the money, yet they had taken part in an injustice. Let us ask God for sincerity, so that we do not appear holy while doing something wrong.
exp.2:10:
John the Baptist says that he baptizes with water as a sign that people are turning away from their sin. But he announces that someone far more powerful than he is coming: Jesus. John does not even feel worthy to carry his sandals, which was the work of a servant. The one who is coming will baptize "with the Holy Spirit and with fire."

John speaks to crowds in the wilderness of Judea, including religious leaders who trusted that they were descendants of Abraham. He asks them for real evidence of change. "Fire" is understood in several ways: purification, judgment, or both; the verses that follow speak of separating the wheat from the chaff.

For today: it is not enough to have an inherited religion or to perform a ritual. Ask God for his Spirit to change your heart, and let that change show in your daily actions, with humility before Jesus.
exp.1:11:
The magi, after worshiping Jesus, received a warning from God in a dream. They were told not to return to Herod. So they withdrew to their own country by another route. The phrase "warned in a dream" tells us that God spoke to them directly while they slept, and "their own country" simply means the land they came from.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Earlier, Herod had asked them to tell him where the child was (Matthew 2:8). But Herod felt threatened by the birth of a new king, and the following text shows that he wanted to kill the child. God protected Jesus by guiding the magi. The Bible does not say how many there were or exactly where they came from.

For today: when God warns us, whether through his Word, through wise counsel, or through our conscience, it is good to obey even if we have to change direction. Obeying God may mean taking a different route.
exp.4:6:
Jesus says that the merciful are happy and blessed, that is, those who feel compassion for others and show it through their actions, by forgiving and helping. The promise is that they themselves will be shown mercy. The word "shown" in the verse means that others will extend mercy to them, or that they will receive it.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples with the crowd around them. This is the fifth beatitude. It describes what the life of those who belong to the kingdom of God is like. Some think mercy comes after hungering for righteousness, because those who recognize their need before God learn to treat others with tenderness. Others read it simply as one more quality of the character of the kingdom.

Today, think of someone who hurt you or who is in need. Take a concrete step: forgive, visit, listen, or help, without expecting anything in return.
exp.5:23:
Jesus says that no one can be a servant of two masters at the same time. Sooner or later, one will be devoted to and the other looked down on. The words "hate" and "despise" show that in the end one of them wins the heart. "Money" is the word Jesus uses for wealth, and he speaks of it almost as if it were a master. You cannot serve both God and money.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Earlier he spoke of treasures on earth and in heaven, and of the eye as the lamp of the body. Afterward he invites them not to be anxious about food or clothing, because the Father cares for them.

Today, ask yourself who truly rules your decisions. Use your money with gratitude and generosity, but do not let worry about it govern you. Trust God and put him first.
exp.26:10:
This verse tells us that Jesus stands before the Roman governor. The governor is Pontius Pilate. Pilate questions him directly: "Are You the King of the Jews?" Jesus replies, "You have said so," an answer that neither plainly denies nor plainly affirms.

The Jewish leaders had brought Jesus before Pilate, because Rome held the authority to condemn someone to death. Calling him "King of the Jews" was a political accusation that could sound like rebellion against Caesar. Jesus does not deny that he is a King, though not in the sense the accusers feared. Some scholars understand his answer as a careful affirmation; others see it as a way of turning the question back to Pilate.

Today, Jesus shows us how to stand firm with calm, even when we are misunderstood or accused. We can trust in the truth without needing to shout or defend ourselves with anger.
exp.3:22:
This verse sums up what Jesus was doing in Galilee. He went from town to town and did three things: he taught in the synagogues (the places where Jews gathered every Sabbath), he announced the good news of the kingdom, and he healed every disease and sickness among the people. The phrase "went throughout Galilee" means he traveled through the whole region.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. He has just told how Jesus called his first disciples, who left everything to follow him. Now Matthew presents the beginning of Jesus' public ministry, just before the Sermon on the Mount. He shows that Jesus had both words and power, and that his fame was spreading quickly.

For today: Jesus cared both for the truth and for people's suffering. We can imitate him by caring for others with words that guide and with concrete help, such as listening, accompanying, or serving.
exp.23:8:
Jesus says that his followers will be handed over to suffer and even be put to death. They will also be hated by people from all nations. The reason is plain: because of his name, that is, because they belong to him. "Handed over" means that others will hand them over to authorities or enemies. "Suffering" means hardship or persecution.

Jesus speaks on the Mount of Olives with his disciples, who had asked him about the end of the age and the sign of his coming. Earlier he spoke of wars, famines and earthquakes, which he called the beginning of birth pains. He warns them ahead of time so that they will not be frightened or lose their faith. Interpreters differ on how much of this was fulfilled in the first century and how much is still to come.

For today: if following Christ brings you rejection or mockery, do not lose heart, for he has already foretold it. Remain faithful, pray for those who mistreat you, and trust that he sustains his own.
exp.20:24:
Jesus asks whether John's baptism came from heaven, meaning from God, or only from people. The religious leaders do not answer honestly. Instead, they talk among themselves about what would be safest for them to say.

Jesus is teaching in the temple when the chief priests and elders challenge his authority. He responds with a question about John the Baptist, who called the people to repent and pointed to Jesus. If the leaders admitted that John's baptism came from heaven, they would have to explain why they did not believe him. If they said it was merely human, they feared how the crowd would react. In the end, they said, "We do not know."

For today: let us be honest before God. Before asking "What answer will serve me best?", let us ask "What is true?" God asks for sincerity, not calculations meant to make us look good.
exp.2:13:
John tried hard to keep Jesus from being baptized by him.

Here John the Baptist speaks. He had called the people to repent and had announced that someone far greater than himself was coming. When Jesus arrives at the Jordan, John is astonished, because baptism was a sign of repentance and Jesus had no sin. Jesus tells him it is right to do this, and John agrees. Interpreters explain the exact meaning of Jesus' words in several ways.

For today: John shows us humility. Sometimes we do not understand what God asks of us, but we can trust Him and obey, even when we cannot see the whole picture.
exp.10:23:
Jesus says that on the day of judgment, the people of Sodom, known for their wickedness, will find it more bearable than the people of Capernaum. The word "bearable" here means that their punishment will be lighter.

Jesus speaks to the cities of Galilee where he did most of his miracles. Capernaum was like his home base, and yet many people did not turn from their sins. He compares their case with Sodom, a symbol of wickedness in the Old Testament. His point is that whoever receives more light has greater responsibility. Scholars understand the details about degrees of punishment in different ways, but the central message of seriousness is clear.

Today, if we have heard the Word of God many times, it is not enough simply to admire it. Ask God for a humble heart, and respond with repentance and obedience to what you already know He asks of you.
exp.25:54:
Jesus speaks to the crowd that has come to arrest him. He asks why they have come out with swords and clubs to seize him as if he were a criminal, when he sat teaching in the temple courts every day and they never arrested him.

The verse is the one quoted above from the Berean Standard Bible, which reads: "At that time Jesus said to the crowd, 'Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? Every day I sat teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me.'"

This happens in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly after Judas betrayed him with a kiss. Jesus has just said that he could ask his Father for help, but he chose not to. His complaint shows that the arrest was happening at night and in secret, away from the people, and was not an open act of justice. He taught in the daylight, hiding nothing.

For today: try to live openly and faithfully according to your convictions. If you ever suffer unfair treatment, follow the calm of Jesus, who trusted in God's plan without answering with violence.
exp.20:21:
Jesus says that if you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer. The word "believe" means truly trusting in God.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after cursing the fig tree that had no fruit, and it withered immediately. They are amazed, and he teaches them about faith without doubt. Shortly after, the religious leaders question his authority. Some understand that the fig tree was also a sign of the lack of spiritual fruit in Israel, although the text here focuses on faith.

For today: pray with confidence in God, not like someone buying a wish, but like a child who draws near to his Father. True faith asks, waits, and submits to what God knows is best.
exp.26:15:
This verse says that at that time the Roman authorities were holding a man who was widely known, named Barabbas. The word "prisoner" means someone held in custody, and "notorious" means that many people knew who he was and what he had done, and not in a good way.

The author, Matthew, recounts Jesus' trial before Pilate, the Roman governor. It was the custom to release a prisoner at the feast of Passover. Matthew introduces Barabbas to show the choice Pilate would put before the people. Other Gospels describe him as someone connected with a rebellion and a murder.

For today: Barabbas, guilty, goes free, and Jesus, innocent, takes his place. This reminds us of God's grace, which does not depend on our merits. We can thank God today for that gift and treat with mercy those who do not deserve it.
exp.7:28:
The two men shouted, "What do you want with us, Son of God?" They asked why he was interfering with them, and they accused him of having come to torture them before the appointed time. "Torture" here means to hurt or punish.

The ones speaking are the demons, who were speaking through the two men. Jesus had just calmed the storm on the sea, and now he arrives in the country of the Gergesenes. The demons recognize who Jesus is and his authority. They speak of a time of judgment that they know is coming. The Bible does not explain every detail of that moment.

For today: recognizing who Jesus is is not enough; it takes trusting him and following him. But we can also rest, because no evil is stronger than Christ, and he can bring freedom to those who suffer most.
exp.9:8:
The verse says the disciples were not to take along money for the journey. The word "prepare" here means to get ready or to acquire. Gold, silver and copper were the coins of that time, and the belts or sashes were where money was kept.

Jesus is speaking to his twelve apostles, before sending them to the cities of Israel to announce that the kingdom of God was near. He asks them to go simply and to trust that God would care for them through the hospitality of others. This was an instruction for that particular mission; at other times, later on, Jesus gave different directions (Luke 22:35-36).

Today this is not about rejecting all planning, but about serving God without money becoming our security. Today you can ask yourself: in what do I trust more, in my savings or in God's care? Serve with generosity and confidence.
exp.20:10:
This verse tells how the people answered the question "Who is this?" They said it was Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee. The crowd is the group of people who were gathered around him. Their answer is true, but it seems incomplete.

Jesus had just entered Jerusalem, and the crowd that was with him, probably many followers and pilgrims, had hailed him as the Son of David. Now, before the stirred-up city, the people give a simpler answer: "the prophet." Some interpret this to show that they regarded Jesus with respect, but without fully understanding that he is the Messiah and King.

Today we can ask ourselves what we think of Jesus. It is easy to admire him as a good teacher or prophet. But he invites us to trust in him as Lord. Today, pray asking him to help you know him more deeply.
exp.9:17:
Jesus says that his followers will be brought before governors and kings on his account. The phrase "the Gentiles" refers to people from other nations, who were not Jews. That situation would be an opportunity to bear witness, that is, to speak about Jesus before them.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples when he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God. He honestly warns them that there will be rejection and persecution. But he also promises that they will not be alone: the Spirit of their Father will give them what to say in those difficult moments. Some believe this passage also looks beyond that first mission, toward the whole history of the church.

For today: if because of your faith you face mockery or pressure, do not see it only as a problem. It can be a door to speak about Christ with humility, trusting that God is with you.
exp.4:29:
If your right hand causes you to stumble into sin, it is better to lose it than to put your whole being at risk. The phrase "causes you to sin" means something that pulls you toward wrongdoing, and "hell" translates "Gehenna," a place Jesus uses as a picture of the final judgment.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and the crowd. He has just taught that sin begins in the heart, not only in actions. He uses a deliberate exaggeration to show how seriously we must take sin. Most readers understand that he is not asking anyone to mutilate themselves, but to cut out at the root whatever makes us fall.

For today: identify one specific thing that leads you to sin, such as certain content on your phone or a harmful friendship, and make a firm decision today to stay away from it, asking God for help.
exp.11:6:
Jesus says that if the Pharisees had understood what "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" means, they would not have condemned the innocent. The phrase "If only you had known" points to understanding that was missing, and "the innocent" refers to those who had done nothing wrong. The saying comes from the prophet Hosea (6:6).

Jesus is responding to the Pharisees, who criticized his disciples for picking heads of grain to eat on the Sabbath. Jesus reminds them that the priests worked in the temple on the Sabbath and were not guilty. He then declares that something greater than the temple was there, referring to himself.

For today: before judging someone for not keeping a rule, ask yourself whether you are showing compassion. God values obedience that comes from a merciful heart, not merely the outward keeping of religious rules.
exp.27:19:
Jesus asks that the new disciples be taught to obey everything he has commanded them. It is not only about knowing things, but about living them out. Then he makes a promise: "I am with you always," that is, "I am with you every day," even to the end of the age, meaning until the close of this present era. The word "Amen" closes the statement, and it means "so be it."

This is the risen Jesus speaking, at the close of the Gospel of Matthew. He has just said that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him, and he sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them. This promise goes along with the mission he entrusts to them: they would not go alone.

For today: if you feel inadequate to speak about Jesus or to live what he teaches, remember that you are not alone. Take one concrete step of obedience this week, trusting that he is with you.
exp.5:8:
Jesus teaches how to pray. "So then, this is how you should pray" means "pray in this way." He begins by calling God "Our Father in heaven," and then says, "hallowed be Your name," that is, that God's name be treated as holy, honored, and respected.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and the crowd. He has just said not to use empty, repeated words as the pagans did, since the Father already knows what we need. For that reason he gives a brief and simple model, not a magic formula.

For today: before asking for things, begin your prayer by remembering that you are speaking with a close and holy Father. Take a few moments to honor him, thank him, and turn your heart toward his presence. Then bring your needs to him with confidence and without many words.
exp.25:28:
Jesus says that from this moment on he will not drink the fruit of the vine, that is, wine, until a day still to come, when he will drink it anew with his disciples in his Father's kingdom. "I tell you" and "I will not drink" and "from now on" point to something that will surely happen.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, just after offering the cup as a symbol of his blood. He knows that his death is near and that the disciples will soon scatter. With these words he assures them that the separation is not the end: there will be a reunion and a celebration in the kingdom. Scholars understand the "day" in several ways, but all agree that it points to the final fulfillment of the kingdom.

For today: when you go through difficult times or loss, remember that Jesus promised a joyful reunion. That hope helps you remain faithful and take the Lord's Supper with gratitude and expectation.
exp.6:21:
Jesus says that on the day of judgment, "that day," many people will speak to him with confidence. They will say, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, and in Your name drive out demons and perform many miracles?" They will present their record of religious activity as proof that they belong to him.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just warned about false prophets and said they are recognized by their fruits. His point is that impressive religious words and works are not enough if there is no real relationship with him and no obedience to the Father's will.

For today: do not trust in your spiritual achievements, your service, or your reputation. Ask yourself honestly whether you truly know Jesus and whether you obey what he says, even in the small and everyday things.
exp.6:20:
Jesus says that simply calling him "Lord" is not enough to enter the kingdom of heaven. The one who enters is the one who does the will of the Father. The word "but" means "but", and "does" means "does" or "practices".

Jesus speaks at the end of the Sermon on the Mount. He has just warned about false teachers and said that trees are known by their fruit. Now he applies that idea to anyone who says they follow him: nice words do not replace a life that obeys. Then he mentions some people who even performed miracles, yet he never knew them.

For today: do not be satisfied with only saying that you believe. Ask God in what area you should obey him this week, such as forgiving, being honest, or helping someone, and take that concrete step, trusting in his grace.
exp.22:29:
Jesus quotes what the scribes and Pharisees used to say: "If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in shedding the blood of the prophets." To be partners in shedding the blood means to be accomplices in the murders. They presented themselves as better than their fathers.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, in his denunciation of the religious leaders. They built and decorated the tombs of the prophets to show respect, but Jesus tells them that their hearts were full of hypocrisy. In the following verse he shows them that, by rejecting him, they were following the same path as their fathers.

For today: it is easy to criticize the mistakes of the past and to believe we are different. Let us ask God to examine our hearts and help us obey him today, when his truth makes us uncomfortable.
exp.23:26:
It says that the coming of Jesus, the Son of Man, will be like lightning that comes from the east and flashes as far as the west. That is, it will be sudden, bright, and visible to everyone.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when they ask him about the signs of the end. He warns them that there will be false christs and false prophets. Some will say, "He is in the wilderness," or "He is hidden in the inner rooms," that is, in private chambers. Jesus says that his return will not be a secret known only to a few.

For today: do not be carried away by anyone who promises to know dates or secret details of Christ's return. Instead, live faithfully, praying, reading the Bible, and loving others, trusting that he will come in plain sight of all.
exp.6:3:
Here Jesus gives an almost comical picture: someone says to his brother, "Let me take the speck out of your eye," while he himself has a beam in his own eye. The "speck" is a tiny piece of straw or splinter; the "beam" is a large piece of timber used in building. The phrase "Let me take" means "allow me" or "let me help."

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount, addressing his disciples and the crowd. He has just warned that we will be judged by the same measure we use with others. With this exaggerated image, he shows how absurd it is to correct others without first examining ourselves. He does not forbid all correction, since he goes on to speak of discernment.

For today: before pointing out someone else's mistake, stop and pray. Ask God to show you your own failings. Then, if you must speak, do so with humility and love.
exp.20:41:
Jesus asks the religious leaders whether they have never read this passage in the Scriptures: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The cornerstone is the stone that joins two walls and holds the whole structure together. "Rejected" means that they threw it away. This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous to see.

Jesus has just told the parable of the wicked tenants, who mistreated the owner's servants and even his son. The leaders themselves answered that the owner would punish those tenants. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22-23 to show that they, as the builders, were rejecting God's messenger: himself. Even so, God would lift him up.

For today: do not measure Christ by what others think of him. If the world rejects him, God still places him as the foundation. Ask yourself whether your life is built on him.
exp.26:37:
Two other men were crucified along with Jesus, one on his right and one on his left. In the Berean Standard Bible the men are called "robbers," a word that refers to people who took others' property by force, not just to people who stole small things.

Here the narrator is Matthew. He has just described how the soldiers kept watch over Jesus and placed a sign above his head reading: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews." Matthew shows that Jesus was treated as a criminal, surrounded by condemned men. Many readers see in this the fulfillment of Isaiah 53:12, which says that he was numbered with the transgressors.

For today: Jesus drew near to those whom society despises. If you feel unworthy or far from God, remember that he was there, among the guilty, and so you can come to him with confidence.
exp.12:9:
The disciples come to Jesus and ask him a straightforward question: why does he speak to the people in parables? "Came" here means they approached him. They have noticed that Jesus often teaches in a way that is not direct, and they want to understand his reason.

The ones asking are the disciples. Jesus has just told the parable of the sower to a crowd, and he ended by saying, "He who has ears, let him hear." The disciples realize that not everyone understands. Jesus will answer that they have been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, that is, truths that God is gradually revealing. Interpreters explain the scope of that answer in several different ways.

When something in the Bible is not clear to you, do as the disciples did: come to Jesus and ask him sincerely. He welcomes the one who comes wanting to understand.
exp.4:47:
He says that his followers must be "perfect," as God is. Here the word "you" is plural, addressing a group, and the verb is "be." The word "perfect" translates a Greek term (teleios) that points to something complete, mature, one that has reached its goal. It does not speak only of never making mistakes, but of loving with a whole heart and without holding back.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just taught them to love their enemies (v. 44). He points out that loving only those who love us is what even tax collectors do. God, on the other hand, makes his sun rise on the good and the evil. His love is the model.

Today, we can choose a person who is hard to love and do a concrete good for them: pray for them, greet them with respect, or help them without expecting anything in return. In this way we practice a love that more closely resembles God's.
exp.19:10:
When the workers who had come first received their pay, they began to grumble against the landowner. Their complaint was not spoken openly but was a bitter resentment they held inside. "On receiving their pay" refers to the denarius they were given. "Landowner" is the master of the vineyard, the employer.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The owner hired workers at different hours of the day and paid all of them the same amount. The first ones expected to receive more, even though they had agreed to a denarius. Many understand that Jesus is teaching about the grace of God, which is generous and is not earned by comparing one person with another. Some also see here a lesson for those who thought themselves better than others.

For today: when you see God blessing others, do not measure his kindness against your own effort. Give thanks for what you have received and rejoice with those who receive his mercy.
exp.8:28:
Jesus touches the eyes of the two blind men and says, "According to your faith will it be done to you." This means: "It will happen in line with the trust you have in me."

The two blind men were following Jesus, crying out that he would have mercy on them, and they called him "Son of David," a title for the promised Messiah. Inside the house, Jesus asked them whether they believed he could heal them, and they answered, "Yes, Lord." Then he touched them and spoke. Their faith was not a power in itself; it was the trust placed in Jesus, who healed them.

Today we can come to Jesus with sincerity, acknowledging our need and trusting in him, even when our faith is small. We do not know how he will respond in every situation, but he invites us to trust.
exp.25:59:
This verse says that the Jewish leaders were looking for evidence against Jesus, but they did not find any, even though many false witnesses came forward. Finally, two came forward. "Finally" is the plain meaning of the phrase here. The term for the high priest is the one used for the chief priest.

Here the writer is Matthew, who describes Jesus' nighttime trial before the Sanhedrin, the religious council. The leaders had already decided to condemn him and were only looking for an excuse that would appear legal. According to the law of Moses, the testimony of two or more witnesses was required, which is why these two appear. Even so, their words about the temple are presented as false or distorted.

For today: the truth does not need lies to stand. Let us ask God for honesty when we speak about others, and if we are ever falsely accused, let us remember that Jesus also went through this and understands us.
exp.13:31:
It says that when Jesus and Peter had climbed back into the boat, the wind died down.

The account is from Matthew. That night the disciples were crossing the lake, and the wind was against them. Jesus came walking toward them on the water, and Peter wanted to go to Him. When he saw the strong wind, he became afraid and began to sink. Jesus reached out and held him up, and when both of them had climbed back into the boat, the storm stopped. The disciples worshiped Him.

Many times we ask that the storm pass first. This passage invites us to look to Jesus in the middle of it. When you feel afraid, cry out as Peter did: "Lord, save me." He is near and He holds you up.
exp.14:12:
Jesus says that every plant which his heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots. He uses the image of a garden: what comes from God remains, and what does not come from Him will not last. The phrase "pulled up by its roots" means removed completely, roots and all.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, after the Pharisees were offended by his teaching. They placed great value on human traditions about washing one's hands and on what counts as clean. Jesus teaches that what truly defiles a person is what comes out of the heart. Many understand the "plant" to be those human teachings, though some think it also refers to the teachers who defended them.

For today: examine whether what you believe and practice comes from the Word of God or only from custom. Ask God to cultivate in you what He has planted.
exp.3:12:
He says that Jesus left Nazareth, the town where he grew up, and went to live in Capernaum. This town was beside the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the old tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali. The word "lived" means that he settled there. The phrase "region" refers to the surrounding area, the territory around the town.

Matthew, the narrator, tells what happened after the temptation in the desert and the arrest of John the Baptist. Jesus begins his public ministry. The next verse explains that this change of place fulfilled what Isaiah had said. Many understand that Matthew wants to show that the light would reach a region mixed with other peoples. Scholars do not agree on why he left Nazareth; the text does not give the details.

God can lead us to new places to carry out his purpose. If today you feel a change of season, ask him to guide you and obey with confidence.
exp.0:1:
It says that Abraham was the father of Isaac, Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers. Judah is one of the twelve sons of Jacob, and the royal tribe would later come from him.

Matthew, the author of the gospel, begins with the genealogy of Jesus to show his Jewish readers that Jesus belongs to the history of Israel. This line follows the promises made to Abraham and then to David. Matthew names Judah and not Joseph, the favorite son, because the line of the Messiah passes through Judah.

For today: God keeps his promises with patience, across generations and through imperfect people. You can trust that he is also at work in your family and your story, even when you cannot yet see the full result.
exp.19:28:
Matthew tells us that as Jesus and his disciples were leaving the city of Jericho, a large crowd was following him. The word "crowd" here means a great number of people gathered together, a throng.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, and he has just taught that true greatness lies in serving, not being served, and that he would give his life to ransom many. This verse changes the scene and sets up the meeting with two blind men who cry out for mercy. Matthew does not explain why so many people were following him; it may have been curiosity, hope, or admiration.

For today: following Jesus is not just going along with the crowd, but learning his heart of service. Today you can ask yourself whom you can serve with humility, and stay alert to the person beside you who is calling out for help.
exp.26:40:
This verse says that the religious leaders of Israel also joined in mocking Jesus on the cross. The verse describes their scorn toward him with the word "mocked." The chief priests were the leaders of the temple, the scribes were teachers of the Law, and the elders were leaders of the people.

Before this verse, the people passing by were already insulting him. Now it is those who had handed him over to be condemned who speak. They mock what Jesus had said about being the Son of God. Without realizing it, they asked for a sign, but they did not understand that Jesus remained on the cross out of love, to save others.

For today: when someone mocks your faith, remember that Jesus was also treated this way. Respond with patience and trust in God, without returning insult for insult.
exp.23:45:
It says the servant is happy when his master, on returning, finds him doing what he was assigned. "Blessed" means happy or favored. "Find" means "come upon him." "Doing so" refers to caring for the household and giving them food on time, as the previous verse says.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after describing the events of the end and his coming. He tells them a parable to encourage them to be ready, because no one knows the hour. The faithful servant represents someone who carries out the task entrusted to him responsibly while the master is away.

For today: this is not about living in fear, but about faithfulness. Do well what God has entrusted to you, such as caring for your family, serving honestly in your work, and helping others, without waiting for someone to watch over you.
exp.17:1:
Jesus invites a little child to come to him and stands him among his disciples, in full view of everyone. It is a simple action, but a very clear one. The phrase "stand among them" means that he placed the child at the center of the group.

The disciples had just asked who was the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Jesus does not answer first with words, but with a gesture. Afterward he explains that one must become like children and humble oneself. Some understand this as referring to a child's trust and dependence; others, to a child's low social standing in that time. Both ideas fit the text.

For today: before seeking recognition or an important place, ask God for a humble and trusting heart. Today, serve someone without expecting anything in return.
exp.2:2:
Matthew explains that John the Baptist is the person the prophet Isaiah spoke about. He is a voice calling out in the wilderness, telling people to prepare the way for the Lord. "Prepare" means getting ready, and "make straight paths for Him" means clearing the way so it is level and free of obstacles.

The one speaking here is Matthew, the author of the Gospel. He quotes Isaiah 40:3 to show that John's mission, which called people to repentance, had already been announced. The verses that follow show John in the desert, wearing simple clothing, with many people coming out to hear him. Preparing the way is understood as preparing the heart to receive Jesus.

Today we can ask ourselves what in our lives gets in the way of God's coming: pride, resentment, or carelessness. Today you can ask him for forgiveness and take a concrete step to make straight that area of your life.
exp.5:4:
Jesus says that when we pray we should not be like the hypocrites, that is, those who act to appear religious. They love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by men. Jesus declares that they already have their full reward: the attention of others is all they will receive.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples and the crowd. Earlier he spoke about giving to others in secret, and now he applies the same idea to prayer.
