He does not condemn praying in public or in the synagogue, but praying in order to impress others. What matters is the motive of the heart.

Today we can ask ourselves: "For whom am I praying?" Make time for simple and sincere prayer, without seeking applause, speaking with God as a child speaks with a father who sees the heart.
exp.19:11:
The workers who were hired first grumble to the owner of the vineyard. The men hired last worked only one hour, they say, yet you have made them equal to us, who bore the burden and the scorching heat of the day. Their complaint is about fairness, and it sets up the owner's reply.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The owner agreed on a denarius, a full day's wage, with the first workers, and out of generosity he gave the same to those who came later. The story follows Peter's question about what the disciples would receive for leaving everything. Many understand it to teach that God's grace is not earned by merit.

For today, when you see God bless someone who seems to deserve it less than you, do not compare. Instead, give thanks for what God has given you and rejoice in his generosity toward others.
exp.22:18:
They taught that swearing by the gift at the altar was more binding than swearing by the altar itself, and Jesus says they were mistaken. He calls them "you blind men," meaning people who lack judgment and cannot see what really matters. The question he asks is plain: which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes it sacred? The answer is clear, because the altar is what makes the gift holy.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees in his teaching against religious hypocrisy. They had invented rules to decide which oaths counted and which could be broken. Jesus shows that these word games were absurd, because every oath, in one way or another, involves God.

For today: let us be people of our word. We do not need formulas or excuses to keep what we have promised. If we say "yes," let it be yes, because God hears everything we say.
exp.25:21:
They were deeply grieved, and each one began to ask him, "Surely not I, Lord?" The word "deeply grieved" means full of sorrow, and "deeply" means very much indeed.

Jesus was eating with his twelve disciples on the night before his crucifixion. He had just said that one of them would hand him over. It is striking that no one pointed to another; each one questioned himself. Matthew does not explain why, and we may think they were aware of their own weakness. Later, Jesus speaks about Judas without leaving any doubt.

For today: instead of quickly judging others, we can humbly ask God, "Surely not I, Lord?" Examining our own hearts helps us to repent and to depend on his grace.
exp.11:12:
Jesus asks a man with a withered hand to stretch out his hand. The man obeys, and his hand is restored to full use, just like the other one. The wording here describes the hand returning to its normal, healthy condition, and healing completely made whole.

Jesus is in a synagogue on the Sabbath. The Pharisees were watching him, looking for a reason to accuse him of breaking the law about rest. Before healing the man, Jesus answers them with the example of a sheep rescued from a pit on the Sabbath, and concludes that a human being is worth far more. For Him, doing good is never out of place. Afterward, the Pharisees make plans to destroy him.

For today: Jesus asked the man for something that seemed impossible, stretching out a useless hand, and healing came as he obeyed. When God asks us for a step that seems beyond our strength, we can trust Him and take it. We should also never put rules or traditions above helping someone who needs it.
exp.21:18:
Jesus asks them to show him the coin used for the tax. The tax was paid to the Roman government. They bring him a denarius, a Roman silver coin worth roughly one day's wage.

The Pharisees, together with others, ask him a question to trap him: whether it was right to pay tax to Caesar. If he said yes, the people would be angry; if he said no, they could accuse him before Rome. Jesus knows their evil intention and calls them hypocrites. By bringing him the coin, they themselves show that they use Caesar's money.

For today: we can fulfill our civic responsibilities, such as paying taxes, without neglecting what is most important. Everything we are belongs to God, so we should give Him our life and our loyalty.
exp.26:29:
They spat on him, then took the staff they had placed in his hand as a mock scepter and struck him on the head with it repeatedly. The word "struck" means they hit him, and the staff was a thin, hollow rod.

Matthew tells what happened in the palace courtyard, after Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified. The soldiers did not believe he was a king; they mocked the charge that he was "King of the Jews." Matthew shows that Jesus endured this humiliation without defending himself. Many Christians see here the fulfillment of Isaiah 50:6, where the Lord's servant does not hide his face from mockery and spitting.

For today: when you are humiliated or treated with contempt, remember that Jesus went through that too and understands you. Ask him for help to respond with patience, without returning mockery for mockery.
exp.0:24:
Joseph had no union with Mary until she gave birth to her Son. Then he gave the child the name Jesus, as the angel had told him to do.

The writer is Matthew. He wants to show that Jesus was born in a miraculous way, as the prophet Isaiah had foretold. Joseph obeys God, takes Mary into his home, and claims the child as his own by giving him a name. The word "until" has been understood in several ways: many believers think that they later had other children, and others believe that Mary remained a virgin always. The text does not make this clear.

For today: Joseph obeyed even though he did not understand everything and even though it was hard for him. Today we can trust God and take the next step of obedience, even when we cannot see the whole picture.
exp.7:21:
Jesus says to a disciple: "Follow Me." He then adds that the dead should bury their own dead.

Jesus uses "dead" in two ways: the first are those who are spiritually lifeless, and the second are those who have physically died.

He is speaking with a man who wanted first to bury his father. Some think the father had already died; others think the man was asking to wait until the father died someday. The text does not make this clear. Earlier, Jesus had said he had nowhere to lay his head, showing that following him costs something. His answer, deliberately strong, teaches that he must be the priority.

For today: ask yourself what good but secondary thing is causing you to put off your obedience to Jesus. Today, take one concrete step of following him, trusting that he guides you.
exp.27:14:
They accepted the money and repeated the story they had been told: that the disciples stole the body while the soldiers were asleep. "Instructed" means they were given directions on what to say. "Circulated" means the account was passed around and talked about among many people. Matthew adds that this version kept spreading among the Jews "to this very day," meaning up to the time when he was writing.

Matthew tells us that the chief priests and the elders, upon learning of the resurrection, paid the soldiers to keep quiet about what had happened. The "governor" is Pilate. Matthew includes this to answer a rumor that was going around in his time about the empty tomb.

For today: the truth can be covered up with money and lies, but it does not disappear. We can ask ourselves whether we are willing to stay silent or bend the truth for convenience. The disciples, by contrast, followed Jesus even while they still had doubts.
exp.27:12:
This verse shows what the chief priests told the soldiers who guarded the tomb to say. They were to report that Jesus' disciples came by night and took the body while the soldiers were asleep. "Stole" means "took secretly, without permission," and "guard" refers to the soldiers who watched over the tomb.

The soldiers had seen what happened at the resurrection and reported it to the religious leaders. These leaders met with the elders and, instead of investigating, paid a large sum of money to cover up the facts. It is strange for anyone to claim they saw what happened "while we were asleep," since sleeping on guard duty was a serious offense; that is why the leaders promise to protect them before the governor.

Today, this passage invites us to be honest even when the truth is uncomfortable. We can ask ourselves whether we ever prefer to hide something instead of facing it. God calls us to seek the truth with humility.
exp.23:18:
It says that there will be very hard times for women who are pregnant and for mothers who are nursing. "Pregnant" means expecting a baby, and nursing mothers are those who feed their babies at the breast. The word "miserable" expresses compassion and sorrow, not punishment. Jesus is lamenting how difficult it will be to flee with so little strength and freedom of movement.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after telling them that the temple would be destroyed. He warns them that when that crisis comes, they must flee quickly, without stopping to gather their belongings. Many believe he refers mainly to the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, and others also see a future fulfillment. Christians have understood it in both ways.

For today: Jesus pays attention to the most vulnerable. We can imitate him by caring for and supporting those who are fragile around us, such as mothers, the sick, or the elderly, before difficulty arrives.
exp.8:27:
Matthew 9:28 says that Jesus entered a house, and the two blind men who had been following him came to him there. Jesus asks them a direct question: do they believe that he is able to do this, meaning restore their sight? They answer without hesitation: "Yes, Lord."

The blind men had followed Jesus down the road, crying out: "Have mercy on us, Son of David," a title that recognized Jesus as the promised Messiah. Jesus did not heal them right away, but let them come into the house and asked them about their faith. Shortly afterward he healed them, saying: "According to your faith let it be done to you."

For today: Jesus invites us to trust him with sincerity. We can bring him our needs and answer him with the same simplicity: "Yes, Lord, I believe."
exp.1:1:
The magi arrive in Jerusalem and ask where the One who has been born King of the Jews is. They say they saw his star in the east, meaning in their own land, and that they have come to worship him. Here, to worship him means to honor him and show him reverence, bowing before him.

These were foreign wise men who studied the stars, probably from the East. The Bible does not say how many there were or what exact country they came from. They ask in the capital because they expected to find the new king there. Their question troubles King Herod, who already held that throne, which is why he is disturbed.

For today: the magi sought Jesus with effort and humility, not caring about the distance. We can do the same by giving real time to seeking him in his Word and in prayer, and by giving him first place in our hearts.
exp.9:36:
Jesus says that anyone who loves father or mother more than him is not fit for him, and the same is true of anyone who loves son or daughter more than him. The word "fit" here means that such a person is not in the right attitude to be his disciple. He does not command us to stop loving our family, but he must hold the first place.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles, whom he is sending out to preach. He warns them that following him would bring division, even within homes, because not everyone would accept his message. For this reason he asks for a loyalty that stands above the strongest bonds. The verses that follow speak of taking up the cross, that is, being willing to suffer for him.

For today: loving Christ first does not make you love your family less, but better. When you have to choose between pleasing someone in your household and being faithful to Jesus, ask him for courage and gentleness to obey him without looking down on anyone.
exp.9:13:
It says that if anyone does not welcome Jesus' messengers or listen to their message, they should leave that house or city and shake the dust off their feet. "Shall not welcome" means will not welcome them. "Listen to" means pay attention to their words.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples, whom he sends to proclaim that the kingdom of heaven is near. For Jewish people, shaking off the dust was a gesture of separation, a sign that they had already done their part. The next verse shows that rejection is a serious matter, though judgment belongs to God, not to the disciples.

We can share our faith with kindness, but without forcing anyone. If someone rejects it, we can move on in peace, without bitterness or resentment, and entrust that person to God.
exp.8:9:
Matthew 9:10 says that Jesus was dining at Matthew's house, and many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with him and his disciples. Tax collectors worked for the Roman rulers collecting taxes, and many people saw them as dishonest and as traitors to their own people. "Sinners" was a label for people of bad reputation or those who did not keep the religious rules.

Matthew is describing a meal in his own home, shortly after Jesus had called him to follow. The verse does not state that the house belonged to Matthew, though many readers believe it did. Sharing a table showed closeness and acceptance, and that is why the Pharisees were scandalized.

Today, Jesus invites us to draw near to those whom others reject, without approving their sin, but with friendship and compassion. Think of someone you could invite to your table this week.
exp.25:69:
Peter answers the servant girl who accuses him of being with Jesus. He denies it in front of everyone present and says, "I do not know what you are talking about." It is a way of pretending not to understand, as if he did not grasp the accusation. The word "But" introduces his reply, and "before them all" means he did it publicly.

Peter is in the courtyard of the high priest's house, while inside they are questioning Jesus. A servant girl recognizes him as a follower of the Galilean. Peter feels fear, and so what Jesus had already foretold comes true: that he would deny him that very night (Matthew 26:34).

All of us can feel afraid to acknowledge Jesus in front of others. If you fail today, remember that Peter was forgiven and restored. Ask God for courage, and when you have the chance, speak of your faith simply and honestly, without waiting to be perfect.
exp.19:13:
The owner of the vineyard tells the worker to take his pay and go. The wage was fair and agreed upon. The owner also wants to give the man who came last the same as the first. The word "last" means "last," and "same" means exactly what it says. "Denarius" was the normal pay for a day's work.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The owner of the vineyard represents God, and the workers are those who respond to his call. Those who worked all day complain because others, who worked only one hour, received the same pay. Jesus teaches that the kingdom rests on God's generosity, not on comparisons. Some understand that he also corrects the pride of those who think themselves superior.

Today, instead of measuring what others receive, we can give thanks for what God has given us. Rejoicing when he is kind to someone else frees us from envy and reminds us that everything is grace.
exp.11:0:
He says that Jesus was walking with his disciples through grainfields on the Sabbath. The disciples were hungry, so they began to pick heads of grain and eat them. "Grainfields" are fields where grain is grown, "to pick" here means to pull off or gather, and "heads" are the tops of the grain plant where the grain grows.

Here the narrator, Matthew, speaks. According to the law of Moses, a person was allowed to take ears of grain by hand from another person's field (Deuteronomy 23:25). But the Pharisees, as we see right away, accuse them of working on the Sabbath, probably because of the way their traditions understood rest. Jesus answers with the example of David.

For today: God gave us rest as a gift, not as a burden. We can care for our times of rest and worship, but without becoming hard toward others or forgetting mercy and the real needs of people.
exp.25:12:
Jesus says with certainty that wherever the gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what this woman did will also be told, so that she will be remembered. The phrase "I assure you" in the Berean Standard Bible conveys the same weight as the old wording, and the perfume she poured out is an expensive ointment, which is what the words "this gospel" and "what she has done" point back to.

Jesus is speaking in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. A woman poured an expensive perfume over his head, and the disciples were upset about the waste. Jesus defends her act and connects it to his burial, which is near. Then Judas goes off to arrange the handing over of Jesus, a strong contrast with the woman.

God values sincere love, even when others see it as excessive. Today we can serve Jesus with generosity and humility, without expecting applause, trusting that he sees and remembers what we do out of love.
exp.2:7:
Produce fruit, then, that shows you have truly repented. Repenting means changing direction, and here you are called to let that change be seen in your life.

John the Baptist is speaking. Many people were being baptized while confessing their sins, and Pharisees and Sadducees also came. John confronts them sharply, because it was not enough to come to the baptism or to take pride in being descendants of Abraham. God was looking for a real change and not merely a religious appearance.

For today: think of one specific area where you have already asked God for forgiveness, such as how you treat your family or your honesty at work, and this week take one visible step of change, such as asking someone for forgiveness or leaving a bad habit behind.
exp.8:24:
What it says: After the crowd had been put outside, Jesus went into the room where the girl was, took her by the hand, and she got up. "Put outside" means the people were sent out of the house. "Took the girl by the hand" means he held her hand to lift her up.

Context: A synagogue ruler had asked Jesus to heal his daughter, who had died. Jesus said she was "sleeping," and the people laughed at him. Matthew tells us that, after the mockers were removed, Jesus acted with calm and authority. Some think "sleeping" speaks of death as something temporary; others think the girl was in a state that looked like death. The text shows that Jesus has power over her.

For today: When mockery or doubt surrounds you, do not lose heart. Come to Jesus with confidence; he can act where others no longer see hope.
exp.12:19:
Jesus says that the seed sown on rocky ground represents the person who hears God's message and at once receives it with joy. "Rocky ground" is ground with a lot of rock and little soil. The initial reaction seems very good.

Jesus is explaining the parable of the sower privately to his disciples, after having told it to the crowds. He clarifies that the same seed, the word of the kingdom, produces different results depending on the heart that receives it. The following verse shows that this joy has no root and does not hold up under difficulties.

For today: hearing the Bible and feeling moved is not enough. Set aside time to meditate on it, put it into practice, and talk with God, so that your faith has roots when trials come.
exp.15:26:
Jesus says that the Son of Man, that is, he himself, will come in the glory of his Father and accompanied by angels. Then he will repay each person according to what they have done. Here "repay" means giving each person what is rightly due.

Jesus speaks to his disciples shortly after announcing his cross. Peter had just rejected that path. Jesus teaches them that following him means giving up one's life, and that what truly matters is the soul, not gaining the world. Christians understand in different ways how works relate to salvation, but many see them as the fruit of faith.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself what value it will have before God. Live today with faith, honesty, and love, knowing that your decisions count.
exp.22:32:
Jesus asks the Pharisees and scribes: "How will you escape the sentence of hell?" He calls them "snakes" and a "brood of vipers," images of dangerous and deceitful people. The word "hell" here translates "Gehenna," a place associated with God's final judgment.

Jesus speaks in the temple, at the end of his ministry, after several woes against the religious leaders. They prided themselves on honoring the prophets, but they acted like those who killed them: they were hypocrites and rejected the truth. Jesus speaks with firmness, but his grief becomes visible later, when he weeps over Jerusalem.

For today: it is not enough to appear religious or to speak well of the faith. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that listens to his correction and practices justice and mercy, not just appearances.
exp.21:5:
This verse says that while some of the invited guests ignored the invitation, others seized the king's servants, mistreated them and killed them. The response was no longer just indifference, but violence against the messengers.

Jesus tells this parable to the religious leaders of Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. The king represents God, and the wedding of the son, his invitation to share in his kingdom. The servants bring to mind the prophets and messengers God sent. Many understand that Jesus is speaking of the rejection those messengers suffered throughout the history of Israel.

Today, let us consider whether we sometimes resent the voice that corrects us or calls us to God. We can ask him for a humble heart to listen, and to treat with respect those who speak to us honestly from his Word.
exp.14:23:
Jesus says that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, that is, to the people of Israel, who were like a flock that had lost its way.

Jesus speaks in response to the disciples, who wanted him to send away a Canaanite woman, a woman who was not an Israelite. She was asking him for help for her daughter. Jesus explains the order of his mission: first to Israel, through whom the blessing would come to all nations. Some think he was also testing the woman's faith, but the text does not say so clearly. What is certain is that she keeps asking right away, and Jesus attends to her.

For today: when God seems silent or says "no," keep drawing near to him with humility and trust. Persevering faith does not tire of seeking him.
exp.11:3:
Jesus reminds them that David, when he was hungry, went into the house of God and ate the consecrated bread. These were holy loaves set before God in the sanctuary, and the law said that only the priests were permitted to eat them. "Not lawful" means not permitted. "But only for the priests" means reserved for the priests alone.

The Pharisees were accusing Jesus' disciples of breaking the Sabbath, because they picked heads of grain to eat. Jesus answers them with an example from Scripture that they knew well (1 Samuel 21). His point is that human need and mercy cannot be ignored, and that he, as one greater than the temple, has authority over the Sabbath. Interpreters explain in various ways how the case of David applies, but the central teaching is clear.

For today: obeying God is not being harsh with people. Before judging someone, ask yourself whether you are guarding the letter of a rule while forgetting the compassion God desires.
exp.8:25:
This verse says that the news of what Jesus did spread throughout that whole region. The word "news" here means what people were talking about, the report that moved from one person to the next. "Region" refers to the area where everything took place.

Matthew, who is writing, has just told how Jesus raised up the daughter of a leading man. People had laughed when Jesus said that she was "sleeping," but after seeing her alive, the amazement spread quickly. Some understand that Jesus was speaking of death as a passing sleep, because He had power to wake her. Right after this, two blind men follow Him, asking for mercy.

For today: when God does something good in your life, do not keep it silent. Tell humbly what He has done, so that others may also trust in Jesus and seek His help.
exp.18:4:
Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24: for this reason a man will leave his father and mother, be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh. To be united means to be joined closely and faithfully, bound together for life. "One flesh" speaks of a deep union that lasts a whole life.

The Pharisees come to test him, asking whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason. Jesus does not begin with rules but with God's original plan in creation. With these words he shows that marriage is a union that God himself establishes, not a simple arrangement that can be broken for any reason.

For today: value your marriage, or the marriages of those around you, as something serious and sacred. Cultivate faithfulness, honest conversation and forgiveness, putting your spouse first after God.
exp.15:19:
Jesus firmly orders his disciples not to tell anyone that he is the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, God's Anointed One. The word "charged" here means that he gave a clear command.

Peter had just confessed that Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus had spoken about his church. Even so, he asks for silence. The exact reason is not stated here. Many think people were expecting a political Messiah, and that Jesus wanted his path of suffering and the cross, which he announces right after, to be understood first.

Today we can learn that knowing Jesus is not just repeating correct titles. We need to understand him as he is: the Messiah who serves, suffers, and saves. Let us ask him to correct our ideas about him.
exp.13:3:
This verse explains why John the Baptist was in prison. John had been telling Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have her," that is, "It is not permitted for you to have her as your wife." The word "lawful" means permitted by God's law.

The one speaking here is the writer of the Gospel, who looks back and tells the reason for the imprisonment. Herod Antipas had taken Herodias, who was the wife of his brother Philip. John, relying on the law of Moses, pointed out to him that this was wrong. For speaking the truth, he ended up in prison, and later Herod wanted to kill him, but he feared the people.

For today: speaking the truth with love can cost dearly, but God calls us to be faithful. Ask him for courage and wisdom to speak with respect, without keeping silent about what is right.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that Mary will give birth to a son and that Joseph is to give him the name Jesus. The reason is that he will save his people from their sins. The phrases "she will give birth" and "you are to give Him the name" carry the same sense as the verse's wording.

"Jesus" comes from the Hebrew Yeshua, which is understood to mean "the Lord saves."

An angel of the Lord speaks, appearing to Joseph in a dream. Joseph was troubled because Mary was pregnant and he intended to leave her quietly, so as not to shame her. The angel calms him and explains that the child comes from the Holy Spirit. When he is told to give the child his name, Joseph accepts to be the child's legal father within the line of David.

For today: Jesus came to rescue us from what harms us most, sin, and not only from the troubles outside us. Today you can bring honestly to him whatever weighs on your conscience, trusting that his name is a promise of forgiveness and help.
exp.18:17:
Here a man asks Jesus, "Which ones?", meaning which of the commandments he was to keep. Jesus answers with four: do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, and do not bear false witness.

The man, a rich young man, had asked how to obtain eternal life. Jesus told him to keep the commandments. He wanted to know which ones, and Jesus named those that deal with how we treat our neighbor. Then he adds honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself. Many understand that Jesus was preparing the young man to show him what truly occupied his heart.

For today: it is not enough to avoid what is wrong at first sight. Ask yourself honestly how you treat those around you: whether you are honest, faithful, and just. Ask God to show you what is in your heart.
exp.25:25:
While they were eating, Jesus takes the bread, speaks a blessing over it, breaks it, and gives it to the disciples. He tells them, "Take and eat," and then declares, "This is My body."

It is the night before the crucifixion, during the Passover supper. Jesus has just spoken of Judas's betrayal, and yet he lets him share the table. With the bread he announces that his body will be given up. Christians understand in different ways how Christ is present at the Supper, but all acknowledge that his sacrifice is remembered there.

Today we can approach the Lord's Supper with gratitude and sincerity, remembering that Jesus gave himself for us. Before taking part, it is good to pause to pray, to thank him, and to ask forgiveness for what we need to set right.
exp.11:15:
This verse says that Jesus firmly warned the people he had healed not to tell others who he was. The phrase "firmly warned" means he gave the instruction with real seriousness. The phrase "make Him known" means to tell openly or publicize who he was.

Matthew records this after the Pharisees had plotted to kill Jesus. He withdrew and continued to heal the crowds. Matthew then explains that this fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah about a chosen servant, beloved of God, who would act with gentleness. Some understand that Jesus was avoiding scandal and conflict before the appointed time; the text gives no further detail.

Today we can learn that serving God does not always need applause or publicity. We can help others with humility, trusting that God sees what is done in silence and knows when and how to make his work known.
exp.17:32:
The king says to his servant: "Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?" The question asks whether the servant ought to have acted with mercy, and "fellow servant" refers to someone who serves the same master.

Jesus tells this parable after Peter asks him how many times he must forgive. A king forgave a servant a huge debt, but that servant refused to forgive a small debt owed to him by another. The king speaks to show him his injustice and his hardness of heart.

For today: when it is hard for you to forgive someone, remember how much you have received from God's mercy. That does not minimize your pain, but it helps you let go of resentment and offer sincere forgiveness, step by step and with God's help.
exp.4:25:
Jesus says firmly that whoever is taken to prison over a debt or a dispute will not get out until they have paid everything. "Truly" is the word he uses to stress that what he says is certain. The "last penny" was a Roman coin of very little value, so the point is to pay down to the very last, even the smallest amount. The "officer" is the official who carries out the sentence.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He is teaching that the righteousness of the kingdom goes beyond not murdering: it includes caring for relationships and seeking peace quickly. Some think the image refers to a real court case and others to a broader spiritual principle; the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: if there is an unresolved conflict with someone, do not let it grow. Take the first step, ask forgiveness, or go and speak calmly, before the problem becomes more costly and harder to resolve.
exp.25:0:
It says that, when Jesus had finished saying everything he had been teaching, he told his disciples. The verse simply reports that he had completed his teaching and then turned to speak to them.

Before this verse, Jesus had given long teachings about the end of the age and the need to be prepared (Matthew 24 and 25). Now the tone changes: he stops speaking to the crowd and addresses his closest friends to tell them that his death is near. It is the beginning of the account of the passion.

For today: Jesus did not run away from what was hard, but faced it with clarity and confidence in God's plan. When you face a difficult moment, you can speak honestly with people of faith and rest in the knowledge that God does not let you go.
exp.5:29:
Jesus says that if God clothes the grass of the field this way, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, then how much more will he clothe you. The word "worry" in this verse means to be anxious or troubled. "Thrown into the furnace" refers to the dry grass being used as fuel. "O you of little faith" is a loving rebuke: they do trust, but their trust is still small.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He teaches them not to be controlled by anxiety about food and clothing. He reminds them that those who do not know God chase after these things, but they have a heavenly Father who knows what they need.

When worry about money or the future troubles you, pause and pray. Name each concern before God and do today what is in front of you, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.9:3:
This verse completes the list of the twelve apostles. It names Simon the Zealot, a title that points to his fervent devotion to a cause, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus, that is, the one who later handed him over. The surname Iscariot may indicate that he came from Kerioth, but this is not certain.

Matthew, who tells the story, presents the twelve whom Jesus chose and sent out to proclaim the kingdom. Jesus called men who were very different from one another, including one who would fail. Matthew mentions the betrayal simply and does not hide it.

Today, this text reminds us that Jesus calls people who are very different and unites them in a single purpose. Try to receive with respect those in the church who think differently, and guard your own heart so that you remain faithful to Christ.
exp.11:19:
He says that the servant chosen by God treats the weak with tenderness. The "bruised reed" is a reed already damaged, and the "smoldering wick" is the wick of a lamp that barely gives off smoke. He will not break the one or snuff out the other. This is how he will act "until he leads justice to victory," that is, until God's justice triumphs completely.

Matthew quotes here the prophet Isaiah (chapter 42) and applies it to Jesus. Earlier, Jesus had healed many people and asked that they not make him known, while the Pharisees were plotting to destroy him. Matthew shows that Jesus is a gentle servant, not loud or violent, and that his mission reaches the Gentiles too. Right after this, he heals a man who was blind and mute.

For today: if you feel tired, hurt, or weak in faith, Jesus does not cast you aside. Come to him with confidence, and treat with the same patience those around you who are fragile.
exp.3:23:
News about Jesus spread all over Syria, and people brought to him everyone who was ill: those with various diseases, those suffering acute pain, the demon-possessed, those having seizures, and the paralyzed. And he healed them.

Matthew is the one telling this story. Jesus had just called his first disciples and was traveling through Galilee, teaching and proclaiming the kingdom of God. The healings went along with his message and showed his compassion and authority. Afterward, large crowds began to follow him from many places.

For today: when you are carrying pain, illness, or fear, you can come to Jesus just as you are, holding nothing back. And if you know someone who is suffering, do as those people did: bring them to Christ in prayer and in your company.
exp.21:7:
The king tells his servants that the wedding banquet is ready. The word "ready" here means prepared. But those who were invited were not "worthy," that is, they did not deserve to be there, because they despised the invitation.

Jesus is telling the parable of the king's son's wedding. He speaks to the religious leaders of his time. Many understand that the guests who refused represent those who did not accept God's call. The mistreated servants recall the messengers God sent. Some also see here a warning about the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem, although this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God invites with generosity, but the invitation must be received with seriousness. Let us not allow work, busyness, or pride lead us to say "later" to his call. Today is a good day to answer him with gratitude and humility.
exp.11:11:
Jesus asks how much more valuable a person is than a sheep, and from this he concludes that it is right to do good on the Sabbath. "Right" here means allowed by the law. "Valuable" refers to the worth a person has in the eyes of God.

He is speaking in a synagogue, on the Sabbath. Some men ask him whether it is right to heal on the Sabbath, but they ask in order to accuse him. He answers with the example of a sheep that has fallen into a pit, which anyone would rescue. Then he heals the man's hand. The Pharisees, on the other hand, go out to plan how to destroy him.

For today: do not use religion as an excuse to ignore the one who suffers. Before setting aside a need because "it is not the right time" or "it is not my task," ask yourself whether God is inviting you to do good right now, and do it with humility.
exp.5:11:
Jesus teaches us to ask God to forgive our "debts," a word that here refers to sins, wrongs, and offenses against God. The verse also says "as we also have forgiven our debtors," meaning that whoever asks for forgiveness has already forgiven those who owe them something, that is, those who have harmed them.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the Sermon on the Mount while he teaches them to pray. This is the Lord's Prayer. After asking for daily bread, he moves on to the need for forgiveness. The verses that follow emphasize this: God expects those who have received mercy to also give mercy. It is not a matter of buying forgiveness, but of showing a heart that has understood grace.

For today: think of someone who hurt you and whom you still carry in your heart. Before you pray, ask God for help in letting go of that resentment, and take a first concrete step, such as praying for that person.
exp.23:21:
Jesus says that if God did not cut short those days of great suffering, no one would survive. The phrase "nobody" in the verse means no human being, and the chosen ones are those who belong to God. For their sake, those days will be cut short.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after announcing the destruction of the temple. He warns them of a very great affliction. Some see it fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70; others also see a future fulfillment. Christians understand it in different ways. What is clear is that God remains in control and protects his people.

For today: when hard times come, remember that God sets limits on suffering and cares for his own. Trust in him, pray, and do not let yourself be frightened or deceived.
exp.0:23:
When Joseph woke up, he did what the angel of the Lord had commanded him and took Mary into his home as his wife. In other words, he brought her in and married her. The verse says he "embraced" her, which here describes him fully and gladly accepting her as his wife.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Before this, Joseph had been planning to quietly end his engagement to Mary, because she was pregnant and he did not understand how. Then the angel explained to him in a dream that the child had been conceived by the Holy Spirit. The text presents this as the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy about Immanuel, "God with us."

For today: Joseph did not wait until he understood everything before obeying. When we know what God asks of us in his Word, we can take the step with confidence, even when it is hard or frightening, because God is with us.
exp.11:26:
Jesus asks the Pharisees: if I drive out demons by the power of Beelzebul, the ruler of demons, then by what power do your sons drive them out? Here "your sons" probably refers to his disciples or to other Jews who performed exorcisms. "They will be your judges" means that they themselves would expose how unjust the accusation was.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees, who accused him of using satanic power after seeing him heal a man who was possessed. He shows them that their accusation makes no sense. If they approve of their own people but condemn Jesus, they are using one standard for themselves and another for him.

For today: let us examine whether we judge others by the same measure we use to judge ourselves. Let us ask God for an honest heart, one that recognizes good even when it comes from someone we do not like.
exp.7:0:
When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed Him. This verse tells us that Jesus left the mountain where he had just taught the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7), and a large crowd began to follow him.

Here Jesus does not speak; instead, Matthew, the narrator, tells us what happened. After teaching with authority, Jesus begins to show through actions what he had said in words. The crowds followed him, perhaps out of curiosity, need, or admiration; the text does not state their reasons. Right away a man with leprosy comes up to him.

For today: following Jesus is not only listening to beautiful teachings. Ask yourself whether you also follow him when it is time to come down from the "mountain" and live in everyday life, drawing near to those who suffer, as he did.
exp.22:14:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees travel over sea and land to win over a single person to their faith. But when they succeed, they make that person twice as much a son of hell as they themselves are. A convert to Judaism, a foreigner who has joined the faith, is the person in view. To travel across an area is what the phrase "traverse land and sea" describes in the verse. The word "hell" here translates a term that pictures judgment.

Jesus speaks in the temple, shortly before his arrest, and denounces the hypocrisy of the religious leaders. His anger is not against the Jewish faith itself, but against a zeal that produced followers of their customs rather than followers of God. How the phrase "twice as much" should be understood is interpreted in several ways, but the general sense is that they were pulling people away from God.

Today, it is worth asking ourselves whether we help others get to know God or only get them to copy our traditions.
exp.16:19:
Jesus explains to his disciples why they could not heal the boy: because they had so little faith. He says that if they had faith the size of a mustard seed (a very tiny seed), they could tell a mountain to move, and it would move. Nothing would be impossible for them.

The phrase "Because you have so little faith" means that their trouble was a lack of trust. The words "Move from here to there" are the command Jesus uses for the mountain. The statement "Nothing will be impossible for you" is a far-reaching claim, not a promise that anyone can have whatever they wish.

Jesus speaks with his disciples, in private, after healing a young man tormented by a demon. They had not been able to help him, and they asked why. Jesus uses an exaggerated image, common in his teaching, to show that what matters is not the size of the faith but the one in whom it is placed: God.

For today: when you face something that seems impossible, do not wait until you have perfect faith. Bring it to God with simple trust, even if it is small, and leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.3:6:
Jesus answers the devil with another sentence from Scripture. The phrase "It is also written" simply means that another passage of Scripture supports what He is saying. The word "test" here means to put God to the test. Jesus says that we should not put God to the test by demanding that He prove His care or His power.

The devil had just used a verse from the Psalms to encourage Jesus to throw Himself down from the temple. Jesus does not argue with ideas of His own, but responds with another word of God (Deuteronomy 6:16). In this way He shows that a text should not be used in isolation, but understood together with the rest of the Bible and with the character of God.

For today: trusting God is not taking reckless risks to see whether He will rescue us. We can ask Him for help, obey Him, and act wisely, resting in His care without demanding signs.
exp.6:8:
Jesus asks a simple question: which of you, if your son asks for bread, would give him a stone? The answer is obvious: none. The wording here is plain, and it matches what we would say today. "Bread" stands for the basic food of each day.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, before his disciples and the crowd. He has just encouraged them to ask, to seek, and to knock on the door. With this example he wants to show that God, as Father, listens to his children and responds with goodness, far more than any human father would.

For today: pray with confidence and simplicity, the way a child talks with their dad. Bring your real needs before God, and trust that he will give you what is good, even when his answer is not the one you were expecting.
exp.24:33:
He says that when Jesus judges all the nations, the King will invite those on his right to enter his kingdom. He calls them "blessed by my Father," meaning people who are favored by God. To "inherit" means to receive something as a gift that passes to you, and the phrase "from the foundation of the world" shows that this kingdom was planned by God from before creation. The words "shall say" carry the same meaning as the modern "will say."

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, shortly before his crucifixion. In this parable of the final judgment, he himself is the King. The image of the shepherd who separates sheep from goats shows that there will be a separation. The verses that follow explain the reason: how they treated those in need.

For today: true faith is shown in concrete acts of compassion. This week, look for someone who is suffering, such as a sick person, someone who is alone, or someone in need, and help them with generosity and simplicity.
exp.26:36:
Matthew says that the soldiers placed above Jesus' head on the cross the written charge against him. It read: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews." The "written charge" in the verse means the official statement of the reason for his execution.

Matthew tells this as the narrator. It was Roman custom to announce the crime of the condemned man. Here the charge was that he was a king, even though the leaders rejected him. The soldiers, without realizing it, wrote a truth that Matthew had already shown from the beginning of his Gospel: Jesus is the promised King.

For today: even when many do not recognize it, Jesus is King. We can ask ourselves in what part of our lives we are not letting him reign, especially when obeying him costs us something, and decide today on one concrete step of trust and obedience.
exp.24:10:
This verse says that the other five virgins, the ones who had gone to buy oil, arrived late and found the door shut. They ask the bridegroom to open the door for them, and they call out "Lord, lord" with urgency. Their request to open the door shows that they want to be let in. The word "later" shows that it was already too late.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples, shortly before his crucifixion, speaking of his return. The bridegroom represents Christ, and the wedding, the joy of his kingdom. The foolish virgins were not ready when he arrived. Some see in the oil true faith or the life of the Spirit; interpreters do not agree on one single meaning.

Today, it is not enough to say religious words or to leave the care of our faith for later. Cultivate your relationship with God every day, in prayer, in his Word and in obedience, so that you are always prepared.
exp.19:19:
This verse tells how the mother of James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to Jesus with her sons. She knelt before him and made a request. "Came to Jesus" means that she approached him.

Jesus had just announced for the third time that he would be handed over, condemned, and crucified, and that he would rise again. Matthew then tells what happened next: the woman asks that her sons be given places of honor in the kingdom. Mark tells a similar scene, but says that the sons themselves made the request. It is likely that all three took part in the request. She acted out of a mother's love, but without understanding the path of suffering that Jesus was describing.

We can bring our desires to Jesus, but it is good to ask ourselves: do I ask to serve, or to be recognized? Let us first ask that his will be done.
exp.4:17:
Jesus affirms with great force that God's law will not lose its value, not even in its smallest detail. The "jot" is the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and the "tittle" is the tiny stroke that distinguishes one letter from another. In the Berean wording, the phrase "not a stroke of a pen" describes this same tiny mark. "Pass away" means to go away or disappear. He says that as long as heaven and earth last, not a single part of the law will disappear, until everything is accomplished.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just said that he did not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them. He wants no one to think that he looks down on Scripture. Christians understand in different ways how the law applies today, but all acknowledge that Jesus brings it to its fullness.

For today: value all of Scripture, including what seems small, and seek to obey God from the heart, not only in appearance.
exp.7:12:
Jesus tells the centurion, a Roman officer: "Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you." The servant in view was a young man who worked for him, and the verse says the servant was healed at that very hour, meaning he was made well at the moment Jesus spoke.

Jesus speaks with the centurion, a man who was not Jewish and who trusted that Jesus could heal his servant just by speaking a word, even without being present. Just before this, Jesus says that many will come from far away into the kingdom, and this scene shows an example of the faith He praises.

For today: we can trust the word of Jesus even when we do not yet see the result. That does not mean God does everything we ask, but that He rejoices when we come to Him with sincere and humble trust.
exp.26:45:
Jesus cried out loudly at about three in the afternoon, the ninth hour. He used Aramaic words, and the text gives their meaning: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" The word "forsaken" means abandoned, left alone.

He speaks from the cross, after three hours of darkness over the land. He quotes Psalm 22:1, a psalm of suffering that ends in trust. Christians understand this cry in different ways: as real pain while he bears the sin of the world, or as a prayer that points to the whole psalm. The Bible does not fully explain it, and it is a mystery that calls for humility. Some of those present thought he was calling for Elijah.

For today: if you feel lonely or without an answer, you can pray with complete honesty, even with questions. Jesus understands your pain and does not ask you to pretend.
exp.24:24:
He says that this servant was afraid, and because of that he hid the talent in the ground. Now he returns it to his master exactly as it was, and tells him: "See, you have what belongs to you." A talent was a large amount of money in that time.

Jesus tells this parable. The one speaking is the third servant, who received only one talent. While the other two worked and multiplied what they had, he did nothing. He justifies himself by saying his master was a hard man. The master calls him wicked and lazy, because he did not even put the money to work to earn interest.

Today, fear can paralyze us and make us hold on to what God has given us: gifts, time, kindness. Ask yourself what you have hidden out of fear, and take a small step today to use it and serve others with trust in God.
exp.26:44:
From the sixth hour until the ninth hour, which is noon until three in the afternoon by our way of counting time, darkness came over all the land. The land could also mean the region, so it is not certain how large the area was.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus is on the cross, and the crowd was mocking Him. In the middle of that rejection, the darkness comes just before His cry to God. Matthew does not explain the cause, and scholars have interpreted it in different ways: as a sign of God's judgment or as a sign of mourning in creation.

For today: when we go through dark moments, let us remember that Jesus was there too, and that we are not alone.
exp.21:16:
The disciples of the Pharisees and the Herodians ask Jesus whether it is right to pay taxes to the Roman emperor, called Caesar. They ask for his opinion: "What do you think?" The question seems simple, but it allows only two answers: yes or no.

The Pharisees wanted to trap Jesus in his own words. First they flattered him to lower his guard. If he said yes, he could lose the favor of the people, who hated Roman rule. If he said no, he could be accused before the authorities of rebellion. The Herodians, supporters of the family of Herod, were there probably for that purpose.

Today, sometimes people ask us questions not to learn, but to corner us. Jesus teaches us to discern intentions and to answer with wisdom, without letting ourselves be pressured by false choices.
exp.10:21:
Jesus says that on the day of judgment, Tyre and Sidon will receive a lighter punishment than the cities of Chorazin and Bethsaida. "More bearable" is his way of describing the lighter outcome for those cities. "You" refers to those Jewish cities of Galilee.

Jesus is speaking. He had done many miracles in those cities, but the people did not change their hearts or turn back to God. Tyre and Sidon were pagan cities, known for their wickedness in the Old Testament. Jesus shows that whoever receives more light has greater responsibility. Christians understand the degrees of judgment in different ways, but here the emphasis is on responsibility.

Today we can ask ourselves: what have I seen and heard of God, and how have I responded? It is not enough to admire Jesus or to know his word. God invites us to truly repent and to obey him with humility.
exp.24:23:
The servant who had received the one talent speaks here. A talent was a very large amount of money. He tells his master that he knew him to be a hard man, that is, demanding and severe. He says that the master reaps where he has not sown, meaning he harvests what someone else has worked for, and gathers where he has not scattered seed, gathering a crop from ground he never planted.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. A master goes on a journey and leaves his goods with his servants. The first two put his money to work and are praised. This third one did nothing, and now he makes excuses by blaming his master. His description of the master is an accusation, and the master, in the following verse, rejects it.

For today: sometimes we avoid serving God with what we have because we hold a mistaken idea of Him, as if He were unjust or hard to please. Let us ask to know Him as He really is, and let us use with confidence and without fear what He has given us.
exp.25:36:
Jesus takes with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, who are James and John. There he begins to feel a deep sorrow and a deep distress. To be sorrowful is to feel pain in the heart, and to be deeply distressed is to feel gripped by a great restlessness. The word "deeply" shows that the feeling was very intense.

The narrator is Matthew. We are in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before Jesus is arrested. Peter had just promised that he would never deny him. Jesus chooses these three, who had already been close to him at other important moments, to accompany him while he prays. The verses that follow show that his sorrow is connected to the cross that was drawing near.

For today: Jesus did not hide his sorrow or live through it alone. When you feel sadness or anguish, do not pretend to be strong. Tell God what you feel and seek out trusted people who will stand with you.
exp.26:12:
Pilate asks Jesus whether he is not hearing all the charges they are bringing against him. The phrase about bearing witness against someone simply means that the people were accusing him and bringing charges against him. Pilate expected Jesus to defend himself.

Here Pilate speaks, the Roman governor. The religious leaders had brought Jesus before him so that he would condemn him. Jesus stayed silent, and this greatly surprised Pilate, because it was normal for an accused man to defend himself. Some believe this silence fulfills what Isaiah 53:7 said about the servant who does not open his mouth.

For today: we do not always have to answer every attack or criticism. Jesus shows us a firm calm, trusting in God. Before responding in anger, we can pray and ask him for wisdom to know when to speak and when to be silent.
exp.25:48:
Judas came straight up to Jesus and greeted him with "Greetings, Rabbi!" (a respectful greeting, like saying "Hello, Teacher!"). Then he kissed him. The word "then" in this verse simply means "immediately". Here the kiss was not a sign of affection, but the signal agreed upon so that the crowd would know whom to arrest.

Matthew tells this on the night Jesus was arrested, in the garden of Gethsemane. Judas, one of the twelve disciples, had agreed with the religious leaders to hand him over. He used a gesture of affection and respect to hide his betrayal. Jesus, however, answered him by calling him "Friend", still giving him an opportunity to reflect.

For today: let us make sure that our religious words and affectionate gestures are sincere. God looks at the heart, and Jesus shows us how to respond to falseness with calm and truth.
exp.19:15:
Jesus says that those who are first will end up last, and those who are last will be first. He adds that many are called, but few are chosen. "Last" here means those who come at the end, and "chosen" means those whom God has picked out. Some old manuscripts do not include the second sentence, and scholars interpret it in several ways.

Jesus tells the parable of the workers in the vineyard. A landowner pays the same amount to those who worked all day and to those who arrived at the last hour. The first workers complain, and the owner answers that he is generous with what belongs to him. Jesus speaks this way after Peter asked what the disciples would receive for having left everything.

For today: God's grace is not earned or compared. Instead of measuring how much we have served or envying the blessing others receive, we can rejoice when God is kind to someone else, knowing that he is kind to us as well.
exp.4:20:
Jesus reminds the people of a commandment everyone knows: "Do not murder." The words "you have heard" mean what they say, and "the ancients" refers to earlier generations, to whom the law was given in the days of Moses. The second part of the verse, "Anyone who murders will be subject to judgment," means that whoever commits murder must answer before the judges.

Jesus is teaching in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just said that the righteousness of his followers must be greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees, who were very careful about outward conduct. Here he begins to show that the law also reaches the heart. That is why, in the next verse, he speaks about anger against one's brother.

For today: it is not enough to avoid the great wrongs. Ask God to help you examine your heart, and if you hold a grudge against someone, take a step today toward peace with that person.
exp.23:1:
Jesus asks his disciples, "Do you see all these things?", pointing to the great buildings of the temple. He tells them, "Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down." In plain terms, everything will be thrown down.

Jesus speaks with his disciples as they leave the temple in Jerusalem. They admired its construction, and he warns them that that impressive place would not remain. Many understand that this was fulfilled when the Romans destroyed the temple in the year 70 AD. The disciples then also ask about the end of the world, and Christians interpret in different ways how the two subjects are related.

For today: it is easy to place our trust in great and apparently firm things, such as prestige, money, or institutions. Jesus invites us to rest in what does not collapse: his word and his kingdom.
exp.14:14:
Then Peter spoke up and asked Jesus to explain the parable. Peter was speaking on behalf of the disciples, who had not understood.

Jesus had just spoken to the crowd about what truly defiles a person, after a discussion with the Pharisees about traditions and washing hands. Then he told the disciples that the Pharisees were blind guides. Many think the parable refers to what was said about what goes into and comes out of the mouth (v. 11), though Peter may also have meant Jesus' words about the plants and the blind. The text does not make this entirely clear.

Today: when something in the Word of God is not clear to you, do not let it pass. Ask God about it in prayer and seek help from the Bible and from mature brothers and sisters. Asking with humility is part of growing.
exp.27:18:
This verse says that Jesus commands his followers to go and make disciples among all nations. "Nations" here refers to peoples or nations in general, not only the Jews. He also commands them to baptize those who believe, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Jesus is speaking after his resurrection, on a mountain in Galilee, to his eleven disciples. Some of them still doubted, but he reminds them that he has all authority. That is why his command has backing. He also promises that he will be with them always, to the end of the world.

For today: you do not need to be perfect or have all the answers. Share with someone close to you what Jesus has done in your life, and help them come to know him, trusting that he walks with you.
exp.14:5:
According to the teaching of the Pharisees, a person who declared their possessions as an offering to God no longer needed to help their parents. "Help" here means aid, especially financial support. "Nullify" means they drained the commandment of its force and value. Jesus states that they had set aside a command of God in favor of a human custom.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees and teachers of the law who were criticizing him because his disciples did not follow the traditions of the elders. He answers by showing that they themselves were disobeying God. They were using a religious practice as an excuse not to care for their parents. Scholars debate exactly how that practice worked, but Jesus' criticism is clear.

For today: do not use your religious activities, your work, or your occupations as a pretext for neglecting your family. Honoring your parents with time, affection, and real help is also obeying God.
exp.26:43:
The same verse says that the two men crucified alongside Jesus also berated him, just as the crowd and the religious leaders did. The word "berated" in this verse means to scold or heap insults on someone, to speak to them harshly and reproachfully. The men are called "robbers," a word that can also be understood as bandits.

Matthew records this moment in the middle of the crucifixion. First the passersby and the chief priests mocked him, and then even those who were suffering the same punishment did. Luke adds that one of them later repented, but Matthew only highlights the complete rejection Jesus received. Shortly afterward come the darkness and his cry to the Father.

For today: when someone treats us badly without reason, let us remember that Jesus knows that pain. We can bring that wound to him in prayer and ask for his help to respond with patience, without returning mockery for mockery.
exp.6:11:
This verse tells us to treat others the way we would want them to treat us. The word "wish" or "want" describes what we hope for from others, and "people" is the word Jesus uses here. Jesus adds that this sums up the Law and the Prophets, which is the heart of what the Old Testament teaches about loving God and our neighbor.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Just before this, he taught that the Father gives good things to those who ask him. After receiving so much kindness from God, he now invites us to show that same kindness to others. Then he speaks of the narrow gate, which calls for a life of sincere obedience.

For today: before you respond to someone with harshness or indifference, ask yourself, "How would I want to be treated in their place?" Then give that same respect, patience, or help.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that the persecution would reach right into the families themselves. A brother would betray his brother to death, a father would do the same with his child, and children would rise against their parents and have them put to death. "Betray" means to hand someone over to the authorities, and the reader can see that the wording points to people turning on their own kin.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to preach. He honestly warns them that proclaiming his message would bring rejection, even from their own loved ones. But first he promises them that the Spirit of the Father would speak through them when they were brought before the authorities.

For today: if following Jesus brings you rejection or misunderstanding, even within your family, do not lose heart. Pray, respond with gentleness, and trust that God sustains you. Keep loving those who reject you.
exp.20:34:
This verse says that the tenants, to whom the owner of the vineyard had rented out his land, seized the servants sent to collect the fruit. They beat one, killed another and stoned a third. The words "beat," "killed" and "stoned" show a growing violence, and "in exchange for a share of the harvest" means that the vineyard was handed to them on the condition that they gave the owner part of what it produced.

Jesus tells this parable in the temple in Jerusalem to the chief priests and the elders of the people. Many understand that the vineyard represents Israel, the servants the prophets, and the son Jesus himself. With this story he shows them how they had treated those whom God sent to them, and the leaders themselves understood that he was speaking about them (v. 45).

For today: let us examine whether we are willing to listen when God corrects us, even when it comes through people who make us uncomfortable. Let us remember that what we have is a gift we manage, not something that belongs to us entirely.
exp.19:5:
He says the owner of the vineyard went out again, around the eleventh hour (about five in the afternoon, when the workday was almost over), and found still others standing around. He asked them why they had been standing there all day long doing nothing. The men had no work, and the owner's question points to the hours they had spent without employment.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. The owner represents God, who keeps calling people to his work, even at the last hour. Jesus tells it after speaking of the first and the last, and to show that God is generous and does not distribute according to our ideas of merit.

For today: it is never too late to respond to God's call. If you feel you have wasted time, today you can begin to serve him, and you can rejoice when he is kind to others.
exp.14:38:
After feeding the crowd, Jesus dismissed them, the verse says. Then he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan. The phrase "dismissed the crowds" means that he sent the people away. Magadan is the name used in this verse. Its exact location is not known for certain, though it was near the Sea of Galilee.

The one acting is Jesus, and the one telling the story is Matthew. Jesus had just multiplied seven loaves of bread and a few small fish to feed about four thousand men, besides women and children. Once that act of compassion was finished, he did not stay to receive applause. He dismissed the people calmly and continued on his way and his ministry.

For today: after serving others, learn to let go. Do good without seeking recognition, and then move on with peace, trusting that God cares for what you did and also for what comes next.
exp.15:7:
Jesus noticed what the disciples were discussing among themselves. He asked them why they were debating about having no bread. He called them "you of little faith," meaning people who do believe in Him but trust Him very little. "Aware" here means that Jesus knew what they were saying without being told.

Jesus had just warned them to beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees, that is, of their influential and harmful teaching. The disciples thought He was speaking of physical bread. Jesus reminds them that He had already fed crowds with a few loaves, so the lack of bread was not the real problem.

For today: when you worry about what you lack, remember how God has already cared for you. Trust Him, and pay attention to what He truly wants to teach you.
exp.21:34:
He says that one of the Pharisees, an expert in the law of Moses, asked Jesus a question. The word "expert" refers to someone who studied and taught the Scriptures. "Tested Him" means he was putting Jesus to the test, hoping Jesus would say something wrong.

The Pharisees heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, another religious group, and they gathered to act. The narrator, Matthew, shows us that this question did not come from a sincere desire to learn, but from a test. Even so, Jesus answered with clarity, and his answer sums up the most important part of the law: loving God.

Today we can ask ourselves what attitude we bring to the Bible. It is possible to study it in order to win arguments, or to love God better. Let us ask him to teach us with a sincere heart, ready to obey.
exp.23:23:
This verse warns that people will appear who claim to be the Christ or who speak in God's name, but they will be false. They will perform great signs and wonders, so impressive that they could deceive, if that were possible, even the elect, that is, those who belong to God.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the signs of the end and of his coming. He prepares them for difficult times and asks them not to believe anyone who says, "Here is the Christ" or "There he is." Some understand this as referring to the years before AD 70, others to the final time, and others to both.

For today: do not measure something only by miracles or by the charisma of the one speaking. Compare what you hear with what Jesus taught in the Bible, and pray for discernment. Christ himself is our security.
exp.20:43:
Jesus describes himself as a firm stone. Whoever falls against this stone will be broken to pieces, meaning hurt and ruined. But the one on whom the stone falls will be crushed, reduced to dust. The verse speaks of two ways of facing Christ: stumbling over him, or being crushed under his judgment.

Jesus speaks to the chief priests and the Pharisees in the temple, shortly before his death. He has just told them the parable of the wicked tenants and quotes Psalm 118 about the stone that the builders rejected. They understood that he was speaking about them, since they were rejecting the Messiah. Some scholars think the verse also echoes Isaiah 8 and Daniel 2.

For today: it is better to surrender to Jesus with humility and let him break our pride than to resist him to the end. Today you can ask him in prayer: "Lord, in what am I resisting you?"
exp.1:16:
This verse says that what happened to the children of Bethlehem came about as something the prophet Jeremiah had already spoken. The word "fulfilled" means the same as "came true."

The one speaking is Matthew, the writer of the Gospel. He has just told of the slaughter ordered by King Herod. The quotation comes from Jeremiah 31:15, where Rachel weeps for her children. Scholars explain in several ways how it is "fulfilled" here: it may be an echo of Israel's ancient sorrow that is repeated in this new suffering. Matthew wants to show that God was not caught off guard by this grief.

For today: when you go through pain you do not understand, remember that God sees it and does not ignore it. You can bring Him your tears with confidence, knowing that He is still at work and brings comfort.
exp.12:48:
What it says: Jesus explains that at the end of the age, the angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous. The word "come" points to the angels going out to do this work, and the separation is the same as in the parable of the net: what is good is kept, and what is bad is thrown away.

Context: Jesus is speaking to his disciples, in a series of parables about the kingdom of heaven. The net gathers all kinds of fish, and the sorting happens only when it is pulled up onto the shore. With this he teaches that, for now, the good and the bad live together, and that the final judgment does not belong to us but to God, through his angels. Then he asks them whether they have understood.

For today: It is not your place to decide who is inside or outside the kingdom. Instead, examine your own heart, live with sincerity, and trust that God will judge with justice in the end.
exp.8:31:
As the two blind men who had just been healed were leaving, people brought to Jesus a man who could not speak and who was under the power of a demon.

Matthew tells this without recording any words from the man or from the crowd. It is simply another encounter of Jesus with someone in need. The man could not ask for help himself, so others brought him. The account also sets up the contrast between the amazement of the crowd and the rejection by the Pharisees, which comes right after.

For today: there are people who cannot or do not know how to ask for help. We can be the ones who bring them to Jesus, through prayer, companionship and care, trusting that he sees them and can help them.
exp.9:10:
Here it says that, on entering any town or village, the disciples were to find out who there was worthy, that is, someone of good standing who was willing to welcome them. There they were to stay until they moved on. "Find out" means to ask carefully, and staying there means lodging, remaining as a guest.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles when he sends them out for the first time to announce that the kingdom of heaven is near. He asks them to trust God and to depend on the hospitality of others. Staying in one house kept them from going around looking for better comforts. Interpreters explain in several ways what "worthy" means exactly, but it points to an open attitude.

For today: when you serve or share your faith, look wisely for people who are open, and do not get distracted looking for comfort. Be thankful for the simple help you receive.
exp.6:16:
Jesus says that the nature of a tree shows itself in the fruit it produces. A healthy tree bears good fruit; a tree that is diseased, meaning damaged or of poor quality, bears bad fruit. The verse says a tree "bears" fruit, which means it produces it, and "fruit" refers to the visible results of a life.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, addressing his disciples and the crowd. He has just warned against false prophets, who look harmless like sheep but do harm like wolves. So he gives them a simple way to discern: look at their conduct, their character, and the effects of their teaching, not only at their pleasant words.

For today: before following a teacher or leader, observe calmly how they live and what they produce in people. Do the same with your own heart, asking God to bear good fruit in you: love, truth, and humility.
exp.25:31:
Jesus says that, after he has risen, he will go ahead of his disciples into Galilee. "Going ahead" is like a shepherd who walks first and leads his flock.

Jesus speaks with his eleven disciples on the way to the Mount of Olives, shortly before he is arrested. He has just told them that they will all abandon him, quoting the prophecy of Zechariah about the struck shepherd and the scattered sheep. But he does not end with their failure: he promises them a reunion. His resurrection is certain, and he wants to restore them. Galilee was the land where they had first begun to follow him.

When we fail or drift away from God, we do not have the last word. Jesus already goes ahead, preparing the way back. We can return to him with confidence, knowing that he waits for us with grace.
exp.15:22:
Jesus turns to Peter and says to him firmly, "Get behind me, Satan!" He tells him that he is a stumbling block to Him, something that gets in His way. Peter was thinking the way people think, not the way God thinks. Telling him to get behind Him means to follow Him, as if Jesus were calling Peter to follow and not to lead.

Jesus had just announced that He would suffer and die in Jerusalem, and that He would rise again. Peter, with good intentions, wanted to prevent it. But Jesus saw in those words the same temptation to take a path without the cross. That is why He called him "Satan", a word meaning adversary. Then He taught that following Him means denying oneself and taking up the cross.

For today: before seeking what is comfortable, ask yourself whether your plans look more like what God wants or like what suits you.
exp.25:35:
Jesus goes with his disciples to a place called Gethsemane, and he tells them to sit here while he goes over there to pray. The word "pray" in the verse means speaking with God, and the phrase "over there" points to a spot a little way off.

Jesus speaks after the Last Supper. He has just said that Peter will deny him, even though all of them promised to stay faithful. Now the hour of his arrest is drawing near, and he looks for a moment alone with the Father.

When hard moments approach, prayer should come first, not last. Jesus did not trust in promises of human strength, but turned to God. Today we too can bring our fears to him before we face them.
exp.14:34:
Matthew says Jesus instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. "Instructed" means he gave clear direction, and the phrase about sitting down means they settled in and took their places, as people did for a meal in those days. The word for the crowd here refers to the large gathering of people.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is recounting what Jesus did. The people had been with him for three days in a deserted place and had nothing to eat. Jesus felt compassion and asked them to sit down before receiving the food. The disciples had only seven loaves of bread and a few small fish.
