For today: sometimes God asks us to obey and to wait with trust before we see his provision. Even when what we have seems small, we can place it in his hands and prepare ourselves to receive whatever he chooses to give us.
exp.20:45:
This verse says that the religious leaders wanted to arrest Jesus. The wording "wanted to arrest Him" shows their intent to seize him. But they did not dare to, because they were afraid of the crowds. The people regarded Jesus as a prophet, that is, someone sent by God to speak on his behalf.

Jesus had just told parables, such as the one about the wicked tenants, in which he showed that these leaders were rejecting God. They understood that he was speaking about them. Instead of reflecting and changing, they became angry and looked for a way to silence him. The speakers in this passage are the narrator, Matthew, and Jesus in the preceding context.

For today: when the Word of God confronts us, we can either harden ourselves or humble ourselves. Let us ask God for a heart willing to listen, and for us to care more about the truth than about what people think.
exp.17:19:
Jesus says that when two or three people gather "in my name," meaning for his sake and in acknowledgment of his authority, he is there with them. Gather means to come together, and the word "or" simply means "or." The size of the group does not matter. His presence does not depend on how many people are there.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples about how to deal with a brother who sins and how the community of believers should act. Just before this, he explained how to seek reconciliation, and just after, Peter asks about forgiveness. So the verse refers to Christ's presence when his people seek truth, restoration, and forgiveness. Some also apply it to prayer and worship in general.

For today: do not look down on small gatherings. When you come together with one or two fellow believers to pray, to resolve a conflict, or to read the Bible, do it with confidence, knowing that Jesus is with you.
exp.1:3:
This verse tells us that King Herod called together all the chief priests and the scribes, the teachers of the law. He asked them directly where the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, was to be born. The word "assembled" means called together, and "chief priests" are the most important religious leaders.

The wise men from the east had arrived asking about the one born King of the Jews, and Herod was troubled. The account does not say with certainty what he was looking for, but the events that follow show that he saw this as a threat. He turned to the experts in the Scriptures, who did know the answer: Bethlehem.

For today: knowing the Bible is not enough; we must respond to it with our hearts. Those leaders knew where the Christ would be born, yet the text does not say they went to look for him. Let us ask God that what we know of his Word will lead us to obey him and worship him.
exp.13:30:
Jesus acted at once: He reached out His hand, took hold of Peter, and asked him why he doubted. The phrase "little faith" does not mean a complete lack of faith, but a weak or divided trust.

Jesus is the one speaking. Peter had asked to come to Him on the water and began to walk. But when he noticed the strong wind, he became afraid and started to sink. He cried out for help, and Jesus rescued him. His question is not only a rebuke; it also invites Peter to think about where he had placed his attention. Afterward, the disciples worship Jesus as the Son of God.

When fear surrounds you, remember that Jesus does not wait for your faith to be perfect before He helps you. Cry out to Him as Peter did: Lord, save me. Then look again to Him, and not only at the problem.
exp.5:30:
Jesus tells us not to be anxious or to live worried, asking: "What shall we eat? What shall we drink? What shall we wear?" The word translated here as "do not worry" means to be troubled or filled with anxiety. The clothing mentioned in the verse is what we put on our bodies.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to the crowd during the Sermon on the Mount. He has just shown how God takes care of the birds and clothes the grass of the field. His point is that if God cares for small things, he will also care for those who are his children. The Gentiles, who did not know the Father, lived consumed by these concerns.

Today, when worry about money, food, or the future overtakes you, stop and pray. Tell God what you need, trust that he knows it, and take the next step responsibly, without anxiety.
exp.9:34:
He says Jesus came to bring division, that is, a split or disagreement, within families: between a man and his father, a daughter and her mother, a daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law. Here "bring" is the word for bringing or causing something. Earlier he spoke of a sword, an image of separation.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to preach. He warns them that following him will bring rejection, even from their own relatives. He does not seek conflict as a goal; it is the consequence of some people accepting his message and others refusing it. Some scholars see here an echo of Micah 7:6.

For today: if your faith in Christ causes tension with someone in your family, do not respond with pride or anger. Follow Jesus with humility, love your family, and ask God for wisdom to be faithful without ceasing to be kind.
exp.16:10:
Jesus answers the disciples' question and confirms what the teachers of the law were saying: Elijah would come before the Messiah. The word "restore" means to bring things back into order or return something to its proper state, and the word "indeed" in the verse stresses that this is certain.

Jesus and three of his disciples had just come down from the mountain of the transfiguration, where they had seen Elijah with Jesus. The disciples were wondering how that fit with the teaching based on Malachi 4:5-6. In the following verse, Jesus explains that Elijah had already come in the person of John the Baptist, and the disciples understood it that way. Some scholars also see a future fulfillment, and this is interpreted in different ways.

God keeps his promises, but sometimes in ways we do not expect. Let us ask him for open eyes to recognize what he is already doing today.
exp.0:8:
It says that Uzziah was the father of Jotham, Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah. In this verse, "was the father of" means a direct parent-child link, and in biblical lists the phrase can also mean "was an ancestor of."

It is part of the family line of Jesus that opens the Gospel of Matthew. Matthew, who writes with Jewish readers in mind, wants to show that Jesus comes from the line of King David and fulfills God's promises. These names are kings of Judah. Matthew does not mention every king; he skips some, which was common in the genealogies of his time. There were good kings, such as Hezekiah, and wicked ones, such as Ahaz.

For today: God carries out his plans even through imperfect families. Your past or your family's past does not limit what God can do with you. Trust that he is still at work in your story.
exp.21:41:
Jesus asks the Pharisees what they think about the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah: whose son is he? They answer, "David's."

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees, who had just tried to test him with difficult questions. Now he is the one asking. The Pharisees were answering correctly, since the Messiah would come from the line of David, but their answer was incomplete. Jesus will soon lead them to Psalm 110 to show that the Messiah is more than a human descendant.

For today: it is not enough to repeat correct answers about Jesus. We can ask ourselves honestly: what do I think of Christ, and do I acknowledge him as Lord of my life?
exp.22:16:
Jesus calls the teachers "blind fools" because they valued the gold more than the temple. He asks them which is more important: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred. The word "makes" means that the temple sets the gold apart for God and gives it a sacred value. In other words, the gold was only special because it was in the temple.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees in a strong public rebuke. They taught complicated rules about oaths: according to them, swearing by the temple did not bind you, but swearing by the gold of the temple did. Jesus shows that this reasoning was twisted, and that they were putting material things above God.

For today: examine which things you value more than you should. Be honest when you speak, without looking for excuses to avoid keeping your word, and put God first, not money or appearances.
exp.6:9:
Here Jesus continues with a simple example: if a child asks for a fish, no father would give him a snake. A fish is good food; a snake would be something harmful or deceptive. The question "will he give" expects an answer, and the answer is "Of course not!"

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just encouraged asking, seeking and knocking. With these examples of ordinary fathers, he wants to show that God is a good Father, far better than any human father.

For today: you can pray with confidence and without fear, knowing that God hears you with love. Although sometimes we do not receive exactly what we ask for, we can trust that He gives what is truly good for us.
exp.14:6:
Jesus calls the Pharisees and scribes "hypocrites," and says that Isaiah prophesied correctly about them. A "hypocrite" was an actor on the stage who wore a mask; here it means someone who pretends to be one thing and is another.

Jesus is speaking with Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem, who criticized him because his disciples did not follow the tradition of washing their hands. He responds by showing that, through their traditions, they were setting aside God's command to honor one's father and mother, using the excuse of giving their goods to God as an offering. Then he quotes Isaiah to point out their false religiosity.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith is only words and customs, or whether it comes from the heart. Before defending a tradition, let us check whether it truly obeys what God asks, such as caring for and honoring our family.
exp.9:14:
Jesus says with great seriousness that on the day of judgment God will deal more leniently with Sodom and Gomorrah, cities famous for their wickedness, than with the town that rejects his messengers. "More bearable" means easier to endure. "Truly I tell you" is a way of saying: "I assure you."

Jesus sends his twelve disciples to announce that the kingdom of heaven is near. He explains how they should act when someone receives them and when someone does not. Rejecting the message is serious, because whoever rejects it rejects God himself. Interpreters understand that there are degrees of responsibility according to what each person has heard.

Today this reminds us that hearing the Word of God is both a privilege and a responsibility. For that reason it is good to receive it with humility and obey it, without hardening the heart. When you share your faith, do so with respect and leave the judgment to God.
exp.25:27:
Jesus says that the wine in the cup represents his blood, which establishes a new covenant, that is, a new agreement between God and people. That blood would be poured out, that is, given up in death, for many, for the forgiveness of sins.

Jesus speaks with his disciples during the last supper, the night before his crucifixion. They were celebrating the Passover, which remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. He gives the meal a new meaning: he announces his death and promises to drink with them again in the kingdom of his Father. Christians understand this in different ways regarding the Lord's Supper, but all recognize its importance.

For today: if Christ gave his life to forgive you, you can come before God with confidence and without fear. Receive that forgiveness with gratitude, and forgive those who have failed you as well.
exp.1:17:
A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning. It is Rachel, weeping for her children, who refuses to be comforted, because they are no more.

Matthew speaks here after the slaughter of the children in Bethlehem ordered by Herod. He quotes the prophet Jeremiah (31:15), where Rachel, a symbolic mother of Israel, weeps for her people carried off into exile. Rachel was buried near Bethlehem, and Ramah was in that region. Matthew joins that ancient sorrow with this new sorrow. Scholars explain in various ways how the word "fulfilled" should be understood, but they all see that God does not ignore the suffering of his people.

Today, when someone suffers a loss, do not hurry them to get over it. Accompany them with patience and prayer. And if you are weeping yourself, remember that God hears the weeping and does not overlook it.
exp.19:24:
Jesus calls his disciples together and reminds them of something they already know: the rulers of the nations (the Gentiles, that is, the peoples who were not Jews) lord it over the people under them. "Lording it over" means acting like owners, and their superiors "exercise authority" by using their power to force themselves on others.

Jesus speaks this after the mother of James and John asked that her sons be given the places of honor in his kingdom. The other ten became angry. Jesus gathers all of them to correct this struggle to be more important, and in the verse that follows he shows them that among them the way must be different.

For today: if you have any authority, at home, at work, or in the church, do not use it to feel superior or to pressure others. Ask yourself each day whom you can serve, and let that service measure your greatness.
exp.17:12:
Jesus says that if the shepherd finds the sheep that had gone astray (that is, had wandered off the path), he rejoices more over that one than over the ninety-nine that never got lost. The phrase "truly I tell you" is a solemn way of saying: "I assure you."

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and earlier he had told them not to despise the little ones. With this parable he shows the heart of God: He seeks the one who turns away, and He does not want anyone to be lost. This leads then to how to treat a brother who sins: go to him to win him back, not to condemn him.

Today, if you know someone who has drifted away from the faith or from the church, do not give them up for lost. Pray for that person and seek them out with care and patience, remembering that heaven rejoices when someone returns.
exp.19:9:
The workers who came first to the vineyard, seeing that the last workers received a denarius, assumed they would be paid more. But each of them also received a denarius. A denarius was the normal pay for one day's work. In this verse, "wage" refers to the payment for a day, and "last" refers to those who came at the end of the day.

Jesus tells this parable about the kingdom of heaven. It comes right after he says that many who are first will be last, and the last will be first. The owner of the vineyard hired workers at different times of the day, and he pays them all the same. Many read this as a lesson about the generosity and grace of God, which is not earned by merit.

For today: when you see God blessing others, perhaps someone who came to faith late, avoid comparing yourself or feeling that you deserve more. Give thanks for what God has given you and rejoice in his goodness toward others.
exp.26:21:
Pilate, the Roman governor, asks the crowd what he should do with Jesus, the one they call the Christ, meaning the Messiah. They all answer together, "Crucify Him!" They are demanding that Jesus be put to death on a cross, the cruelest punishment the Romans used.

Pilate speaks with the people gathered at the trial. He had already given them a choice between Jesus and Barabbas, and they chose Barabbas. The religious leaders had persuaded the crowd. Pilate knew that Jesus had done nothing wrong, but he did not have the courage to defend him. Then he washed his hands, as if that could leave him free of guilt.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we go along with the group even when we know what is right. Let us ask God for courage to speak the truth and do good, without washing our hands of it.
exp.25:55:
Jesus says that all of this is happening so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled. Then the text tells us that all the disciples deserted him and fled. "But" is simply a word that signals a contrast with what came before, and "deserted him" means they left him on his own.

Jesus had just been arrested in Gethsemane. He speaks to the crowd that came with swords and clubs, and reminds them that he taught every day in the temple and they never seized him. With this he shows that he is not caught by surprise: he accepts God's plan. The disciples, full of fear, run away. Some believe this also fulfills what is said in Zechariah 13:7, although the text here does not name it.

We all fail when we are afraid. But Jesus did not abandon his disciples even though they left him; afterward he restored them. If today you have failed in your faith, return to him with confidence: his faithfulness is greater than your weakness.
exp.22:31:
Jesus says to the scribes and Pharisees: "Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers." The phrase "Fill up" means to fill a cup or a vessel to the brim. It is an ironic and very serious statement: he invites them to complete the sin of their ancestors.

Jesus speaks in his last public teaching in the temple, in Jerusalem. He has just pronounced woes against the religious leaders for their hypocrisy. They said they would never have killed the prophets, but their rejection of Jesus showed they had the same heart. Many understand that Jesus already saw what they would do to him.

For today: it is not enough to criticize the mistakes of the past. Ask God to examine your heart and show you whether today you resist his truth, even if you say you respect it.
exp.0:6:
This verse continues the line of descendants from King David down to Jesus. It says that Solomon was the father of Rehoboam, Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asa. The phrase "the father of" simply names each person's direct father, and in the Bible it can sometimes also indicate a wider line of descent, such as a grandfather or an ancestor.

Matthew, who writes his Gospel to show who Jesus is, begins with this genealogy. He wants to demonstrate that Jesus is the promised Messiah, heir to David's throne. These names are kings of Judah, some faithful and some not so much. Matthew does not hide the fact that Israel's history was imperfect.

For today: God keeps His promises even through imperfect families and difficult generations. If your family history has failures or wounds, remember that God can work in it and carry out His purpose through you.
exp.11:20:
This verse says that the nations that are not Jewish, the "Gentiles", will put their hope in the name of Jesus. "Put their hope" here means to rely on someone and place one's trust in them. The "name" represents his whole person and his authority.

Matthew is speaking, and he quotes the prophet Isaiah (42:1-4) to explain what Jesus is like. After healing many people, Jesus asked that they not make him known. Matthew sees in this the gentle and humble servant that Isaiah announced, who does not shout or crush the weak, and whose work reaches all peoples.

For today: Jesus treats with tenderness the one who is wounded or weary. If you feel like a bruised reed, come to him with confidence. And remember that his invitation is for everyone, so we can share it with kindness.
exp.4:11:
Jesus says: "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you." The word "reward" here means recompense or payment. The verse also gives the reason for joy: the prophets who came before you were persecuted in the same way.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just said that those who are persecuted for the sake of righteousness are blessed. Here he gives them a reason to rejoice: suffering for following Jesus places them in the same line as the prophets who were faithful to God. Next he will tell them that they are salt and light.

For today: if someone mocks you or rejects you for living with honesty and faith, do not lose heart. Pray for that person, keep doing good, and remember that God sees what others do not see.
exp.23:7:
The passage says that wars, famines, plagues and earthquakes are only the beginning of birth pains. The word "birth pains" points to the pains of labor: discomforts that come before something greater, and that come closer and closer together. That is why Jesus says the end is not yet.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the signs of the end. He does not want to frighten them or let them be deceived, but to prepare them for difficult times, including persecution, as the following verse says. Christians understand in different ways how much of this has already been fulfilled and how much is still to come.

For today: when the news frightens you, do not be troubled or obsessed with dates. Trust that God is in control, remain faithful to Jesus, and keep loving others.
exp.5:12:
Here Jesus teaches us to ask God not to lead us into situations where we might fall, and to deliver us from evil, or from the Evil One, since the word can be understood in both ways. The word "temptation" can also mean trial. The closing praise is not part of our verse, so we can leave it aside, though many scholars believe it was added later as a doxology used in the church's prayer.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the Sermon on the Mount. He teaches the Lord's Prayer as a model of simple, trusting prayer, not of empty words or outward show. He ends this prayer with a request for protection, and immediately stresses the importance of forgiving others.

Today, we can begin the day by asking God for strength to avoid places and decisions that we know make us stumble, and by recognizing that only with his help can we resist.
exp.0:21:
This verse says that everything that happened with Mary, Joseph and the child who was to be born was no accident. Matthew explains that it took place "to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet," that is, so that what God had already spoken through a prophet would come true.

Here Matthew, the author of the gospel, pauses the account of the angel and Joseph. He wants to show his readers, most of whom were Jews, that the birth of Jesus is joined to the promises of the Scriptures. The prophet quoted is Isaiah (7:14), as the next verse shows. Some scholars debate how that prophecy applied in its own time and in Jesus, but Matthew sees it fulfilled in Christ.

For today: God keeps what He promises, even when it takes a long time. When life seems confusing, trust that He continues to work faithfully.
exp.19:23:
This verse says that the other ten disciples were very upset when they learned what the two brothers, James and John, had asked for. The phrase "they were indignant" here means they were filled with anger toward them.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Shortly before, the two brothers (together with their mother, according to the earlier passage) had asked Jesus for places of honor in his kingdom. The others were angry, perhaps because they also wanted that position, although the text does not state this clearly. Jesus uses the moment to teach them that greatness in his kingdom is measured by service.

Today, when someone receives recognition, it is easy to feel envy or resentment. Before reacting, ask yourself whether your anger comes from a hidden desire to be first. Ask God for a humble heart that serves with joy.
exp.9:16:
Jesus tells his disciples to be careful about people, because some of them will hand them over to the councils, which were local Jewish courts. They will also flog them in the synagogues, which were the places where people gathered to worship and to be taught. The word "be careful" in this verse means to watch yourselves and stay alert.

Jesus speaks to the twelve apostles when he sends them out for the first time to proclaim the kingdom of God. He sends them out as sheep among wolves, and he does not promise them an easy road. He warns them honestly so that they will not be taken by surprise. Then he assures them that the Spirit will give them what to say in that hour.

Today, being faithful to Christ can bring rejection or mockery. Be wise, not naive, but do not be afraid. Trust that God is with you, and he will give you words and strength when you need them.
exp.19:27:
This verse says that Jesus, whom it calls "the Son of Man," did not come into the world to be served by others, but to serve others. It also says that he came to give his life as a ransom for many. A ransom was the price paid to free a captive or a slave.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Two of them, James and John, together with their mother, had asked for the most important places in his kingdom, and the others became angry. Jesus explains to them that among his followers greatness is measured the opposite way from the world: whoever wants to be great must serve. And he points to himself as the example.

For today: before looking for recognition, ask yourself whom you can serve this week, at home, at work, or in your church, without expecting applause. Do it with gratitude for what Christ did for you.
exp.9:32:
Jesus says that whoever publicly denies him, that is, whoever says they do not know him or do not belong to him, will be denied by him before God the Father. The word "deny" here means to disown him or refuse to acknowledge him, and "whoever" means anyone at all. It is the opposite side of the promise in the verse before it.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples when he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom. He warns them that there will be rejection and persecution, but he asks them not to be afraid, because God cares for them even more than for the sparrows. Christians understand this text in different ways: some see it as a serious warning about persistent denial, and others remember that Peter denied Jesus and was restored (John 21).

Today we can ask God for the courage to acknowledge Jesus simply and with love, at work, in the family, or with friends, even when it costs us some embarrassment or rejection.
exp.26:18:
While Pilate was seated on the judgment seat, that is, in the place where he pronounced sentence, his wife sent him a message. She urged him to have nothing to do with "that innocent man," that is, with Jesus. She explained that she had suffered terribly that day in a dream because of Him.

Matthew is the only evangelist who tells this story. Pilate, the Roman governor, already knew that the Jewish leaders had handed Jesus over out of envy. Just as he was about to give his decision, this message from his wife arrives. The text does not say who sent the dream or what it contained; some believe it was God who warned her, but the Bible does not make this clear.

God can place warnings in our path, even through unexpected people. When we know what is right, we should obey and not give in to the pressure of others, as Pilate did, since he later gave in.
exp.26:42:
They said that the religious leaders were mocking Jesus on the cross. They said He trusts in God, so let God rescue Him now, if God wants Him. They mocked Him because Jesus had said that He was the Son of God. The word "deliver" in the verse means "to set free" or "to rescue."

The speakers are the chief priests, the scribes, the Pharisees, and the elders. Their words recall Psalm 22:8, which describes similar mockery. They thought that if God did not rescue Him, it would be proof that Jesus was wrong. Christians understand that Jesus remained on the cross out of love, to fulfill the plan of saving others.

Today, when God does not respond as we expect, we should not conclude that He has abandoned us. His silence is not always rejection; sometimes He works in a way that is deeper than we can see.
exp.6:23:
Jesus says that everyone who hears his words and acts on them is like a wise man, that is, a sensible and careful person. That man built his house on a rock, meaning on solid, firm ground.

Jesus is finishing the Sermon on the Mount. Just before this, he warned that it is not enough to say "Lord, Lord," or even to do impressive things in his name. What matters is a real relationship with him, which shows itself in acting on what he says. That is why he closes with this comparison: two builders, two foundations, and a storm that reveals the difference.

For today: choose a teaching of Jesus that you already know, such as forgiving, being honest, or not worrying, and decide on one concrete action to put it into practice this week. Hearing is the beginning; acting on it is what gives firmness.
exp.12:27:
The owner of the field makes clear that the weeds did not come from any carelessness on his part: "An enemy did this." The servants then ask him whether he wants them to go and pull the weeds up.

Jesus is telling the parable of the weeds to the crowds. The owner represents God, and the enemy, as Jesus explains later in the same chapter, is the devil. The servants are worried and want to act quickly, but the owner stops them so they do not harm the wheat.

For today: we are not always called to judge or to separate others from us. We can live patiently among people who are different, guard our own hearts, and trust that God will bring justice in his own time.
exp.24:6:
It says that, when they heard the midnight cry, the ten virgins woke up and trimmed their lamps. "Trimmed" is a word that in the verse above reads "trimmed," and it means getting something ready or put in order. It probably refers to trimming the wick and making the flame burn brighter.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in the parable of the ten virgins. With it he encourages them to be ready for his return, the time of which no one knows. Here they all get up and do the same thing, but it will soon become clear that not all of them were equally prepared: five of them were missing oil.

For today: it is not enough to look ready when the decisive moment arrives. Cultivate a real faith starting now, with prayer, the Word, and daily obedience, so that your heart is prepared when you need it most.
exp.26:46:
Some of those standing near the cross heard Jesus' cry and said, "He is calling Elijah." Hearing it, they spoke this way.

Jesus had just cried out, "Eli, Eli," which means "My God, my God." Those words sound similar to "Elijah." It may be that the bystanders misheard the name, or that they were mocking him. Scholars do not agree. In addition, many Jews expected that Elijah would come to help the righteous. They spoke this way while Jesus was suffering, after three hours of darkness.

When we suffer, others may misunderstand our pain or fail to grasp it. Jesus knows that kind of loneliness. We can speak to God honestly, even when we feel he is far away, because Jesus himself prayed this way.
exp.13:32:
This verse tells us that the disciples who were in the boat came to Jesus and worshiped him. They said, "Truly You are the Son of God!" The word "worshiped" here means bowing down in respect and recognition. Some scholars think it was full worship, and others believe it was a reverence that was still growing in understanding.

Matthew is the one who tells the story. Jesus had just walked on the water, rescued Peter when he was sinking, and calmed the wind. The disciples were frightened, and on seeing all of this they understood that Jesus was much more than a teacher. Their declaration comes from what they had seen with their own eyes.

For today: when you pass through storms, remember what Jesus has done in your life and respond to him with gratitude and worship. Even if you doubt like Peter, he takes you by the hand.
exp.5:28:
Jesus says that not even King Solomon, with all his wealth and splendor, was adorned as beautifully as one of the wildflowers of the field. In other words, the beauty God gives a flower surpasses the luxury of the most famous king of Israel.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He is teaching them not to live anxious about what they need, such as food and clothing. To be anxious means to worry with distress. He uses the lilies as an example to show God's care. Scholars do not agree on which exact flower those "lilies" were.

For today: when worry about money or your needs unsettles you, pause for a moment, look at something in creation, and remember that God cares for you. Then pray, take the responsible step that is yours to take, and entrust the rest to Him.
exp.26:9:
This verse says that the thirty pieces of silver, the money Judas returned, were used to buy the potter's field. This happened "as the Lord had commanded me." The "pieces of silver" were coins, and "potter" refers to someone who makes clay vessels. Some scholars understand the potter's field to have been a plot of land used for burying strangers.

The one speaking is Matthew, the author of the Gospel. The priests did not want to keep that money in the treasury because it was the price of blood, so they bought a piece of land. Matthew attributes the words to Jeremiah, although the wording seems to come mainly from Zechariah 11:12-13, with echoes of Jeremiah 18 and 32. Scholars explain this in several ways, and there is no single answer accepted by everyone.

For today: God can guide events, even unjust ones, toward his purpose. If today you face something that seems unfair or meaningless, trust that God is still at work, and ask him to help you not be carried away by greed as Judas was.
exp.11:37:
Here some of the scribes and Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign. They address him as "Teacher," as a sign of respect, and say, "We want to see a sign from You," that is, they want to see a miracle that would prove God sent him.

Jesus had just healed a man who was possessed by a demon, and some of the leaders accused him of acting by the power of the devil. Then Jesus spoke about the seriousness of words. Now they ask him for a sign, even though they had already seen many. For this reason Jesus calls them an evil and adulterous generation, speaking of their unfaithfulness to God, and promises them only the sign of Jonah.

For today: faith does not grow by demanding proofs from God, but by listening humbly to what he has already shown. Ask him for a heart willing to believe and obey.
exp.4:36:
Jesus says that our speech should be simple: when we say "yes," let it be yes, and when we say "no," let it be no. "Speech" here refers to the way we express ourselves. Anything added to strengthen what we have said, such as oaths or exaggerations, comes from the evil one. Some scholars understand "the evil one" as a reference to the devil, and others as wickedness in general.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Before this, he corrects the custom of swearing by heaven, by the earth, or by one's own head to give more weight to a promise. His teaching shows that a person of integrity does not need embellishments in order to be believed.

Today we can take care that our words are trustworthy. Avoid promising more than you can deliver or exaggerating to persuade others. If you say you will go, go; if you cannot commit, say "no" kindly. In this way your word will have value on its own.
exp.24:31:
All the nations will be gathered before the Son of Man when he comes as King, and he will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. The word for "nations" can also mean peoples or Gentiles. The picture is simple: a shepherd sorting his flock into two groups.

Jesus speaks these words to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, shortly before his crucifixion. They come after the parables of the ten virgins and the talents, which stress being ready and being faithful. This scene of the final judgment closes his teaching. Some scholars think "all nations" means all of humanity; others think it means the non-Jewish nations. This is debated, but the central point is clear.

For today: God looks at how we live out our faith in everyday life. Today you can ask yourself who near you needs help, and respond with one concrete act of kindness.
exp.1:0:
Matthew 2:1 says that Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea during the time of King Herod. Soon after, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem. "Magi" were men who studied the stars and signs; the Bible does not say how many there were or what their names were.

Matthew is the one who writes, and he presents Jesus as the King promised to Israel. That foreigners come looking for him shows that his coming matters to other peoples as well. Herod ruled under the power of Rome. Exactly where the Magi came from is not known; it is debated whether they were from Persia, Babylon, or some other place.

These men made a long journey to find Jesus. Today we can ask ourselves: how much effort am I willing to make to seek Christ and worship him? Seeking him truly is worth any road.
exp.15:10:
Jesus tells his disciples that they have misunderstood him. He was not talking to them about bread to eat. When he said "beware of the leaven," he was using a picture. Leaven is what makes dough rise, and it spreads through the whole batch. The warning means to be careful.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after they worry that they have not brought any bread. He reminds them that he has already fed thousands with very little, so bread was not the real problem. In the next verse, Matthew explains that the "leaven" was the teaching of the Pharisees and the Sadducees.

Today we can ask ourselves which ideas shape our hearts without our noticing. Just as a little leaven changes the whole dough, a false teaching can keep growing. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and trust that God cares for what we need.
exp.1:18:
This verse says that, after King Herod died, an angel of God appeared to Joseph in a dream while he was sleeping. Joseph was in Egypt with Mary and the child Jesus.

Matthew tells this after the killing of the children in Bethlehem. Joseph had fled to Egypt to protect Jesus from Herod's plan. Now that the danger is over, God gives him new instructions. Matthew shows that God watched over Jesus at every step.

For today: God does not forget us in times of fear or waiting. We can trust that he knows when a difficult season will end. In the meantime, let us do as Joseph did: listen to God and obey calmly, one step at a time.
exp.21:2:
It says that the king sent his servants to tell the invited guests that the banquet was ready. Those people had already been invited earlier, but now they were given the final notice. They refused to come. The word "call" in the verse refers to the guests who had been invited.

Jesus is speaking to the religious leaders of Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He uses a parable about a king who prepares a banquet for his son. Many understand that the king represents God, and that the guests who refuse are those who heard his call and did not respond. Some see here a reference to Israel, although the parable has a broad message.

God invites us with love, but the invitation calls for a response. Today we can ask ourselves what things distract us from saying "yes" to him, and look for time to listen to him sincerely.
exp.20:40:
Here the people listening to Jesus answer his question about the parable. They say that the owner would bring those wretches to a wretched end, and would rent the vineyard out to other tenants who would give him his share of the fruit at harvest time.

Jesus tells the parable to the chief priests and the elders of the people. Without realizing it, they themselves pass judgment on themselves. Jesus then explains that the kingdom of God would be taken away from them and given to a people who produce fruit. Many understand that the vineyard represents Israel and the tenants represent its leaders.

God has entrusted us with gifts, time, and opportunities, and he expects fruit: love, justice, and obedience. Let us ask him today for a humble heart that listens to his correction instead of resisting it.
exp.20:2:
Jesus tells his two disciples what to say if anyone asks them why they are untying the animals. They are to say, "The Lord needs them," and the owners will send them right away.

Jesus speaks near Jerusalem, in Bethphage, just before his entry as King. He gives clear instructions, and Matthew explains that this fulfills what the prophet Zechariah announced: a humble king riding on an animal. The Bible does not explain how everything was arranged; some think Jesus knew the owner, and others think he knew by supernatural means.

For today: what we have, whether time, talent, or resources, can be useful to the Lord. Let us trust his guidance and be willing to obey, even when we do not understand every detail.
exp.20:1:
Jesus sends two disciples to the village ahead of them. He tells them that there, right away, they will find a donkey tied up, with her colt beside her, and that they must untie them and bring them to him.

Jesus speaks as he approaches Jerusalem, near Bethphage on the Mount of Olives. He is preparing his entry into the city, a few days before his death. Matthew explains right away that this fulfills what the prophet said, that is, Zechariah 9:9, which announces a humble king riding on a donkey. Jesus presents himself as King, but with gentleness and not with military force.

For today: Jesus asks for something simple and the disciples obey without arguing. He trusts that God has already prepared the way, even when you do not understand the whole plan. Obey today what he asks of you, even when it seems small.
exp.7:24:
This verse says that the disciples went to Jesus, who was sleeping in the boat, and woke Him. They cried out, "Lord, save us! We are perishing!" That is, "We are going to die!" The word "perishing" means that they felt they were sinking and that their lives were in danger.

The ones speaking are the disciples, frightened by a violent storm on the lake. The waves were filling the boat, and Jesus was asleep. They come to Him as "Lord," for they trusted that He could help them. Jesus then asks them why they are afraid, and He calms the wind and the sea. In this way, the disciples see who He is.

For today: when you feel that life is sinking, do not wait until you have everything under control. Cry out to Jesus with sincerity, even if your prayer is short and full of fear. He hears you and can give you peace, even in the middle of the storm.
exp.23:25:
Jesus says that if someone tells you the Christ is out in the wilderness, do not go out looking for him. And if they say, "Here he is, in the inner rooms," do not believe it. The inner rooms are private, hidden places inside a house.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives as he explains what will come before the end. He has just warned them that false christs and false prophets will rise up and perform impressive signs. Then he makes clear that his return will not be hidden, not even from a few people, but will be as visible as lightning flashing across the whole sky.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away by anyone who promises a secret or special revelation about Christ. Test every teaching against what the Bible says, and keep your trust in Jesus, not in people who draw attention to themselves.
exp.8:12:
Jesus tells the Pharisees to go and learn what a line of Scripture means: "I desire mercy, not sacrifice." That is, God values our treating others with compassion more than carrying out religious rituals without love. He adds that he has not come to call the righteous, but sinners, so that they change their hearts and their direction. "Go" here means go and learn, and "repentance" means turning back to God.

Jesus speaks after the Pharisees criticized him for eating with tax collectors (people looked down on in those days) and sinners. He answers with irony: he quotes Hosea 6:6 and shows that his mission is to heal the spiritually sick, not to flatter those who believe they are well.

Today, before judging someone, ask yourself whether you are showing mercy. Approach with respect and kindness the person who is far from God, remembering that you too need his grace.
exp.27:7:
They left the tomb with two feelings at the same time: fear and great joy. They did not stop; they hurried to tell the news to his disciples.

Matthew recounts what happened after an angel had announced to them that Jesus had risen. The angel gave them a task: go and tell the disciples. They obeyed right away. Moreover, in the next verse Jesus himself meets them on the way, which shows that their obedience was not in vain.

For today: you do not need to have everything clear or to stop feeling fear in order to share the good news of Jesus. We can speak of Him with mixed emotions, yet with a willingness to obey. God often meets us while we are on the way.
exp.22:2:
Jesus says that what the scribes and Pharisees teach should be obeyed, but their conduct should not be copied. "Practice and observe" means to carry out and obey, and phylacteries are small boxes containing passages of the Law that were tied to the arm or the forehead. The problem is that they do not practice what they preach: they teach one thing and live another.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, in the temple at Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. The scribes and Pharisees taught the Law of Moses (the seat of Moses), so their teaching, when it agreed with the Law, was valid. But Jesus rebukes their hypocrisy, since they loaded others down with burdens and sought to appear religious.

For today: value the truth of God's Word even when the one who teaches it fails, but do not use their mistakes as an excuse. And examine your own life: make sure that what you say with your mouth is also seen in your deeds.
exp.2:5:
This verse tells us that people were baptized by John in the Jordan River and, as they did so, confessed their sins. The phrase "by him" means that John was the one doing the baptizing.

Confessing means openly acknowledging the wrong one has done, without hiding it or excusing it.

Here the speaker is the narrator, Matthew. He describes the ministry of John the Baptist, who called the people to turn back to God. Many people came from Jerusalem and from all of Judea. Shortly afterward, John speaks sharply to the Pharisees and Sadducees, because he wanted to see true repentance and not merely an outward act.

Today, this passage invites us to be honest with God. We can bring before him, with sincerity, what we have done wrong, without excuses, and ask him for forgiveness and help to change. A change of heart is then seen in the way we live.
exp.4:13:
Jesus tells his disciples that they are "the light of the world." Here "you" addresses his followers directly.

He compares his followers to a city on a hill: it can be seen from far away and cannot be hidden.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, before his disciples and the crowd. He has just spoken of the Beatitudes and of persecution, and earlier he called his own "the salt of the earth." Now he reminds them that their lives have a visible effect. He then explains that light is meant to shine, not to be covered up, and that their good works should lead others to glorify God.

Today we can ask ourselves where we are hiding our faith out of fear or shame. This week, do one concrete act of kindness, without seeking applause, so that others may see God in you.
exp.20:8:
Matthew tells us that the crowds walking ahead of Jesus and those following behind were shouting with joy: "Hosanna to the Son of David!" "Hosanna" was a cry meaning "save us, please," and over time it became an expression of praise. "Son of David" is a title for the promised king. The "crowds" are the large groups of people.

Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a donkey, and the crowd welcomes him as a king. Their words come from Psalm 118:25-26, a psalm that was sung at the festivals. Only a few days later, the same city would be divided over him. Some understood Jesus as the Messiah; others saw him only as a prophet.

For today: praising Jesus is good, but it is worth asking ourselves whether we follow him also when there is no festival. Today you can thank him and ask him to help you trust him every day.
exp.15:2:
Jesus says that people know how to read the sky: if the morning sky is red and overcast, they announce that a storm is coming that day. The red sky is the reddish, cloudy look he describes, and the overcast sky is the dark, threatening appearance that suggests bad weather. He then calls them "hypocrites," because they can interpret the weather but do not understand the signs of the times, that is, what God was doing at that moment.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees and Sadducees, who were usually rivals, but who join together to test him. They ask him for a sign from heaven, even though they had already seen healings and miracles. The problem was not a lack of evidence but a closed heart. Some early manuscripts do not include these lines, and scholars debate them, but the message fits the rest of the passage.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we are paying attention to what God is already showing us in his Word and in our lives, or whether we keep asking for more proof so that we do not have to obey.
exp.7:19:
Jesus says that foxes have dens to live in and birds have nests to rest in, but he, called "the Son of Man," has no place of his own where he can rest his head, that is, where he can rest and sleep.

A scribe, a teacher of the Law, promises to follow him wherever he goes. Jesus does not turn him away, but honestly shows him what following him involves: a simple life, without guaranteed comforts. "Son of Man" is a title Jesus used for himself; many relate it to Daniel 7. The Bible does not say what the scribe decided.

Before we commit to Christ, it is wise to think about the cost. Following him may ask us to give up comfort, security, or our own plans. Today you can ask him: "Lord, what comfort do I find it hard to let go of so that I can truly follow you?"
exp.23:17:
Matthew 24:18 says that a person who is working in the field when danger comes should not turn back to get their cloak. The cloak here is the outer garment that workers would often set aside while they labored in the fields.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, answering questions about the future of Jerusalem and the final times. He warns them that when a certain sign appears, they must flee without delay. Many link this to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, and some also see a future fulfillment. Scholars understand it in different ways.

For today: when God shows us that it is time to obey, it is not wise to delay because of attachments or comforts. Ask yourself what things are holding you back, and ask God to help you let them go with trust.
exp.23:30:
Jesus says that, when he comes, he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call. They will gather his chosen ones, that is, those who belong to God, from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other. The phrase "from one end of the heavens to the other" means from the farthest reach of the sky to the far side. No one will be overlooked or left far away.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the signs of the end. He describes his glorious return, which will be visible to everyone. Christians have understood some details of this passage in different ways, but the central message is clear: Christ will return and gather his people.

If you belong to Christ, you can live with hope and without fear. No distance, loneliness, or hardship will separate you from his care. Today, pray with confidence and live faithfully, knowing that he will keep his promise.
exp.13:28:
Jesus says just one word to Peter: "Come." Then Peter gets out of the boat, walks on the water, and comes toward Jesus.

It is night, and the disciples are in the middle of the lake, frightened because they see someone walking on the water. Jesus tells them not to be afraid, and Peter, with his impulsive character, asks Jesus to command him to come to Him. Jesus answers with an invitation. Peter steps out trusting in that word, not in himself.

For today: when you sense that God is calling you to take a difficult step, lean on His word and not on your own strength. Take the step, and keep your eyes on Jesus, not on the difficulties around you.
exp.26:32:
This verse tells us that Jesus and the soldiers came to a place called Golgotha, a name from Aramaic that Matthew explains as "the place of the skull." Matthew is the one telling the story. He has just described how Jesus was mocked and led away to die, and how Simon of Cyrene carried his cross. It is not known for certain why the place had this name; some think it was because of the shape of the ground, others because it was a place of executions. The Bible does not make this clear.

For today: Jesus did not turn away from this harsh place; he went there out of love for us. When you go through difficult moments, remember that he knows pain and walks with you. You can come to him with confidence and thank him for his sacrifice.
exp.12:52:
This verse says that when Jesus had finished telling the parables of chapter 13, those simple stories about the kingdom of heaven, He withdrew from that place.

The narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just asked his disciples whether they had understood, and they said yes. Matthew marks with this sentence the close of one block of teaching and the start of another moment. Soon Jesus comes to his own country, Nazareth, where the people are amazed, but also doubt him.

For today: when we hear the Word, saying "yes, I understand" is not enough. What we have learned must go with us into the next step of life, where it will be tested. Let us ask God that what we hear becomes obedience and trust, even when others doubt.
exp.21:13:
This verse says that God's invitation is for many, but few end up being "chosen," that is, approved or accepted. The "called" are the invited guests; the "chosen" are those who respond in the right way. The word "chosen" can also be understood as "elect."

Jesus speaks to the religious leaders and tells the parable of a king who invites people to a wedding feast. The first invited guests reject the invitation, and then everyone is invited. One man comes in without a wedding garment and is thrown out. Interpreters explain the garment in different ways: a life that responds to the invitation with faith and obedience, or the righteousness that God himself gives. Jesus says this with a serious warning.

Today, it is not enough to hear God's invitation or to be close to religious things. Respond with a humble heart, trust in Christ, and let him transform your life.
exp.5:21:
The eye works like a lamp for the body: it lets light in. In the Berean Standard Bible, Jesus says, "If your eyes are good, your whole body will be full of light." The word translated "good" comes from a Greek word that can mean simple, clear, or without deceit, and some also understand it to mean generous. If the eye is like this, the whole body, that is, the whole person, is full of light.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Just before this, he spoke of treasure in heaven and of how the heart follows the treasure. Right after, he speaks of not being able to serve both God and money. Many understand the eye to represent where we direct our gaze and desires, although some interpret it as generosity.

For today: examine what draws your gaze and your attention. Ask God for a clear, undivided heart, so that your decisions about money and time show that He comes first.
exp.0:10:
Josiah was the father of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin or Coniah, and of Jeconiah's brothers. This happened at the time of the exile, when the people of Judah were taken away to Babylon. The word "father" here means the direct ancestor in the family line. The exile was the forced removal of people from their homeland to another land.

Matthew includes this genealogy to show his Jewish readers that Jesus comes from the family line of King David. This verse marks a turning point: the kingdom falls and the people are taken into exile. Some scholars note that Matthew leaves out some names, and that "father" can indicate descent in a broader sense. Even so, the royal line continues.

For today: even in the darkest times, such as an exile, God keeps fulfilling his promises. If you are going through a hard season today, remember that God is still at work in your story.
exp.17:34:
Jesus says that his heavenly Father will treat each of us in the same way if we do not forgive our brother from the heart. The word "you" here is the plain "you" of the verse, and the wrongs done against us are what we are called to forgive. Saying "I forgive you" with the lips is not enough; forgiveness must be sincere and come from within.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples after Peter asked how many times he had to forgive. Jesus answers with the parable of the servant whose master forgave him an enormous debt, but who then refused to forgive a small debt owed to a fellow servant. This verse is the final application of that story. Some read it as a sign of how seriously God regards the failure to forgive; others stress that someone who has received so much grace should be willing to give it.

Today, think of someone who hurt you and ask God for help to let go of resentment, remembering how much He has forgiven you.
exp.13:34:
This verse tells that the people of Gennesaret recognized Jesus as soon as he arrived. Then they sent word to everyone in the surrounding region, and people brought him all the sick. The phrase "when the men of that place recognized Jesus" means that they knew who he was.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus and his disciples had just crossed the lake after Jesus walked on the water and calmed the storm. The people in the boat had worshiped him as the Son of God. When they reached the shore, the local people, who had already heard about him, did not waste the opportunity and sought his help for their loved ones.

Today we can imitate those people: when we recognize who Jesus is, we do not keep the news to ourselves. Think of someone who is suffering and bring them to Christ in prayer, or invite them to get to know him.
exp.14:13:
Jesus tells his followers not to worry about the Pharisees. He calls them "blind guides": people who cannot see the truth yet still lead others. "Disregard them" means leave them alone and do not give them your attention. The "pit" is a deep hole in the ground, and if a blind person leads another blind person, both will fall into it.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, who tell him that the Pharisees were offended. Shortly before, Jesus had taught that what defiles a person is what comes out of the heart, not what goes into the mouth. The Pharisees placed more value on their human traditions than on what God had said.

For today: before following a teacher or leader, check what they teach against Scripture. And if you are guiding others, ask God for the humility to see clearly yourself first.
exp.23:24:
Jesus says: "See, I have told you in advance." The word "See" draws attention, as if saying "take careful note." And "I have told you in advance" means that He warned them before it happened.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the signs of the end and of his coming. He warns them that false christs and false prophets will appear, with impressive signs, able to deceive even the elect, that is, those who belong to God. With this statement Jesus makes it clear that the deception will not catch them by surprise.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away by anyone who claims to have a special message or miracles. Compare what you hear with what Jesus taught in the Bible, and ask God for wisdom to discern.
exp.8:32:
This verse tells how, when Jesus drove out the demon, the man who had been unable to speak began to talk. The crowd was amazed. The word "amazed" means that they were greatly astonished. They said that nothing like this had ever been seen in Israel.

The one telling the story here is Matthew, who reports what the crowd saw. They had brought a man who could not speak because of a demon, and Jesus set him free. Right away the Pharisees, who were religious leaders, responded harshly and said that Jesus drove out demons by the power of the prince of demons. In this way, one and the same event produced wonder in some and rejection in others.

Today we can ask ourselves how we respond to what God does. We can open our hearts with gratitude and wonder, or harden ourselves with doubts and prejudices. A good practice is to thank God each day for one of his works, great or small.
exp.21:27:
The Sadducees ask Jesus: if a woman married seven brothers, one after another, and all of them died, whose wife will she be in the resurrection? The verse says that all seven were married to her.

The speakers are the Sadducees, a religious group who, according to the same Gospel, denied the resurrection. They based their story on the law of levirate marriage, in which a brother married the widow of the man who had died. They were not seeking to learn but to make the idea of resurrection look foolish and to put Jesus in a difficult position. He answered that they were mistaken because they did not know the Scriptures or the power of God.

For today: before we ask hard questions about God, let us examine whether we seek to understand or only to win an argument. Let us approach the Bible with humility, trusting that God is greater than our ideas.
exp.6:24:
This verse describes a storm that strikes a house: the rain falls, the torrents rage, and the winds blow and beat against it. But the house does not fall, because its foundation was on the rock. The rock here means firm, solid ground, and the verse's "beat against" means the storm struck the house with force.

Jesus speaks at the end of the Sermon on the Mount. Just before this, he warns that saying "Lord, Lord" is not enough; one must obey. With this image he closes his teaching: whoever hears his words and puts them into practice is like a wise builder. Many understand the storm as the trials of life and also as the final judgment.

For today: choose a teaching of Jesus that you already know, such as forgiving, not worrying too much, or being honest, and practice it this week. Faith becomes firm when it moves from hearing to action.
exp.19:25:
In Jesus' group, things work the opposite way from the world. The words "It shall not be this way among you" mean that among his followers, this should not be the pattern. "Whoever wants to become great" means whoever desires to rise to greatness, and "servant" is someone who attends to and serves others. Whoever wishes to become great must learn to serve.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples. The brothers James and John, through their mother, had asked for the best places in the kingdom. The other ten became angry, perhaps because they also wanted that place. Then Jesus called them all together and corrected them, comparing the power of the rulers of the nations with the path of service. He himself is the example: he came to serve and to give his life.

Today we can ask ourselves: "Whom can I help without expecting recognition?" Choose one concrete act of service today, at home, at work, or in the church, and do it with humility.
exp.18:21:
When the young man heard this, he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth. The verse notes that the young man was simply a young man, and that he left in sorrow because he owned much.

The young man had asked what he still lacked to have eternal life, and he said that he had already kept the commandments. Jesus looked at him and told him to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow him. That command touched exactly what he held most tightly in his heart. Afterward Jesus warned his disciples how hard it is for a rich person to enter the kingdom. Scholars disagree about whether this command is for everyone or only for him, but it is clear that Jesus wanted his whole heart.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: is there something, whether money, comfort, or security, that I would find hard to let go of if Jesus asked me for it? Give it to God today in prayer, and ask for a generous and free heart.
exp.15:27:
Jesus says that some of those standing with him will not die before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. "Taste death" is an expression that means to die. "Earn" means to gain.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after announcing his suffering and calling them to follow him, even though it may cost them their lives. He promises them that his kingdom is real and that his glory will be seen. Christians understand this in several ways: as the transfiguration, which is described in the passage that follows; as the resurrection and the birth of the church; as the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70; or as a broader reference to his kingdom. There is no single view accepted by everyone.

For today: when following Jesus seems costly, remember that his kingdom is secure. Entrusting your life to him is worth more than gaining everything the world offers.
exp.23:0:
This verse tells us that Jesus left the temple in Jerusalem and was walking away from it. His disciples came up to him to point out the buildings of the temple. The phrase "left the temple" simply means that he had gone away from it, and "came up to Him" means that they drew near to him.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just been teaching in the temple and had spoken sharply against the religious leaders. The disciples admired the beauty and size of the structure. Jesus answers at once that all of it would be destroyed. Many understand this to refer to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70 AD, and Christians interpret what follows about the end in different ways.

For today: it is easy to be impressed by what looks large and solid. Let us ask God to teach us to place our hope in him and not in buildings, achievements, or institutions that pass away.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that the eye works like a lamp for the body. If your eyes are bad, your whole body is left in darkness. If the light you think you have is really darkness, that darkness is enormous. In the Bible, a bad eye is often linked to envy or greed, though some readers understand it more broadly as a distorted way of looking at things.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Just before this, he spoke about storing up treasures in heaven rather than on earth. Right after it, he warns that no one can serve both God and money. This verse connects both ideas: what we look at and desire shapes our whole inner life.

For today: examine which things catch your eye and your desire. Ask God to help you look with generosity and trust, not with ambition or envy.
exp.4:10:
Jesus says that those who are blessed, or happy, are those who are insulted, persecuted, and falsely spoken against. The word "insult" here means to treat someone with contempt or to humiliate them. But he sets a clear condition: that all of this happens "because of Me." He is not speaking of suffering for one's own mistakes, but for following Christ.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Before this, he has described the character of those who belong to his kingdom. Now he makes clear that living this way will bring rejection, as it did to the prophets before them. For this reason he encourages them to rejoice, since their reward is great in heaven.

For today: if someone mocks you or speaks badly of you for living with honesty and faith in Jesus, you do not have to respond with hatred or fear. You can stand firm, pray for that person, and remember that God sees what others do not see.
exp.9:31:
Here Jesus says that whoever acknowledges him, that is, whoever recognizes him and openly speaks of belonging to him, will be acknowledged by Jesus before his Father in heaven. "Everyone who confesses me" means anyone who does so, and "before men" means publicly, in plain view of others.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples before sending them out to preach. He warns them that there will be rejection and persecution. So he reminds them that the Father cares about every detail of their lives, even the hairs of their heads, and that they should not be afraid. Acknowledging him would have a cost, but it also carries a promise. The next verse shows the other side: denying him has consequences too.

For today: you do not need to give great speeches. You can acknowledge Jesus simply, for example by praying in public, speaking honestly about your faith, or acting as he taught, even when it feels awkward or costs you something. Do it trusting that the Father cares for you.
exp.9:15:
Jesus tells his disciples that he is sending them out like sheep among wolves, that is, as defenseless people surrounded by hostile people. For this reason he tells them to be shrewd as snakes, meaning alert and careful so as not to walk into unnecessary dangers, and innocent as doves, which means sincere, without malice or deceit. The word "shrewd" can be understood as clever, and "innocent" can be understood as pure or without guilt.

Jesus speaks to the twelve apostles when he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God. He warns them that there will be rejection and persecution. He does not promise them an easy mission, but he does give them a way to act: to use good judgment without losing their integrity. The verses that follow show that they will face courts and authorities.

Today we can be shrewd when we make decisions and deal with difficult people, but without lying or repaying evil with evil. Seeking God's wisdom in prayer helps us keep that balance.
exp.4:38:
Jesus tells his listeners not to answer evil with evil. In the Berean Standard Bible wording, "not to resist an evil person" means not paying back a blow or seeking revenge. "Slaps" means striking someone with the hand, and "turn to him the other also" means offering the other cheek.

Being slapped on the right cheek, usually with the back of the hand, was above all an insult rather than a serious injury.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just quoted the old law, an eye for an eye, which limited revenge so that it would not go too far. Now Jesus goes further and shows the character of the Kingdom: not repaying in kind. Christians understand differently how far this applies, for example in cases of self-defense or justice.

Today, when someone insults you with harsh words, try not to answer with another insult. Breathe, respond calmly or stay silent, and seek to do good.
exp.14:1:
The scribes and Pharisees ask Jesus why his disciples break the tradition of the elders. The word "break" here means to go against it or disregard it. Their complaint is that the disciples do not wash their hands before they eat. They were not talking about hygiene, but about a ceremonial custom of purity.

The ones speaking are teachers of the law and Pharisees who had come from Jerusalem, perhaps to watch over or question Jesus. They placed great value on the teachings that earlier leaders had handed down. Jesus does not respond by defending a small detail, but turns the question back on them: they themselves set aside God's commandment for the sake of their traditions.

For today: let us examine our religious customs with humility. Traditions can help us, but they must never take the place of God's Word or of truly loving people.
exp.24:7:
The foolish ones lacked good judgment. When they realized their lamps were going out, they asked the wise ones, the sensible ones, to give them some of their oil. The word "prepared" is used here to mean that they got their lamps ready.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples to speak about his return. The bridegroom represents Christ, and the virgins represent those who await his coming. All of them waited and all of them fell asleep, but only some were truly prepared. Many understand the oil as a living and true faith, although it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: do not live on the faith of others. Cultivate your own relationship with God day by day, through prayer and his Word, so that you are ready at any moment.
exp.4:43:
Jesus says we must love our enemies. That means praying for those who persecute us. It also means being willing to do good to people who hate us and to speak well of those who treat us badly.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples and the crowd. Before this, he refers to what the people had been taught: "You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy." That second part does not appear in that form in the law of Moses, so it likely reflects a popular teaching of his day. Jesus calls for a love that reflects the character of the Father, who gives sun and rain to everyone.

This week, pray by name for someone who annoys you or has hurt you. Ask God to bless that person, and look for one small act of kindness toward them.
exp.14:3:
Jesus recalls what God commanded: to honor father and mother. He also cites the law that said anyone who curses their father or mother must be put to death. Here the words that matter are "curses" and "must be put to death." They mean that anyone who spoke against their parents with disrespect or contempt was to be condemned to death. With this he shows that God took the treatment of parents very seriously.

The Pharisees and scribes accused the disciples of not following the tradition of the elders, because they did not wash their hands before eating. Jesus answers with a question of his own and confronts them. They used a tradition to avoid helping their parents, saying that their possessions were dedicated to God. In this way they set aside a clear commandment.

Today we can ask ourselves whether some custom or excuse keeps us from caring for our parents. Honoring them includes respect, time, affection, and practical help when they need it.
exp.1:22:
Matthew tells us that Joseph took Mary and the child Jesus and went to live in a town called Nazareth, in Galilee. He says this fulfilled what the prophets had spoken: that Jesus would be called a Nazarene. The word "Nazarene" appears here as a quoted term, and the verse above uses the same English word.

Matthew also explains why the family did not return to Judea. Joseph was afraid of Archelaus, the son of Herod, and God guided him in dreams. It is striking that no prophet writes exactly these words, so the verse is understood in several ways. Some think Matthew is pointing to Nazareth being a despised town, and that the Messiah would be looked down upon. Others see a play on a Hebrew word meaning "branch" or "shoot." It is not certain which idea is correct.

For today: God can guide your life simply, even toward small or little-valued places. If you feel overlooked, remember that Jesus also grew up in a humble place, and God continues to work there.
exp.10:25:
Jesus says that he agrees with his Father's plan. "Yes, Father" is his way of saying a full and willing agreement. "For this was well-pleasing in Your sight" means that this was your will and it pleased you. "Well-pleasing" means that it was delightful to him and seemed right in his eyes.

Jesus speaks after rebuking cities that saw his miracles and did not repent. He praises the Father because the truths of the kingdom were hidden from those who think themselves wise, but were revealed to the humble. That is the Father's decision, and Jesus accepts it with joy. Right after, he invites the weary to come to him.

For today: draw near to God with humility. You don't need to understand everything to know him; trust in his good will and come to Jesus with your weariness.
exp.5:0:
Jesus says we should take care not to practice our "righteous acts," that is, good works such as giving, praying, or fasting, only so that people will see us and admire us. If we do it that way, "no reward" means that we will not receive a reward from our heavenly Father.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Shortly before, he had spoken of a righteousness greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees. Now he warns against religion that is only for show. The verses that follow give examples, such as giving to those in need, and show that God looks at the heart and not at applause.

Before doing something good, ask yourself: "Am I doing this to please God or to look good in the eyes of others?" This week, do an act of kindness in secret, without telling anyone, and offer it to God.
exp.23:22:
Jesus warns that, at that time, someone may say to you, "Look, here is the Christ!" or "There He is!" His instruction is clear: do not believe it. "Christ" means "the Anointed One," the promised Messiah.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after announcing the destruction of the temple. He describes a time of great distress and warns them so that they will not be deceived. The verses that follow explain that false christs and false prophets will arise with impressive signs. Interpreters differ on how much of this refers to the fall of Jerusalem and how much to the end of the age.

For today: do not follow anyone who presents a spectacular message about Christ. Compare what you hear with the teachings of Jesus in the Bible, and ask God for wisdom.
exp.6:18:
This verse says that every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. The image of a tree stands for people, and the fruit stands for what their lives produce.

Jesus is speaking at the end of the Sermon on the Mount. He has just warned about false prophets, who look like sheep but are not. He tells his listeners that they are recognized by their fruits, that is, by their conduct and their teaching. Right after this, he makes clear that saying "Lord, Lord" is not enough, but that one must do the will of the Father. The fire is understood as a picture of God's judgment.

For today: do not be satisfied with religious words alone. Ask God to examine you, and look at whether your life shows love, truth, patience, and kindness in everyday matters.
exp.27:6:
The angel tells the women to go quickly and tell the disciples that Jesus has risen from the dead. He also tells them that Jesus is going ahead of them into Galilee and that they will see him there. "Quickly" means fast, "going ahead" means that he leads the way in front of them, and "See, I have told you" is a way of stressing that the message is certain.

The angel speaks to Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, who went to the tomb early. He takes away their fear and shows them the empty tomb. Then he sends them as the first messengers of the resurrection. Galilee was the region where Jesus had spent much of his ministry, and there he had promised to meet them.

God can give us good news even when we are frightened or sad, and he invites us to share it without delay. Jesus is alive and goes ahead of us on every path. Today we can move forward with confidence and tell someone close to us the hope we have in Christ.
exp.13:19:
