They all ate and were satisfied. "Satisfied" means they ate until they had enough, with nobody left hungry. Afterward, the disciples picked up the broken pieces that were left over and filled twelve baskets.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus was in a remote place with a crowd, and the disciples had only five loaves of bread and two fish. Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and distributed it through them. Some see in the twelve baskets a possible allusion to the twelve tribes of Israel or to the twelve disciples, but the text does not say so.

For today: the little we have, placed in the hands of Jesus, can be enough for others. Give him with confidence what you have, and he will know how to multiply it.
exp.9:11:
Jesus says that when the disciples enter a home, they should greet its occupants. In that time, greeting a household was more than saying "hello": it meant wishing them peace, as was customary in the Jewish world. It is a gesture of respect and goodwill toward those who receive them.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles as he sends them out for the first time to the villages of Israel to proclaim the kingdom of heaven. He asks them to go with simplicity and to seek a home that will welcome them. He then explains that this peace will rest on the house that receives them, and will return to them if they are rejected.

For today: before speaking about our faith, let us begin with kind and respectful treatment. A sincere greeting and an attitude of peace open doors and show the character of Christ in everyday life.
exp.10:11:
Jesus says that, from the time John the Baptist began to preach until that moment, the kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence, or pressing forward with force. "The violent lay claim to it" describes people who take hold of it with determination and energy. Scholars understand this in different ways: some see hostile opposition to the kingdom; others see people who seek it with burning determination.

Jesus speaks to the crowds after John, who was in prison, sent messengers to ask whether He was the Messiah. Jesus defends John as the promised messenger, the one who prepares the way. With John a new time begins, and the kingdom is announced with urgency, amid both rejection and enthusiasm.

For today: do not seek God with indifference. If the kingdom matters to you, give it your determination: devote time to prayer, to the Bible, and to obedience, even when there are obstacles.
exp.14:15:
Jesus asks Peter and the other disciples, "Do you still not understand?" The word "understand" means to grasp the meaning of something. The question means they had not yet grasped what He was teaching.

Jesus had just explained that what makes a person unclean is not eating without washing one's hands, as the Pharisees' tradition held. Peter asked Him to explain that saying. Jesus answers with a tone of surprise and firm affection, because they had been with Him for a long time and still thought like the religious teachers. Right away He explains that what truly defiles comes out of the heart.

For today: do not be discouraged if you do not understand something in the Bible. Ask God, as Peter did, and let Him correct your way of thinking with patience.
exp.16:18:
Afterward the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked him a sincere question: why couldn't they drive the demon out? The word for coming near is "came," the word for being alone is "privately," and the phrase for casting out means driving it out.

The ones asking are the disciples, and they are puzzled. Jesus had just healed the boy, and a worried father had reported that the disciples were unable to help him. They had earlier received authority to drive out demons (Matthew 10:1), so their failure surprised them. They chose to ask in private, perhaps out of embarrassment or out of respect. Jesus will answer by pointing to their little faith.

For today: when we fail or do not understand something, we can come to Jesus honestly, without hiding our confusion. He does not turn away the one who asks with humility; rather, he teaches us to trust and to depend on God in prayer.
exp.3:19:
Matthew 4:20 says that Simon Peter and Andrew, when they heard Jesus' call, at once left their nets and followed him. The phrase "at once" in the verse means without delay. Their nets were their tools and their livelihood, so leaving them was a very real step.

Jesus was walking by the Sea of Galilee and called these two fishermen, saying, "Follow Me," that is, "come after Me." He promised to make them "fishers of men," an image that draws on their trade to speak of a new mission. The text does not say whether they had known him before; it only shows their prompt response to the call.

For today: following Jesus calls for concrete obedience. You may not leave your work, but you can ask yourself what keeps you from answering him promptly, and take one simple step of faith today.
exp.11:25:
Jesus says that if Satan drives out Satan, he is fighting against himself. Then his kingdom would be divided and could not last. "Drives out" means to force someone to leave, and "last" means to continue and hold on.

The Pharisees had just watched Jesus free a man who was controlled by a demon. Instead of recognizing that power, they said he was acting with the help of Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons. Jesus, knowing their thoughts, shows them with simple logic that their accusation makes no sense. Then he points out that the power of God is the one at work, and that the kingdom of God had already arrived among them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, out of pride or prejudice, we call evil what is clearly the work of good. The verse also reminds us to care for unity in the family and the church, because division wears down and destroys.
exp.16:1:
He says that Jesus was transfigured, that is, his appearance changed before Peter, James, and John. His face shone like the sun, and his clothes became as white as the light. It was something visible and real to the three disciples.

Matthew tells what his witnesses saw. Jesus took them aside to a high mountain, six days after Peter had recognized him as the Christ and Jesus had announced his coming death. This moment revealed his divine glory before the cross. The verse does not say which mountain it was, and it is uncertain.

When the road gets hard, remember who Jesus is. His glory is real, even when we do not see it. Take a moment today to look at him with confidence and to listen to him.
exp.25:20:
Jesus is at the table with his twelve disciples, sharing the Passover meal. In the middle of the meal, he tells them seriously that one of them is going to betray him. He introduces the warning with "Truly I tell you," which means "I assure you, this is true," and then states it plainly. To betray someone means to hand them over to their enemies.

He speaks shortly before his arrest and crucifixion. He knows what is coming and does not hide it. The disciples become deeply saddened, and each one asks, "Is it I, Lord?", which shows that none of them felt completely sure of himself. Jesus endures this betrayal coming from someone very close to him.

Today we can examine our own hearts with humility, without thinking ourselves more faithful than others. Let us ask the Lord to keep us from turning away from him, and let us trust that he knows even our weaknesses.
exp.7:10:
Jesus says that many people will come from the east and the west, that is, from all parts of the world, and they will share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.

Jesus then speaks of his amazement at the faith of a Roman centurion, a foreigner who trusted that Jesus could heal his servant with only a word. Jesus says he had not found such great faith even in Israel. With this, he announces that God welcomes people from all nations, and he warns that inherited privileges do not replace personal trust in him.

For today: do not take your relationship with God for granted because of your family, your church, or your history. Trust in Jesus simply, like the centurion, and welcome with joy those who come from places and backgrounds different from yours.
exp.25:43:
He left them again, went away once more, and prayed a third time, saying the same thing as before. The cup is an image of the suffering that awaited him, the cross.

Jesus is in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before he is arrested. He feels deep anguish. Meanwhile, his disciples cannot manage to stay awake. He seeks his Father and gives his will over to God's, for he knows what is coming.

For today: there is nothing wrong with praying several times about the same thing. Jesus did not look for new or impressive words, but once again laid his burden before God with honesty. When you are going through something hard, you can repeat your heart to God, and finish by saying, "Your will be done."
exp.14:26:
She does not argue with Jesus. She accepts what he says and turns his words to her advantage. The word "dogs" here is a gentle one, the kind that speaks of animals kept as pets in the home. "Crumbs" are the small pieces of bread that fall while people eat. She says, "Yes, Lord," and asks for even a small share of his goodness.

She is a Canaanite woman, not an Israelite, who comes to Jesus to ask for help for her daughter. Jesus had said that it was not right to take the children's bread and give it to the dogs. Many understand that he was testing her faith, though the text does not explain his reasons. She answers with humility and trust, and Jesus praises her faith and heals her daughter.

We can come near to God with humility and not give up when the answer is slow. A simple faith trusts that his goodness reaches even to the crumbs.
exp.11:5:
Jesus says that someone greater than the temple is here with them. "One greater" refers to Himself. The temple was the most sacred place for the Jews, so this claim is very strong. The words "I tell you" show that He speaks with authority of His own.

Jesus is responding to the Pharisees, who accused his disciples of picking heads of grain on the Sabbath. He reminds them of two examples: David eating the consecrated bread, and the priests who worked in the temple on the Sabbath without being guilty. If the temple allowed those exceptions, then all the more Jesus, who is greater, can say what is right. Interpreters agree that Jesus presents Himself with divine authority.

For today: Jesus deserves first place, above our traditions, buildings, and rules. We can ask ourselves whether we care more about religious forms than about mercy and about Christ Himself.
exp.15:17:
Jesus tells Peter that he is Peter, and that on this rock he will build his church. He promises that the gates of Hades, the place of the dead, will not be able to overcome it. To prevail means to win out or gain the upper hand.

Jesus speaks this after Peter confessed: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Christians have understood "this rock" in different ways: Peter himself, his confession of faith, or Christ. There is a play on words, since "Peter" means "rock." Jesus speaks of his church as something he himself builds and protects.

For today: if Christ builds his church, you do not have to carry the weight of holding it up. Serve with confidence and humility, and rest in the fact that faith in Jesus as the Son of God is the firm foundation, even in difficult times.
exp.4:33:
Jesus says that we should not swear at all. "Swear" means to affirm something by calling on God or something sacred as a witness. Here he mentions heaven, and he explains that we should not swear by it because it is "God's throne," that is, the place where God rules.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Earlier he had quoted the old law: do not swear falsely, and keep what you have promised to the Lord. Some people used oaths to sound more believable, or to look for excuses. Jesus goes to the heart of the matter: the truth needs no decoration. Christians understand in different ways whether this forbids every oath, such as an oath in court, or only the casual ones.

Today, try to be a person so honest that your simple "yes" or "no" deserves to be trusted. Keep what you promise, without showing off or exaggerating.
exp.17:20:
Peter comes to Jesus with a sincere question: how many times must he forgive a brother who wrongs him? He even offers a number of his own: up to seven times? The phrase "came to Jesus" means "approached Jesus," and the phrase "sins against me" means "wronged me or hurt me."

Peter speaks after Jesus has taught about correcting a brother who fails and about the life of the community gathered in his name. Peter probably thought seven times was already generous, since many teachers of his time asked for forgiveness fewer times. Jesus will answer with a much broader teaching about mercy.

For today: instead of keeping count of the offenses, ask God for help to forgive a specific person. Forgiving does not mean saying the harm did not matter, but letting go of the desire for revenge and trusting in God's justice and grace.
exp.20:19:
The disciples see that the fig tree dried up right away, and they are amazed. They ask how it could happen so quickly. "Right away" here means "at once." "Amazed" means very surprised.

The speakers are the disciples, and they speak after Jesus told the fig tree that no one would ever eat fruit from it again. It had leaves, but no figs, and that seemed to promise something it did not deliver. Many understand this as a sign about the lack of true fruit in Israel, though some interpret it in other ways. Jesus uses their amazement to teach them about faith and prayer.

For today: it is not enough to appear to have a spiritual life; God looks for real fruit. And when we pray, let us do so with simple faith, trusting God and bringing our requests to him.
exp.8:30:
This verse tells how the two blind men whom Jesus healed, as soon as they went out, began to spread the news about him throughout the whole region. The word "but" marks a contrast with what Jesus had asked of them, and "spread the news" means they made him known to everyone.

Here Matthew is telling the story. Jesus had just restored their sight because of their faith, and he firmly told them not to tell anyone. The men, full of joy, did not stay quiet. It is not known for certain why Jesus asked for silence; some think he wanted to avoid crowds who would come looking only for miracles. Whatever the reason, their disobedience is striking.

For today: gratitude is natural when God works in our lives. But let us learn from this passage to join joy with obedience, asking for wisdom to know when and how to speak of what God has done.
exp.26:22:
This verse shows Pilate asking the crowd, "Why? What evil has He done?" The word "governor" here refers to the Roman authority who was judging the case. But the people do not answer with reasons; they only shout all the louder, "Crucify Him!"

Pilate speaks with the crowd gathered in front of his judgment seat in Jerusalem. It was the custom to release a prisoner at the feast, and the people asked for Barabbas. The verses before this one say that the chief priests and the elders had persuaded the crowd. Pilate asks because he sees no crime in Jesus, but in the end he gives way to the pressure.

For today: the pressure of the group can drown out truth and justice. Before you join in with what everyone is saying, ask as Pilate did: "What evil has He done?" And, unlike him, have the courage to act according to what you know is right.
exp.7:31:
Jesus answers with a single word: "Go!" The demons come out of the two men and enter the pigs. The whole herd rushes down the steep bank into the sea and dies in the waters. A herd is a group of animals, and the steep bank is the slope that drops to the water.

Jesus speaks with authority, and the demons ask his permission, which shows that they are under his command. He had just freed two men controlled by demons. Instead of rejoicing, the people of the town ask him to leave. We do not know for certain why: some think it was fear, others that they cared more about the economic loss.

For today: Jesus has real power over evil and values people more than possessions. Examine what matters most to you when God works in your life, and do not let fear or self-interest drive you away from him.
exp.26:27:
They stripped Jesus of his clothes and put a scarlet robe on him, a deep red cloak like those worn by soldiers or kings. Being stripped meant he was left exposed in front of everyone.

Matthew tells what happened after Pilate, the Roman governor, ordered Jesus to be flogged and handed over to be crucified. The soldiers, in the praetorium, mocked him for claiming to be King. It is an account of humiliation, but Matthew writes it to show who Jesus really is.

Jesus endured the mockery and shame without answering with hatred. Today, when someone humiliates us or mocks us, we can remember that Christ went through this first, and ask him for strength to respond with patience and trust in God.
exp.7:4:
It says that Jesus arrived in Capernaum, a town in Galilee. There a centurion came to him, that is, an officer of the Roman army who was in charge of about a hundred soldiers. This man came pleading with him, that is, asking with humility and need. The phrase "came to him" shows that the centurion took the first step.

Matthew tells this right after the healing of the leper. First Jesus touches an outcast Jew; now he attends to a foreigner with authority. The centurion belonged to the power that dominated Israel, yet he recognizes that he needs help. The next verse shows that he pleads for his sick servant, not for himself.

For today: we can come to Jesus with confidence, no matter who we are, and ask him also for others. Intercessory prayer is born from love and humility.
exp.21:29:
Jesus says that after the resurrection people will no longer marry. The words "marry" and "given in marriage" refer to getting married. They will be "like the angels in heaven," meaning they will live in a different condition from the present one, without any need for earthly marriage.

Jesus is answering the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They presented him with the case of a woman who married seven brothers, one after another, to make the idea of rising from the dead look absurd. Jesus tells them they are mistaken because they do not understand the Scriptures or the power of God.

For today: we do not measure what God prepares by the limited ideas of this world. We can trust that his promise of eternal life is real and greater than we can imagine. In the meantime, let us value our relationships, serving and loving with our hope placed in God.
exp.5:6:
Jesus says that when we pray we should not babble on like pagans, saying the same empty things over and over. To "babble on" means speaking at great length, like someone who chatters endlessly. The pagans were people who did not know the God of Israel. They thought they would be heard because of the great number of their words.

Jesus is speaking in the Sermon on the Mount. Earlier he corrected those who prayed in order to be seen by others. Now he corrects another mistake: believing that many words will convince God. Right after this he gives the reason: the Father already knows what we need. Then he teaches the Lord's Prayer, a simple and brief prayer.

For today: pray with sincerity and simplicity, like a child speaking with their Father. You do not need long sentences or special words. Tell him with confidence what is in your heart, knowing that he hears you.
exp.16:9:
The disciples ask Jesus a question as they come down from the mountain. They want to know why the scribes, the teachers of the Law, say that Elijah must come first. The verse reads "Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?", so the reader will see that wording in the question itself. If Elijah has to come before, they ask, how does that fit with what they have just seen?

The disciples have just seen Jesus transfigured, standing with Moses and Elijah. Jesus had told them to keep quiet about that vision until his resurrection. This confused them, and they remembered the teaching that Elijah would come before the Messiah, based on Malachi 4:5. Jesus will answer that Elijah has already come, and most interpreters see in this John the Baptist.

For today: when something about God does not add up for you, ask sincerely, as they did. Jesus does not reject honest questions; he uses them to teach us.
exp.10:8:
Jesus asks the crowd what they went out into the desert to see when they went to find John. He answers that John was indeed a prophet, and more than a prophet. The question about what they went out to see is the same question, and the words "Yes, I tell you" carry the same sense of "I assure you."

Jesus speaks to the crowd after John's disciples, while John was in prison, had left with their question. Jesus wants the people to value John: he was not weak like a reed swaying in the wind, nor was he looking for luxury. Then he explains that John was the messenger announced by God to prepare the way for the Messiah.

Today, this invites us to ask what we are looking for when we draw near to God and to his Word. We can value those who point us to Christ with firmness and humility, and ask God to make us people of firm convictions, not moved by every wind.
exp.12:54:
What it says: The people of Nazareth wonder how Jesus can teach with such wisdom. They know him as the carpenter's son, and they mention his mother, whose name is Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas.

Context: The speakers are the people of his hometown, who watched him grow up. They are amazed at his teaching in the synagogue, but they do not believe, because they see him as someone ordinary. About who these brothers were, some Christians understand them as children of Mary and Joseph, others as cousins or as children of Joseph from an earlier marriage. That is why Jesus says that a prophet is not honored in his own country.

For today: Let us not judge people only by their background or by what we already think we know about them. Let us keep our hearts open to recognize the work of God in ordinary places and people.
exp.11:14:
Here the verse says that Jesus, once he became aware of the Pharisees' plot against him, withdrew from that place. Large crowds followed him, and he healed all of them.

The narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just healed a man's hand on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees, angered, plotted together to kill him. Jesus does not respond with confrontation but quietly withdraws. Matthew then connects this with Isaiah's prophecy about a gentle servant. Scholars generally agree that Matthew wants to show the humility of Jesus, though not everyone agrees on every detail.

Today, when we face opposition or unfair criticism, we do not always need to argue. We can step away in peace and keep doing good for those who need us.
exp.4:26:
Jesus reminds his listeners of a very well-known commandment from the law of Moses: "Do not commit adultery." To commit adultery means to have sexual relations with someone who is not your husband or wife. The phrase "You have heard that it was said" simply points back to the teaching the people already knew.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, before his disciples and the crowd. He is explaining the true meaning of God's law. Here he begins to show that God does not look only at outward actions, but also at what is in the heart, as the verses that follow say.

For today: it is not enough to avoid visible sin. Today you can ask God to help you guard your eyes and your thoughts, and to respect other people and your own marriage from the heart.
exp.23:27:
It says that wherever there is a dead body, the vultures gather there. Vultures are birds that feed on carcasses. "Wherever" is the plain modern word for the phrase, and the verse is a common saying: what is out in the open is noticed and draws attention.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives about his return. He warns them not to believe those who say that the Messiah is hidden somewhere. His coming will be as clear as lightning. Some think the saying points to how obvious his coming will be; others think it speaks of judgment. Interpreters understand it in several ways.

For today: do not live in anxiety or be swept along by anyone who promises to know dates or secret places. Measure every teaching against the words of Jesus, and live in faith, ready for his return.
exp.11:32:
Jesus says that a tree cannot be separated from its fruit. If the tree is good, it will produce good fruit; if the tree is bad, it will produce bad fruit. The wording "make a tree bad" points to the tree itself being unsound, and here the idea is simply bad. The conclusion is clear: a tree is known by what it produces.

Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees, who had just seen him free a man possessed by a demon, and they said he did it by the power of Beelzebub. Jesus shows them that their wicked words reveal a hardened heart. Attributing to the devil the work of the Holy Spirit was a very serious accusation, and that is why he speaks with such firmness.

For today: what we say and do reflects what is in our heart. Instead of only polishing our words, let us ask God to transform our inner life, and his fruit will be seen.
exp.10:9:
Jesus says that John the Baptist is the one about whom Scripture spoke when it announced a messenger sent ahead.

Jesus speaks to the crowd that had gone out into the wilderness to hear John, who was now in prison. He asks them what they expected to see: someone weak or luxuriously dressed? No, a prophet, and more than a prophet. The quotation comes from Malachi 3:1, and Jesus applies it to John, who announced the coming of the Messiah.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are getting our hearts ready for Christ. John did not seek attention for himself, but pointed to Jesus. We can imitate him by living simply and pointing others toward Christ through our words and our lives.
exp.18:15:
A man comes up to Jesus and asks what good thing he must do to obtain eternal life. He calls him "Teacher," a respectful title for someone he admires. The phrase about coming up to him simply means that he approached Jesus.

The account goes on to say that he was a young and wealthy man, and the scene follows right after Jesus blessed the children, who receive the kingdom with simplicity. This man, by contrast, thinks that eternal life is earned by doing something. Jesus will lead him to think about the goodness of God and about the commandments.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek God only to complete a list of good works, or whether we trust in him with a humble heart, like a child. Let us ask that question honestly and be willing to hear his answer, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.12:28:
Here the owner of the field tells his workers not to pull up the weeds. The wording in your verse is "if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them." The reason is that, in pulling out the weeds, they could also uproot the wheat. The weed is a plant that looks very much like wheat while it is young, and its roots can become tangled with the wheat's roots.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd in the parable of the weeds. The servants ask whether they should clean up the field, but the owner asks for patience: the separation will happen at the harvest. Later, Jesus explains that the field is the world and that the harvest represents the end of the age.

For today: it is not our place to decide who belongs to God and who does not. Instead of judging or looking down on others, we can live with patience, love, and good witness, and trust that God will do justice in his own time.
exp.24:4:
It says the bridegroom was delayed for a long time before he arrived, and that the ten virgins became drowsy. "Became drowsy" means they began to nod off, and then they fell fast asleep. "Was delayed" means he came later than expected. Both the wise and the foolish ones fell asleep.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, teaching with a parable about his return. The important point here is that they all fell asleep, so the difference between them was not the sleep, but that some had brought spare oil and others had not. Interpreters explain the oil in various ways, and there is no single certain reading.

For today: do not be anxious about the waiting; prepare in a simple and steady way. Grow your faith every day, with prayer and the Word, so that it does not depend on the moment or on what others have.
exp.12:45:
It says that a merchant who was looking for fine pearls found one very precious pearl. He went away, sold everything he had, and bought it. The verse notes that the wording of this verse is plain and modern, and that the merchant is simply a person who buys and sells goods.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, teaching in parables about the kingdom of heaven. This parable goes alongside the one about the hidden treasure. In both, someone discovers something of enormous value and gives up everything to obtain it. The difference is that here the man was searching, while in the earlier one he found the treasure without looking for it. Some see in the pearl Christ or the kingdom; others stress the value of responding to God wholeheartedly.

Today: think about what things compete with God in your heart. Ask him for help to put him first, with joy and not out of obligation.
exp.0:2:
This verse continues the list of Jesus' ancestors. "Father of" means that the man named was the parent of the one who follows. Judah had two twin sons with Tamar, Perez and Zerah. Then Perez became the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram.

The names in your Bible are given in their modern spellings: "Judah" is Judah, "Tamar" is Tamar, and "Perez" is Perez.

Matthew, the author of the Gospel, begins by showing that Jesus is the promised Messiah, a descendant of Abraham and of David. He writes especially for Jewish readers, who valued genealogies greatly. It stands out that he mentions Tamar, a woman whose story (Genesis 38) was complicated and painful. Why he includes her is not stated here; many think it shows the grace of God.

For today: God can work through imperfect family stories. If your past or your family's past carries wounds or mistakes, they do not define you; God can bring redemption and purpose.
exp.10:3:
Jesus answers John's disciples: go back and tell John what you yourselves are hearing and seeing.

Jesus is the one speaking. John the Baptist is in prison, and he sends word asking whether Jesus is the expected Messiah or whether they should look for someone else. Jesus does not simply say "yes." Instead, he points to his works: healings and good news for the poor, which fulfill what the prophets announced. It is not known for certain why John asked; some think he had doubts, others that he wanted to strengthen his own disciples.

For today: when you have doubts or go through a hard time, do not stay silent. Bring your questions to Jesus honestly, and remember what he has already done, both in the Bible and in your own life.
exp.17:5:
Jesus says that whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in him to stumble would be better off with a large millstone hung around his neck and sunk in the depths of the sea. The word "stumble" means to cause someone to fall, to sin, or to lose their faith. A millstone was so heavy that a donkey would turn it to grind grain.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, who had just asked who was the greatest in the kingdom. He set a child in the middle of them as an example of humility. Many understand the "little ones" to be simple and humble believers, not only children; the text allows both ideas. The image is harsh to show how serious this is before God.

For today: take care with your words and your example, especially with those who are new in the faith or more vulnerable. Ask yourself whether what you say or do brings them closer to Jesus or makes them doubt.
exp.20:16:
Jesus left the religious leaders who were angry with him, went out of Jerusalem, and went to Bethany. There he spent the night.

"Spent the night" describes simply where he stayed. The verse does not say whose home he stayed in.

This is Matthew's account, written about Jesus. He had just entered Jerusalem and healed people in the temple. The children were praising him, and the chief priests and scribes became indignant. Jesus answered them with Scripture and then withdrew. Bethany was a nearby village, and many believe his friends Martha, Mary, and Lazarus lived there, though this text does not say so.

Jesus does not always stay to argue. Sometimes he withdraws to rest and pray. If a conversation brings only anger and no listening, we can do the same: speak with truth, then step away in peace and return to God.
exp.25:51:
Jesus tells one of his disciples to put his sword back in its place. He warns that those who choose violence to fight will themselves end up dying by violence.

Jesus speaks in the garden of Gethsemane, just as he is being arrested. One of the disciples, whom John identifies as Peter, struck a servant of the high priest. Jesus stops him because he did not come to establish his kingdom by force. In the verses that follow, he explains that he could ask for help from angels, but the plan of God announced in the Scriptures had to be fulfilled. Some understand the statement as a general principle; others see it as a warning for that particular moment.

When we feel hurt or treated unfairly by someone, we can ask God for patience before responding with anger or revenge, and seek peace.
exp.14:24:
Matthew tells us that the Canaanite woman, after Jesus seemed to ignore her, came closer and knelt before Him. Kneeling shows respect and humility. Her prayer is very short and direct: "Lord, help me!"

This woman was not an Israelite, and she had been pleading for her daughter, who was tormented. Jesus had kept silent and had said that He was sent first to the lost sheep of Israel. She did not give up. Scholars interpret Jesus' silence in several ways, but the account shows that her faith came to light and grew stronger.

When you are in need and feel that God is silent, do not walk away. Come near with humility, be sincere, and ask for help in simple words. Persisting with trust is also faith.
exp.23:47:
This verse speaks of a servant who, instead of being faithful, thinks to himself, "My master will be away a long time." He is called "wicked" because his inner attitude leads him to live as if no one were going to call him to account.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, as he teaches them about his return. He has just praised the faithful servant who keeps doing his work. Now he presents the contrast: the one who, expecting a long absence, stops being responsible. The following verses show the consequences of that carelessness.

For today: do not use the waiting as an excuse for living without commitment. Although we do not know when Christ will come, we can be faithful each day, treating others well and honestly carrying out what God has entrusted to us.
exp.20:42:
Jesus tells his hearers that the kingdom of God, that is, the place of those who live under God's rule and blessings, will be taken away from them and given to a people who produce its fruit. "I tell you" means the same as "I say to you," and "fruit" refers to the works and the life that please God.

Jesus speaks in the temple to the religious leaders, right after the parable of the wicked tenants. They had rejected God's messengers, and soon they would reject the Son. The verses that follow show that they understood he was speaking about them. Interpreters debate who this "people" is: many see the followers of Jesus, both Jews and non-Jews, and others see a new people of God.

For today: having a religious name or belonging to a church is not enough. Ask God to show you which fruits are missing in your life, such as love, justice and humility, and obey him today in one concrete action.
exp.18:8:
Jesus says that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery. He also says that whoever marries a woman who has been divorced commits adultery. People today understand what the exception covers, and whether it allows a new marriage, in different ways.

Jesus is responding to some Pharisees who are testing him about divorce. He reminds them that Moses allowed it because of the hardness of their hearts, but that from the beginning God intended marriage to be a lasting union. His disciples are surprised at how demanding his words are.

For today: value your marriage as a serious covenant. Care for honest conversation, forgiveness, and faithfulness, and if there is a crisis, seek pastoral help. Someone who has lived through a divorce can also draw near to God with humility, for his grace remains available.
exp.20:0:
This verse tells us that Jesus and his disciples were already close to Jerusalem. They arrived at Bethphage, a village on the Mount of Olives. From there, Jesus sent out two of his disciples to carry out a task.

The name "Jerusalem" refers to the city they were approaching, and Bethphage is the place they reached just outside it. The phrase "approached Jerusalem" means they were already very near the city.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Matthew. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, in the days before his crucifixion. With what follows, Matthew shows that Jesus enters the city as King in a humble way, and that this fulfills what was spoken by the prophet Zechariah. Jesus knows what is about to happen and prepares for it calmly.

Today we can learn to obey even when an instruction seems small or strange. The disciples did not see the whole plan, but they trusted Jesus and went. We can take the step God shows us today, trusting that He sees the whole path.
exp.8:35:
This verse tells us that Jesus looked at the crowds and was moved with compassion for them. He saw that they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd to care for them or guide them.

It is part of Matthew's account. Jesus went through cities and villages teaching, proclaiming the kingdom and healing the sick. Meanwhile, the Pharisees accused him of acting by the power of the demon. In the face of that hardness, Jesus responds with tenderness toward the people. Right after this, he asks his disciples to pray that the Lord of the harvest will send workers, because the need is great.

For today: when we see people worn down or lost, let us not judge them from a distance. Let us ask God for a compassionate heart, pray for them, and be ready to help them with a concrete gesture of kindness and truth.
exp.10:1:
This verse says that John the Baptist was in prison when he heard about what Jesus was doing. "The works of Christ" means what Jesus was doing: his healings, his teaching, and his signs. So John sent some of his disciples to ask Jesus something.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. John had announced Jesus, but now he was in prison, and as far as we know, Herod had put him there. His question, in the verses that follow, shows that he had doubts or was seeking confirmation. Scholars understand this in different ways, and the Bible does not explain it fully.

For today: when you have doubts or go through difficult times, do not turn away from God. Do as John did: bring your questions directly to Jesus, with sincerity, and look for his answer in his Word.
exp.24:0:
Matthew 25:1 says that the kingdom of heaven will be like ten young unmarried women who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom, that is, the groom of the wedding. The phrase "will be like" means "will resemble" in this sentence. "At that time" points back to the time of Christ's return, which was mentioned earlier.

Jesus speaks on the Mount of Olives, answering his disciples about his coming and the end of the age (Matthew 24). This is a parable: a simple story meant to teach a truth. Many understand the bridegroom to represent Christ. The details of wedding customs of that time are explained in several ways, so it is best not to claim too much.

For today: the parable invites us to live prepared, not merely with an appearance of faith. Today you can set aside a few minutes to pray and read the Bible, so that your faith is real and steady, ready for when Christ returns.
exp.9:2:
This verse continues the list of the twelve apostles: Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew the tax collector, James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. A tax collector was a man who collected taxes for the Roman government, a job that was looked down on by the Jewish people.

The one speaking in this passage is the account by Matthew. Jesus has just called his twelve disciples and given them authority to heal and to drive out spirits. Matthew includes himself in the list and remembers that he had been a tax collector, without hiding his past.

For today: Jesus calls people who are very different from one another and ordinary, with varied pasts. If you feel unqualified, remember that God can use you just as you are. Respond to his calling with humility and a willingness to serve.
exp.14:8:
This passage says that the worship of some people is worthless, because they teach as if rules made up by people were commands from God. "They worship me in vain" means they show respect to God through words or religious practices, but it accomplishes nothing. "Precepts of men" refers to human rules placed on the same level as the word of God.

Jesus is the speaker. Some Pharisees and scribes had come from Jerusalem to challenge him because his disciples did not follow the tradition of washing their hands before eating. Jesus answers them by quoting Isaiah: they were careful about outward things, but their hearts were far from God. Then he teaches the crowd that what truly defiles a person comes from within.

For today: check whether you are giving more importance to human customs or rules than to loving God from the heart. Before demanding something of others, ask yourself whether the Bible actually teaches it, and seek sincere worship.
exp.8:7:
This verse tells how the crowd responded when they saw Jesus heal the paralytic. They were filled with awe, which means they were deeply amazed, and they glorified God. The phrase "who had given such authority to men" points to the authority to act that God had given. They recognized that God had given this authority to men.

Matthew records this after Jesus told the paralytic that his sins were forgiven. Some of the scribes thought this was blasphemy. Jesus healed the man to show that he had authority to forgive sins. The words "to men" can be understood in several ways: the people may not have grasped everything, but they recognized that God was at work.

For today: when you see God's hand in the lives of others, do not stay silent. Give thanks to him and praise him simply.
exp.2:1:
John the Baptist proclaims: "Repent." That means change your mind and your direction, leave sin behind, and turn back to God. The reason he gives is that "the kingdom of heaven is near," meaning that God's rule was close at hand, because the Messiah was about to appear.

John speaks in the wilderness of Judea, and Matthew explains that he fulfills what was spoken by Isaiah: a voice preparing the way of the Lord. His plain clothing and simple food show a serious message without decoration. His call was to prepare the heart before Jesus arrived.

For today: repentance is not only feeling guilty, but changing direction. Think of a habit, an attitude, or a relationship where you need to turn back to God, and take one concrete step today, such as asking forgiveness or letting go of something that pulls you away from Him.
exp.3:15:
This verse says that the people living in darkness have seen a great light. It speaks of those living in the land of the shadow of death, that is, a place marked by sorrow, spiritual ignorance, and hopelessness. For them a light has dawned, that is, it has shone and the day has broken.

Matthew is the one who writes. He quotes the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 9:1-2) to show that Jesus came to Galilee, an area with many mixed peoples, called "of the Gentiles." Matthew sees in this the fulfillment of God's promise. There Jesus began to preach and to call his first disciples.

For today: if you find yourself in a dark moment, Jesus is not far away. Draw near to him in prayer and in his Word, and let his light guide you, even if it is one step at a time.
exp.25:68:
It says that Peter was sitting outside, in the courtyard. A servant girl came up to him and told him that he too was with Jesus, the Galilean. The words "the Galilean" point to the fact that Jesus came from the region of Galilee, which was also where Peter was from.

While inside they were mistreating Jesus, Peter had followed from a distance and sat down among the people. The servant girl speaks because she recognizes him as a follower of Jesus. This is the beginning of the three denials that Jesus had already foretold. Peter, who earlier promised he would not abandon him, now feels fear.

For today: the fear of looking foolish or being hurt can keep us from speaking about our faith. If we have failed, let us remember that Peter was restored afterward. Let us ask God for courage and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.25:7:
When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and asked, "Why this waste?" The word "waste" here means the perfume was being poured out for nothing. "Indignant" points to real anger, not just a doubt.

The account takes place in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a few days before the crucifixion. The ones speaking are the disciples, and from the context they think the perfume could have been sold to help the poor. Their concern seems good, but they did not understand the value of that act. Jesus called it a "good work" and defended the woman.

For today: before criticizing someone's act of love toward God, it is wise to pause and ask what is in their heart. We can serve the needy without looking down on sincere worship.
exp.20:3:
This verse says that what Jesus was about to do, entering Jerusalem riding on a donkey with its colt, was no accident. It took place to bring about what a prophet had spoken long before. To fulfill something means to make it come true.

Matthew, the writer, explains why Jesus sent his disciples to fetch the animals. The verses that follow quote words from Zechariah 9:9, with an echo of Isaiah 62:11. Jesus presents himself as the promised King, yet he comes humbly, without a warhorse or military force. Some scholars see in this a gesture of humility and peace.

For today: God keeps what he promises, though sometimes in surprising ways. We can trust his Word and follow the example of Jesus, seeking to influence others with gentleness and service, not with pride or force.
exp.10:17:
What it says: Jesus tells us that John the Baptist lived with great simplicity and self-discipline, not joining in banquets or ordinary meals, and the people rejected him, saying, "He has a demon!" The phrase "neither eating nor drinking" does not mean that John went without nourishment, but that he lived a very sober and set-apart life.

Context: Jesus is the speaker. He compares "this generation" to children playing in the marketplace who complain that their friends will not dance when they play the flute or mourn when they sing a funeral song. He wants to show that the people were looking for excuses: they rejected John for being too serious and rejected Jesus for mixing with everyone. No form of God's call seemed acceptable to them.

For today: Let us examine our hearts to see whether we truly want to hear God or are only looking for excuses. Sometimes we criticize the manner of the messenger so that we do not have to face the message. Let us ask for humility to receive the truth, even when it comes in a way different from what we expected.
exp.8:26:
As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed Him, calling out, "Have mercy on us!" "Mercy" means compassion that moves someone to help one who is suffering. "Son of David" was a title for the promised Messiah, the king God would send.

Shortly before this, Jesus had raised a man's daughter back to life, and the news had spread throughout the whole region. The account here is Matthew's, and it is the blind men who call out. By calling him "Son of David," they show that they believed Jesus was the Messiah, even though they could not see him with their eyes.

For today: when you find yourself in need, cry out to Jesus sincerely and without pretense. You do not need elegant words, only a heart that trusts in his compassion and keeps seeking him.
exp.26:54:
This verse says that many women were there, watching the crucifixion of Jesus from a distance. They had followed him from Galilee to care for him, that is, they had helped him with his daily needs. The word "minister" here speaks of practical and constant care.

The one speaking here is Matthew, the narrator of the Gospel. After telling of Jesus' death and the reactions of the centurion, he shows us those who were still present. The verses that follow name some of them: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. While many fled, they stayed, though at a distance.

For today: faith is sometimes shown by being present and serving faithfully, even when it hurts or when we do not understand everything. Ask yourself whom you can accompany and serve faithfully this week, without seeking applause.
exp.23:31:
Jesus tells us to learn this lesson from the fig tree. As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near. The word "tender" here describes a branch that turns soft and full of new life. It is a simple comparison, drawn from nature.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after they asked him about the signs of the end. He has just described his coming in glory. Now he teaches them that certain signs show that his coming is near. Scholars disagree about how to apply the phrases "this generation" and "these things," and it is honest to acknowledge this.

For today: live alert and awake, without anxiety or excessive curiosity about dates. Just as one watches the fig tree, look at your life with faith, pray, and remain faithful to Christ each day, ready for his return.
exp.25:15:
This verse says that, after accepting the payment, Judas began to watch closely and look for the right moment to hand Jesus over. The phrase "the right moment" means a suitable time, and "hand Jesus over" means putting him into the hands of his enemies. Judas did not act on impulse; he planned it with care.

The one telling the account is Matthew. Judas, one of the twelve disciples, had already agreed with the chief priests to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver. Matthew shows that the betrayal was a deliberate decision. At the same time, Jesus continues to prepare the Passover calmly, knowing that his hour is drawing near.

For today: a wrong decision often grows little by little, when a person keeps turning it over and looks for the moment to carry it out. It is wise to bring our thoughts and temptations to God early, before they become plans, and to ask him for a faithful heart.
exp.27:4:
The angel spoke to the women who had come to the tomb. He told them not to be afraid, because he knew whom they were looking for: Jesus, the one who was crucified.

The angel had just appeared with a look like lightning, and the guards were left as if dead from fright. The women were frightened too. He speaks to them calmly to prepare them for the good news that follows: Jesus has risen. Notice that he recognizes them and knows what they are looking for.

Today, when something frightens us or we do not understand what God is doing, we can remember that he knows what we are seeking and speaks to us with tenderness. Let us seek Jesus with sincerity, and he will give us hope in the midst of fear.
exp.9:35:
This verse says that, when people follow Jesus, those closest to them, their own family, can become opponents. "Enemies" here are members of the home who oppose or reject. The word means opposition or rejection, not that Jesus wants hatred within families.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples when he sends them out to preach. He warns them that their message divides, because not everyone will accept it. Here he cites an idea from the prophet Micah (7:6). The "sword" is an image of division, not of violence. Jesus asks that loyalty to him come above everything, even above family.

If your faith brings misunderstanding at home, do not lose heart or answer with harshness. Follow Christ with love, patience and respect, praying for your loved ones, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.6:25:
Jesus says that whoever hears his words but does not act on them is like a foolish man, a man without wisdom. That man built his house on sand, ground that may look like it will hold but offers no firmness. The "rock" mentioned in the previous verse refers to the solid foundation chosen by the wise man. The phrase "I will liken him" means that Jesus is about to compare the person to this picture.

Jesus is finishing the Sermon on the Mount, where he taught how someone who belongs to the kingdom of God lives. He speaks to his disciples and to a crowd. With this comparison he makes clear that it is not enough to admire his teachings: they must be put into practice. The people were astonished at his teaching.

For today: listening to a sermon or reading the Bible is good, but it is not enough. Choose one teaching of Jesus, such as forgiving or being generous, and practice it this week, even if it costs you a little. In this way your life is built on something firm.
exp.8:29:
Matthew tells us that Jesus healed two blind men: their eyes were opened. Right away he warned them sternly, ordering them firmly that they should tell no one. The sentence can stay as it is, with its plain meaning that he spoke to them with serious force.

The narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just asked them whether they believed he could heal them, and they answered that they did. Why he asked for silence is not stated here. Some think he wanted to avoid crowds who would come only for miracles, or misunderstandings about his mission as the Messiah. Others see humility. What is certain is that the blind men did not obey, and the news spread.

For today: faith in Jesus is also shown in obedience. They were eager to share what had happened, but Jesus had asked them for something else. We can ask ourselves whether, when we speak about what God has done for us, we are doing what he actually asks of us.
exp.24:39:
The King answers the righteous, who are amazed. He says that whatever they did for one of these least brothers of His, they did for Him.

Jesus speaks at the end of His teaching on the Mount of Olives, describing the judgment of the nations. The righteous ask when they cared for Him, since they do not remember doing so. Some understand the "least brothers" to be believers in general; others, the disciples sent by Christ. Both readings stress that practical love shows a real faith.

Today, think of someone close to you who is in need, such as a sick or lonely neighbor, and help them this week with a meal, a visit, or a phone call. Do it as if for Christ.
exp.3:9:
Jesus commands Satan to leave. He answers with Scripture: God alone is to be worshiped and served. "Away from Me" means "go away," and "Him only" means God and no one else.

Jesus speaks here after fasting forty days in the wilderness. The devil offers him the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:13, where Moses reminded Israel that they must not follow other gods. This is the third temptation, and Jesus rejects it firmly. Immediately the devil leaves, and angels come and minister to him.

Today we can ask ourselves what things compete for first place in our hearts: money, success, or the approval of others. When something promises us a great deal in return for putting God in second place, let us remember this verse and respond as Jesus did: God first.
exp.26:61:
This verse tells that on the day after Jesus' death, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate, the Roman governor. "Preparation Day" was the day of getting ready for the Sabbath, that is, Friday. So this meeting took place on the Sabbath.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Just before, Joseph of Arimathea buried Jesus, and the women were watching the tomb. Now the religious leaders, who had sought his death, are worried about what Jesus said about rising again. They are going to ask for the tomb to be guarded.

For today: We may try to silence the truth, but we cannot stop it. If we are uncomfortable with the words of Jesus, instead of resisting them, it is good to listen to them with humility and honesty.
exp.21:15:
They sent their disciples to Jesus, along with the Herodians, and called him "Teacher." They praised him: they said he is honest, teaches the way of God in accordance with the truth, and seeks favor from no one. The phrase "you pay no attention to external appearance" means he does not judge people by how important or impressive they look.

Those who speak are followers of the Pharisees and the Herodians, a group linked to the power of Herod. They usually did not get along, but they joined forces against Jesus. Their words were true, but not sincere: they wanted to trap him with a question about paying the tax to Caesar, as the following verse shows.

For today: let us be wary of flattery that seeks to manipulate. Let us ask God for a sincere heart, so that our kind words are honest and not a means to get something.
exp.13:21:
Right after Jesus fed the five thousand men, not counting women and children, Jesus immediately made his disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of him to the other side of the lake, while he dismissed the crowds. The word "immediately" means right away, and "made" here means that Jesus told them to go. "Dismissed" means he sent the people back to their homes.

Matthew tells us that Jesus was the one who took the initiative to separate the disciples from the crowd. The text does not explain the reason. John 6:15 suggests the people wanted to make him king, but Matthew does not say so.

For today: sometimes God tells us to move forward toward a place where we cannot see clearly, and then leaves us a time of waiting. Obeying without understanding everything is trusting that he remains close, even when we do not see him.
exp.7:2:
This verse tells how Jesus reached out and touched the man with leprosy. Then he said, "I am willing. Be clean!" and the leprosy was cleansed at once. The word "immediately" here means "right away," and the phrase "was cleansed" means the man was healed.

The man with leprosy had come to Jesus, knelt before him, and said, "Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean." In that time, the law of Moses kept people with leprosy apart from everyone else, and touching them made a person ceremonially unclean. Jesus touches him anyway. Afterward he tells him to show himself to the priest, as the law required (Leviticus 14), so that his healing would be confirmed.

For today: we can come to Jesus honestly, even with our wounds and shame. He does not turn away from us. We can also follow his example by approaching with compassion those whom others avoid.
exp.21:43:
It says that God the Father spoke to another "Lord," who is the Messiah: "Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet." To sit means to take a seat; the right hand means the place of honor and authority; and putting enemies under someone's feet is a picture of complete victory.

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees in the temple, shortly before his death. He quotes Psalm 110:1, which David wrote under the guidance of the Spirit. The Pharisees taught that the Christ would simply be a son of David. Jesus shows them that David calls him "Lord," so he is more than a descendant: he has a higher dignity. They could not answer him.

For today: if Christ reigns at God's right hand, we can trust that he has the final word over our fears and problems. Today, in prayer, hand over the situation that weighs on you and acknowledge him as Lord in truth.
exp.8:8:
This verse tells how Jesus, as he went on from there, saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. He told him, "Follow Me," and Matthew got up and followed him. The tax booth is where the government's taxes were collected, and the wording here is simple: Jesus speaks, and Matthew responds at once.

Here the narrator is describing the scene. Jesus has just healed a paralyzed man. Tax collectors were looked down on because they worked for Rome, and many of them collected more than they should. Even so, Jesus calls Matthew. Afterward, Matthew shares a meal with Jesus and other people who were rejected, and the Pharisees are scandalized.

For today: Jesus calls ordinary people, even those others despise. If you feel his invitation, respond with simplicity and obedience. And look at others with the same grace with which Christ looks at you.
exp.9:19:
When Jesus's disciples are brought before rulers because of their faith, they should not worry about what they are going to say. The verse speaks to "you all," and the word for worry means to be anxious or troubled. The Spirit of the Father will speak through them.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles when he sends them out to preach. He warns them that there will be opposition, trials, and even betrayal by family members. The promise is given for those difficult hours of persecution. Some think it applies mainly to those moments of witness under pressure, not as an excuse for failing to prepare in other situations.

If today you find yourself having to explain your faith in a tense moment, do not carry the fear of not having the perfect words. Pray, trust that God is with you, and speak with simplicity, love, and courage.
exp.18:13:
Jesus tells his disciples to let the little children come to him and not to stop them. "Let" means "allow," and "do not hinder them" means "do not get in their way." He says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to "such as these," that is, to those who are like them.

Some parents brought their children to Jesus so that he would place his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked them, perhaps thinking that Jesus was too busy. Jesus corrects his disciples and shows his affection for the little ones. Interpreters explain in various ways how they resemble the kingdom: in their trust, their humility, or their dependence.

Today we can welcome children with patience and give them a place in the church and in the family. We can also draw near to God with simplicity and trust, like a child running toward his father.
exp.26:34:
The verse tells us that the soldiers crucified Jesus and then divided up his clothing among themselves. To decide who would keep each piece, they cast lots, something like rolling dice. The verse for this comes in the next part of the verse, which says that it fulfilled what the prophet had spoken.

Here the narrator, Matthew, wants to show that what happened was not an accident. The words he has in mind come from Psalm 22:18, a psalm of David describing a righteous sufferer. The Roman soldiers were only doing what was customary: keeping the belongings of the condemned man. Without knowing it, they were fulfilling what had been written centuries before.

For today: when life feels unjust or out of control, remember that God does not lose the thread. Jesus suffered with a purpose, and that truth invites you to trust that God can also work in your darkest moments.
exp.23:3:
Jesus gives a very simple warning: be careful, do not let yourselves be deceived. "See to it" means "pay attention, be alert." "Anyone" includes everyone who hears him. It is a call to stay awake and think clearly.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They have just asked him when these things will happen and what the sign of his coming will be. Before giving signs, Jesus begins with this warning. Then he explains that many will come claiming to be the Christ, and there will be wars and rumors of wars. Christians understand in different ways how these words are fulfilled.

Today we can come to know well what Jesus taught by reading the Gospels faithfully. That way, when someone says something striking in his name, we can compare it with his word and not be carried away by fear or by excitement.
exp.23:32:
Just as the new leaves of the fig tree announce that summer is near, so the disciples should recognize the signs Jesus described. The text does not state in exact words who is near: the verse says "He is near, right at the door," and the wider passage speaks of the coming of the Son of Man.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after they asked him about the signs of the end. He teaches them with a simple parable so that they will stay alert. Christians interpret in different ways what "all these things" and "this generation" refer to.

For today: live with attention and without fear. Instead of obsessing over dates, keep your heart awake, your accounts clear with God, and your life full of love and obedience to Christ.
exp.16:5:
The verse tells how the disciples, Peter, James and John, reacted when they heard the voice of God from the cloud. They fell facedown to the ground in terror. The words "when the disciples heard this" refer to the voice of the Father, and "in terror" means they were filled with a deep and reverent fear.

Jesus had just been transfigured on a mountain, and Moses and Elijah appeared with him. Peter was speaking of making three shelters, and then God himself interrupted with his voice: "This is my beloved Son... hear him." Their reaction shows that they were in the holy presence of God. Afterward Jesus touched them gently and told them not to be afraid.

For today: when you sense the greatness of God, do not run away. Listen to Jesus, who draws near, touches you, and says: "Do not be afraid." He is the one who deserves all our attention.
exp.26:50:
This verse tells what happened right after Jesus died. The curtain of the temple, a thick, large cloth that hung between the rest of the temple and the Most Holy Place, was torn in two, from top to bottom. At the same time, the earth shook and the rocks were split apart.

Here the narrator, Matthew, presents the signs that accompanied the death of Jesus. That curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple. That it was torn from top to bottom suggests it was the work of God. Many Christians understand that it means the way to God was opened through Jesus (Hebrews 10:19-20). Some scholars debate the exact extent of its meaning.

Today we can draw near to God with confidence, without fear or barriers. You can pray today, just as you are, knowing that God receives you.
exp.24:32:
Here Jesus describes the moment of the final judgment. Like a shepherd who separates his sheep from the goats, He will place some people on his right and others on his left. The right side was the place of honor.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, shortly before his crucifixion. It is the closing of his teaching about his return. He uses the image of the shepherd, familiar to his listeners, to show that there will be a real and just separation. The verses that follow explain that the criterion is how the needy were treated.

For today: true faith shows itself in concrete love. This week, seek out someone with a nearby need, a neighbor, a relative or a coworker, and help them with something practical, such as a meal, a visit or your time.
exp.4:21:
Jesus says that it is not only murder that is serious, but also anger that is held onto against a brother. "Raca" was an insult meaning something like "empty-headed" or "good for nothing"; "fool" means someone foolish or senseless. The "council" refers to the higher court, and "the fire of hell" translates "Gehenna," a place Jesus uses as an image of God's judgment. Scholars debate how much of this is literal punishment and how much is emphasis.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just said that their righteousness must surpass that of the scribes and Pharisees. He does not want only outward obedience, but a clean heart. So he goes to the root of the commandment "You shall not murder": hatred and contempt.

Today, before you speak a hurtful word, stop and ask God for calm. If you have already offended someone, seek reconciliation soon.
exp.4:22:
If you go to the temple to offer your gift to God, and right there you remember that a brother has something against you, something is wrong. "Gift" here means an offering or present. "Altar" was the place where sacrifices were offered.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just explained that the commandment "You shall not kill" reaches to anger and contempt in the heart. That is why he teaches that broken relationships matter greatly to God. The verses that follow say that reconciliation must come first.

For today: if you know you have wronged someone, do not ignore it while you carry on with your life of faith. Take the first step: call, ask forgiveness, or seek to talk. Your worship becomes more sincere when you work for peace.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that Jesus spoke once more, and he did so in parables. The verse does not mention anyone asking him a question, so the wording does not suggest that. The phrase "once again" simply means he spoke to them another time. A parable is a simple story that teaches a spiritual truth.

The speaker is Jesus, in the temple in Jerusalem, in the last days before his crucifixion. The religious leaders were rejecting him and looking for a way to trap him. With this parable of the wedding feast, Jesus shows them that God invites everyone, but many respond with indifference or refusal.

For today: God invites us to know him, and that invitation deserves a sincere response. Today you can ask yourself whether you are letting other concerns pull you away from God. Set aside a few minutes to listen to him in prayer and in his Word.
exp.20:14:
The verse says that the chief priests and religious leaders saw two things in the temple: the wonderful works Jesus was doing, such as healing the blind and the lame, and the children shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David." "Hosanna" was a cry that means "save us, we beg you," and "Son of David" was a title for the promised Messiah. Seeing this, they were indignant, meaning they were filled with anger.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Jesus had just entered Jerusalem and driven out those who were making the temple a place of business. The chief priests and scribes were the religious authorities, and they were upset because Jesus was receiving praise as the Messiah. The children recognized him, and they did not.

Today we can ask ourselves whether pride or habit keeps us from rejoicing in what God does. Let us be humble and praise Jesus simply, like the children.
exp.21:25:
This verse says the same thing happened to the second brother, then to the third, and so on down to the seventh: each one married the widow and died without leaving children.

The speakers are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They present to Jesus this extreme case, based on the law of Moses about marrying a brother's widow, to make the idea that the dead rise look ridiculous. Jesus answers them afterward that they are wrong because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.

For today: sometimes we ask complicated questions in order to argue, not to learn. Before we test God with clever doubts, let us come to his Word with humility, willing to be corrected and to trust in his power.
exp.25:63:
Jesus answers the high priest directly. "You have said it yourself" means "yes, that is so." Then he adds that they will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, that is, in the place of honor and authority beside God, and coming on the clouds of heaven.

Jesus is being tried that night before Caiaphas and the council. Up to that point he had kept silent, but in response to the solemn oath he declares who he is. His words recall Daniel 7:13 and Psalm 110:1. The leaders understood this as a claim to divinity and charged him with blasphemy.

For today: Jesus did not hide the truth even though it cost him his life. We can trust that he reigns and will return, and that gives us courage to be honest about our faith with humility and firmness.
exp.26:28:
The Roman soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and set it on Jesus' head. They put a staff in his right hand, as if it were a royal scepter. They knelt down before him and mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" The word "Hail" is a greeting, like "Long live!" or "May you live long!" "Mocked" means that they laughed at him and made fun of him.

Here no particular character speaks, but Matthew narrates what the governor's soldiers did. After Pilate handed him over to be crucified, they imitated the honor given to an emperor, but to humiliate him. Without realizing it, they named a truth: Jesus is King, although his kingdom is not like the kingdoms of this world.

Today we can remember that Jesus endured scorn out of love for us. When someone mocks your faith or treats you with contempt, turn to him, who understands you, and respond with patience and humility.
exp.21:45:
After Jesus asked his question, no one was able to answer him. From that day on, no one dared to question him any further.

Jesus is in the temple in Jerusalem, surrounded by Pharisees and other leaders who wanted to trap him with difficult questions. Now it is he who asks the question. He quotes Psalm 110:1, where David calls the Messiah "Lord." If the Messiah were only a son of David, why would David call him Lord? Jesus showed that the Messiah is more than a simple human descendant. The text does not say what they thought inside; it only says they were silent.

Today we can come to Jesus with sincere questions, not to win an argument, but to know him better. He is Lord, and before him it is good to listen with humility.
exp.0:12:
This verse continues the list of Jesus's ancestors: Zerubbabel was the father of Abiud, Abiud was the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim was the father of Azor. The names are spelled in a slightly different form than in some older Bibles, but they are real people in the family line.

Context: the author of the gospel, traditionally Matthew, presents the genealogy of Jesus to show that He comes from the line of David and Abraham. These names, after Zerubbabel, do not appear in the Old Testament, so almost nothing is known about them. Some scholars think Matthew summarized or drew on family records; this is understood in several ways.

For today: God also works through people who are unknown and through ordinary lives. Your daily faithfulness, though no one notices it, can be part of what God is doing in your family and in future generations.
exp.1:15:
Matthew tells us that King Herod realized the wise men had outwitted him and would not return to tell him where the child Jesus was, and he was filled with rage. So he gave orders to kill all the baby boys in Bethlehem and the surrounding area who were two years old or younger. He based that age on the time the wise men had told him about when the star appeared.

Matthew is the one telling the story. Herod ruled as king under the power of Rome, and he feared losing his throne to a newborn "king of the Jews." Matthew shows that Jesus was born into a hostile world, and that God protected him. We do not know how many children died; the Bible does not give a number.

For today: power used out of fear and pride destroys others. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that does not defend its own position at the cost of others, and let us trust that God sees the suffering of the innocent.
exp.26:63:
The religious leaders ask Pilate to place a guard at Jesus' tomb until the third day. The phrase "make sure" in the verse means to keep watch over and protect the tomb. To "steal" means to take something dishonestly, here to take the body away. The word "last" means final. They fear that the disciples will come at night, take the body, and tell the people that Jesus has risen, and that this final deception would be worse than the first, that is, worse than the belief that Jesus was the Messiah.

The chief priests and the Pharisees speak before Pilate, the Roman governor. They remembered that Jesus had said He would rise on the third day. They wanted to prevent any rumor that would strengthen His message. Pilate granted them a guard, and they sealed the stone.

For today: human efforts cannot stop the plans of God. If something worries you, trust that God is stronger than any seal or guard. You can come to Jesus honestly, without fear of investigating who He is.
exp.24:16:
This verse says that the servant who received two talents did the same as the first one: he worked with that money and managed to earn two more. "Earned" means he made a profit, and in the verse before, the wording "gained" meant that he traded or worked with the money to multiply it. A talent was a very large sum of money.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, in the parable of the talents. Before his departure, a master distributes his goods to his servants according to their ability, that is, according to their capacity. Jesus teaches them to live faithfully while they wait for his return.

For today: God does not ask you for what you do not have, but for faithfulness with what he has given you. Do not compare yourself with others; use your time, your gifts and your resources diligently, serving God and others.
exp.5:1:
Jesus says that when we help the poor with a gift, we should not sound a trumpet to draw attention to ourselves. Giving money or help to people in need is what is meant here by "alms." The "hypocrites" were those who acted in order to appear good. They wanted to be honored by people, and that admiration was the only reward they received.

Jesus is teaching his disciples and the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Earlier he had spoken about not practicing righteousness in order to be seen. Here he gives a first example: giving. It is not known for certain whether the trumpet was literal or an exaggerated way of speaking; many believe it is an image for showing off.

For today: before helping someone, ask yourself why you are doing it. Try to give without advertising it or looking for praise, trusting that God sees your heart.
exp.4:34:
Here Jesus continues teaching about oaths. The "footstool" is the small stool where a king rests his feet, and "the great King" is God. Jesus says that one should not swear by the earth or by Jerusalem, because they belong to God.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. Some people used oaths by heaven, the earth, or Jerusalem to sound convincing, thinking that this way they did not bind the name of God. Jesus shows that all of these belong to him, so no oath is "small." Scholars debate whether he forbids every legal oath or mainly the misuse of oaths in everyday speech.
