Today: take care with your words so that you do not need to decorate them with dramatic promises. Strive to be a person whose "yes" and whose "no" can be trusted, by doing what you say.
exp.12:0:
That same day Jesus left the house where he was and sat down by the shore of the lake. The word "sea" here refers to the Sea of Galilee, which is a large lake. "That day" tells us that what follows happens right after the events of the previous chapter.

Jesus is the one acting, and the author is Matthew. Shortly before, Jesus had faced rejection from some religious leaders. Now he leaves the house and goes out to the people, who gather around him. There he will begin to teach in parables, simple stories with a deep message. The texts do not say which house it was; some think it was the house in Capernaum, but this is not certain.

For today: Jesus went out to where the people were. We can ask ourselves whether we are willing to step out of our comfort zone to draw near to others with kindness and share the hope we have in God.
exp.26:8:
It says that what happened with the thirty pieces of silver fulfilled what a prophet had spoken. The words "was fulfilled" mean that the event matched what had been foretold. The phrase "the price set on Him" refers to the amount the people of Israel put on Jesus, and with those coins a field was bought.

Matthew, the author, explains what happened after Judas handed Jesus over. Judas returned the money, and the priests used it to buy the potter's field. Matthew names Jeremiah, but the wording is closer to Zechariah 11:12-13, although there are also echoes of Jeremiah 18, 19 and 32. Scholars explain this in several ways, and there is no single certain answer.

For today: Jesus was sold for a low price, but his worth is infinite. We can ask ourselves what things we value more than Christ, and give him first place again.
exp.6:22:
Jesus says that on the day of judgment he will plainly tell certain people: "I never knew you." He commands them to depart from him. Here the BSB's "Then I will tell them plainly" conveys the same idea of a clear, open declaration. "You workers of lawlessness" refers to those who practice injustice or live without obeying God.

Jesus speaks at the end of the Sermon on the Mount. He has just warned that calling him "Lord, Lord" is not enough. Some will do impressive things in his name, such as prophesying or performing miracles, but without a life surrendered to the Father's will. Afterward he speaks of building on the rock, which is hearing and obeying.

For today: do not settle for words or religious activities. Ask God to help you truly know him, to trust in Jesus, and to obey him every day in concrete matters, such as forgiving, being honest, and serving with humility.
exp.0:22:
This verse says that a virgin will become pregnant and will give birth to a son, and they will call him Immanuel. Matthew explains that this name means "God with us."

Matthew quotes here the prophet Isaiah (7:14). An angel had just spoken to Joseph in a dream to tell him that Mary was expecting a child through the work of the Holy Spirit. Matthew shows that this fulfills what the prophet had announced. Some scholars think that Isaiah was also speaking about his own time, but Matthew sees in Jesus the full fulfillment. Notice that Jesus is not called Immanuel as an everyday name, but the name describes who he is.

For today: if God chose to be with us in Jesus, you are not alone. In your fears or burdens, you can pray today with confidence: "Lord, you are with me."
exp.23:36:
Jesus says that his coming will be like what happened in the days of Noah. The word "as" in the verse introduces the comparison, and "coming" refers to his return. "Son of Man" is a title that Jesus uses for himself. The comparison is not about how wicked the people were, but about how they lived without noticing what was approaching.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when they asked him about the signs of the end. He had just said that no one knows the day or the hour, only the Father. That is why he uses Noah as an example: the people carried on with ordinary life, eating and marrying, and the judgment came suddenly. Christians understand this passage in different ways, but all agree on the call to stay alert.

Today we can live calmly with the tasks of each day, but without forgetting God. A good habit is to set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible, so that the heart is ready, without fear or distraction.
exp.23:34:
Jesus says that everything that seems firm and lasting, heaven and earth, will one day come to an end. But his words will never run out or lose their worth. "Will pass away" means they will stop existing; "will never pass away" means they will always be fulfilled and remain.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the future of the temple and the signs of the end. He tells them of difficult events and of his return. Christians interpret in different ways what "this generation" refers to, but all agree that Jesus wants to give his followers certainty: what he says is sure, even though no one knows the day or the hour.

Today we can build our lives on the words of Jesus and not on what changes. Set aside a few minutes each day to read the Gospels and obey one concrete teaching.
exp.26:5:
The chief priests picked up the thirty pieces of silver that Judas had thrown into the temple. They said it was unlawful to put this money into the treasury, the box for the offerings, because it was blood money, payment for handing a man over to death.

Judas, in remorse, had confessed that he betrayed innocent blood. The priests did not want to take responsibility. They themselves had paid that money to condemn Jesus, but now they were careful about what the law allowed. Matthew shows this contradiction: they worry about a rule, but not about having taken part in an injustice.

Today we too can keep religious forms and still have a hardened heart. God wants sincerity, not appearances. Let us ask him to show us where we ignore our guilt, and let us respond with repentance and justice.
exp.1:10:
On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh. "Fell down" describes bowing low, down to the ground, as a sign of deep respect. "Gifts" are presents. Frankincense is a fragrant resin that was burned in worship.

This is Matthew's account. The magi had come from the east, guided by a star, looking for the one born king of the Jews. After this moment, God warns them in a dream not to return to Herod, who wanted to harm the child. The Bible does not say how many magi there were. Some see a symbolic meaning in the gifts, but the text does not explain it.

The magi searched diligently for Jesus and gave Him the best they had. Today we too can draw near to Him with humility and offer Him what is precious in our lives: our time, our talents, and our hearts.
exp.10:13:
Jesus says that John the Baptist is the Elijah who was to come. The phrase "if you are willing to accept it" points to the choice the listeners must make. He does not mean that John was literally the prophet Elijah returned to life, but that John carried out the mission that had been announced.

Jesus speaks to the crowds after some of John's disciples asked him whether he was the Messiah. He refers to Malachi 4:5, where a messenger like Elijah was promised before the day of the Lord. Jesus makes clear that John prepared the way, but that accepting this requires an open heart. That is why he adds: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."

For today: God speaks in ways we do not always expect. Let us ask him for a humble and willing heart, to recognize his voice even when it comes through simple means, and to obey it without making excuses.
exp.22:9:
This verse says that Jesus' followers should not seek to be called "instructors" in a way that shows superiority, because the true Instructor is one alone: Christ. The word "instructors" here refers to guides or teachers with authority.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, shortly before his death. He has just criticized some scribes and Pharisees who loved titles, the best seats, and public greetings. He does not forbid teaching, but seeking honor and power through it. Christians are brothers and sisters, and the following verses speak of serving and of being humble.

For today: if you teach or lead, do it to serve and not to show off. Always point to Christ, and receive correction with humility, as one more brother or sister.
exp.18:5:
Jesus says that marriage joins a man and a woman so closely that they are no longer two separate people but one shared life. For this reason, what God has joined together, no one should separate. The word translated "separate" means to pull apart or break.

Here Jesus is speaking. Some Pharisees were testing him by asking whether it was lawful to divorce. He takes them back to the beginning, to Genesis, to show God's original plan for marriage. Later, when he speaks of Moses, he explains that the permission to give a certificate of divorce was a concession because of the hardness of heart. Christians discuss how to apply this in difficult cases.

Today, if you are married, care for your marriage as something precious: forgive quickly, speak honestly, and pray together with your spouse. If you are going through a separation, seek pastoral counsel with humility and hope.
exp.25:26:
Jesus took the cup of wine, gave thanks to God, and passed it to his disciples. He told them all to drink from it. "Gave thanks" means that he prayed in thanksgiving, and "drink from it, all of you" is a gentle command, an invitation for each of them to take a drink.

Jesus is speaking with the twelve at the Passover supper, shortly before he is arrested. He has just announced that one of them will betray him, and even so Judas is at the table. Through the bread and the cup, Jesus explains the meaning of his death. In the verses that follow, he says that his blood seals a new covenant for the forgiveness of sins.

Jesus invites all of them to receive what he offers. When you take part in the Lord's Supper, do it with gratitude and humility, remembering that forgiveness is a gift that Christ paid for you. You can also do this in your daily prayer, thanking him for his sacrifice.
exp.26:49:
This verse describes the moment Jesus dies on the cross. He cried out again in a loud voice and then gave up his spirit. "Cried out" means he shouted, and "gave up his spirit" means he died, freely giving his life.

The narrator is Matthew. Earlier, someone offered Jesus vinegar, and others mocked him, waiting to see whether Elijah would come to save him. Matthew shows that Jesus did not die defeated, but in full surrender. Right after this, the veil of the temple is torn in two and the earth shakes, signs that many understand as the end of the separation between God and people.

For today: if Jesus gave his life out of love, we can trust that our forgiveness does not depend on our own merits. Today you can come to God simply and thankfully, and hand over your burdens and your fears to him.
exp.13:16:
The disciples answer Jesus that they have only five loaves and two fish. The word "only" here means "just" or "nothing more than." They point out how little they have, as if it would not be enough for anything.

The disciples are speaking as evening falls, in a deserted place and with a great crowd. Jesus had said to them, "You give them something to eat." They had suggested sending the crowd away, and now they look at what they have and see that it is very little. But Jesus asks them, "Bring them here to me."

For today: sometimes we feel that what we have is far too little for the need we see. Instead of keeping silent about it or being left paralyzed, we can place in Jesus' hands what we have, our time, talents, or resources, and trust that he can use it.
exp.23:35:
Jesus says that no one knows the exact day or hour of his return. Not even the angels in heaven know it, nor the Son; only the Father knows. The word "but" marks the contrast, and the phrase "no one knows" means that no created being has that information.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the signs of the end. He gives them warnings, but he makes clear that the exact date is not revealed. He then compares that day to the days of Noah, when people went about their normal lives and were not watching.

Today, instead of trying to calculate dates, we can live each day with faith, honesty, and love, ready to meet God. Trusting the Father also gives us peace, because the future is in his hands.
exp.13:29:
Peter, while walking toward Jesus on the water, noticed the strength of the wind and became afraid. Then he began to sink and cried out, "Lord, save me!"

The account is told by Matthew. The disciples were in a boat at night, in the middle of a storm, when Jesus came walking on the sea. Peter asked to go out to Him, and Jesus said, "Come." Peter walked well while he kept his eyes on Jesus, but his fear grew when he saw how strong the wind was. His cry was brief, but it was sincere.

When fear overwhelms us, we can do what Peter did: call out to Jesus plainly. A perfect prayer is not required. A simple sentence, spoken with trust, is enough. And Jesus responded at once, reaching out his hand.
exp.20:25:
This verse shows what the religious leaders were thinking as they debated among themselves. If they answered that John's baptism was from men, they feared the reaction of the crowd, because everyone regarded John as a prophet. The phrase "if we say, From men" refers to the answer they would give, and "regard John as a prophet" means to consider him a prophet.

Jesus is in the temple, and the chief priests and the elders ask him by what authority he does these things. He answers them with a question of his own about John the Baptist. They are trapped: if they say "from heaven," they must admit they did not believe John; if they say "from men," they face the people. So in the end they say, "We do not know."

For today: before answering about something important, ask yourself whether you are seeking the truth or only trying to please others. Speaking honestly before God is worth more than protecting our image.
exp.13:27:
Here Peter answers Jesus after hearing him say, "Take courage, it is I." The phrase "if it is You" means "if it really is You." Peter asks that Jesus command him to come to Him on the water.

The disciples were in the boat, at night, frightened because they thought they were seeing a ghost. Jesus calmed them with his voice. Peter, impulsive and full of enthusiasm, does not stay still: he wants to be where Jesus is. Notice that he does not act alone, but waits for the Master's command.

For today: when you want to take a step of faith, seek first the word of Jesus, not only your enthusiasm. And if you are afraid on the way, remember that you can cry out as Peter did: "Lord, save me."
exp.19:26:
Whoever wants to be first among you, that is, the most important or the one with the highest position, must make himself a slave to the others. The word "slave" here speaks of someone who serves, even to the point of being owned by another. The verse says "whoever wants" to be first, and "you" refers to all of you.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples. Earlier, the mother of James and John asked him for places of honor for her sons, and the other ten became angry. Jesus explains to them that in the world, rulers dominate others, but among his followers greatness is measured by service. He himself is the example: he came to serve and to give his life.

For today: before seeking recognition, ask yourself whom you can help this week, without expecting applause. Serve in something simple, at home, at work, or in the church.
exp.8:4:
Jesus asks which is easier: to say "Your sins are forgiven," or to say "Get up and walk." The word "or" here is the same "or" we use today, and "are forgiven" means forgiven by God.

Jesus speaks with some scribes, the teachers of the law, who were silently accusing him of blasphemy. He knew their thoughts. He had just told a paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven. Saying that is easy, because no one can check it. So Jesus heals the man in front of everyone, to show that he truly has authority to forgive.

For today: Jesus is concerned with what is within us, not only with what can be seen. You can bring him with confidence your deepest need, forgiveness and healing of the heart, knowing that he has the authority to give them to you.
exp.20:39:
Jesus asks a simple question: when the owner of the vineyard returns, what will he do to those tenants? Jesus does not give the answer; he lets his listeners give it.

Jesus is speaking to the chief priests and the elders of the people, in the temple, after telling a parable. In it, the tenants mistreat the owner's servants and kill his son. With the question, Jesus leads his listeners to condemn themselves by their own words. Many understand that the vineyard represents Israel and that the son announces Jesus himself.

For today: God has entrusted us with things that are not ours, such as time, gifts, and faith. Let us ask ourselves with humility whether we are bearing good fruit for him or only looking after what is our own.
exp.25:19:
When evening came, Jesus was reclining at the table with his twelve disciples to eat the Passover supper. "When evening came" means that it was already getting dark, and "reclining" describes how he settled in to eat with them.

Matthew, the narrator, is the one telling what happened. The disciples had already prepared the supper, just as Jesus had asked them to. It was the Jewish feast of Passover, which remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Jesus knew his death was near. He was about to tell them that one of them would betray him, and still he reclined with all of them, including the one who would betray him.

For today: Jesus valued being at the table with his own just before his hardest moment. We can follow his example by giving sincere time to the people we love, especially in days of trial.
exp.15:12:
Jesus arrives in the region of Caesarea Philippi, an area north of Israel. There he asks his disciples who people say the Son of Man is. The title "Son of Man" was one that Jesus used for himself. The phrase "came to" means "arrived at."

Jesus had just warned his disciples to beware of the false teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Now he takes them away, to a quiet place, and prepares them for a very important question. First he asks what people think, and then he will ask what they themselves believe. That question leads to Peter's confession.

For today: it is not enough to repeat what others say about Jesus. Take a quiet moment to ask yourself honestly: who is Jesus to me? Read about him in the Gospels and answer sincerely in prayer.
exp.16:8:
As they came down the mountain, Jesus gave His disciples a clear command: they were not to tell anyone about what they had seen until the Son of Man had been raised from the dead. Peter, James and John had just witnessed the transfiguration, and Jesus told them to keep the vision to themselves for now. "Son of Man" is a title Jesus uses for Himself.

Jesus speaks to His three disciples. They have just seen His glory, along with Moses and Elijah. Many people expected a glorious Messiah without the cross. If the disciples had spoken about the vision beforehand, people could have misunderstood it. After the resurrection, everything would make sense.

For today: there are things of God that we understand fully only in the light of the cross and the resurrection. If today you experience a moment of great spiritual clarity, do not use it to boast. Keep it with humility and let it draw you closer to Jesus, who walks with you in the hard times too.
exp.12:34:
Matthew explains that Jesus taught in parables so that what a prophet had said long ago would come true. "I will open my mouth in parables" means that he would speak in stories and comparisons. "I will utter" means that he would bring things out freely, like something pouring forth. The "things hidden since the foundation of the world" are truths of God that had not been clearly understood since the beginning of the world.

The speaker is Jesus, who has just told the parables of the mustard seed and the yeast. Matthew quotes Psalm 78:2, written by Asaph, whom the Bible also calls a seer. Matthew sees that Jesus fully carries out that announcement. Afterward Jesus will leave the crowd and explain things to his disciples.

For today: do not be content with hearing God from a distance. Come close to Jesus with your questions, as the disciples did, and he will make his word clear to you.
exp.13:11:
This verse tells how John the Baptist's disciples, after his death, came and took his body and buried it. Then they went and informed Jesus of what had happened. The word for the news here is simply "informed," which is the plain sense of the verb.

Here the narrator is Matthew. John had been imprisoned and put to death on the orders of King Herod. His followers did not abandon him even after he was dead, and they brought the news to Jesus. The text that follows says that Jesus withdrew to a lonely place, but the crowds followed him, and he felt compassion and healed the sick. The Bible does not explain in detail why he went away, and it can be understood as a moment of grief or of prayer.

For today: when pain or loss comes, bring your sorrow to Jesus with sincerity, just as they did. He understands you and receives you.
exp.5:14:
Jesus says that if we do not forgive people for the wrongs they have done to us, our Father will not forgive our wrongs either. The wrongs are the bad actions we commit against others. The word "neither" means "in the same way, not," so the verse is saying that God treats us the way we treat others in this matter.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, and this verse clarifies what he said right after the Lord's Prayer, where we ask: "forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." He teaches his disciples that whoever receives God's mercy must show it to others. Some scholars understand that this is not about earning forgiveness through effort, but that a hard and unforgiving heart shows it has not valued the grace received.

Today, think of someone who hurt you and whom you still hold in your heart. Ask God for help to let go of that resentment, and take a concrete step: pray for that person, or seek reconciliation if it is possible and healthy.
exp.15:8:
Jesus asks his disciples whether they still don't understand, and whether they have forgotten the miracle of the five loaves that fed five thousand people. He also asks them how many basketfuls of leftovers they gathered afterward. "Basketfuls" refers to the small baskets of leftovers they collected.

Jesus had warned them: "Watch out for the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees." The disciples assumed he meant bread, because they had forgotten to bring some. Jesus, aware of their thoughts, gently corrects them. If they had already seen that he could multiply bread, they had no reason to worry about food. Later he explains that he was speaking of the false teaching of those groups.

For today: when we worry about what we lack, let us remember how God has already cared for us before. That grateful remembrance strengthens faith and helps us listen better to what God is truly telling us.
exp.27:8:
Matthew 28:9 says that the risen Jesus suddenly met the women as they were hurrying away from the tomb. He greeted them with the word "Greetings!", a common greeting of the time. They came to him, grasped his feet, and worshiped him, that is, they fell down before him, recognizing him as Lord.

The one telling the story is Matthew. The women had heard the angel and were leaving with fear and great joy to tell the disciples. On the way, Jesus himself met them. Then he calmed them and charged them to carry the message to his brothers. Thus they were the first to see him risen.

For today: Jesus draws near to those who seek him in faith, even when they feel fear. He responds with sincere worship and obedience, and calls us to bring others the good news that Christ lives.
exp.25:61:
This verse says that the high priest stood up in front of everyone and asked Jesus, "Have You no answer?" He wanted Jesus to respond to what the men were testifying against Him. Here "testifying" simply means giving testimony against someone.

This happens during the night trial before the Sanhedrin, at the house of the high priest Caiaphas. They were looking for accusations to condemn Jesus, but the false witnesses did not agree with each other. Caiaphas, frustrated, presses Jesus to speak. Jesus remains silent, and this matches what Isaiah 53:7 says about the servant who does not open his mouth.

For today: it is not always necessary to defend yourself against every unjust accusation. Jesus knew when to be silent and when to speak the truth. Ask God for wisdom to answer with calm, trusting that He defends the truth.
exp.4:14:
Here Jesus says that no one lights a lamp and puts it under a basket. The normal thing is to set it on a stand, so that it gives light to everyone in the house. The point of the picture is that a lamp is meant to be seen and to be useful.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. He has just told them that they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. With this simple image he explains that their life of faith is not meant to be hidden, but to be seen. He then makes clear that good works lead others to glorify the Father.

Today, you do not have to boast about your faith, but neither should you hide it out of fear or shame. Be kind, honest, and helpful at home, at work, and in your neighborhood, so that others can see God in the way you live.
exp.9:5:
Jesus tells his twelve disciples to go first to "the lost sheep of Israel." The word "rather" introduces this contrast, and the phrase "go first" means "go before anyone else." "The lost sheep" is an image of the Jewish people, who needed guidance and care.

Jesus speaks to the twelve apostles as he sends them out on their first mission. Before that, he told them not to go to the Gentiles or to the cities of the Samaritans. This does not mean that other peoples were excluded forever, since later Jesus would send his followers to all nations. Here the point is one of order: first, the promises made to Israel.

For today: God sometimes asks us to begin with those closest to us. Think of someone in your family, your workplace, or your neighborhood who feels lost, and offer them your time, your patient listening, and a word of hope.
exp.7:22:
This verse says that Jesus got into the boat and that his disciples followed Him. The boat was probably a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee. "Followed Him" means they went after Him, climbing into the boat with Him.

The one telling the story is Matthew. Shortly before, Jesus had spoken with a man who wanted to wait to bury his father, and Jesus answered him, "Follow Me." Some understand that his father had already died; others, that the man asked to wait until his father died. The text does not make this clear. What is certain is that following Jesus comes first. Now the disciples follow Him into the boat, and soon the storm will come.

For today: following Jesus does not always lead us to peaceful places. If today you feel that you are walking with Him and difficulties still come, do not think you took the wrong path. He is with you in the boat.
exp.24:37:
The righteous keep asking the King: "When did we see you as a stranger and take you in? Or naked, and clothe you?" Here the word for "stranger" means someone who is a traveler without a home, and "took you in" means they welcomed him and hosted him. "Clothe" means to give clothing.

Jesus speaks in the parable of the judgment of the nations, at the close of his teaching about the last days. The King praises the righteous for their compassion. They are surprised, because they did not know they were serving Christ himself when they helped those in need. Their question shows humility: they were not keeping count of their good deeds.

Today we can serve with simplicity, without seeking applause. Think of someone close to you who needs food, clothing, company, or help, and do something concrete this week. Jesus teaches that practical love for those in need has very great worth before God.
exp.17:22:
It says that the kingdom of heaven is like a king who decided to settle accounts with his servants. Jesus does not say that the whole kingdom is like this, but he uses this story to teach something about how God acts.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Peter has just asked him how many times he must forgive, and Jesus answers with "seventy times seven," that is, forgiving without keeping count. With this parable, which begins here, he explains why forgiveness must be so great: God has forgiven us first.

Today we can remember how much God has forgiven us before we demand anything from another person. If someone has offended you, ask God for a humble and generous heart to take the first step toward forgiveness.
exp.9:26:
Jesus says that what He teaches in private, His disciples must proclaim openly and without fear. The words "in the dark" and "whispered in your ear" speak of teaching given quietly, among a few. "In the daylight" means openly. The housetops were the flat roofs of houses, from which a person could speak so that many would hear.

Jesus speaks to His twelve apostles as He sends them out to preach. He warns them that they will be rejected, as He Himself was. For this reason He tells them: do not be afraid of people. What He taught them quietly was not to be kept hidden out of fear of opposition.

For today: if God has taught you something through prayer or through His Word, do not hide it out of shame. Look for a simple opportunity this week to share it with someone, with respect, love, and trust that the Father cares for you.
exp.7:27:
When Jesus arrived on the other side of the lake, in the region of the Gadarenes, two men controlled by demons came out to meet him. They were coming from the tombs, that is, from the graves. They were so violent that no one could pass that way.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Just before this, Jesus calmed the storm, and the disciples wondered who he was. Now Matthew shows another answer: Jesus also has authority over evil spirits.

For today: Jesus does not avoid people whom others fear or reject. We can approach those who suffer and seem lost with compassion, trusting that Christ has the power to set them free.
exp.17:2:
Jesus says with great seriousness that unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. The phrase "unless you change" points to turning around, or being converted, and that is the heart of the verse.

The disciples had just asked who was the greatest in the kingdom. Jesus answers by placing a child in the middle of them. He shows them that greatness is not sought through power or importance, but through humility. The verses that follow make clear that the humble person, like this child, is the greatest.

For today: this is not about being naive, but about trusting God with simplicity, without pride or the desire to be more than others. Today you can recognize that you need God and serve someone without seeking applause.
exp.18:10:
Jesus says that not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given. The word "given" here means "granted to them."

Jesus has just taught that marriage is very serious and that divorce, except for sexual unfaithfulness, is not what God intended. The disciples respond by saying that then it would be better not to marry. Jesus answers with this verse and then speaks of those who live unmarried for the sake of the kingdom. Scholars discuss whether "this word" refers to the disciples' statement or to the teaching about marriage and remaining single.

Both marriage and singleness are a calling and a gift from God. Today we can take our commitments seriously and respect, without judging, the path God gives to each person.
exp.25:22:
Jesus answers the disciples and says that the one who will betray him is someone who eats with him, who dips his hand into the same bowl. Here "betray" means handing him over, putting him into the hands of his enemies. "The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me" means that this is how it will happen.

We are at the Last Supper, the Passover meal, shortly before the crucifixion. Jesus announces that one of the twelve will betray him, and everyone grows sorrowful and asks, "Lord, is it I?" Sharing the same bowl was a sign of friendship and trust, so the betrayal hurts all the more. Jesus does not give a name here; shortly afterward Judas asks, and Jesus answers him, "You have said so."

For today: Jesus knows our hearts and still invites us to his table. We can imitate the disciples and ask ourselves humbly, "Is it I?", asking God to help us be faithful.
exp.24:5:
At midnight the cry rang out: "Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!" The shout announces that the man the virgins had been waiting for is finally arriving, and they must go out to greet him. "The bridegroom" is the man getting married, the one the virgins were waiting for.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in his teaching about the last times. He tells the parable of ten virgins who were waiting for the bridegroom. He uses it to encourage readiness, because the bridegroom delayed and came when no one expected him. Many understand that the bridegroom represents Christ and his return, although the parable itself does not explain this in detail.

For today: do not live waiting for the "perfect moment" to prepare yourself. Nurture your relationship with God each day through prayer, Bible reading and obedience, because that personal faith cannot be lent to someone else or left until the last minute.
exp.23:12:
This verse says that whoever keeps standing firm in the faith to the end, that person will be saved. The word "perseveres" here means to keep going steadily and not give up.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when they ask him about the signs of his coming. He warns them that there will be deception from false prophets, an increase of evil, and love that grows cold. He tells them this to prepare them and to encourage them not to lose heart in hard times. Christians understand in different ways how this promise relates to salvation and the end.

Today we can cultivate a steady faith: praying each day, reading the Bible, and staying close to a community of believers. Then, when weariness or doubt comes, we do not depend on our own strength, but on the faithfulness of God.
exp.25:17:
Jesus tells his disciples to go into the city, to a certain man's house, with a short message: "The Teacher says, My time is near." He plans to keep the Passover at that man's house with his disciples. The man is not named, and the verse does not say how the disciples are to recognize him.

Jesus speaks just after Judas has looked for a way to betray him. The disciples ask where to prepare the Passover meal. Jesus gives calm and precise instructions, like someone who knows what is coming. By "my time" he probably means his death, which is near, though some understand it more broadly, as the hour appointed by God.

For today: Jesus faced what was hard with calm and obedience to the Father's plan. When you go through difficult moments, trust God, faithfully do what is yours to do, and do not stop sharing the table with those you love.
exp.21:37:
Jesus says that loving God is the most important commandment of all. The phrase "the first and greatest commandment" means the first in order and the greatest in value. Nothing stands above this commandment.

Jesus is speaking with an expert in the law, who asks him a question to test him, as Matthew 22:35 tells us. It was a common question among Jewish teachers: which commandment is the chief one? Jesus answers by quoting Deuteronomy 6:5 and teaches that all the law and the prophets depend on love for God and for our neighbor.

Today we can begin the day by giving God first place, with a simple prayer or a few lines of Scripture. When he is first in the heart, it becomes easier for us to love others with patience and kindness.
exp.23:9:
In times of great pressure, many will fall away from their faith and turn their backs on Jesus. Beyond that, they will betray one another, handing each other over, and they will hate one another. The verse of "offended" here is not about gossip or taking offense at a remark. It means falling away or stepping back from following Christ.

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They ask him about the end of the age and the sign of his coming. He warns them ahead of time about persecution, betrayal, false prophets, and love growing cold. He wants them not to be caught off guard or lost. Scholars disagree about how much of this was fulfilled in the first century and how much still lies ahead.

For today: when pressure or disappointment comes, do not let bitterness pull you away from Christ or from your brothers and sisters. Seek forgiveness, prayer, and community, and stay firm in his Word.
exp.22:35:
Jesus states with complete seriousness that the consequences of all the rejection and violence against God's messengers will fall on the people of his own time. The word translated "truly" means "surely" or "in truth." "Generation" refers to the people living at that time.

Jesus speaks in the temple, in the last days before his crucifixion. He has just pointed out the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees. He reminds them that, throughout history, God sent prophets and many were rejected and killed. Many understand that the judgment announced relates to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, although some also see a broader scope. What follows shows his grief: Jesus laments, he does not rejoice.

For today: when God corrects us through his Word or through other people, let us not harden our hearts. Let us listen with humility and return to him in time.
exp.22:5:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees love the places of honor: the best seats at banquets and the front seats in the synagogues. The word "banquets" refers to meals, where one's place at the table showed how important each person was.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, and he criticizes the religious teachers of his time. His problem was not that they taught the law, but that they did their works so that others would see them, seeking applause more than pleasing God. Then he reminds his disciples that they are brothers and that only Christ is their Teacher.

Today we can ask ourselves why we serve: are we seeking recognition, or loving God and others? A simple practice is to do some service quietly, without expecting anyone to notice it, and to give thanks when others are honored.
exp.16:17:
Here Jesus spoke with firmness to the demon that was troubling the boy, and the demon came out of him. The word "rebuked" means that he spoke to it with authority and gave it a command, and "he was healed from that moment" means that the boy was made well at that same instant.

A desperate father had brought his son to the disciples, but they could not help him. Jesus, with sadness, spoke of the lack of faith of that generation and asked that the boy be brought to him. Afterward, in private, he explained to his disciples that they could not heal him because of their little faith.

For today: when you face something that is beyond you, do not rely only on your own strength. Bring the situation to Jesus with a simple faith, even if it is small, and trust that he has the power to help you.
exp.26:39:
Those passing by the cross mocked Jesus. They reminded him that he had said he would tear down the temple and rebuild it in three days. They said to him, "Save Yourself!" and challenged him, "If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!" The word "destroy" here refers to tearing down, and the phrase "rebuild it" means putting it back up again.

The ones speaking were passersby, people going along the road. They had heard a false accusation from the witnesses at the trial (Matthew 26:61). Jesus was speaking of the temple of his body, according to John 2:19-21. They doubted that he was the Son of God, and the mockery repeated the temptation in the desert: "If You are the Son of God..."

Jesus did not come down from the cross, but not because he lacked power. He stayed there out of love for us. When someone mocks your faith, or when God seems silent, remember that his way of acting is sometimes different from what we expect. Trust in him.
exp.24:25:
Jesus tells how the master answers the servant who hid the talent. He calls him "wicked and lazy", that is, a bad person and careless about his duty. Then the master repeats the servant's own words: "You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I have not scattered seed." To reap means to harvest, and to scatter seed means to plant it. The master does not admit that what the servant said is true; he uses the servant's own words to show that his excuse does not hold up.

Jesus speaks in the parable of the talents, during his teaching to the disciples about his return. The servant said he was afraid and did nothing. The master answers that, if he truly believed him to be so demanding, he should have worked harder. Some interpreters see here a warning about living without fruit.

Today, do not use fear or a distorted image of God as an excuse for not serving. Ask yourself what God has given you, whether time, abilities or resources, and take one small step today to use it well.
exp.25:3:
This verse says that the religious leaders met together and agreed on a plan to arrest Jesus secretly, and then to kill him. "Arrest" means to take someone into custody. "Secretly" means in hiding, without the people noticing.

The narrator is Matthew. Jesus had just announced that he would be handed over to be crucified. Meanwhile, the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders gathered together in the house of Caiaphas, the high priest. They feared the crowd that followed Jesus, so they sought to act in secret and not during the festival.

For today: when we feel that someone threatens our position or our comfort, we can fall into pride and deceit. Let us ask God for a humble and sincere heart, one that seeks the truth even when it costs us to change.
exp.9:18:
In this passage, when the disciples are handed over to others, they should not worry about how to respond or what to say. Jesus promises that in that very hour they will be given what to say.

Jesus speaks to his twelve apostles as he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom. He warns them that there will be rejection and persecution. The next verse explains that the words will come from the Spirit of the Father speaking through them. This is a situation of persecution for the sake of Jesus, not just any occasion.

If you face pressure or ridicule for your faith, do not freeze up out of fear of speaking badly. Pray, trust God, and prepare yourself simply, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.18:28:
Jesus says that whoever gives up houses, brothers or sisters, father or mother, wife or children, or fields for the sake of his name will receive a hundred times as much and will inherit eternal life. The phrase "a hundred times as much" means a reward far greater than what was lost.

Peter had just asked what the disciples would gain, since they had left everything to follow Jesus, after seeing the rich young man go away sad. Jesus promises them a place of honor in his kingdom and extends the promise to every one of his followers. Many understand the reward as a spiritual blessing, such as a new family in the church, in addition to eternal life. The next verse warns that the first may be last.

For today: if following Christ costs you something, trust that he will not leave you empty-handed. Serve him with humility, without boasting about what you have given.
exp.14:10:
Jesus says that what a person eats does not make them unclean before God. What truly defiles a person is what comes out of their mouth, that is, their words, which express what is in the heart. "Listen and understand" is an invitation to pay close attention.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd, after the Pharisees criticized his disciples for not following certain washing rituals before eating. They valued human traditions more than what God asks for. That is why the Pharisees were offended, and Jesus answered them firmly.

Today we can take care not only of outward religious appearances, but also of our words. Before you speak, ask yourself: does this reflect a clean heart? Ask God to heal your inner life, so that your words bring life and not harm.
exp.6:10:
Jesus compares a human father with God. If an earthly father, though imperfect, knows how to give good things to his children, how much more will your Father in heaven, who is perfect, give good things to those who ask him. The verse speaks of "good gifts," and the words "you who are evil" remind us that people have flaws, yet we are still able to love and give well.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching his disciples and the crowd. Just before this, he invited them to ask, seek, and knock. With the example of a parent giving to a child, he wants them to trust that God listens and responds with kindness, not with deception or indifference.

For today: pray with simple trust, like a child who talks with his father. Tell him your needs, without fear of bothering him. Trust that his answer will come from his love and wisdom, even when it is sometimes not what you imagined.
exp.21:44:
Jesus asks the Pharisees a question. He quotes Psalm 110:1, where David calls someone else "Lord." The Jews understood that the Messiah would be a son of David, that is, a descendant of David. But if David, who was the king, calls him "Lord," how can he be only his son?

The Psalm's picture of the enemies being placed under his feet means that they are completely defeated.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, at the end of several debates in which the religious leaders tried to trap him with difficult questions. Now he asks them the questions. He does not do this to humiliate them, but so that they will think about who the Messiah really is: a descendant of David, and at the same time greater than David. Christians see here a sign of his divinity, although they did not know how to answer.

For today: it is not enough to have correct ideas about Jesus secondhand. Ask yourself honestly: who is he to me? If he is Lord, I can entrust him with my fears and my decisions.
exp.25:23:
Jesus says that he will go to his death, just as the Scriptures said long ago. But he also warns with sorrow: woe to the one who betrays him! The word "woe" expresses grief and judgment. The statement that it would have been better for that man if he had never been born shows how serious that betrayal is. To "betray" him means to hand him over to his enemies.

Jesus speaks during the Last Supper with his twelve disciples. He has just said that one of them will betray him. The disciples grow sorrowful and ask, "Is it I?" Jesus does not say this to shame them, but to show that he knows all things and that his death does not take him by surprise. Even so, Judas is responsible for his own decision.

For today: instead of pointing at others, we can ask ourselves humbly, "Is it I, Lord?" Let us ask him to examine our hearts and keep us faithful to him.
exp.6:4:
Jesus says that before helping to correct another person, one must first remove what is wrong in his own life. To "take out" means to remove. The "speck" is a tiny particle, like a grain of dust, and the "beam" is a large piece of timber. A "hypocrite" is someone who pretends to be better than he really is.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just warned against judging others harshly. He does not forbid helping one's brother, for he says that afterward you will be able to see clearly enough to remove the speck. What he corrects is the blindness and pride of someone who criticizes without examining himself.

For today: before pointing out a fault in someone else, pray and honestly ask yourself what is in your own heart. Acknowledge your own failings, and then, with humility and kindness, help your brother.
exp.11:18:
This verse says that the Servant chosen by God will not quarrel or cry out loudly. "Quarrel" means to argue or fight with force, and "cry out" means to shout to draw attention. No one will hear his voice in the streets, as someone seeking fame would make it heard.

Matthew quotes Isaiah 42 here and applies that prophecy to Jesus. Earlier, Jesus had healed many people and asked that they not make him known, while the Pharisees were plotting to destroy him. Matthew shows that Jesus did not act with noisy force or a spirit of rivalry, but as the gentle servant God had promised.

For today: we can follow Jesus' example by serving with humility, without seeking applause or winning arguments by shouting. When we must defend the truth, let us do it with firmness, but with kind and calm treatment.
exp.5:7:
Jesus says, "Do not be like them," meaning like the pagans who keep piling up words when they pray. The reason is simple: your Father knows what you need before you ask.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just corrected the prayer offered to be seen by others and the prayer that believes speaking at length obliges God to listen. Right after this, he gives them the Lord's Prayer as a brief and simple model.

For today: pray with sincerity and trust, without worrying about sounding eloquent. Speak with God as a child speaks with a father, and remember that prayer is not informing him, but drawing near to the one who already cares for you.
exp.7:9:
Jesus was amazed when he heard this, and he turned to the people who were following him and said with great seriousness, "Truly I tell you, I have not found anyone in Israel with faith this great." Here "Truly I tell you" is the same phrase that opens the verse, and the saying itself shows that he was surprised.

Jesus is the one speaking. The centurion was a Roman officer, that is, a foreigner, who asked for healing for his servant. He recognized that Jesus had authority and that his word was enough, just as his soldiers obeyed his commands. Jesus praises that trust, and in the verses that follow he shows that people from everywhere will enter the kingdom.

For today: trust that the word of Jesus is enough. Even if you do not yet see the answer, you can pray with humility and believe that he has power and that he is good.
exp.5:32:
Matthew 6:33 says that the most important thing in life is to seek first the kingdom of God, that is, his rule and his will, and also his righteousness, meaning living in the upright way that pleases him. If we do that, God promises to give us what we need. The word "but" introduces the contrast, and "added" means given in addition to what we seek first.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. They lived with worries about food and clothing. He reminds them that the Gentiles, who did not know God, were concerned with these things, but that the heavenly Father already knows what they need. For this reason he invites them to trust.

Today, before you begin your day, set aside a few minutes to pray and ask God to guide you to live as he wants. Then hand your worries over to him and confidently do what you have to do.
exp.18:3:
Jesus answers the Pharisees with a question: "Have you not read...?" He says that the Creator, who made everything from the beginning, made human beings "male and female," that is, man and woman. The word "made" in this verse refers to creating.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees who wanted to test him. They asked him whether a man could divorce his wife "for any cause." Instead of joining their arguments, Jesus takes them back to the book of Genesis and to God's original plan for marriage.

For today: before we give our opinion about marriage, let us go back to what God said from the beginning. Let us value our spouse as a gift from God, and care for the union with respect, patience, and commitment.
exp.12:49:
This verse says that at the end of the age, the angels will throw the wicked into a fiery furnace. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, which expresses pain, anguish, and despair. The word "age" here refers to a period or era of time.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and explains the parable of the net. The net gathers all kinds of fish, and then the good are separated from the bad. With this image he teaches that there will be a final judgment and a separation. Many understand the "fiery furnace" as a serious picture of punishment; Christians debate how to interpret the details.

For today: do not take your spiritual life lightly. God is patient now, but the judgment is real. Ask him to examine your heart, and live with sincerity, not just outward appearance.
exp.0:4:
This verse continues the list of Jesus's ancestors. It says that Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, and that Boaz was the father of Obed by Ruth. After that, Obed was the father of Jesse.

Here Matthew, the author of the gospel, opens his book by showing that Jesus is the promised Messiah, a descendant of Abraham and David. It stands out that he names Rahab and Ruth, two women from outside Israel. Some believe Matthew wants to show that God's grace reaches all peoples. That this Rahab is the one from Jericho is the most common view, but the Bible does not make that clear here.

God can use anyone, regardless of their origin or their past. If today you feel far away or out of place, remember that God welcomes you and can give you an important place in his plan.
exp.10:20:
Jesus says "Woe to you!" to two cities, Chorazin and Bethsaida. That "woe" expresses grief and a serious warning. He tells them that if the miracles performed there had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, pagan cities, their people would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Sackcloth and ashes were signs of mourning and humility before God.

Jesus is the speaker. He has just shown that the people rejected both John the Baptist and him, making excuses. Chorazin and Bethsaida, in the region of the Sea of Galilee, saw many miracles, but did not change their hearts. The texts do not detail which miracles occurred in Chorazin.

For today: seeing or hearing things about God is not enough; God expects a response. Today you can ask yourself: what area of my life do I truly need to surrender to him, with humility and sincere change?
exp.13:24:
This verse says that, as dawn was nearly breaking, Jesus came toward his disciples walking on the sea. The last part of the night, roughly between three and six in the morning, is what the verse refers to. The lake of Galilee is the sea in view here.

The one acting here is Jesus. Earlier he had sent the crowds away and gone up the mountain to pray alone. Meanwhile, the disciples were in the boat, battered by the waves and with the wind against them. Jesus saw them in their trouble and went out to them. Afterward he calmed them by saying: "Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid."

For today: sometimes we feel the night is long and the wind is against us. This passage reminds us that Jesus is neither far away nor absent. He may come in an unexpected way, but he does come. Today, in the middle of your difficulty, speak to him honestly and trust that he is with you.
exp.4:42:
The people had heard it said that they should love their neighbor and hate their enemy. Jesus is pointing back to that common teaching. The word "neighbor" refers to the person who lives close to us.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. The first part, "Love your neighbor," comes from Leviticus 19:18. The words "Hate your enemy" are not found in that law, and they seem to reflect a popular teaching of the time. Jesus is going to correct that idea and show a wider love, like the love of God.

For today: think of someone who rubs you the wrong way or has hurt you. This week, pray for that person and do one simple act of kindness toward them, without expecting anything in return.
exp.0:0:
This is the record of the family line of Jesus Christ, the son of David and the son of Abraham. The word "genealogy" here means lineage, the list of his ancestors. He is presented as the son of David and the son of Abraham, that is, a descendant of both. The word "son" is used in a broad sense: descendant.

The author is Matthew, according to Christian tradition. He writes mainly with Jewish readers in mind, and that is why he begins with a genealogy. David was the promised king on whose throne an eternal descendant would reign, and Abraham received the promise that he would bless all the nations. Matthew shows that Jesus is the one who fulfills both of God's promises.

For today: God keeps his promises, even when generations pass. If you are waiting for something God has promised, trust that he is working with patience and faithfulness, even when you cannot see it. Your story also fits within his plan.
exp.7:26:
What it says: After Jesus calmed the storm, those who saw the miracle were amazed. They asked what kind of man Jesus was, since even the winds and the sea obeyed him. "Were amazed" means they were filled with wonder and astonishment.

Context: The ones speaking are the men who were in the boat with Jesus and his disciples. A great storm had terrified them, and Jesus, who was sleeping, was woken up. With a single command he calmed everything. Their question shows that they did not yet fully understand who he was. Soon afterward, the demons call him "Son of God," so the contrast is clear.

For today: When a storm in your life makes you feel you are sinking, come to Jesus honestly, as the disciples did, and cry out to him. He has authority over what frightens you, and you can trust his care even when you do not understand everything.
exp.26:48:
Some of those standing there said, "Leave him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to save him." "Leave him alone" means "wait" or "don't interfere," and "save him" means rescue him or deliver him.

The speakers are people standing near the cross. They had heard Jesus call out and thought he was calling for Elijah. There was a Jewish belief that Elijah could come to help the righteous. It is not certain whether they were speaking with mockery, curiosity, or both. What we do see is that they did not understand what was happening. Shortly afterward Jesus dies, and extraordinary signs take place.

Today we can learn not to judge lightly what we do not understand about God. Sometimes his answer does not come the way we expect, but he is still at work. Let us listen with humility before we mock or doubt.
exp.15:15:
Peter answers with a clear confession: Jesus is the Christ, the Anointed One, the Messiah promised by God. He also calls him the Son of the living God, meaning someone with a unique relationship with the Father, and the true God, who acts and is not like dead idols.

Jesus had just asked what people were saying about him. Some thought he was a prophet risen from the dead. Then he asks his disciples directly, and Peter speaks on his own initiative. Jesus tells him that this truth was revealed to him by the Father, not a human opinion. As to what "this rock" is, Christians interpret it in different ways: Peter, his confession, or Christ himself.

Today, Jesus also asks us: "But who do you say that I am?" Repeating what others think is not enough. Take a moment to answer him honestly in prayer, and ask him to strengthen your faith.
exp.14:17:
Jesus says that the things that come out of our mouth come from the heart, and that these are what truly defile a person. "Defile" means to make impure, and here it refers to impurity before God. The source of the problem is not outside us but within us.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, after the Pharisees and scribes criticized them for not washing their hands before eating, as the tradition of the elders required. He answers that true impurity does not come from food, but from within the person.

Before correcting my words, I can ask myself what is in my heart. Today I can pray, "God, cleanse my heart," and seek for my words to reflect honesty, kindness, and respect toward others.
exp.7:1:
He tells us that a man with leprosy came up to Jesus and knelt before him in a posture of deep respect. The word used for this may mean that he fell down or bowed low in reverence. He said to him, "Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean."

Here "make me clean" means to heal him and set him free from the disease.

The man speaking is a leper, who at that time lived apart from other people and was considered unclean under the law of Moses. This happens right after the Sermon on the Mount, when many people were following Jesus. The man does not doubt Jesus' power; he puts himself in his hands. Some believe that the act of kneeling here is only reverence; others see a recognition of who Jesus is.

Today we can pray as this man did: with humility, trusting in the power of Jesus and placing our need in his hands, not demanding, but letting his good will decide.
exp.4:44:
Jesus says that we should love and pray for our enemies so that we may be children of God. In other words, this shows that we resemble our heavenly Father. He causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous alike, whether or not people deserve it.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. He corrects the common idea of loving your neighbor and hating your enemy. He teaches them that God's love is not limited to those who deserve it or whom they happen to like, and that his followers should reflect that same generosity.

For today: think of someone who has treated you badly. This week, pray for that person and do one simple act of kindness toward them, such as greeting them respectfully or helping them with something, without expecting anything in return.
exp.11:7:
Jesus says that the Son of Man, a title he uses for himself, has authority over the Sabbath. Here "Lord" means master, the one who holds authority. The statement that he is Lord of the Sabbath means that the Sabbath is under his authority.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees, who accused his disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking heads of grain to eat. He answers them with examples from Scripture and with the words of Hosea: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice." He teaches that God looks at the heart, not only at rules. Soon after, he will heal a man on the Sabbath.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we care more about rules than about people. Jesus is Lord of all, so we should obey him with a compassionate heart, seeking to do good and to show mercy to those who need it.
exp.26:20:
Here Pilate, the Roman governor, gives them a choice between two prisoners: Jesus and Barabbas. The word "release" means to set free. The crowd answers that they want Barabbas.

Pilate asks the question because it was the custom to release one prisoner at the feast of the Passover. The chief priests and the elders had persuaded the people to ask for Barabbas. Matthew also tells us that Pilate knew Jesus was not guilty. The Gospels describe Barabbas as a well-known prisoner, and Mark and Luke say that he had committed murder.

For today: It is easy to be carried along by the opinion of the majority. Before deciding, let us ask God for wisdom and ask ourselves: is this just and true? Choosing Jesus is worth more than following the crowd.
exp.15:23:
Jesus tells his disciples that if anyone wants to come after him, they must deny themselves, which means stop putting their own desires first. They must also take up their cross, which means accept the cost of following him, and then follow him.

Jesus had just announced that he would suffer and die. Peter rebuked him, thinking the way people naturally think. Jesus answered him firmly and then taught everyone that following him is not a path of comfort. The cross was a tool of execution, so he was speaking of total surrender. The verses that follow explain that losing your life for Jesus is truly gaining it.

Today, following Jesus may mean forgiving when it hurts, telling the truth even when it costs you, or giving up a habit that controls you. Ask yourself today: where must I say "no" to myself in order to say "yes" to Christ?
exp.9:21:
Jesus tells his followers that everyone will dislike them because of his name, that is, because they belong to him. But whoever perseveres to the end, staying firm and faithful, will be saved. To persevere means to keep going with patience, and to be hated means to be disliked or rejected.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as he sends them out for the first time to announce the kingdom in the towns of Israel. He honestly warns them that opposition will come, even from within their own families, and he promises that the Spirit of the Father will speak through them. Scholars debate whether "the end" refers to death, to the coming of the Son of Man, or to a later time.

For today: if following Christ brings you mockery or rejection, do not give up. Stay firm one day at a time, trusting that God sustains you by his Spirit.
exp.12:6:
Another part of the seed fell among thorns. The thorns grew up alongside the young plant and did not let it develop. They choked it, which means they took away its room, its light, and its nourishment until it died.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. He tells the parable of the sower using an image everyone knew: the field. Later in the same chapter, he explains to his disciples that the thorns stand for the worries of this world and the deceitfulness of riches (Matthew 13:22). His purpose is to show how the heart responds to the word of God.

For today: review what things are growing alongside your faith. Worries and the desire for more can gradually fill all of your time. Remove one of them today and give that space to listening to the word of God.
exp.16:13:
When Jesus and his three disciples came down from the mountain and reached the crowd, a man came up to him and knelt before him. The phrase "knelt before him" means that he got down on his knees out of respect and need. The word "crowd" refers to a large gathering of people.

Here the narrator, Matthew, is speaking. Jesus had just come down from the mountain of the transfiguration and had explained that Elijah had already come in the person of John the Baptist. On reaching the bottom, he meets an urgent need. The verses that follow say the man asks for help for his son, and that the disciples were not able to heal him.

For today: when your burden is greater than your strength, do not stay silent. Come to Jesus with humility and bring him your need with confidence, as this father did.
exp.26:31:
Along the way, the Roman soldiers came upon a man from Cyrene, a city in North Africa, named Simon, and they forced him to carry Jesus's cross. This was the cross Jesus had to carry on his way to be crucified.

Matthew is the one telling the story. After flogging and mocking Jesus, the soldiers were leading him away to be crucified. It was common for condemned people to be made to carry their cross, or part of it. Matthew does not say why they chose Simon; he only tells us that they found him. Mark adds that he was the father of Alexander and Rufus.

For today: Simon did not choose to carry the cross, but he ended up walking alongside Jesus on his hardest road. We can help those who are suffering, even when we did not expect to, and in this way serve Christ in others.
exp.25:65:
Here the high priest asks the members of the council what they think of Jesus. They answer: "He deserves to die." "Deserves to die" means that, in their judgment, he has done wrong and the punishment is death. "Blasphemy" means speaking about God with disrespect or claiming for oneself something that belongs only to God.

Jesus had just said that he would be seen sitting at God's right hand and coming on the clouds. The high priest took this as blasphemy, tore his clothes, and called for a verdict. The Jewish leaders, gathered in a night trial, condemned him without recognizing who he was.

For today: when the truth about Jesus makes us uncomfortable, we can either harden ourselves or humble ourselves. Let us ask God for an open heart to listen to Christ, even when he contradicts what we already think.
exp.16:4:
While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud enveloped the disciples, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!" The voice is God the Father speaking about Jesus, saying that he delights in his Son. It also gives a command: listen to him.

Jesus was transfigured on the mountain with Peter, James, and John. Moses and Elijah, whom many understand to represent the Law and the Prophets, appeared with him. Peter proposed making three tents, as if the three were equal. Then the Father speaks and makes it clear that Jesus has a unique place. Afterward, Jesus himself comforts the frightened disciples.

For today: before deciding or seeking answers, put Jesus first. Read the Gospels carefully and practice what he teaches, without fear.
exp.22:19:
Jesus says that whoever swears by the altar does not swear only by the stone or the structure, but also by everything that is placed on it: the offerings and the sacrifices.

Jesus is speaking to the scribes and Pharisees, whom he calls blind fools. They had made rules about which oaths were binding and which were not. In this way they could look very religious while still escaping the need to keep their word. Jesus shows them that every oath leads back to God, who is holy.

For today: let us be people of our word. We do not need clever phrases or excuses to avoid what we have promised. If we have said "yes," let us keep it, remembering that God hears every one of our words.
exp.4:8:
He says that those who work for peace are happy. "Blessed" means happy or favored. "Peacemakers" are not merely people who are calm, but those who work to reconcile and build peace between others. Jesus says they will be called "sons of God," that is, they will be recognized as people who resemble their Father, who is a God of peace.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in the Sermon on the Mount. He is describing what life is like for those who belong to his kingdom. This beatitude comes between mercy and purity of heart, and persecution. That suggests that seeking peace is a fruit of a transformed heart, even though it sometimes brings opposition.

For today: if there is a conflict in your family, work, or church, take a concrete step toward reconciliation. You can listen calmly, ask forgiveness, or speak well of the other person, without waiting for the other to go first.
exp.24:13:
This verse begins another parable of Jesus. It says that the kingdom of heaven is like a man going on a journey. Before leaving, he called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them. "Going on a journey" means "leaving on a trip"; "servants" are the employees or household workers.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, in his teaching about his return. Just before this, he had asked them to stay alert, because no one knows the day or the hour. This parable shows how to live while we wait: not only with our eyes on heaven, but serving with what has been entrusted to us.

For today: everything we have, such as time, abilities, and resources, is a trust from God. Think of one specific thing God has given you and use it this week to bless someone.
exp.25:71:
It says that Peter denied Jesus a second time, and this time he did it with an oath, that is, solemnly declaring that he was telling the truth. He says, "I do not know the man!" as if Jesus were a stranger to him. The statement is a complete denial of any connection with Jesus.

Peter speaks in the courtyard of the high priest, on the night Jesus was arrested. A servant girl recognizes him as a follower of Jesus the Nazarene. Peter is afraid. Shortly before, Jesus had told him that he would deny him three times, and Peter had insisted that he never would. Now he is falling, step by step.

For today: all of us can fail when we feel pressure or fear. It is wise to be humble and not trust in our own strength. But Peter's story also reminds us that Jesus forgives and restores anyone who returns to Him with repentance.
exp.9:25:
So do not be afraid of them. Jesus tells us not to fear those who oppose us. The ideas here are things being concealed or hidden, and things being disclosed or made known to everyone. What is hidden will come to light, and what is not known today will become known.

Jesus is speaking to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to preach. He has just warned them that they will be rejected and insulted, just as he was. He tells them not to fear, because the truth of the gospel will not be kept silent. Interpreters also see here a promise that God will do justice in the end. Both ideas fit with what follows.

For today: if you feel afraid to speak about your faith, or if mockery wounds you, remember that God sees everything and the truth is not lost. Be honest and speak with love, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.27:3:
This verse says that the soldiers who were guarding the tomb were so overcome with fear at seeing the angel that they trembled and became like dead men. "Guards" are the soldiers who stood watch. Here "trembled" means they were struck with terror and shook. "Became like dead men" means they lay still, without strength, as if they had no life in them.

Matthew tells what happened on the morning of the resurrection. The guards had been posted there to keep anyone from taking the body of Jesus (Matthew 27:62-66). The narrator is Matthew, and he shows that neither human power nor the seal on the tomb could stop God. Then the angel speaks to the women and tells them not to be afraid, because Jesus has risen.

For today: the same power that made the guards tremble is the one that gives hope to those who trust in Christ. When you feel fear, remember that Jesus lives and has the final word.
exp.8:23:
Jesus tells the crowd to leave, because the girl is not dead but asleep. The words "go away" mean "get out of here" or "make room." A "girl" is a young child. At his words, the people laughed at him, mocking him with scorn.

Jesus arrives at the house of a leader, a ruler or official, whose daughter has just died. Already there were flute players and many people making noise for mourning. Jesus speaks calmly and with authority. Many believe he calls death "sleep" because for him it is not the end; others think it is simply a way of speaking. Then he takes the girl by the hand and she rises.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless and others laugh at your faith, do not lose heart. Keep trusting in Jesus, because his power and his word are greater than the noise around you.
exp.25:62:
This verse says that Jesus remained silent in the face of the accusations. Then the high priest put him under oath: "I charge you under oath by the living God", that is, "I bind you in the name of God", to tell whether he was the Christ (the Messiah, the promised king) and the Son of God.

Jesus is being tried at night by the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council. The false witnesses could not agree with one another. Caiaphas, the high priest, seeks to have Jesus himself declare who he is. Jesus breaks his silence and answers, "You have said it", a clear affirmation. That provokes the charge of blasphemy.

For today: Jesus stayed silent before the lies, but he spoke when the truth about who he is was at stake. We can ask for wisdom to know when to be silent and when to speak with courage and gentleness about our faith.
exp.20:5:
This verse says that the disciples went to the place Jesus had pointed out and did exactly what He directed them to do.

This is the account of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. Matthew, who tells the story, explains that Jesus sent two disciples to bring a donkey and her colt. Matthew links this to the prophecy of Zechariah, which announced a gentle King riding on a humble animal. The disciples do not argue or ask for explanations; they simply obey.

For today: sometimes God asks us for something simple whose purpose we do not fully understand. The disciples trusted and obeyed, and so they took part in something much greater than they imagined. Today you can take a small step of obedience, trusting that Jesus knows what He is doing.
exp.1:19:
An angel speaks to Joseph in a dream while he is in Egypt. He says, "Get up! Take the Child and His mother and go to the land of Israel," and gives the reason that those who were seeking the Child's life are now dead.

The angel speaks to Joseph after the death of King Herod. Herod had wanted to kill Jesus, and that is why the family fled to Egypt. Matthew shows that God watched over his Son and guided every step. Many scholars understand that "those seeking the Child's life" refers to Herod and those who supported him, although the text gives no further details.

For today: God knows when a difficult season will end. We can wait for his guidance and obey step by step, as Joseph did, without rushing ahead.
exp.9:7:
Jesus tells his twelve disciples to heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, and drive out demons. The commands are plain, and the phrase "freely" means without charge. They received this power without paying for it, so they must give it without payment.

Jesus speaks when he sends out the Twelve to "the lost sheep of the house of Israel," that is, to the Jewish people who were wandering without a guide. His message was that the kingdom of heaven had drawn near. These signs showed that the kingdom brought power and compassion. Then he asks them to go out trusting, without carrying money, because the worker deserves his provision.

Everything good we have from God we receive as a gift. Therefore, we can serve others generously, without seeking profit or pride: helping, listening, praying, and sharing what God has given us.
exp.0:5:
This verse continues the list of Jesus's ancestors. It says that Jesse (called "Isaí" in this version) was the father of King David, and that David was the father of Solomon. Solomon's mother is described as the woman who had been the wife of Uriah, that is, Bathsheba, though she is not named.

Matthew writes to show that Jesus is the promised Messiah, a descendant of David. By mentioning Uriah, Matthew recalls David's sin with Bathsheba, told in 2 Samuel 11. It is notable that he also includes women such as Rahab and Ruth, who were not Israelites by origin. Scholars explain in several ways why he does so, but all see a message of grace.

For today: God does not hide the flaws in the history of Jesus. If your past carries shame or mistakes, God can work in it and continue to fulfill his purpose with your life.
exp.10:6:
