Jesus begins to speak to the crowds about John the Baptist, after John's disciples had already left. He asks them what they went out into the wilderness to see: "A reed swaying in the wind?" The phrase "as John's disciples were leaving" means "when they had gone away," and "swaying" means "moving back and forth."

John was in prison, and he had sent messengers to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come. Jesus answers with his works and then speaks up for John. His question suggests that John was not weak or changeable like a reed. He was firm, even though he was going through a hard trial. Some believe the reed was also a common image of the area, but the text does not explain this.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith depends on our mood or on our circumstances. God can hold us firmly, and we can bring our doubts to him honestly, as John did.
exp.12:22:
This verse speaks of the good soil, which represents the person who hears the word, understands it, and bears fruit. Not everyone produces the same amount: some yield a hundredfold, others sixty, and others thirty. The phrase "bears fruit" simply means that the word produces real results in a person's life.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd and then explains the parable of the sower to his disciples. Before this, he described three kinds of soil where the seed does not thrive: the path, the rocky ground, and the thorns. With this fourth soil, he shows what a heart looks like when it truly receives the message of the kingdom.

For today: do not stop at hearing the word; take time to think about it, ask God to help you understand it, and put it into practice this week through one concrete decision. God does not ask you to compare yourself with others, but to be faithful and bear fruit with sincerity.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that people who suffer mistreatment for doing what is right are happy, or blessed. The word "blessed" here means happy or favored. "Being persecuted" means being pursued or treated badly. The promise is that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.

Jesus speaks this at the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount, addressing his disciples and the crowd. This is the last of the Beatitudes. In the verses that follow, he makes clear that this persecution comes from following him, and he reminds them that the prophets of old were also mistreated. Their reward is great.

For today: if you are ever criticized or left out for acting with honesty and faithfulness to Christ, do not lose heart. Keep doing good without repaying evil with evil, and trust that God sees and rewards.
exp.20:27:
Jesus begins a parable by asking, "What do you think?" In other words, he invites them to consider it carefully. He speaks of a man who had two sons. He went to the first one and said, "Son, go and work today in the vineyard." A vineyard was a field of grapevines, and in the Bible it often represents God's people. The word "today" shows that the invitation is urgent.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with the chief priests and the elders, who had just questioned his authority. They would not answer about John the Baptist because they feared the crowd. So Jesus tells this story to show how they respond to God.

For today: God calls us to obey now, not just to speak well. Today you can ask yourself what God is asking of you, and do it sincerely, without putting it off for later.
exp.11:34:
Jesus says that each person has within the heart a kind of storehouse or "treasure." Whatever is kept stored there is what comes out afterward. A person with a good heart brings out good things, and a person with an evil heart brings out evil things. The word "idle" in the following verse means empty or of no use.

Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees, who had just accused him of driving out demons by the power of Satan. He shows them that their harsh words revealed what was really in their hearts. He calls them a brood of vipers because of their harshness. Just as the fruit shows what kind of tree it comes from, words show what is inside us.

For today: when a harsh word slips out, do not look only at the mouth, look at the heart. Ask God to cleanse it, and fill it each day with his Word and prayer, so that something good will come out of it.
exp.7:18:
A certain scribe, an expert teacher of the Law of Moses, comes to Jesus and says he will follow him wherever he goes. The wording here is simple: "Teacher" is the respectful way he addresses Jesus, and "I will follow You wherever You go" means exactly what it says.

Jesus had just healed many sick people, and a crowd was gathered around him. Then he told his disciples to cross to the other side of the lake. At that moment the scribe speaks, perhaps moved by enthusiasm. Jesus's reply in the following verse shows that he is speaking of a path of sacrifice and without comforts. The Bible does not say what happened afterward to this man.

It is easy to say "I will follow You" when everything is going well. Before we commit ourselves, it is wise to think honestly about what it means to follow Jesus. We can ask him to give us a steady heart, one that remains faithful to him even when it costs something.
exp.18:6:
The Pharisees answer Jesus with a question: if God joins a man and a woman together, why did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away? That certificate was a written document that a husband handed over to send his wife away.

The Pharisees, who wanted to test him, use the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 24:1) as their defense. Jesus had just recalled God's original plan: two people united as one flesh. They reply by pointing to a permitted exception. Jesus will answer that Moses allowed it because of the hardness of their hearts, and not because it was God's desire from the beginning.

Today we can avoid asking "how far am I allowed to go?" and instead ask "what does God want for my marriage?" Let us care for the covenant with humility, forgiveness, and a tender heart.
exp.12:57:
This verse says that Jesus did not do many miracles in Nazareth, because the people did not believe in him. The word "unbelief" means a lack of faith, or refusing to believe.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Jesus had returned to his hometown and was teaching in the synagogue. His neighbors had known him since childhood, knew who his family was, and were offended, that is, they stumbled over him and rejected him. They thought that someone so ordinary could not have such wisdom. Mark 6:5 adds that he did heal a few sick people, so it was not that he lacked power, but that unbelief closed the door.

For today: do not let habit or prejudice keep you from seeing God at work. Come to Jesus with an open and trusting heart, and ask him to increase your faith.
exp.13:33:
This verse tells how Jesus and his disciples crossed the lake and landed on the other shore, at a place called Gennesaret. The phrase "the other side" means the far shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Here the narrator is Matthew. Shortly before, Jesus had walked on the water and calmed the wind. The disciples, amazed, worshiped him and said he was the Son of God. Now the story continues with a peaceful landing, and soon the people of that place recognize Jesus and bring him their sick.

For today: after the storms, God keeps guiding us to the next shore. We can trust that Jesus leads us to places where he wants to work, and we can stay alert to help those who need his mercy.
exp.13:15:
Jesus tells his disciples that the people do not need to go away to find food. Then he says something surprising to them: "You give them something to eat." The disciples are the ones he asks to take action.

Jesus speaks after he has healed the sick. The afternoon was already advancing, the place was deserted, and the disciples asked him to send the crowd away so they could buy food. Jesus had felt compassion for the crowd, and he wants his disciples to take part in caring for it too. Although they had only five loaves of bread and two fish, Jesus invites them to bring that to him.

For today: when you see a need that seems too large, do not ignore it or leave it to others. Offer Jesus whatever little you have, your time, your help, or your money, and trust that he can use it.
exp.24:40:
Jesus, the King, speaks to those on his left at the final judgment. He tells them to depart from him and calls them "cursed." Their destination is the eternal fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels, not for people.

Jesus is telling the parable of the sheep and the goats. Earlier, he spoke to those on his right, who cared for his brothers, the least of these. Now he addresses those who did not. The reasons appear in the next verse: they gave no food, no drink, and did not visit. Interpreters debate who these "brothers" are, but the emphasis falls on practical compassion.

For today: true faith shows itself in simple acts of love. This week, look for someone in need, a sick person, a lonely one, or a hungry one, and help them with something concrete.
exp.10:5:
It says that the one who is blessed, or happy, is the person who does not fall away or stumble because of Jesus. Here, falling away means doubting or being troubled because Jesus is not what one expected, not being frightened. To be "blessed" means to be deeply favored by God.

Jesus is the speaker. John the Baptist was in prison and sent word to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come. Jesus does not give a simple yes, but points to his works: healings and good news for the poor, as Isaiah had foretold. Then he adds this sentence, like a tender invitation to trust him even when his way is not the one people expected.

For today: when life does not turn out as you asked and God seems silent, do not turn away from Jesus. Look at what he has already done, bring your doubts to him honestly, and keep trusting him.
exp.14:21:
This verse tells how a Canaanite woman from that region came to Jesus, crying out, "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me!" Her daughter was miserably possessed by a demon, meaning she was suffering terribly under the control of an evil spirit. "Canaanite" was an old name for the people of that area, who were not Jews.

Jesus had just taught that what defiles a person comes out of the heart, not from eating with unwashed hands. Then he went toward Tyre and Sidon, land of the Gentiles. The woman is the one who speaks, moved by a mother's pain. She calls him "Son of David," a title for the Messiah promised to Israel.

When you are in despair, come to Jesus with humility and faith, without keeping silent. Tell him sincerely what hurts you and ask for his mercy, even if you do not understand his answer.
exp.0:9:
This verse continues the list of Jesus's ancestors. It says that Hezekiah was the father of Manasseh, Manasseh the father of Amon, and Amon the father of Josiah. Here "the father of" means that the person named was an ancestor of the one who follows.

Matthew writes this Gospel and begins by showing that Jesus comes from the line of King David. These names are kings of Judah. Among them is one who was very faithful, like Hezekiah, and others who were very wicked, like Manasseh and Amon. Matthew does not hide that mix. Some scholars note that the list summarizes the genealogy and may leave out some people, which was common in ancient lists.

God can keep his promises even through imperfect families and crooked stories. Your past or your family's past does not limit what God can do with you. Trust that his grace is greater than your mistakes, and try to live faithfully today.
exp.8:19:
A woman had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, a long and continuous flow of blood. She came up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of his cloak. "Suddenly" marks how unexpected her move was.

Matthew tells this as Jesus is on his way to the house of a leader whose daughter had died. The woman interrupts the journey without making a sound. Many understand that, because of her illness, she lived under the purity restrictions of the law, and that is why she came up in secret. She believed that just by touching him she would be healed.

Today, if you feel tired or worn out from a long problem, come to Jesus as you can, even with a simple and trembling prayer. He hears you and stops for you.
exp.26:17:
This verse says that Pilate understood the real reason they had brought Jesus before him. It was not for a real crime, but out of envy. The Jewish leaders handed Jesus over to the Roman authorities.

The one who "knew" was Pilate, the Roman governor. The narrator, Matthew, explains why Pilate offers the crowd a choice between Barabbas and Jesus. Pilate probably expected the people to ask for Jesus to be set free. The chief priests felt that Jesus was taking away their influence over the people, and that is why they were accusing him.

For today: envy can lead us to harm others, even disguising it as justice. Let us ask God to examine our hearts. When someone else is blessed or recognized, let us learn to rejoice with them instead of resenting them.
exp.20:23:
Jesus answers a question with a question. He says that He will also ask them one question, and that if they answer Him, He will tell them by what authority He is doing these things. The word "answer" in this verse means to respond or reply, and "one question" is the single question He asks in return.

Jesus is in the temple teaching, a day after He drove out the sellers. The chief priests and the elders ask Him who gave Him permission to do that. He does not avoid the question: He uses a question about John the Baptist to show whether they were truly seeking the truth or only wanted to trap Him.

For today: before demanding answers from God, let us examine our hearts. Sometimes we ask to sincerely learn, and other times to defend what we have already decided. Let us ask for humility to accept the truth, even when it costs us.
exp.24:1:
It says that of the ten young women who were waiting for the bridegroom, five were prudent, that is, sensible and far-sighted, and five were foolish, the word the verse uses for those who lacked sense or judgment. The point is not that some looked good and others looked bad at first glance, since all of them carried a lamp and all of them went out to meet the bridegroom.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he teaches them how to be ready for his return. This parable follows his warnings about staying alert. The ten seem alike on the outside; the difference will show later, in what each one did to be ready.

Today it reminds us that it is not enough to seem like believers or to stay near the things of God. It is good to cultivate a real faith every day: to pray, read the Bible, and obey, so that we do not live carelessly or depend on the preparation of others.
exp.5:5:
Jesus says that when you pray, you should go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. An inner room is a private room in the house, a place where you can be alone. Your Father, who sees what is done in secret, is the one who notices what no one else can see, and he will reward you.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and to the crowd. Just before this, he has criticized hypocrites who prayed in the synagogues and on the street corners so that people would admire them. Jesus does not forbid praying in public; he corrects the motive of the heart.

For today: set aside a quiet time each day, without phones or distractions, to speak with God honestly. Do not pray to impress anyone, but to be with your Father, who listens to you and knows you.

sum.18: Jesus teaches that God designed marriage to be a lasting union, and he blesses the children, saying that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who are like them. A rich young man walks away sad because he is not willing to give up his possessions, and Jesus teaches that all things are possible with God and that those who follow him will receive a reward.
sum.11: Jesus defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath and heals a man's withered hand, teaching that it is good to do good on that day. The Pharisees accuse him of healing by the power of Beelzebul, but he answers that his works show the kingdom of God has arrived, and he warns that words reveal the heart. When they ask for a sign, he speaks of Jonah, and he says that whoever does the will of the Father is his family.
sum.23: Jesus announces that the temple will be destroyed. He warns his disciples about deception, wars, persecution, and a great affliction that will come before his glorious return. No one knows the day or the hour, so he calls them to stay alert and to serve faithfully while he is away.
sum.5: In this chapter Jesus teaches people to give, pray, and fast simply, without seeking the praise of others, because the Father sees what is done in secret. He teaches the Lord's Prayer, speaks about forgiveness and about storing up treasure in heaven, and warns that no one can serve both God and money. He ends by inviting people not to worry about material needs and to seek God's kingdom first.
sum.17: Jesus teaches that the greatest in the kingdom is the one who humbles himself like a child, and he warns against causing little ones to stumble, since the Father wants to seek out and save each person who is lost. He also explains how to seek reconciliation with a brother and the importance of always forgiving, with the parable of the servant who was forgiven a great deal but would not forgive a small debt.
sum.19: Jesus tells the parable of a vineyard owner who pays the same wage to all his workers, even though some worked the whole day and others only one hour, to show his goodness and generosity. Then he announces his death and resurrection, teaches that whoever wants to be great must serve, and heals two blind men who cried out for mercy.
sum.8: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls Matthew, and eats with sinners, saying that he came for the sick, not for the healthy. He also teaches about new and old, and heals a woman, a dead girl, two blind men, and a mute man. Seeing the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, he feels compassion and asks that people pray for workers.
sum.24: Jesus teaches with three scenes about his coming. There are ten virgins: five wise ones who brought oil, and five foolish ones who did not. There are servants who receive talents: two multiply them, and one hides his out of fear. And there is the final judgment, where the King separates people according to whether or not they helped those in need. Everything calls for staying alert, being faithful, and loving through actions.
sum.16: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, and a voice from heaven says, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." Then he heals a boy whom the disciples had been unable to heal, and he teaches that faith, even if it is as small as a mustard seed, makes the impossible possible. He also announces his death and resurrection, and he instructs them to pay the temple tax.
sum.9: Jesus calls his twelve disciples and gives them authority to heal the sick and drive out evil spirits. He sends them to the lost sheep of Israel to proclaim that the kingdom of heaven is near. He warns them that they will face rejection and persecution, but he tells them not to be afraid, because God cares for them. Whoever follows him must love him above all else and take up their cross.
sum.2: John the Baptist preaches in the desert that people must repent because the kingdom of heaven is near, and he warns that being descendants of Abraham is not enough; they must produce good fruit. He announces that someone more powerful than him is coming. Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father says, "This is my beloved Son."
sum.12: Jesus teaches using parables: the sower and the different kinds of soil, the wheat and the weeds, the mustard seed, the yeast, the treasure, the pearl, and the net. They show how the kingdom of God grows and that in the end there will be a separation between the righteous and the wicked. In his own hometown, the people reject him and do not believe.
sum.25: Jesus announces that he will be handed over, and while the leaders plan to kill him, Judas betrays him for thirty pieces of silver. At the Last Supper, Jesus offers the bread and the cup as his body and his blood of the new covenant, prays in anguish in Gethsemane, and is arrested. He is condemned by the council, and Peter denies him three times and weeps bitterly.
sum.3: Jesus is led into the wilderness, and after fasting for forty days he resists the devil's three temptations by quoting Scripture. He then goes to Galilee, announces that the kingdom of heaven has come near, and calls four fishermen to follow him. He teaches and heals many people, and large crowds follow him.
sum.1: Some wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem looking for the newborn King. They travel to Bethlehem, guided by a star, to worship him and give him gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Herod, filled with fear, tries to kill the child, but God warns Joseph in a dream. Joseph flees with the family to Egypt and later settles in Nazareth.
sum.15: The Pharisees and Sadducees ask Jesus for a sign, and he rebukes them and warns his disciples to beware of their false teaching. Peter declares that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus announces that he is going to suffer, die, and be raised. He then teaches that following him means denying yourself and taking up your cross.
sum.10: John the Baptist, from prison, asks whether Jesus is the one who was to come, and Jesus answers by pointing to his works. He then praises John as a messenger sent by God. Next he rebukes the towns that did not repent despite his miracles. At the end, he thanks the Father and invites the weary to come to him and find rest.
sum.22: Jesus warns the crowds and his disciples not to imitate the scribes and Pharisees, who say one thing but do another. He teaches that whoever is greatest must be a servant, and that whoever humbles himself will be exalted. He then pronounces seven "woes" against them for their hypocrisy, and he ends by mourning with sorrow over Jerusalem's rejection of him.
sum.26: The Jewish leaders hand Jesus over to Pilate, who, although he sees that Jesus is innocent, gives in to the crowd, releases Barabbas, and orders Jesus to be crucified. After he is mocked, Jesus dies on the cross amid extraordinary signs, and a centurion acknowledges that he was the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and his tomb is sealed and guarded.
sum.0: Matthew 1 presents the family tree of Jesus, which links him to Abraham and to King David, and divides it into three groups of fourteen generations. It then tells how Mary conceived through the Holy Spirit, and how an angel told Joseph to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus, because he would save his people from their sins. Joseph obeyed.
sum.7: Jesus comes down from the mountain and shows his power and compassion. He heals a man with leprosy, the servant of a centurion who believed in his word, Peter's mother-in-law, and many other sick people. Then he calls people to follow him with complete commitment, calms a storm, and frees two men who were possessed by demons, even though the crowd asks him to leave.
sum.21: Jesus tells the parable of a king who invites guests to the wedding feast of his son. The invited guests refuse to come, so the king calls in everyone he can find, and one man arrives without wedding clothes. Then Jesus answers questions about paying the tax to Caesar, the resurrection, and the greatest commandment: to love God and to love your neighbor. At the end, he asks how the Messiah can be both the son and the Lord of David.
sum.6: In Matthew 7, Jesus teaches not to judge hypocritically, to ask God with confidence, since he is a good Father, and to treat others the way we want to be treated. He warns that we must choose the narrow gate, beware of false teachers, and obey his words, like someone who builds their house on rock. The crowds were amazed at his authority.
sum.20: Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a young donkey, and the crowd welcomes him as the Son of David. He then cleanses the temple, heals the sick, and dries up a fig tree that bears no fruit to teach about faith. When the leaders question his authority, he answers with parables that show their rejection and the danger of not bearing fruit.
sum.13: Herod had John the Baptist killed, and Jesus withdrew, but he had compassion on the crowd and fed more than five thousand people with five loaves of bread and two fish. Afterward he walked on the sea, rescued Peter when Peter began to doubt, and his disciples worshiped him as the Son of God. In Gennesaret, sick people who touched his cloak were made well.
sum.4: Jesus goes up the mountain and teaches his disciples. He calls blessed the humble, those who mourn, and those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, and he tells them that they are the salt and light of the world. He then explains that he came to fulfill the law, and he calls for a deeper kind of righteousness: purity of heart, reconciliation, honest speech, and love even for enemies.
sum.27: At dawn, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary go to the tomb, and an angel tells them that Jesus has risen and that they will see him in Galilee. The religious leaders pay the soldiers to say that the disciples stole the body. Jesus appears to his followers, declares that he has all authority, sends them to make disciples of all nations, and promises to be with them always.
sum.14: Jesus tells the Pharisees that their tradition nullifies God's command, and he teaches that what defiles a person comes out of the heart, not what goes into the mouth. He then heals the daughter of a Canaanite woman because of her great faith. Finally, he heals many sick people and feeds four thousand men, besides women and children, with seven loaves of bread and a few small fish.
